trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? YES — Nairobi (East Africa hub). Natural Justice keeps 3 hubs: Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar. A hub means staff on the ground rather than a project relationship. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Business Registration Service
trackers.desc: Kenya's Business Registration Service company registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC)
trackers.desc: Kenya’s statutory anti-corruption body — investigates graft, enforces integrity law and recovers corruptly-acquired assets.

trackers.name: e-GP Kenya
trackers.desc: Kenya's national electronic government-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Kenya, and for how much.

trackers.name: ICJ Kenya (Kenyan Section, International Commission of Jurists)
trackers.desc: Nairobi-based NGO of jurists drawn from the Bar and Bench (founded 1959) that works to develop and protect the independence of the judiciary and legal profession in Kenya, monitor judicial reform and integrity, and advance freedom of information.

trackers.name: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA-Kenya)
trackers.desc: Independent Kenyan public-policy think-tank (est. 1994) producing analysis of the national budget, taxation and economic policy and promoting informed public debate. Here you can trace Kenya's budget, taxation and economic policy, analysed independently.

trackers.name: Kenya Law
trackers.desc: National Council for Law Reporting: official free database of Kenyan judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Kenyan case-law, the Kenya Gazette and legislation (National Council for Law Reporting / Kenya Law).

trackers.name: Public Procurement Portal
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Kenya, and for how much.

trackers.name: Transparency International Kenya (TI-Kenya)
trackers.desc: Transparency International's Kenya chapter (since 1999). Anti-corruption research and advocacy, runs Advocacy and Legal Advice Centres, and works on transparency in public procurement, devolved government, the extractives sector and humanitarian aid.

trackers.name: TISA — The Institute for Social Accountability
trackers.desc: Kenyan civil-society institute (since 2008) promoting social accountability and good governance, with a strong focus on devolution and county governments. Tracks national and county public finance management and budgets, campaigns on public debt and fiscal accountability (Okoa Uchumi), and equips citizens and oversight institutions to hold duty-bearers to account between elections.

trackers.name: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics
trackers.desc: Kenya's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Kenya.

trackers.name: NEMA — EIA/SEA reports & licensed-experts register
trackers.desc: Kenya's National Environment Management Authority (NEMA). You CAN get: EIA/SEA reports for download, and — as public documents inspectable for a small fee — the register of licensed EIA/EA experts and every issued EIA licence. You CAN'T get: some files released only on request. For activists: match a project's EIA to the firm or expert who signed it via the experts register, and check the licence is valid.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Constitutional auditor of public funds. Here you can trace public-audit findings on waste, irregularity and misspending in Kenya.

trackers.name: Commission on Administrative Justice (Office of the Ombudsman, Kenya)
trackers.desc: Kenya's ombudsman and the oversight body for the Access to Information Act — maladministration complaints and ATI enforcement. — Holds to account: public bodies that hold records — find information-commissioner decisions and appeals.

trackers.name: Kenya Open Data
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Kenya.

trackers.name: National Treasury Kenya
trackers.desc: Publishes Kenyan budget documents and fiscal data. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Kenya.

trackers.name: Katiba Institute — strategic litigation and the NET appeal route
trackers.desc: HOW A COMMUNITY STOPS A PROJECT HERE: an EIA licence issued by NEMA can be appealed to the National Environment Tribunal, and it works. Save Lamu filed at the NET in 2016 against the licence for the proposed 1,050 MW Lamu coal plant, supported by Natural Justice, Katiba Institute and the DeCOALonize campaign; the NET revoked the licence in 2019; and on 16 October 2025 the Environment and Land Court at Malindi dismissed the developer's appeal, holding the EIA failed on ash disposal, air pollution and climate impacts and that the licence violated Articles 42 and 69 of the Constitution. THE TRAP: the Statute Law (Miscellaneous Amendment) Act 2018 amended section 129 of EMCA and removed the automatic maintenance of status quo on filing an appeal — lodging at the NET no longer freezes the works by itself, so orders must be sought separately or you win a ruling about a site already built on. AND THE ODDS: appeals lose too — in the Sosian Energy geothermal case at Menengai the Tribunal found against the community, which then had to appeal to the Nakuru Environment and Land Court.

trackers.name: Community Land Act 2016 — register collectively or lose the commons
trackers.desc: THE ROUTE OUT OF INSECURE TENURE. Act No. 27 of 2016, giving effect to Article 63(5) of the Constitution, lets communities register land collectively, obtain title, set up governance and enter legally binding conservancy agreements. Before it, land occupied for generations was government trust land and vulnerable to expropriation. HOW: notice to the community and to national and county administrators constitutes the first assembly; the assembly elects a community land management committee of 7 to 15 members which compiles a register of all community members, drafts the community's own rules and constitution, and records the minutes authorising registration. Women and youth must be represented on the committee. A registered community may reserve areas expressly for community conservation and for cultural and heritage sites, and reserved land must be used exclusively for that purpose. The Act also requires registered communities to protect critical ecosystems and habitats, create incentives for conservation investment, and enable co-management of forests and water by those with customary rights.

trackers.name: The subdivision trap — how the same Act loses the land
trackers.desc: READ THIS BEFORE THE COMMUNITY VOTES. The Community Land Act also permits conversion and allocation of land to individual members — and research on Maasailand records that its introduction led many group ranches to dissolve communal land into private individual parcels rather than register as community land, producing enclosures and unsustainable use and threatening forests, grasslands and wildlife. Subdivision fragments wildlife corridors unless the community chooses collective registration. The choice made at the assembly is the decisive one, and it is effectively irreversible. WHERE SUBDIVISION HAPPENED ANYWAY, one documented mitigation: three community conservancies were created inside the subdivision process, each registered member receiving 8 acres within a conservancy plus 21 acres for settlement — and landowners were deliberately not shown the precise coordinates of their conservancy parcels, to discourage building on them. Each conservancy is run by an elected committee handling operations and investors. SUPPORT: the Kenya Wildlife Conservancies Association, which proposed 24 amendments to the Bill and had 12 adopted, plus Northern Rangelands Trust and TNC.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: NEMA environmental assessment — only high-risk study reports are gazetted; project reports never leave the licensing portal
trackers.desc: THE PROJECT NEXT TO YOU PROBABLY GENERATES NO NEWSPAPER NOTICE AT ALL, AND THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL THING TO KNOW ABOUT THE KENYAN SYSTEM. The Authority's own clarification states that project reports are not uploaded to nema.go.ke unless requested; only study reports, meaning high-risk projects, are published in the Kenya Gazette and in newspapers and put on the website. A medium-risk project sits on the licensing portal, reachable only by someone who already knows to look. Check the portal by name and location rather than waiting for a notice. WHERE A STUDY REPORT IS INVOLVED, THE PUBLICITY DUTIES ARE SPECIFIC AND CHECKABLE: within fourteen days of receiving the report the Authority must invite public comment; it must publish a notice once a week for two successive weeks in the Gazette and in a newspaper with nationwide circulation and in particular wide circulation in the project area; and it must announce the notice on nationwide radio, in both official and local languages, at least once a week for two consecutive weeks. The notice must state the anticipated impacts, the proposed mitigation, and the times and place where the full report can be inspected. The radio announcement in local language is the duty least often performed and least often checked — its absence is a documented defect in public participation, which is the ground on which EIA licences have actually been revoked in Kenya. Separately, the proponent must hold at least three public meetings, give notice at least a week before each, and appoint a coordinator to receive and record oral and written comments, and the assessment must be done by an expert registered and licensed by the Authority. Licence fees run at 0.1 per cent of total project cost, minimum KSh 10,000, with no upper cap. Environmental incidents: 0741 101 100 or incidence@nema.go.ke. Director General, Popo Road off Mombasa Road, P.O. Box 67839, Nairobi. CAVEAT: the fourteen-day, two-week and radio requirements above were read from the assessment and audit regulations as published by Kenya Law, not from this page, which sets out fees and process at a higher level.

trackers.name: National Environment Tribunal — 60 days to appeal a decision nobody is required to tell you about, and six copies of the notice
trackers.desc: THE APPEAL RIGHT IS OPEN TO ANY AGGRIEVED PERSON, NOT ONLY THE APPLICANT — AND THE CLOCK CAN EXPIRE BEFORE YOU LEARN THE LICENCE EXISTS. Under the framework environment Act any person aggrieved by a decision of the environment authority — the grant, refusal or conditions of an assessment licence among others — may appeal to the Tribunal, and the Tribunal's procedure rules require six copies of a written notice of appeal to reach it not later than sixty days after the date the disputed decision was given to or served upon the appellant. The notice states the decision challenged, its reference number, its date and the grounds. A party objecting to the Tribunal's jurisdiction or to the admissibility of an appeal must do so in writing within thirty days of being notified of the appeal, which is worth knowing because it is the first thing a well-resourced respondent will do. THE GAP THAT MATTERS: the authority must communicate its decision to the project proponent, and there is no corresponding duty to publish a grant to the public — a point put in issue before the Environment and Land Court in 2026, seeking an order that assessment decisions be published. Until that changes, write to the authority asking to be served with the decision, and diarise sixty days from the date of communication rather than from the date you heard about it. The Tribunal also hears matters under the forest and wildlife conservation statutes, may appoint specialist advisers, and its decisions go on appeal to the Environment and Land Court. Its record includes revoking an assessment licence for a coal power plant on the ground of inadequate public participation. CAVEATS: the Tribunal has no website of its own; its cause lists are published by Kenya Law, the state law reporter, whose site blocks automated access, so the list has to be opened in a browser. Commentators consistently describe the Tribunal as under-resourced, and its jurisdiction has been read narrowly in some rulings, so an appeal filed on the wrong subsection has been dismissed on time limits before.

trackers.name: National Land Commission compulsory acquisition — get your own survey before the inquiry date, not after; the County Gazette is the notice people miss
trackers.desc: THE INQUIRY IS THE HEARING, AND ALMOST EVERYTHING THAT DECIDES YOUR COMPENSATION IS FIXED THERE. Acquisition begins when a Cabinet Secretary or a County Executive Committee Member asks the Commission to acquire; the Commission certifies in writing that the land is needed for a public purpose and publishes a notice of intention in the Kenya Gazette and in the relevant County Gazette — the county publication is the one nobody watches. It must also require the acquiring body to produce the parcel list, title searches, cadastral maps and a resettlement action plan naming the affected persons. A further notice must issue at least thirty days after the notice of intention, fixing a date for an inquiry into the propriety of the acquisition and into claims for compensation, at which the Commission determines who is interested in the land and makes a separate award for each of them. THREE THINGS PEOPLE LEARN TOO LATE: commission your own surveyor before the inquiry, not after it. In a reported appeal a landowner proved the road actually took 75 per cent of his parcel against 50 per cent gazetted, and the point failed because his survey post-dated the inquiry by nine months. Second, you may elect the form of compensation — alternative land, money, or another form — rather than accepting whatever is offered. Third, where a partial taking leaves you an unusable remnant you can require the acquiring authority to take the whole, and that has to be raised, not assumed. An award you refuse is paid into a special compensation account the Commission holds, and possession has in practice been taken before every procedural step was complete. CAVEATS: the section numbering and the thirty-day interval above were read from the Land Act 2012 and from Environment and Land Court judgments published by Kenya Law, not from this site, which does not publish the acquisition procedure, an inquiry calendar or a claim form. The Commission's own conduct of inquiries has been found wanting in litigation over the Lamu port and coal projects, where communities said notices never reached them.

trackers.name: Land Acquisition Tribunal — 30 days to appeal an award, and going to court first gets your case struck out
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE FORUM YOU MUST USE BEFORE A COURT, AND MISSING THAT IS HOW COMPULSORY ACQUISITION CLAIMS DIE ON A PRELIMINARY OBJECTION. The Land Act directs that disputes relating to compulsory acquisition be lodged first with the Tribunal, with judicial proceedings as a last resort; appeals filed straight into the Environment and Land Court have drawn objections that the suit was premature and belonged to the Tribunal. An appeal against a National Land Commission decision must be filed within thirty days of that decision, and the Tribunal must determine it within sixty days; it may extend time where sufficient cause is shown. It can direct the Commission to pay interest on the shortfall where it finds the award should have been larger, which is the remedy most people do not ask for. The Tribunal was created by a 2019 amendment, became operational only in 2023, sits as three members with a chairperson nominated by the Judicial Service Commission, and its registry is on the ground floor of Kenya Re Towers, Upper Hill, Nairobi. It is not decorative: in 2025 it dismissed a multi-billion-shilling claim and quashed five National Land Commission gazette notices on the ground that the acquisition lacked authorisation from the county government said to have requested it — which is worth reading if a county denies having asked for an acquisition being carried out in its name. The Tribunal has no website of its own. Its judgments are published by Kenya Law, the state law reporter, under the code KELAT; this link opens one month's listing and the year and month in the path can be changed to browse others. Because it only began sitting in 2023 the body of decisions is thin, and older acquisitions were litigated in the courts instead.

trackers.name: Access to information — 21 days to answer, 30 days to appeal, and a non-complying officer pays you KSh 10,000 a day
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE REPAIR FOR EVERY NOTICE THE KENYAN SYSTEM DOES NOT SEND YOU — THE PROJECT REPORT THAT NEVER LEAVES THE LICENSING PORTAL, THE ASSESSMENT LICENCE NOBODY MUST PUBLISH, THE COUNTY GAZETTE NOTICE YOU DID NOT SEE. Under the Access to Information Act 2016 a public entity must process a request within 21 days. You pay nothing to make the request — a charge may be made only for copying and supplying — and you do not have to say why you want it from a public entity, and your reasons cannot be held against you. The reverse applies to a private body: there you must state a reason, and it has to relate to protecting a right or freedom. If your request is sent to the wrong entity it must be transferred within five days and you must be told within seven. IF THEY MISS THE 21 DAYS, OR REFUSE, OR DEFER, OR CHARGE A FEE YOU THINK IS WRONG, APPLY TO THE COMMISSION ON ADMINISTRATIVE JUSTICE FOR REVIEW WITHIN 30 DAYS of being notified of the decision; the Commission can extend that period, and silence counts as a decision to review. On review the Commission can order the release of information withheld unlawfully and recommend compensation, its orders bind both national and county governments, and they are executed through the High Court as if they were High Court orders. The teeth are real and rarely quoted: an order can require release within 21 days and provide that the responsible officer personally pays the applicant KSh 10,000 for every day of continued non-compliance — the Commission has issued exactly that order and published the compliance. Dissatisfied with the Commission's own decision, you have 21 days to the High Court. Commission on Administrative Justice, 2nd Floor West End Towers, Waiyaki Way, Westlands; P.O. Box 20414-00200 Nairobi; info@ombudsman.go.ke; +254 20 2270000. CAVEAT: the section numbers and the five, seven, twenty-one and thirty day intervals were read from the Act and from the Commission's own best-practice handbook rather than from this page, and the Act's exemptions were not examined here — a refusal citing an exemption is a different argument from a refusal by silence.

trackers.name: Kenya Conservancies Fund — money and technical help to hold land as a conservancy, but your boundaries must already be undisputed
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a fund launched in April 2026 by the Kenya Wildlife Conservancies Association — a landowner-led national membership body representing over 200 community and private conservancies — giving financial and technical assistance to conservancies, aimed squarely at emerging ones with limited institutional capacity, governance systems or infrastructure rather than established operations. It grew out of an earlier small grants fund piloted in the Mara and Taita landscapes and is intended as micro-financing for new, nascent and needy conservancies underserved by competitive funding models. What it will pay for includes habitat restoration, species protection and monitoring, governance and management capacity, infrastructure, and diversified revenue — tourism, livestock, carbon and biodiversity credits — with explicit weight on the participation of women and youth in governance. WHO IT SUITS — AND THE ELIGIBILITY LINE THAT WILL DECIDE YOUR CASE: the published criteria require a registered conservancy entity, demonstrated community participation, sound governance and financial management, membership of KWCA and of a landscape association, and — the one that matters — well-defined land ownership and legally recognised boundaries free from disputes. Read that plainly: this is money for securing land you already hold cleanly, not for winning back land somebody else is claiming. A community already in a boundary fight or facing an acquisition will struggle to qualify, which is the argument for registering the conservancy and settling the boundaries before a project appears rather than after. Conservation significance must also be shown — high biodiversity, a wildlife corridor or a buffer zone — so the case is made in ecological terms, not in terms of the threat. CAVEAT: no grant ceiling, application window or decision timetable was published on the page consulted; the fund is new, and its first cycle terms should be confirmed with the association directly.

trackers.name: A Rocha Kenya — buys threatened forest outright at a published price: one acre costs $350 or KSh 35,000 to secure
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: an organisation whose stated method is buying land to stop it being cleared, with a price a community or a campaign can quote to donors: one acre costs US$350, or KSh 35,000, to secure. It has been working in the Dakatcha Woodland since 2000 and is assembling the A Rocha Dakatcha Nature Reserve parcel by parcel — 1,517 acres acquired against a planned 10,500-acre reserve, expanded with other funders to 3,797 acres. WHY THE PRICE MATTERS MORE THAN THE ECOLOGY HERE: Dakatcha covers about 465,000 acres, it receives no protection from the state, half of it has already been converted to farmland or grazing, and it is being cleared for charcoal, timber and pineapple plantations, with outside investors and land speculation adding to the pressure. Against an unprotected landscape, purchase is one of the few things that actually stops a clearance. DONATIONS ARE TAKEN THROUGH ROUTES A KENYAN CAMPAIGN CAN USE, INCLUDING M-CHANGA — the Kenyan crowdfunding platform — as well as GoFundMe and the international parent body, so money can be raised locally rather than only from abroad. It publishes a written land purchase strategy alongside its conservation strategy. WHO IT SUITS: a community or campaign next to unprotected forest with willing sellers and a species or habitat case — the organisation's stated basis for buying is biodiversity, so the argument that wins is what lives there, not who is threatening it. Its neighbours' programme works on sustainable management, restorative farming and beekeeping on adjoining land, so a purchase does not end the relationship. CAVEAT: this is a specific landscape programme, not a national land-purchase fund — nothing indicates it buys outside Dakatcha, and no application route for a landowner or community elsewhere in Kenya was found.

trackers.name: Nature Kenya land purchase programme — 2,573 acres bought at Dakatcha and handed to local groups to manage
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Kenya's oldest conservation society, which runs an actual land purchase programme rather than an advocacy campaign — it has acquired 2,573 acres of Dakatcha Woodland, created the Kamale Nature Reserve out of it, and separately finalised the purchase of another 773 acres at Kibaoni-Marafa. It funds those purchases by assembling money from outside: the World Land Trust, the African Bird Club, RESOLVE, TiME and Danish civil society funding are named as the financial backers — which is the model to copy, since the money for a purchase almost never comes from one source. THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR A COMMUNITY DECIDING WHETHER TO INVITE THEM IN: the reserve is managed by local organisations — the Dakatcha Woodland Conservation Group and the Kamale Mazingira community-based organisation — with a community warden engaged to run forest patrols and biodiversity monitoring. The land is bought and then run by the people already there, rather than becoming an outsider's estate. Areas identified for purchase are mapped in advance and assessed for suitability, so an approach works better with a defined parcel and a willing seller than with a general appeal. WHO IT SUITS: communities beside unprotected coastal forest under pressure from charcoal, logging, pineapple expansion and speculation. CAVEATS: no published application route, price per acre or purchase criteria were found — approach is by contact rather than by form; and the entries above are drawn from the society's own dated reports, so the acreages are a snapshot rather than a current total.

trackers.name: RECONCILE, Nakuru — publishes the communities' guide to registering community land, and litigates in the public interest on natural resources
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Resource Conflict Institute, established 1999 and registered in Kenya as a regional NGO in 2001, based in Nakuru rather than Nairobi — which its own profile treats as the point, because it puts the organisation next to the rural communities it works with. It conducts policy and legal research on environmental and natural resource governance, undertakes public interest environmental and natural resource litigation and education, and runs programmes across Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. WHAT TO GET FROM IT FIRST: it publishes a Communities' Guide to Registration of Community Land, written with pastoralist communities in the arid and semi-arid lands specifically in mind, covering the process, the requirements and the skills needed to register. WHY REGISTRATION IS THE WHOLE GAME IN KENYA: under the Community Land Act 2016 unregistered community land is held in trust by the county government, and that trusteeship ends the moment the community registers — registered community land carries a certificate of title and is private to that community. Until then the county holds it, holds any compulsory-acquisition compensation for it in a special account, and county interference in unregistered land can be substantial and lawful. An unregistered community facing a project is arguing through its county; a registered one is a titleholder. THE STEPS, AND THE PLACE IT STALLS: the community land registrar advertises a public meeting in a national newspaper and on national radio to elect the community land management committee; the community then prepares a register of members, adopts by-laws, harmonises boundaries with neighbours and applies. Paralegal-supported communities in Isiolo, Marsabit, Samburu, Laikipia and Tana River have done exactly this — and in one documented case eleven communities completed everything only to find that the government had not appointed community land registrars to the counties, so there was no official to receive the applications. Check that your county has a registrar before you begin. WHO IT SUITS: pastoralist and rural communities in Kenya seeking registration, and anyone needing public interest litigation on natural resources outside Nairobi. Off Oginga Odinga Road, Ngei Estate, Nakuru; P.O. Box 7150-20110. CAVEATS: a research, advocacy and capacity-building institute — its litigation is strategic rather than a general legal-aid service, and no intake route or fee information was published. Several Kenyan organisations named in this field — community paralegal partners in the pastoralist counties — may merit their own entries.

trackers.name: Maasai Mara Wildlife Conservancies Association — landowners are paid an annual lease to keep their land open, which is the answer to subdivision and fencing
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY WITHOUT SELLING: MMWCA, a membership association established as a legal entity in 2013, coordinates a network of conservancies in the Mara built on a partnership between landowners and tourism partners, with the association as coordinator. THE INSTRUMENT: individual landowners lease their parcels into a conservancy and receive a fixed annual lease fee paid regardless of how many tourists actually come that year — the distinctive feature of the Mara model is that the benefit is direct and guaranteed to each landowner, not pooled into a committee's budget. Reported scale: 15 established conservancies covering 347,011 acres, involving 14,528 landowners, with lease payments over US$4.8 million a year, and 24 conservancies at various stages of development. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND WILDLIFE, and it is the reason it is in this file: across southern Kenya formerly communal group ranches have been subdivided into tens of thousands of individual parcels, and once individuals hold parcels they can sell or fence them — which fragments grazing land and lets outsiders buy in. Elsewhere in the same ecosystem, communities have used the identical logic explicitly as a defence: one landowner noted that it is now very hard for newcomers to purchase land because it has already been leased out, and in another conservancy the terms mean members cannot sell to anyone other than another member for conservation purposes, and cannot put up fences. A lease is a way of taking land off the market for a term without giving up ownership. In the Amboseli system, foundations pay annual leases to thousands of Maasai landowners on similar terms. WHO IT SUITS: individual titleholders in wildlife landscapes who want income without selling, and communities whose group ranch has just been subdivided. CAVEATS: this depends on a tourism market and a paying partner, so it works where wildlife draws visitors and nowhere else; conservationists caution the model holds only while landowners keep receiving benefits and remain in decision-making; and leases are for a term — what happens at renewal is the risk. It secures land against fencing and sale; it does not stop a state project.

trackers.name: Tanzania-Bondeni Community Land Trust, Voi — Africa's first CLT: residents hold the land collectively so nobody can sell the neighbourhood out from under them
trackers.desc: WHAT THIS IS AND WHY IT IS HERE: a community land trust — the community owns the land collectively and permanently while households hold their homes — established at the Tanzania-Bondeni informal settlement in Voi, about 350 km south-east of Nairobi, between roughly 1991 and 2004 as part of an upgrading project. At launch the settlement held some 4,370 residents in 530 structures on 22 hectares. It is the first CLT in the Global South and the first in an informal settlement, and the closest thing in this file to a body that acquires land and holds it against resale. THE PROBLEM IT WAS BUILT TO SOLVE, which is the reason to consider it anywhere: after an upgrading or regularisation project, residents with individual titles sell to higher-income buyers and the cycle of land concentration resumes — the community is improved and then displaced by its own improvement. A resident put it plainly: if we take individual title deeds, some will start selling them, and where will the children live? The CLT separates land from buildings so that the land cannot be sold. HOW IT WAS MADE TO WORK IN KENYAN LAW, since the same obstacles exist elsewhere: Kenyan law did not permit the separation of ownership over land and buildings, so residents organised and registered as a private organisation, entered into trust deeds applying the CLT's management rules, had public land transferred to the trust, and the trust then issued individual titles to member families. Legal support came from the Kenyan legal aid NGO Kituo Cha Sheria, working with the municipal council, the local government ministry and the Commissioner of Lands, with a housing cooperative union supplying individual credit. WHAT WENT WRONG, AND YOU SHOULD READ THIS BEFORE COPYING IT: researchers record that the arrangement is legally intricate and daunting, that residents' unfamiliarity with the model meant rules on re-electing the managing committee and overseeing absentee owners went unenforced, and that mobilisation weakened and distrust of the trust's managers grew. Without strong and continuous community mobilisation the model does not reach its potential. WHO IT SUITS: urban and peri-urban communities facing displacement by their own upgrading, or wanting collective tenure that survives individual sales. CAVEATS: THIS IS A CASE AND A MODEL, NOT A SERVICE YOU CAN RING — the trust has no site; this entry points at the international CLT centre's Africa page documenting it. Kituo Cha Sheria, which did the legal work, has its own entry in this file. For registering community land under the 2016 Act, Kenya's RECONCILE entry is the route.

trackers.name: Kituo Cha Sheria — Kenya's oldest legal aid organisation, free representation on evictions and land, with an SMS line and directions to the door
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Kituo Cha Sheria, the Legal Advice Centre, founded on 9 July 1973 by young lawyers who sat under a tree in Ngara, Nairobi, giving free legal advice — now the oldest and most experienced legal aid and human rights organisation in Kenya, with around 60 professionals and a network of volunteer advocates. WHAT IT HANDLES THAT MATTERS HERE: land rights, housing evictions and land grabbing, alongside labour, family and refugee matters; it provides free consultations, legal representation and alternative dispute resolution, and has run legal aid clinics across eight regions of Kenya rather than only in Nairobi. It litigates in the public interest against forced evictions and unconstitutional policies, and its own account is that as a result, evictions have significantly reduced and land grabbing does not happen without a fight. It did the legal work behind Africa's first community land trust, recorded separately in this file. HOW YOU REACH IT, WHICH ALMOST NO ENTRY IN THIS FILE CAN SAY: an SMS line on 0700 777 333, an online portal for free legal services, info@kituochasheria.or.ke, a head office at Ole Odume Road off Argwings Kodhek Road in Nairobi — published with the bus and matatu route number and the stage to alight at — plus a Mombasa office at Tudor and a Nairobi branch at Pangani. It also trains community paralegals in informal settlements and rural areas and runs community justice centres, the flagship being Nyando in Nyanza since 2006. WHO IT SUITS: Kenyan households and communities facing eviction, land grabbing or a land dispute they cannot afford to litigate. CAVEATS: demand far exceeds capacity and the caseload spans many fields, so approach early; the state National Legal Aid Service is a separate route with its own application form; and for community land registration Kenya's RECONCILE entry is the specialist.

trackers.name: Kenya Land Alliance — national land network that maps community land interests and pushes Community Land Act registration county by county
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Kenya Land Alliance, a non-partisan umbrella network of civil society organisations and individuals working on land law and policy, formed 1999, a Trust from 2001 and registered as an NGO in 2013, based at Nakuru with declared operations including Turkana, Tana River, Mombasa, Kisumu and Nakuru. WHAT IT DOES FOR COMMUNITIES RATHER THAN FOR POLICY: it maps out, through SOCIAL CARTOGRAPHY, the land interests of minority groups and communities across counties — including pastoralists and communities living with mining and oil drilling — and pushes for more registration of Community Land under the 2016 Act, working at county as well as national level through peer-to-peer learning between communities. It convened, with a land rights institute, a multi-stakeholder platform (the Ardhi Caucus) bringing state and non-state actors together to unblock community land registration a decade after the Act. ON THE GROUND: workshops with an urban settlement cooperative society in Nakuru on displacement and evictions, matrimonial property, succession and problematic land use; a women's land rights reporting tool piloted in Kakamega and Taita Taveta counties; and public tracking of land grabbing cases — noting the anti-corruption commission's report of 130 court cases over grabbed property in Mombasa county. Its own diagnosis of why women lose land is the useful part: lengthy, adversarial and technical access-to-justice processes, poor access to information, a multiplicity of laws, and weak enforcement of the laws that exist. WHO IT SUITS: Kenyan communities seeking community land registration, pastoralists, and residents of counties with heavy land-grabbing or extractive pressure. CAVEATS: an advocacy and networking umbrella — casework and representation happen at member organisations; for community land registration fieldwork Kenya's RECONCILE entry, for free representation Kituo Cha Sheria, and for the collective-tenure model, the Tanzania-Bondeni community land trust entry.

trackers.name: GROOTS Kenya's Community Land and Property Watch Dog groups — neighbours who camp at a widow's house so the title deed cannot be taken during the funeral
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: GROOTS Kenya, a national network of community-based organisations and women's self-help groups founded in 1995, which in 2005 built its flagship Community Land and Property Watch Dog model in response to women being stripped of property and disinherited. HOW A WATCH DOG GROUP IS BUILT, and it is copyable by any village without money: each group is volunteer women and men — community health workers, traditional leaders, TRAINED PARALEGALS and government stakeholders sitting together; GROOTS runs an intensive eight-week programme training ONE member of each group as a paralegal, who then trains the rest of their own group. The group monitors disinheritance locally, mediates land disputes within families, refers unresolved cases to formal adjudication, and educates the community on land tenure and property rights. Reported reach: watch dog groups in more than 30 locations in central and western Kenya, having handled more than 200 cases of women's property rights violations. WHY THE TIMING IS THE WHOLE POINT: dispossession happens in the days after a husband's death, so a group in Kiambu County moves as soon as news of a death arrives, visits the bereaved family and STAYS PRESENT THROUGH THE MOURNING PERIOD to deter attempts to seize land documents and title deeds — in one member's words, so that the widow cries with one eye while the other stays alert. Chiefs in the county reportedly refer women directly to local paralegals. The courts are too slow and too expensive to stop a title deed walking out of a house during a funeral; presence is the only remedy that operates on that timescale. Divyam House No. 2, Cedar Road off Lantana Road, Westlands, Nairobi; +254 720 898 222. WHO IT SUITS: Kenyan widows, orphans and families facing property grabbing or disinheritance, and communities wanting to build a watch dog group of their own. CAVEATS: members are VOLUNTEERS — support runs to transport and meals rather than salaries, so capacity is uneven; the model mediates and refers rather than litigating, and paralegals doing this work report threats from powerful individuals. For free representation Kenya's Kituo Cha Sheria entry; for community land registration, RECONCILE.

trackers.name: Northern Rangelands Trust — supports 39 community-owned conservancies, and its financing model is the thing to interrogate before joining
trackers.desc: WHERE THE MONEY COMES FROM: NRT brings together 39 community-owned and community-run conservancies in northern and coastal Kenya, reported as protecting over 10 million acres and home to more than 300,000 indigenous people from 18 ethnic groups, across 10 counties. It is a founding member of the national conservancies association already recorded in this file, and it assists county governments that want to establish their own community conservancies. THE FINANCING ARCHITECTURE, WHICH IS WHAT TO INTERROGATE BEFORE YOUR COMMUNITY SIGNS ANYTHING: NRT states it seeks financial sustainability on a THIRDS MODEL — a third of conservancy operations financed by commercial enterprise, a third by government, a third by donors; it supported conservancies with a reported Ksh 854 million for operations in one year. County money is real and increasing: all 10 county governments actively support these conservancies and six provide financial support, with a 50 per cent COST-SHARE model agreed with one county government for operational budgets, and counties asking NRT to help draft county legislation enabling that support — which is what locks funding in across successive administrations, rather than leaving it to a friendly governor. Coastal conservancies received Ksh 155 million from a national water sector trust fund with 15 per cent county co-funding, and tripartite memoranda between conservancies, NRT and county governments have been signed in three counties. The Conservancy Management and Development Plan is the instrument that links a conservancy to the County Integrated Development Plan — so getting your plan written is how community priorities enter county budgets. WHO IT SUITS: northern and coastal Kenyan communities considering forming or joining a conservancy, and anyone negotiating county co-funding. CAVEATS: THE MODEL IS CONTESTED — researchers and some community members have questioned governance, consent and the degree of genuine community control in large conservancy programmes, and carbon projects on communal rangeland have drawn particular criticism; read the conservancy's own constitution and ask who signs the carbon and tourism agreements before joining. Conservancy status is not a land title. For the Mara lease model see the Maasai Mara association entry, for grants the Kenya Conservancies Fund, and for community land registration, RECONCILE.

trackers.name: National Legal Aid Service — Kenya's statutory free-lawyer scheme, toll-free 0800720640, and it takes LAND cases
trackers.desc: WHAT YOU ARE ENTITLED TO: the National Legal Aid Service (NLAS), established under the Legal Aid Act No. 6 of 2016 to provide affordable, accessible, sustainable, credible and accountable legal aid to INDIGENT PERSONS, to promote legal awareness, to FUND JUSTICE ADVISORY CENTRES and to promote alternative dispute resolution. It matters here because its civil remit expressly includes property and LAND disputes — ownership and boundaries — alongside constitutional and PUBLIC INTEREST matters. HOW TO REACH IT: offices in Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru and Eldoret, and a TOLL-FREE NUMBER, 0800720640, to book an appointment for free legal services. HOW THE APPLICATION WORKS, so nobody is turned away at the counter: you apply on the form prescribed in the FIRST SCHEDULE of the Legal Aid (General) Regulations 2020, showing your financial situation — income statements, savings and assets — and the nature of the case; eligibility covers citizens, children, refugees, stateless persons, internally displaced persons and victims of trafficking. Two details worth knowing in advance: the Service may grant PARTIAL legal aid on condition that you contribute financially to the fund; and it maintains a REGISTER OF ACCREDITED LEGAL AID PROVIDERS under section 60 — so if NLAS itself cannot take you, ask for the register and go to an accredited provider near you. Bring identification and any court summons or contracts. WHO IT SUITS: indigent Kenyans with a land, boundary, succession or public interest matter who need a funded lawyer or a referral. CAVEATS: A STATE SERVICE WITH A MEANS TEST AND A MERITS ASSESSMENT, concentrated in urban centres, and accreditation of providers carries fees under the 2020 regulations — it is not a route for opposing a government project you are fighting. For free representation from an NGO, Kenya's Kituo Cha Sheria entry; for constitutional and environmental litigation, Katiba Institute.

trackers.name: Conservation Alliance of Kenya, open to community-based organisations — and the leasing model paying 15,000 Kenyan landowners to keep their land unfenced
trackers.desc: FIFTEEN THOUSAND LANDOWNERS PAID TO LEAVE IT UNFENCED, AND THE UMBRELLA A VILLAGE GROUP CAN JOIN: THE CONSERVATION ALLIANCE OF KENYA IS A LIMITED LIABILITY MEMBERSHIP ORGANISATION REGISTERED IN KENYA AS THE UMBRELLA BODY TO ADVANCE THE PRESERVATION, PROTECTION AND MANAGEMENT OF WILDLIFE AND ITS HABITATS; PLACES OF NATURAL BEAUTY; LOCATIONS OF ZOOLOGICAL, BOTANICAL, GEOGRAPHICAL AND SCIENTIFIC INTEREST; AND FEATURES OF LANDSCAPE WITH GEOLOGICAL AND PHYSIOGRAPHICAL VALUE IN KENYA. Read that object clause carefully: places of NATURAL BEAUTY and features of landscape with GEOLOGICAL value are inside its mandate, not only wildlife. A hill, an outcrop, a waterfall with no endangered species on it still falls within what this body exists to protect — which is rarer than it sounds. AND MEMBERSHIP IS OPEN TO REGISTERED INTERNATIONAL NGOs, DOMESTIC NGOs, CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS AND COMMUNITY BASED ORGANISATIONS, with a governance structure of BOARD OF DIRECTORS, COUNCIL OF ADVISORS AND SECRETARIAT, and a named board head. CBOs can join as members alongside international NGOs. A registered village organisation sits in the same body as the largest conservation organisations in the country — register the CBO first, then apply. THE INCOME MODEL, WITH THE NUMBER: IN A NAMED CONSERVATION AREA, WITH OPERATIONAL SUPPORT FROM A CONSERVATION ORGANISATION AND A DEVELOPMENT AGENCY, 15,000 LANDOWNERS ARE EARNING AN INCOME BY LEASING THEIR LAND AND CREATING UNFENCED AREAS FOR WILDLIFE, TOURISM AND LIVESTOCK — with the area board chaired by a NAMED LOCAL TEACHER. Fifteen thousand individual landowners each paid to keep their own parcel unfenced, and the board chaired by a schoolteacher rather than a conservationist. That is the answer to the question of what a smallholder gets for not selling: a lease payment, an intact herd route, and a seat. Ask what the per-acre lease rate is and how long the term runs before you agree to anything. WHO MAY FORM ONE, DEFINED: A WILDLIFE CONSERVANCY IS LAND MANAGED BY AN INDIVIDUAL LANDOWNER, A BODY CORPORATE, A GROUP OF OWNERS OR A COMMUNITY FOR PURPOSES OF WILDLIFE CONSERVATION AND OTHER COMPATIBLE LAND USES TO BETTER LIVELIHOODS. An INDIVIDUAL landowner can declare a conservancy in Kenya. You do not need a community first — one owner is enough to start, and other compatible land uses is written into the definition, so livestock and farming are not excluded. THE LEVERAGE, IN THE STATE'S OWN TERMS: KENYA AIMS TO PUT 30% OF ITS LANDS UNDER CONSERVATION MANAGEMENT BY 2030 — AND THE RECORD STATES PLAINLY THAT THE GOVERNMENT HAS MAXIMISED WHAT IT CAN DO WITH ITS OWN LANDS; THE ONLY WAY TO CLOSE THE GAP WILL BE TO SUPPORT COMMUNITIES TO MANAGE THEIR LANDS. The state cannot reach its own target without community land. That is the strongest bargaining position any Kenyan landholding community has ever had — you are not asking for a favour, you are the only way the commitment gets met. Say so. ALSO RECORDED: community conservancies lead strategies including ROTATIONAL GRAZING, CARBON CREDITS AND WATER STORAGE; a PROJECT FINANCE FOR PERMANENCE mechanism is being developed to establish a CONSERVATION TRUST FUND FOR THE LONG TERM, bringing together governments, indigenous peoples and local communities, funders and partners TO SECURE LONG-TERM CONSERVATION, FULL AND SUSTAINED FUNDING, AND COMMUNITY BENEFITS; and the honest constraint is stated too — MOST COMMUNITY CONSERVANCIES DO NOT HAVE FUNDING FOR SOCIAL PROJECTS, MANAGEMENT PLANS, AND ECONOMIC INVESTMENTS. Most conservancies are underfunded for exactly the three things that make them work. Budget the management plan and the social projects into the deal at the start, not afterwards. WHO IT SUITS: Kenyan landowners, group ranches and CBOs considering a conservancy or a lease. CAVEATS: LEASING MEANS SIGNING A TERM AGREEMENT over your land — read it with counsel. For money and technical help to hold land as a conservancy, Kenya's Kenya Conservancies Fund entry; for 2,573 acres bought outright, Nature Kenya; for forest bought at auction, A Rocha Kenya; for land leased from Maasai landowners, the Maasai Mara Wildlife Conservancies Association entry; for 39 community-owned conservancies, Northern Rangelands Trust.

trackers.name: The Grassroots Justice Network — 12,300+ members from 3,430 organisations that any community justice group can join, with flexible grants, a legal empowerment resource library, and the push to get community paralegals recognised in AU Agenda 2063
trackers.desc: TWELVE THOUSAND MEMBERS, AND A GRANT THAT IS NOT TIED TO A PROJECT — placement note first: THIS IS A GLOBAL NETWORK AND THE FILE HAS NO GLOBAL KEY. It is filed under Kenya because Kenya is one of the six countries in the convenor's own country programme and because the network's senior Africa officer and a named Kenyan member leader appear in this record. Membership spans 175 countries, so it applies wherever you are. THE GRASSROOTS JUSTICE NETWORK, FORMERLY THE LEGAL EMPOWERMENT NETWORK, HAS GROWN FROM FEWER THAN 50 PEOPLE IN ONE ROOM TO 12,300+ MEMBERS FROM OVER 3,430 ORGANISATIONS ACROSS 175 COUNTRIES, DESCRIBED AS THE LARGEST COMMUNITY OF JUSTICE DEFENDERS IN THE WORLD — AND ITS PURPOSE IS CONNECTING, STRENGTHENING, AND EXPANDING THE NUMBER OF COMMUNITY PARALEGALS AROUND THE WORLD. Fewer than fifty people in one room. Every network in this file started that way, and this one names the number — which is the encouragement a village association needs before its first meeting. Membership is open to organisations and to individuals: if your community has one person doing paralegal work, that person can join a global body of twelve thousand who do the same thing. THE PART THAT IS MONEY: THE NETWORK RUNS A MODEL OF FLEXIBLE GRANTS THAT RESPONDS TO THE NEEDS OF GRASSROOTS GROUPS TAKING ON STRUCTURAL INJUSTICES — with grantees recorded describing what the flexible funding let them achieve. Flexible is the same principle this file recorded with unrestricted funding two rounds ago, and it matters for the same reason: a group fighting a land taking cannot predict what next month costs. Ask the network what its grants require and when they open — a small flexible grant to a village paralegal is worth more than a large restricted one to somebody else's project. THE LIBRARY, WHICH IS FREE: THE NETWORK BUILT THE WORLD'S MOST COMPREHENSIVE RESOURCE LIBRARY ON LEGAL EMPOWERMENT, and its members co-produced A PRACTICAL GUIDE FOR LEGAL SERVICE PROVIDERS IN RURAL AREAS ACROSS THE WORLD, plus A COLLECTION OF RESEARCH BRIEFS REVIEWING THE NATURE OF THE WORK UNDERTAKEN BY COMMUNITY PARALEGALS IN DIFFERENT COUNTRIES AND HOW THAT WORK IS RECOGNISED AND FUNDED BY THE GOVERNMENT. How paralegal work is recognised and FUNDED BY THE GOVERNMENT, country by country. That brief answers the question every group in this file eventually reaches: is there a public budget line for what we are doing, and has any state created one. Look up your own country in it before asking your ministry. THE CONTINENTAL ASK WORTH JOINING: A SENIOR NETWORK OFFICER AND A NAMED KENYAN MEMBER LEADER CALL FOR THE AFRICAN UNION'S AGENDA 2063 TO INCLUDE TARGETS FOR THE LEGAL RECOGNITION AND FINANCING OF COMMUNITY PARALEGALS. Legal recognition AND financing, as targets in the AU's own framework. If that lands, community paralegals stop being a donor project and become a funded category. It is the single policy ask in this file that would change the position of the most organisations at once — and it is being made by Africans inside the network, so an African member group adding its name carries weight. WHAT THE MODEL PRODUCES, WITH TWO NUMBERS FROM DIFFERENT COUNTRIES: IN SIERRA LEONE, PARALEGALS AND COMMUNITIES HAVE TAKEN ON OVER 300 LAND AND ENVIRONMENTAL INJUSTICES IN A DECADE, INCLUDING UNFAIR LEASE AGREEMENTS; AND IN MOZAMBIQUE, COMMUNITY PARALEGALS KNOWN LOCALLY AS DEFENSORES DE SAÚDE HAVE HELPED IDENTIFY OVER 29,000 GRIEVANCES, 81% OF WHICH HAVE BEEN RESOLVED. Eighty-one per cent resolved. That is the resolution rate of a paralegal working inside their own community, and it is higher than anything a court in this file achieves. The lesson is not that lawyers are unnecessary but that most grievances are settled before they need one — if your community is choosing where to spend, a trained local paralegal resolves more cases per shilling than litigation. AND WHAT A PARALEGAL IS TRAINED IN, WHICH IS BROADER THAN LAW: PARALEGALS TRAINED IN THE BASICS OF LOCAL LAW, AS WELL AS COMPLEMENTARY SKILLS LIKE COMMUNITY ORGANIZING, TRAINING, ADVOCACY, AND STRATEGIC MEDIATION — intended as A FRONTLINE THAT CAN BE IN TOUCH WITH COMMUNITY NEEDS, ADJUST LEGAL TRAINING AND ADVOCACY TO LOCAL CONTEXTS, AND EMPOWER PEOPLE TO KNOW AND USE THEIR RIGHTS. Strategic mediation sits in the same training as law. Most land disputes end in an agreement rather than a judgment, and the person who can hold that room is the one who was taught both. WHO IT SUITS: any African community group doing paralegal or legal empowerment work, and anyone seeking flexible funding or free materials. CAVEATS: A NETWORK AND A CONVENOR, not a law firm — and its country programmes cover six countries only. For paralegals who renegotiate leases already signed, Sierra Leone's Namati entry; for community paralegals in Kenya, the entries under Kenya's legal aid organisations.

trackers.name: The Isiolo judgment — 165 residents got two conservancies on their community land declared unconstitutional, with a permanent injunction and 53 rangers barred, and the documenting organisations behind it
trackers.desc: ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-FIVE RESIDENTS, FOUR YEARS, ONE JUDGMENT — and it is the most important community win in this file's recent African record: A THREE-JUDGE BENCH OF THE ENVIRONMENT AND LAND COURT FOUND THAT A LARGE CONSERVATION ORGANISATION AND ITS PARTNERS HAD ESTABLISHED AND OPERATED WILDLIFE CONSERVANCIES ON UNREGISTERED COMMUNITY LAND WITHOUT PROPER PARTICIPATION FROM THE PUBLIC, IN TWO NAMED WARDS OF ISIOLO COUNTY — RULING THE ESTABLISHMENT UNCONSTITUTIONAL AND FINDING THAT IT VIOLATED THE CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS OF THE 165 PETITIONERS, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO PROPERTY RIGHTS. UNREGISTERED community land is the hinge. The land had not been registered, and the court treated establishing a conservancy on it without proper public participation as unconstitutional. If your community land is unregistered and somebody is operating on it, that is the finding to put in front of a lawyer — and registering your land is the thing to start now regardless. THE ORDERS, WHICH ARE WHAT MAKES IT WORTH READING: THE CONSERVANCIES WERE ORDERED TO SHUT DOWN OPERATIONS EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY; THE COURT ISSUED A PERMANENT INJUNCTION PROHIBITING THE ORGANISATION AND ITS PARTNERS FROM CONDUCTING ANY CONSERVANCY OPERATIONS, INCLUDING RECRUITMENT AND DEPLOYMENT OF RANGERS, IN THE AFFECTED AREAS; AND 53 COMMUNITY WILDLIFE RANGERS WERE PROHIBITED FROM OPERATING OR DEPLOYING IN THE SUBCOUNTY. A permanent injunction naming recruitment and deployment of rangers. Where armed or uniformed personnel are the daily face of a project on your land, that is the specific order to ask counsel about — shutting an operation and barring its personnel are two different remedies, and this community got both. WHO BROUGHT IT: 165 RESIDENTS FROM THE TWO CONSERVANCIES FILED THE PETITION IN 2021, AND THE LEAD PETITIONER — A PASTORALIST AND HUMAN RIGHTS ADVOCATE — SAID AFTERWARDS: I'M NOT OPPOSING THE CONCEPT OF CONSERVATION, BUT HOW IT'S DONE AND THE LEGITIMACY CREATED A LOT OF CONFUSION AND DOUBTS. A hundred and sixty-five named petitioners, filed 2021, decided 2025. Four years. That is the honest timeline for a constitutional land case, and the number of petitioners is the other lesson: this was not one brave individual but a body of residents, which is harder to intimidate and harder to dismiss as unrepresentative. And read the lead petitioner's framing — not against conservation, against how it was done. That framing is why it won. WHAT IT REACHED: the conservancies fed a soil carbon removal project promoted as the WORLD'S LARGEST, whose credits have been BOUGHT BY NAMED MULTINATIONAL CORPORATIONS INCLUDING A STREAMING COMPANY, A SOCIAL MEDIA COMPANY, A BANK AND AN AIRLINE — and a certifying body had earlier SUSPENDED CREDIT ISSUANCE from one of the conservancies after an advocacy report accused the project of OVERESTIMATING ITS CARBON SAVINGS AND VIOLATING INDIGENOUS RIGHTS, before later reversing course. The buyers are named companies with reputations. A carbon project on your land has customers, and those customers can be written to — and a certifier can suspend issuance, which is a second pressure point that does not require a court. Find out who certifies the scheme and who buys the credits. THE PRECEDENT VALUE, PUT BY A KENYAN LAWYER: WHAT THIS CASE MIGHT HAVE DONE IS INTENSIFY THE NEED FOR PEOPLE TO UNDERTAKE PUBLIC PARTICIPATION WITH THE PEOPLE WHO HAVE THE RIGHTS OVER LAND — NOT ONLY HAS THIS CASE INFORMED US ABOUT WHERE TO GO AND FIND OUT PREVIOUS JUDGMENT PRECEDENTS, BUT ALSO SHOWS THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF COUNTY GOVERNMENTS, THE MINISTRY OF LANDS, THE WILDLIFE SERVICE AND OTHER STAKEHOLDERS, AS WELL AS THE ROLE OF COMMUNITIES. LITIGATION CREATES AWARENESS. And the judgment is recorded as potentially AFFECTING HOW CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS OPERATE ON COMMUNITY LANDS ACROSS KENYA, emphasising THE NEED FOR CONSERVATION EFFORTS TO ALIGN WITH CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES AND RESPECT COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS. THE DOCUMENTING ORGANISATION: a research institute published a report on community conservancies in northern Kenya, quoting named elders and professionals from five named communities, and has separately responded to a due diligence report commissioned by the project's own donors. A body that publishes named community testimony and then publicly criticises the donors' own review is the kind of ally that keeps a case alive between hearings. If your case has an international funder behind the project, somebody is probably already investigating it. THE CAVEAT, RECORDED PLAINLY: THE ORGANISATION HAS ASKED THE COURT FOR A STAY OF EXECUTION AND IS APPEALING THE DECISION. A first-instance win is not the end. Plan for the appeal from the day you file — and note that in the same period the organisation also lost a major donor and had a carbon project suspended, which is a reminder that litigation is one of several pressures and rarely the only one that works. WHO IT SUITS: Kenyan communities on unregistered community land, anyone facing a conservancy or carbon project established without their participation. CAVEATS: THIS IS ONE JUDGMENT UNDER APPEAL, and communities differ on conservancies — this file also records the leasing model that pays 15,000 landowners. For how a community becomes a registered conservancy, Kenya's Conservation Alliance and KWCA entries; for the communities' guide to registering community land, RECONCILE; for constitutional litigators, Katiba Institute; for 60 days to appeal a decision, the National Environment Tribunal entry.

trackers.name: The BIOPAMA grant facility — €50,000 small grants answered in six weeks and €100,000–200,000 medium grants for community-based organisations, both with NO co-financing required, with the money reserved country by country
trackers.desc: NO CO-FINANCING REQUIRED, AND AN ANSWER IN SIX WEEKS — placement note first: THIS FACILITY COVERS AFRICAN, CARIBBEAN AND PACIFIC COUNTRIES, FILED UNDER KENYA BECAUSE THE WORKED EXAMPLE BELOW IS KENYAN AND KENYA IS IN THE RESERVED-FUNDS LIST; THE ELIGIBLE AFRICAN COUNTRIES ARE NAMED IN FULL BELOW. NO CO-FINANCING REQUIRED is the phrase that matters most, and it appears on BOTH windows. Most funders in this file want the community to bring a share of the money, which is exactly what a community facing a project does not have. Here the fund covers the whole amount. THE SMALL WINDOW: A MAXIMUM OF EUR 50,000 WITH NO CO-FINANCING REQUIRED, FOR INTERVENTIONS OF UP TO 12 MONTHS, ON AN OPEN-ENDED CALL WHERE APPLICANTS CAN APPLY AT ANY TIME — AND THE FINAL DECISION IS AIMED TO BE TAKEN WITHIN 6 WEEKS OF RECEIPT OF PROPOSALS. Apply any time, answer in six weeks. That is fast enough to matter when something is happening on your land this season rather than next budget year. THE MEDIUM WINDOW, AND ITS STATED PURPOSE NAMES YOU: GRANT SIZE VARIES FROM A MINIMUM OF 100,000 EUR TO A MAXIMUM OF 200,000 EUR, WITH NO CO-FUNDING NECESSARY FROM THE APPLICANT — TO ENABLE AND SUPPORT COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANISATIONS ENGAGED IN THE CONSERVATION OF BIODIVERSITY TO CARRY OUT SUSTAINABLE CONSERVATION MEASURES IN PROTECTED AND CONSERVED AREAS, AND TO SUPPORT LOCAL COMMUNITIES' INITIATIVES AIMING TO ENHANCE THE LIVELIHOODS OF LOCAL PEOPLE WHILST EFFECTIVELY CONTRIBUTING TO PROTECTED AREAS MANAGEMENT. COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANISATIONS written into the purpose of a two-hundred-thousand-euro window. Not an NGO applying on your behalf — the CBO is the intended applicant. AND THE MONEY IS RESERVED COUNTRY BY COUNTRY, WHICH TELLS YOU YOUR ODDS BEFORE YOU WRITE: 2.5 MILLION EUR IN TOTAL, OF WHICH APPROXIMATELY 1.5 MILLION IS RESERVED FOR ETHIOPIA, KENYA, RWANDA, TANZANIA, UGANDA, MADAGASCAR, MOZAMBIQUE AND ZAMBIA — AND THE REMAINING 1 MILLION FOR ANGOLA, BOTSWANA, COMOROS, DJIBOUTI, ERITREA, ESWATINI, LESOTHO, MAURITIUS, MALAWI, NAMIBIA, SEYCHELLES, SUDAN, SOMALIA, SOUTH AFRICA, SOUTH SUDAN AND ZIMBABWE. A million euros ring-fenced for sixteen countries that rarely appear in conservation funding at all — Comoros, Djibouti, Eritrea, Eswatini, Lesotho and Somalia among them. If you are in one of those, the competition for that ring-fenced million is far thinner than for the general pot, and this file has recorded how few funders reach those countries. WHERE THE WORK MUST HAPPEN: PRIORITY AREAS INCLUDE KEY LANDSCAPES FOR CONSERVATION, KEY BIODIVERSITY AREAS, MARINE MANAGED AREAS OR OTHER PROTECTED AND CONSERVED AREAS, WHERE THEIR IMPORTANCE IS JUSTIFIED BY DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS OR STRATEGIC DOCUMENTS. OTHER PROTECTED AND CONSERVED AREAS is broad, and the justification can come from a strategic document rather than a formal designation. A community-conserved area that appears in a national strategy or a recognised diagnostic can qualify — so find out first whether your place is already named in one, because that reference is the eligibility. THE THREE CONDITIONS TO SATISFY: COMPLY WITH AN ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM; ENABLE DATA AND INFORMATION SHARING FROM THE PROJECT WITH THE REGIONAL OBSERVATORIES; AND BE OF PRACTICAL FIELD APPLICATION AND LIMITED IN TIME TO AVOID DEPENDENCY ON THE SUPPORT PROVIDED. Read the second one twice: your project data goes to the regional observatory. That is a cost and a benefit — your monitoring enters a regional record that outlives the grant, but plan what you are willing to publish about your own area before you agree. HOW TO APPLY: THROUGH THE GRANTS MANAGEMENT PORTAL — CREATE YOUR ACCOUNT, LOG IN AND APPLY. THE WORKED EXAMPLE, AND IT SHOWS WHAT 50,000 EUROS BUYS: A GRANT ENHANCES COMMUNICATION, SECURITY AND WILDLIFE AND HABITAT MONITORING IN A NAMED KENYAN FOREST RESERVE, IMPLEMENTED BY A NAMED COMMUNITY FOREST ASSOCIATION OVER 12 MONTHS — ITS OVERALL OBJECTIVE BEING TO ENSURE THE ASSOCIATION'S RANGERS CAN ENGAGE EFFECTIVELY IN SECURITY AND CONSERVATION MEASURES, ALLOWING THEM TO JOIN THE RADIO NETWORK OF THE SECURITY FORCES IN THE LANDSCAPE AND TO JOIN THE WILDLIFE MONITORING EFFORTS, WITH 25 COMMUNITY FOREST USER GROUPS AND THEIR FAMILIES GAINING ADDED SECURITY. Joining the radio network of the security forces is the specific thing the money bought. Community rangers who can talk to the police and the wildlife service on the same channel are treated as part of the security landscape rather than as trespassers on it — and 25 user groups benefited from one grant to one association. AND THE EXCEPTIONS TO KNOW BEFORE APPLYING: SOUTH AFRICA CANNOT BE A BENEFICIARY OF CONTRACTS FINANCED BY THIS FUND, THOUGH PERSONS ESTABLISHED THERE MAY PARTICIPATE IN THE PROCEDURES; AND TRANSBOUNDARY ACTIVITIES INVOLVING SOUTH SUDAN ARE ELIGIBLE. WHO IT SUITS: African community forest associations, conservancies, CBOs and community-managed marine areas in the named countries. CAVEATS: CALL WINDOWS OPEN AND CLOSE — check the portal for the current round rather than relying on a past deadline, and note the data-sharing condition. For rapid response grants under a different fund entirely, Kenya's Urgent Action Fund–Africa entry; for the West African marine network in the same programme, The Gambia's RAMPAO entry; for flexible grants and a paralegal funding brief, the Grassroots Justice Network entry.

trackers.name: The Strategic Legal Response Centre — rapid legal support when land defenders are criminalized, attacked or killed, and help forcing implementation of judgments already won — with the Kenyan community organisations and the 13-community women-led assembly
trackers.desc: THE JUDGMENT WAS WON AND STILL NOT IMPLEMENTED — that is the problem this entry exists for, and it is stated on the record: DESPITE A 2017 LANDMARK JUDGEMENT BY THE AFRICAN COURT ON HUMAN AND PEOPLES' RIGHTS IN FAVOUR OF A NAMED KENYAN FOREST PEOPLE, THEY ARE STILL EXCLUDED FROM THEIR ANCESTRAL FOREST LANDS — AND THE ORGANISATION IS SUPPORTING THEM TO SEEK THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THIS RULING, AND TO PURSUE LITIGATION TO HALT EVICTIONS. A continental court ruled in their favour and years later they are still off their land. Winning is not the end of the case, and this file has recorded the same pattern from Isiolo to the Endorois. Budget for the implementation fight as a separate campaign with its own funding — and note there is an organisation whose stated work is exactly that second fight. WHAT THE CENTRE OFFERS: THE ORGANISATION AMPLIFIES ITS SUPPORT THROUGH A STRATEGIC LEGAL RESPONSE CENTRE, IN COLLABORATION WITH ITS COUNTRY TEAMS AND NETWORKS OF LOCAL LAWYERS AND PARTNERS — FACILITATING THE STRATEGIC USE OF A WIDE RANGE OF JUDICIAL AND NON-JUDICIAL MECHANISMS AT NATIONAL, REGIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL LEVELS TO ENSURE ACCESS TO JUSTICE AND RAPID RESPONSE WHENEVER LAND AND SELF-GOVERNANCE RIGHTS ARE VIOLATED, OR WHENEVER LAND DEFENDERS ARE CRIMINALIZED, THREATENED, ATTACKED OR KILLED. NETWORKS OF LOCAL LAWYERS is the operative phrase — the centre connects you to counsel in your own country rather than flying someone in. And CRIMINALIZED is listed first among the harms, before threatened or attacked: the commonest thing that happens to a land defender in this file is a charge, not a bullet. AND THE SECOND HALF, WHICH ALMOST NOTHING ELSE IN THIS FILE OFFERS: IT SUPPORTS PEOPLES TO PROACTIVELY DEMAND IMPLEMENTATION OF LEGAL DECISIONS UPHOLDING THEIR RIGHTS. East African assemblies it supported focused on DEALING WITH SETBACKS, SUCH AS LEGAL VICTORIES THAT ARE NOT IMPLEMENTED BUT ARE FOLLOWED BY HARASSMENT, CRIMINALIZATION, AND FURTHER RIGHTS DENIAL. Communities teaching each other how to survive winning is a subject nobody plans for and everybody meets. ITS OPERATING PRINCIPLE, WRITTEN PLAINLY: CRUCIALLY, WE DON'T CALL THE SHOTS — WE SUPPORT FOREST PEOPLES TO MAKE THEIR OWN DECISIONS THAT WILL SHAPE THEIR FUTURE; and it aims to ensure LEGAL STRATEGIES ARE DESIGNED AND DIRECTED BY INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND FOREST PEOPLES. The legal strategy is directed by the community, not the lawyers. Ask any organisation offering you legal help who decides when to settle — that answer tells you whose case it is. THE KENYAN BODIES IT NAMES, AND THE NETWORK THEY BUILT THEMSELVES: A NAMED PEOPLES DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM FOR ONE FOREST COMMUNITY; AND FOR ANOTHER, AN INDIGENOUS PEOPLES DEVELOPMENT PROJECT DESCRIBED AS A VERY EFFECTIVE COMMUNITY BASED ORGANISATION, WHICH HAS DEVELOPED LINKS AND WORK WITH OTHER FOREST AND PASTORALIST COMMUNITIES IN KENYA — WHO TOGETHER HAVE CREATED THE VERY EFFECTIVE COMMUNITY LAND ACTION NOW! NETWORK. Forest people and pastoralists in one network, built by the communities rather than for them. Those two groups are usually set against each other over the same ground; a network that holds both is far harder for an administration to split. AND THE ASSEMBLY, WITH ITS EXACT COMPOSITION: AN EAST AFRICA WOMEN-LED INDIGENOUS PEOPLES ASSEMBLY NETWORK THAT SPANS 13 COMMUNITIES — 7 FROM KENYA, 3 FROM TANZANIA, 2 FROM UGANDA AND ONE FROM EASTERN DRC. Thirteen communities across four countries, women-led, meeting to share legal strategies. If your community has women who carry the land knowledge but never sit in the negotiations, that assembly is the room they belong in. THE CONSERVATION ROUTE, WITH BOTH DOORS: WHERE PARTNERS IDENTIFY PROBLEMS, IT CAN HELP SET UP DIALOGUE WITH GOVERNMENTS AND CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS WHERE COMMUNITIES CAN PUSH FOR REFORMS IN POLICY AND PRACTICE, INCLUDING THROUGH A NAMED MECHANISM — AND THESE DIALOGUES CAN PREVENT WIDESPREAD EXCLUSION, EVICTION AND DISPOSSESSION; WHERE DIALOGUE IS DIFFICULT OR IMPOSSIBLE, IT CAN SEEK ACCOUNTABILITY AND REDRESS THROUGH LEGAL CASE WORK. A named mechanism exists for communities to bring a conservation organisation into a mediated dialogue — which is the route to try before litigation when the body on your land is an NGO rather than a company. Ask for it by name. AND THE CONTINENTAL REFERENCE DOCUMENT: A BRIEFING PAPER PROVIDES A CONTINENT-WIDE ASSESSMENT OF PROGRESS AND PERSISTENT CHALLENGES IN SECURING COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS IN AFRICA, BASED ON A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF LAND, CONSTITUTIONAL, AND RELATED SECTORAL LAWS IN 53 AFRICAN COUNTRIES, FINDING THAT LEGAL RECOGNITION OF CUSTOMARY AND COMMUNITY LAND TENURE HAS EXPANDED SIGNIFICANTLY SINCE THE 1990s AND IS NOW FIRMLY EMBEDDED IN MANY NATIONAL LEGAL FRAMEWORKS. All fifty-three countries reviewed in one document, with the finding that the law is now on your side in more places than most people assume. Look your own country up before anyone tells you no legal basis exists. WHO IT SUITS: African forest and pastoralist communities facing eviction, criminalized defenders, and anyone holding a judgment nobody is enforcing. CAVEATS: IT WORKS THROUGH PARTNERS IN 18 COUNTRIES — check whether yours is one. For the grant windows with no co-financing, Kenya's BIOPAMA entry; for the Isiolo judgment won by 165 residents, the Isiolo entry; for flexible grants and the paralegal funding brief, the Grassroots Justice Network entry.

trackers.name: Conservation organisations that buy African land — the deal forms they offer (easements for schools, payment for ecosystem services, conservation enterprise) and the 6,920-hectare purchase after which the residents were violently evicted
trackers.desc: SOMEBODY BUYS THE LAND — ASK WHO WAS LIVING ON IT. THIS ENTRY IS FILED WITH BOTH HALVES ON PURPOSE: THESE ARE ORGANISATIONS THAT WILL PAY FOR LAND AND PROTECT IT, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT A COMMUNITY FACING A DEVELOPER OFTEN NEEDS — AND THERE IS A DOCUMENTED CASE IN WHICH THAT PURCHASE ENDED IN THE EVICTION OF THE PEOPLE WHO LIVED THERE. A COMMUNITY DECIDING WHETHER TO DEAL WITH ONE NEEDS BOTH. WHO THEY ARE: A CONTINENTAL CONSERVATION FOUNDATION HEADQUARTERED IN NAIROBI AT A NAMED ROAD AND SUBURB, DESCRIBED AS ONE OF AFRICA'S LARGEST AND OLDEST CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS WITH A SOLE FOCUS ON AFRICA, AND AS THE AFRICAN UNION'S OFFICIAL CONSERVATION PARTNER — WITH FIVE MAIN STRATEGIES: CONSERVING LAND; UNDERSTANDING AND PROTECTING SPECIES; CREATING CONSERVATION-FRIENDLY BUSINESSES; EMPOWERING PEOPLE THROUGH EDUCATION AND TRAINING; AND ENGAGING GOVERNMENTS. THE DEAL FORMS THEY OFFER, EACH NAMED, AND WORTH KNOWING BY NAME BEFORE ANYONE PROPOSES ONE TO YOU: AN EASEMENTS FOR EDUCATION PROGRAM; SIX SCHOOLS REBUILT IN RETURN FOR COMMUNITIES' CONSERVATION COMMITMENTS; PAYMENT FOR ECOSYSTEM SERVICES; COMMUNITY SCOUTS; LAND USE PLANNING AND ZONING; COMMUNITY CONFLICT RESOLUTION; TOURISM PLANS AND CONCESSION GUIDELINES; AND CONSERVATION ENTERPRISE, DEFINED AS A COMMERCIAL ACTIVITY THAT GENERATES ECONOMIC BENEFITS THAT SUPPORT CONSERVATION AND COMMUNITIES. A SCHOOL IN RETURN FOR A CONSERVATION COMMITMENT is the trade being offered, and six have been built. That can be a good bargain — but read what the commitment binds, for how long, and what happens to the school if the community later wants the land back. An easement is a permanent restriction on your own land; the building is not. AND IT WORKS AT STATE LEVEL TOO: IT PILOTED THREE CONSERVANCIES WITH A NATIONAL WILDLIFE AUTHORITY AROUND THREE NAMED NATIONAL PARKS, WHICH BECAME THAT COUNTRY'S FIRST DESIGNATED CONSERVANCIES — and it initiates PAN-AFRICAN LEADERSHIP PLATFORMS FOR CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS AND PROTECTED-AREA AGENCIES AND LINKS THEM INTO GLOBAL AND REGIONAL POLICY PROCESSES. NOW THE RECORD, WHICH THIS FILE OWES ANY COMMUNITY BEING APPROACHED: IN NOVEMBER 2011 TWO CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS PAID US$2 MILLION EACH TO BUY AN AREA OF 6,920 HECTARES FROM A FORMER HEAD OF STATE, AND GAVE IT TO THE GOVERNMENT TO CREATE A PROPOSED NATIONAL PARK. TWO MILLION DOLLARS EACH, PAID TO A FORMER PRESIDENT. That is the price of seven thousand hectares in that market, and it tells you what conservation money can move when it wants to. It is also the number to hold up when you are told there is no money to buy land your community needs.
