AND WHAT HAPPENED TO THE PEOPLE: A TELEVISION DOCUMENTARY BROADCAST THAT YEAR DOCUMENTED THE VIOLENCE BEHIND THE CREATION OF THE PARK. THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLE WHO LIVED IN THE AREA WERE SUBJECTED TO A SERIES OF BRUTAL EVICTIONS, AND TOLD THE JOURNALIST THAT POLICE BEAT PEOPLE, TOOK THEIR PROPERTY AND BURNT VILLAGES. NONE OF THESE PEOPLE WERE MENTIONED IN THE PRESS RELEASE ABOUT THE HANDOVER CEREMONY. The purchase was lawful, the transfer was ceremonial, and the residents appear nowhere in the announcement. That is the shape to watch for: land can be bought over your heads from someone who holds paper title while your claim is customary and unregistered. This file's LandMark entry names the same mechanism — unmapped land reads as empty — and its mapping entries are the answer. AND THE ESCALATION THAT FOLLOWED: AN INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATION WROTE TO A UN COMMITTEE ON THE ELIMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION ABOUT THE GRAVE SITUATION CONFRONTING THE COMMUNITY, NOTING THAT POLICE HARASSMENT CONTINUED. A UN treaty committee received a written submission about an eviction from a conservation purchase. That route exists and it does not require a lawyer in-country — an organisation abroad can file it. Know that before the bulldozers, not after. THE PRACTICAL RULE THIS PRODUCES, AND IT IS THE POINT OF FILING BOTH HALVES: when a conservation organisation offers to buy land near you, ask four things in writing — WHO IS SELLING AND ON WHAT TITLE; WHO IS RECORDED AS LIVING OR GRAZING THERE; WHO WILL HOLD THE LAND AFTERWARDS; AND WHAT HAPPENS TO RESIDENTS IF THE STATE DECLARES A PARK. Those four questions are answerable before signing and unanswerable afterwards. OTHER NAMED BODIES IN THE SAME FIELD, FOR COMPARISON: an organisation founded in 2000 using a PUBLIC-PRIVATE-PARTNERSHIP APPROACH TO MANAGING PROTECTED AREAS; a community-driven conservation organisation founded in 2005; a foundation REGISTERED IN NIGERIA LED BY EXPERIENCED AFRICANS which CO-MANAGES A NAMED NATIONAL PARK AND IS COMMENCING A SECOND PROJECT IN ANOTHER, AND AIMS TO ATTRACT AFRICAN CAPITAL INTO THE SECTOR; and an international foundation established 1999 working in named African countries which BUILDS IN-COUNTRY CAPACITY BY PROVIDING TECHNICAL AND FUNDRAISING SUPPORT TO LOCAL PARTNERS. FUNDRAISING SUPPORT TO LOCAL PARTNERS is the offer to ask that last one for — help raising money in your own organisation's name rather than money spent on your behalf. And a conservation foundation led by Africans and registered in an African country is a different counterparty from a foreign one; ask where the organisation is registered and who sits on its board. WHO IT SUITS: African communities offered a conservation deal, easement or land purchase, and those seeking a buyer for land under threat. CAVEATS: THE EVICTION RECORD ABOVE IS THE CAVEAT, and it is filed here rather than buried. For the fund that grants toward buying land in perpetuity, South Africa's World Land Trust entry; for the eviction case filed alongside it, that entry's caution; for the mechanism a community can invoke against a protected area, Tanzania's Whakatane entry; for the platform showing concessions over community land, Mali's LandMark entry.

trackers.name: Public interest litigation to protect Nairobi's public open spaces (EALJ)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a University of Nairobi East African Law Journal study of how public interest litigation has been used to defend public open spaces in Nairobi, written around the actual filings rather than the theory. It walks through Green Belt Movement and 4 others v NEMA and China Road and Bridge Corporation, filed at the National Environment Tribunal on 2 June 2020, whose grounds are the template for a city open-space challenge: an EIA licence issued without adequate public participation as required by law, without a proper Strategic Environmental Assessment, and where the proponent omitted substantial information. It also covers a private-title dispute over land in Jamhuri estate arising from allocations by the former Nairobi City Council. USE IT: these three grounds — participation, missing SEA, incomplete information — are what a Nairobi filing is built on.

trackers.name: County planning appeal — and the exhaustion trap
trackers.desc: WHERE A KENYAN DEVELOPMENT IS ACTUALLY DECIDED, AND HOW TO CHALLENGE IT. Under the Physical and Land Use Planning Act No. 13 of 2019, an applicant or interested party aggrieved by a County Executive Committee decision on an application for development permission may appeal to the County Physical and Land Use Planning Liaison Committee — and ‘interested party’ is the phrase that lets a neighbour or community group in, not only the developer. OBJECT EARLIER IF YOU CAN: the Act sets objection points during plan-making — notice and objections to an inter-county plan (s.32), public participation in preparing a county plan (s.40), and notice and objections to a local plan (s.49). Objecting at plan stage is cheaper and earlier than fighting a permission. THE TRAP THAT LOSES CASES: a court has been asked to strike out an entire suit on the ground that it contravened the mandatory provisions of sections 129 and 130(1) of EMCA with Regulation 46 of the EIA and Audit Regulations 2003, because the plaintiffs went to court without first taking the grievance to the National Environment Tribunal — the court lacking original jurisdiction and its jurisdiction being invoked prematurely. USE THE LADDER IN ORDER: object at plan stage, then the County Liaison Committee, then the NET, and only then the Environment and Land Court. Going straight to court can lose you the case on jurisdiction with no hearing on the merits.

trackers.name: County Environment Committee — and complaints against NEMA itself
trackers.desc: TWO COUNTY-LEVEL LEVERS UNDER EMCA (Cap 387). Every County Environment Committee preparing a county environment plan must undertake public participation, and must take account of other county plans already adopted so they stay consistent; those plans go to the Cabinet Secretary for incorporation into the national environment action plan. That is a statutory hearing you are entitled to, before permissions are ever issued. AND WHEN THE REGULATOR IS THE PROBLEM: the National Environmental Complaints Committee investigates allegations or complaints against any person or against NEMA itself in relation to the condition of the environment in Kenya — the route when your objection is that the authority failed to act, rather than that a company did something.

trackers.name: NLAS — free lawyer, land disputes and public interest included
trackers.desc: THE FREE LAWYER FOR THE LADDER. NLAS is a body corporate under the Legal Aid Act 2016, in the Office of the Attorney General. WHAT IT COVERS MATTERS HERE: under section 35(2) its civil work expressly includes land disputes, and it covers constitutional matters involving violation of fundamental rights and matters of public interest that affect the rights of communities or groups — so a community land or environmental case sits inside the mandate, not at its edge. WHO QUALIFIES: Kenyan citizens, refugees under the Refugees Act, victims of human trafficking, internally displaced and stateless persons, and children needing representation. APPLY on form NLAS1, prescribed in the first schedule to the Legal Aid (General) Regulations 2020; bring national ID, your case documents, and proof of income — or a sworn affidavit if you have none. THE COVERAGE GAP, PLAINLY: although the service is described as available across all 47 counties, physical offices are in only 5 — Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru, Eldoret — with more planned for Lamu, Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Isiolo, Marsabit and Tana River. Elsewhere use the toll-free line 0800 720 640, email the nearest county office, or catch a community legal aid clinic. AND NOTE: the Service may grant partial legal aid on condition you contribute financially to the fund. OTHER ROUTES: Kituo Cha Sheria, whose M-Haki platform gives legal advice by mobile phone, FIDA Kenya, and the Law Society of Kenya pro bono programme.

trackers.name: Oxpeckers (investigative outlet)
trackers.desc: Independent accountability-journalism outlet (GIJN member); Oxpeckers — South African environmental-crime investigations.

trackers.name: Centre for Environmental Rights (CER) — strategic environmental litigation
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: South Africa's leading public-interest environmental law organisation — runs strategic litigation and supports community groups, with a record of judgments against coal and industrial projects. WHO IT SUITS: be realistic — they take on only a limited number of strategically selected cases capable of systemic change, so a single local application may not qualify. Their legal-services page carries self-help steps, including the environmental complaints hotline, for matters they cannot take. DO YOU QUALIFY? THERE ARE TWO FILTERS. Under Law Society requirements CER will only consider cases where the person or organisation is unable to afford private environmental attorneys, or unable reasonably to access the resources to engage them — the second applying particularly to non-public-interest organisations. Separately, the Centre takes on only a limited number of strategically selected cases, so passing the means test is not enough and CER should not be your only plan. USE THIS EVEN IF THEY DECLINE YOU: CER records that departments have committed to releasing documents automatically, by email, without a formal access-to-information request — from the environment department, environmental authorisations, waste management licences, atmospheric emission licences and Biodiversity Act permits for named facilities; from water and sanitation, water use licence applications, water use licences, and audit and compliance reports. That is 7 document categories obtainable without a lawyer and without a PAIA application. Current named officials are on CER's page; where a document is not automatically available, a formal PAIA request can be made and the South African History Archive publishes a guide to preparing one.

trackers.name: Environmental Justice Fund (South Africa)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a movement-driven, feminist NGO funding environmental and climate justice organisations in South Africa. WHO IT SUITS: South African community and environmental-justice groups looking for domestic rather than foreign funding. NOTE: canonical domain not yet verified; named as a grantmaking partner on greengrants.org. READ THE ELIGIBILITY RULES FIRST — they are the point of this fund. EJF does not consider applications from established NGOs: it exists because most funding goes to established NGOs while community-based organisations cannot reach money directly. Decisively for small groups, you do not need to be formally registered to apply. It does not fund companies, other profit-making entities or state bodies including municipalities. Grants run R50,000–R100,000 over 6 months to 1 year, with capacity-strengthening and networking support alongside the money. Your proposal must make the link to environmental justice explicit — the fund's own example is that distributing food parcels would probably not qualify, while establishing a community food garden with training in organic farming and permaculture would. It is a fund by activists, for activists, using participatory grant-making in which decisions are taken by activists from the sector rather than philanthropic gatekeepers, founded jointly by groundWork, Earthlife Africa, the Centre for Environmental Rights, WoMin, the Vaal Environmental Justice Alliance, the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance, the Benchmarks Foundation, Women on Farms and the Mining & Environmental Justice Community Network of South Africa. It currently supports 35 community-based organisations.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? YES — Cape Town (headquarters and hub). Natural Justice keeps 3 hubs: Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar. A hub means staff on the ground rather than a project relationship. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Centre (LRC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: South Africa's largest public-interest law centre. Its Land and Natural Resources work litigates for rural communities, small-scale fishers and farmers on access to land, mining and extractive projects, customary governance and, increasingly, environmental and climate justice, alongside a long housing-and-evictions practice. Offices in Johannesburg (with the Constitutional Litigation Unit), Cape Town, Durban and Makhanda. WHO IT SUITS: a community or a class of vulnerable clients rather than an individual dispute — the LRC is client-based but works on a strategic-impact model and selects matters through its focus areas, so approach the nearest office with a community-level problem.

trackers.name: SANBI — Biodiversity Stewardship
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: explains South Africa's biodiversity stewardship system — the route by which private and communal landowners enter agreements with a provincial conservation authority to protect land in a biodiversity priority area. Several of the agreement types are formally declared as protected areas under the Protected Areas Act 57 of 2003, which gives long-term legal security to the site, and since 2016 a landowner declaring a Nature Reserve or National Park can deduct 4% of the land value from taxable income each year for 25 years (per UNDP South Africa). USE IT: to find out which agreement type gives real statutory protection rather than a non-binding partnership, before approaching your provincial authority about land you are trying to keep out of development.

trackers.name: Conservation Outcomes
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a KwaZulu-Natal-based non-profit that walks private and communal landowners through biodiversity stewardship — planning, establishment and governance of conservation areas, the declaration process itself, and the post-declaration management support that declaration alone does not provide: annual plans of operation, veld and fire management, alien species control, and help applying for the tax deduction and rates exemptions. It also develops tourism, ethical hunting and natural-resource ventures so protected land can pay for itself. USE IT: when you have land worth protecting but need someone who has done the declaration paperwork before.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: amaBhungane
trackers.desc: South African nonprofit investigative newsroom exposing state capture, corruption and money laundering, and litigating for transparency.

trackers.name: Information Regulator (South Africa)
trackers.desc: South Africa's independent regulator enforcing access to information (PAIA) and data protection (POPIA). — Holds to account: public bodies that hold records — find information-commissioner decisions and appeals.

trackers.name: Legal Aid South Africa
trackers.desc: Statutory body providing legal representation to those who cannot afford it. · Find here: South Africa's state-funded legal-aid provider (Legal Aid SA). THERE IS A SEPARATE, HIGHER MEANS THRESHOLD FOR LAND MATTERS — ask for it by name. Legal Aid SA states that if you are employed and applying for legal aid for a land matter, you must earn less than R13,625.00 per month after tax. The ordinary civil threshold is R8,200 per month, or R9,000 where the applicant is a member of a household. A land matter carries a threshold roughly 50–65 percent higher than an ordinary civil one, so someone refused on the general civil figure may still qualify on the land figure. Asset limits: movable not above R151,700, immovable not above R711,700 — check current figures, since the Means Test is revised against CPI (set from 1 April 2023, revised again from 1 April 2025). A REFUSAL IS NOT THE END: appeal first to the Provincial Executive, then to a second level — the Chief Legal Executive in civil matters — and at each stage you may write an additional motivation as to why the appeal must succeed. The National Office Executive's decision is final within Legal Aid SA, so the second appeal closes the internal route. TWO ELIGIBILITY STATEMENTS SIT TOGETHER ON THE RECORD: legal aid is available to anyone who lives in South Africa, not only citizens — but also that in civil cases legal aid is not available to non-citizens. A non-citizen with a civil land matter should establish which governs before relying on the broader statement. Asylum seekers are expressly covered under Chapters 3 and 4 of the Refugees Act 130 of 1998. CALIBRATE YOUR EXPECTATIONS: in 2021/22 it assisted 487,552 people — but only 40,143 new civil matters (11 percent) against 314,998 criminal, alongside advice to 132,411 people. Civil work is about one matter in nine, and advice volumes are growing faster than representation — the same pattern recorded here for Ireland. The Legal Aid Manual (version 7), the Legal Aid Regulations and Government Gazette 44936 of 6 August 2021 are published — bring the Manual's own words to your nearest Justice Centre, with ID and proof of income.

trackers.name: Municipal Money (Treasury)
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in South Africa.

trackers.name: Public Service Accountability Monitor (PSAM)
trackers.desc: Research, training and advocacy institute based at Rhodes University (active since 1999) that monitors public-resource management — budgeting, planning, expenditure and performance — across southern Africa. Here you can trace how public money is budgeted, spent and delivered across southern Africa, tracked through PSAM's social-accountability monitoring.

trackers.name: Master of the High Court Trust BO Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.name: Vulekamali
trackers.desc: South Africa's online budget data portal. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in South Africa.

trackers.name: Auditor-General South Africa
trackers.desc: Constitutional supreme audit institution. Here you can trace public-audit findings on waste, irregularity and misspending in South Africa.

trackers.name: CIPC
trackers.desc: South Africa's Companies and Intellectual Property Commission register. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Constitutional Court of South Africa
trackers.desc: Official Constitutional Court judgments. · Find here: the judgments of the Constitutional Court of South Africa.

trackers.name: eTenders Portal
trackers.desc: South Africa's national public-tender publication portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in South Africa, and for how much.

trackers.name: Financial Intelligence Centre (FIC)
trackers.desc: South Africa's financial intelligence unit, identifying proceeds of crime and combating money laundering and terrorist financing. Here you can trace how suspicious transactions are reported and money-laundering intelligence is produced in South Africa.

trackers.name: SAFLII
trackers.desc: Southern African Legal Information Institute: free judgments from South African and regional courts. · Find here: free South African and wider Southern-African case-law and legislation (SAFLII).

trackers.name: Special Investigating Unit (SIU)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of South Africa — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Statistics South Africa (Stats SA)
trackers.desc: South Africa's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in South Africa.
