Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Uruguay.

trackers.name: Fondo Uruguay Socioambiental — funds rights defence, not just conservation
trackers.desc: A FUND WHOSE OBJECT IS THE THING THIS MAP IS FOR. Its stated purpose is strengthening the defence of socio-environmental rights in Uruguay through financial and technical support to community groups and civil society initiatives. Note both halves of that framing: it says grupos comunitarios, not registered NGOs — so an unincorporated neighbourhood group is within the intended audience — and it says defence of rights, not conservation projects. Most funders in this map finance conservation activity and are uneasy about advocacy; naming rights defence as the object is unusual and worth using in how you frame an application. Technical support is offered alongside the money, which matters for a group applying for the first time.

trackers.name: Vigilancia Ambiental — a citizen platform wired into the ministry
trackers.desc: CIVIL SOCIETY ASKED TO BE PLUGGED INTO THE STATE, AND WAS — a model worth copying elsewhere. The Red Uruguaya de ONG Ambientalistas, an asociación civil de segundo grado grouping environmental organisations and professionals, built Plataforma de Vigilancia Ambiental, where any person can file an environmental report and georeference it, developed with support from AGESIC, the digital government agency. IT POINTS BOTH WAYS: the Ministry of Environment's own complaints service page links out to the Red's citizen monitoring platform, and the platform provides access back to the ministry's complaints system. The Red reports interconnection with several departmental intendencias including Salto, Soriano, Colonia and Rocha. Under an open government commitment, a single national environmental complaints system was to integrate the state's Sistema Único de Respuesta with Vigilancia Ambiental — and interconnection with the civil society reporting system was added at the express request of the Red. The commitment states the aim that civil society play a fundamental role in oversight and enforcement of environmental regulation. ALSO: Denuncias Ambientales UY, an app built by COENDU, carries reporting tools to report breaches to the police and to the ministry.

trackers.name: Mapeo de la Sociedad Civil — find the group already working on your place
trackers.desc: A CATEGORISED DIRECTORY OF URUGUAYAN ORGANISATIONS, including conservación ambiental and organisations of promoción de derechos e incidencia — the fastest way to find whether someone is already working on your site, and to find co-applicants for the funds that require partnership. WHAT THE LISTINGS SHOW IS ITSELF USEFUL: the entries include a balneario neighbours' association formed around a single beach with the slogan ‘recuperemos nuestra playa’, an interdisciplinary group of biologists, geographers, sociologists, writers and naturalists working on one sierra range, and a group focused on a triple-border area. Small single-place groups are the norm here, not the exception — worth knowing if you are wondering whether your own group is too small or too local to count as an organisation.

trackers.name: CEJIS — Centro de Estudios Jurídicos e Investigación Social
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Bolivian non-profit founded in 1978 that has accompanied the titling of 24 indigenous territories in the lowlands and helped write indigenous rights into the 2009 Constitution. It now works on agrarian recovery of ancestral land, territorial autonomies, and control and defence of territory, with offices in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Trinidad, Riberalta and La Paz. WHO IT SUITS: indigenous and peasant organisations of the Amazon, Chiquitanía and Chaco, and the Movimiento Sin Tierra — it works through representative organisations, not individual households. You CAN also use its territorial-monitoring guide and heat-spot reporting, which documents fire inside titled territories and is usable evidence when the state says nothing is happening.

trackers.name: COICA — Coordinadora de las Organizaciones Indígenas de la Cuenca Amazónica
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the basin-wide confederation of Amazonian Indigenous organisations, founded to act for 511 Indigenous peoples across the nine Amazon countries, around 66 of them in voluntary isolation or initial contact. It works through one national member organisation per country — in this country that is CIDOB, Confederación de Pueblos Indígenas de Bolivia — and its governing Council brings those presidents together. Its standing work areas are territorial rights and natural resources, human and sociocultural rights, and international law, and it has issued a formal declaration on the defence of Amazonian Indigenous defenders. USE IT: go to CIDOB first — COICA is the regional weight behind a national organisation, not a direct service. It is the route to carry a territorial case or a threat against leaders from your community into regional and international forums.

trackers.name: FUNDESNAP — Fundación para el Desarrollo del Sistema Nacional de Áreas Protegidas
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Bolivia's protected-areas fund, and the national operator of Conserva Aves — a Bezos Earth Fund-backed initiative led by American Bird Conservancy, Audubon, BirdLife, Birds Canada and RedLAC — running open public convocatorias with Asociación Armonía as technical partner. WHO IT SUITS: the calls co-finance proposals to CREATE OR EXPAND subnational protected areas, and the eligible categories are unusually wide — departmental, municipal, indígena originario campesina, and private natural-heritage reserves. So a community or municipality wanting to declare an area is squarely in scope, not just one already managing one. The site must fall inside the published priority areas, which are shown on a geographic viewer with the call documents. HOW IT DIFFERS: it funds the act of protecting a place, rather than the running costs of a place already protected.

trackers.name: Instituto Nacional de Estadística
trackers.desc: Bolivia's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Bolivia.

trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Instituto de Acceso a la Información Pública (IAIP)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority; El Salvador’s IAIP is the guarantor body under the LAIP (2011) — resolving access appeals, training officials and overseeing the Portal de Transparencia, El Salvador.

trackers.name: FIAES — Fondo de la Iniciativa para las Américas El Salvador
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a debt-for-nature fund created by Legislative Decree 585 of 1993 under the Enterprise for the Americas agreement with the United States and extended in 2001 by the Tropical Forest Conservation Act. It funds work in protected areas, the coastal-marine ecosystem and their buffer zones, prioritising by national poverty index as well as biodiversity. WHO IT SUITS: NGOs and ADESCOs — legally recognised community development associations — acting as organizaciones ejecutoras; individuals cannot apply. HOW IT DIFFERS: its council is chaired by the environment minister, so it is quasi-public money with published operating manuals you can read before applying.

trackers.name: UNES — Unidad Ecológica Salvadoreña
trackers.desc: El Salvador's principal environmental organisation working alongside community groups defending territory — indigenous communities in resistance in the Sensunapán-Banderas river basin, mangrove management on the coast, and the long fight over metallic mining. It accompanies and strengthens local committees rather than acting for them, and it articulates nationally with the Juzgado Ambiental, the human rights ombudsman (PDDH) and municipal governments, which is the practical value: it knows which of those doors to use. It has also run a strategic environmental litigation diploma with the Universidad de El Salvador. WHO IT SUITS: organised community committees and campesino and indigenous groups; UNES accompanies and trains, it does not litigate your case for you.

trackers.name: El Faro
trackers.desc: Salvadoran investigative newsroom reporting on corruption, organized crime and power.

trackers.name: El Salvador — Centro Nacional de Registros (CNR)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Registro de Comercio registers companies & commercial entities (consultable online) alongside property & IP registries, El Salvador. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in El Salvador, and for how much.

trackers.name: Corte de Cuentas de la República
trackers.desc: National — supreme audit institution of El Salvador. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in El Salvador.

trackers.name: Juzgados Ambientales — they order remedies; plan to fight for the compliance record
trackers.desc: SPECIALIST ENVIRONMENTAL COURTS THAT HAVE ORDERED REMEDIAL MEASURES AGAINST MINING DAMAGE — few countries in this map have one. The Juzgado Ambiental de San Miguel ordered in 2019 a series of measures to reduce the damage caused by mining at San Sebastián. BUT RECORD WHAT HAPPENED NEXT, BECAUSE IT DEFINES THE LIMIT: on 31 January the Ministry of Environment (MARN) declared as reserved information the compliance with those court-ordered measures, refusing to release it and stating the data would stay reserved until the case concludes in February 2030. So the order exists and the compliance record is sealed for years. If you win an order from an environmental court here, assume you will have to fight separately for the compliance information, and build the access-to-information request into the litigation plan rather than treating it as a follow-up. NOTE ALSO the cost-recovery provision from the 2017 law: MARN was required, at the cost of the responsible persons, to close old metallic mines and recover affected regions — worth checking whether an equivalent survives in the current law.

trackers.name: The 2017 mining ban — a model statute, and a lesson about durability
trackers.desc: THE STRONGEST CITIZEN-WON ENVIRONMENTAL LAW IN THIS MAP — AND IT WAS REPEALED. In March 2017 El Salvador became the first country in the world to prohibit metallic mining in all its forms, after a citizen campaign backed by environmental organisations, the Catholic Church and local communities. THE DRAFTING IS THE MODEL: art. 2 definitively prohibits exploration, extraction, exploitation and processing in any possible form, and bans toxic chemicals such as cyanide and mercury in any mining process; art. 3 reaches terrestrial, maritime and subterranean mining; and art. 9 declares the law special, of national interest, prevailing over any other that contradicts it — a supremacy clause inside an environmental statute is rare and is the feature to copy. Artisanal miners and güiriseros got 2 years to convert to another activity, so subsistence work was transitioned rather than criminalised. IT WAS REPEALED IN DECEMBER 2024 by the Ley General de Minería Metálica; the Dirección General de Energía, Hidrocarburos y Minas is now the principal authority, with MARN and the Autoridad Salvadoreña del Agua overseeing environmental and water conditions, and the reglamento due within one year. Opponents including UNES, the Church and the UCA warn the Río Lempa could receive toxic waste; a campaign for a million signatures to have the law declared unconstitutional is running, though its own leaders judge a favourable response very unlikely. THE LESSON FOR THE WHOLE MAP: a law won by citizens, carrying a supremacy clause, was still repealed by a later legislature. Durability comes from constitutional entrenchment or treaty status, not from statutory language however strong.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Fundación Moisés Bertoni — reservas bajo dominio privado
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: works with landowners who want part of their property declared a private nature reserve recognised by the Paraguayan state, handling the technical justification, the declaration and the subsequent management. Private conservation became a formal category with the SINASIP in 1994; the Reserva Natural del Bosque Mbaracayú was created by Ley 112/91 as Paraguay's first private reserve, and Reserva Tapytá was recognised by Decreto 5831 of 2005 as protected in perpetuity. USE IT: to convert threatened Atlantic Forest, Cerrado or Chaco land into a declared reserve — the technical dossier is the bottleneck, and this is who writes it.

trackers.name: Guyra Paraguay — Conservación de Sitios
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: has been acquiring land for conservation in perpetuity since 2001 and now runs four conservation units, including the Guyra Retã complex of over 6,000 hectares inside the Tekoha Guasu / San Rafael national park reserve, Cañada El Carmen created by Ley 2073/05, Campo Iris and Tobich in the Chaco. Its private reserve category runs under Resolución SEAM 200 of 2001 within Ley 352/94 on protected areas. Critically, it buys land for Indigenous territorial reclamation as well as for conservation: in 2008 it bought 548 hectares in socio-environmental condominium under a deed committing it to cede the land outright after ten years, and in 2023 it transferred that title to the Mbya Guaraní community of Tapy Kanguekua–Arroyo Morotí. USE IT: where an Atlantic Forest or Chaco property is for sale over ancestral territory and the community needs a buyer that will hand the title on.

trackers.name: FAPI — Federación por la Autodeterminación de los Pueblos Indígenas
trackers.desc: An autonomous third-level Indigenous federation of 13 member organisations across both regions of Paraguay, registered since 2007 and recognised as a legitimate interlocutor before the Paraguayan state. Its most directly usable output is tierrasindigenas.org.py, the interactive platform it coordinates with UCINY, CLIBCH, Tierraviva, GAT and others, which maps Indigenous lands and territories against forest-change and fire data — most Indigenous territory is absent from official maps, so the platform exists to make it visible and to drive territorial restitution. Its member associations also drafted the national free, prior and informed consent protocol over nine years. WHO IT SUITS: Indigenous communities in Paraguay working through their own association — FAPI acts through its 13 members, not for individual claimants.

trackers.name: Contraloría General de la República
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Paraguay, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: DNCP – Contrataciones Públicas
trackers.desc: Paraguay's procurement agency, an open-contracting pioneer publishing all state tenders. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Paraguay, and for how much.

trackers.name: Administrative Registry of Final Beneficiaries
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.name: Poder Judicial del Paraguay
trackers.desc: Official judiciary portal with jurisprudence and case search. · Find here: the portal, case search and rulings of Paraguay's Judiciary.

trackers.name: Paraguay — Dirección General de los Registros Públicos (DGRP)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the Judiciary’s DGRP maintains the Registro Público de Comercio & Registro de Personas Jurídicas with an online registral-information service, Paraguay. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Artículo 38 — any person, alone, may demand measures from the authorities
trackers.desc: THE BROADEST STANDING PROVISION IN THIS MAP. Article 38 gives toda persona the right, individually or collectively, to claim measures from the public authorities for the defence of the environment, the integrity of the habitat, public health, national cultural heritage and other interests that by their nature belong to the community and relate to quality of life and collective patrimony. FOUR THINGS TO USE: any person — no residence, ownership or membership requirement; individually — you do not need an organisation, unlike Mongolia where a missing charter clause defeated an NGO's standing; integrity of the habitat is named separately from the environment, so it is its own protected interest; and the right is to claim measures from the authorities, making it a demand on the state rather than only a defence against a private party. IT SITS BESIDE TWO OTHERS: article 40, the right to petition authorities ‘individual o colectivamente y sin requisitos especiales’ in writing, to which they must respond within the period set; and article 39, the right to just and adequate compensation for damage caused by the State.

trackers.name: Supervisión de cumplimiento — the stage after judgment, and it works
trackers.desc: PARAGUAY IS WHERE THE INTER-AMERICAN INDIGENOUS LAND DOCTRINE WAS BUILT — Yakye Axa (2005), Sawhoyamaxa (2006) and Xákmok Kásek (2010), in each of which the Court ordered restitution of ancestral lands and required the State to supply basic goods and services in the interim. The doctrine, with Moiwana and Saramaka: property under article 21 of the American Convention is not limited to the Western concept and covers communal property of traditional peoples, including natural resources on their lands as a means of maintaining religion, agriculture, hunting, fishing and their way of life. THE STAGE MOST CAMPAIGNS OVERLOOK: after judgment the Court opens supervisión de cumplimiento, and it is active — in Sawhoyamaxa it issued supervision resolutions in 2015 and 2019, recorded the 2014 law expropriating the community's traditional lands as a concrete advance, and in 2017 sent a delegation on an in situ visit to the Paraguayan Chaco. A judgment is not the end of the case; supervision is where implementation is argued. WHAT PRODUCED THE RESULT was the combination: court supervision, plus monitoring with periodic meetings with the community and with Congress, plus public campaigning. BE REALISTIC: Amnesty assessed the 2005 and 2006 violations as not addressed and therefore continuing, with state action insufficient — roughly two decades passed between expulsion and concrete restitution.

trackers.name: Ley 3001 art. 11 — roads, dams and pipelines must buy environmental certificates
trackers.desc: A LAW THAT MAKES DEVELOPERS PAY THOSE WHO CONSERVE. Ley 3001/2006 creates a certification mechanism for environmental services, with economic valuation attached. Article 2 defines environmental services as those generated by human activities of management, conservation and recovery of ecosystem functions — so it pays for activity, not merely for owning intact land, and recovery of a degraded ecosystem is inside the definition. ARTICLE 11 IS THE OPERATIVE PROVISION: works of high environmental impact — construction and maintenance of roads, hydraulic works, power plants, electricity transmission lines, pipelines, port works, high-emission industries, and discharge of urban and industrial effluents — must include within their investment scheme the compensation for environmental services through acquisition of Certificados de Servicios Ambientales, expressly without prejudice to other mitigation and conservation measures. So a road, dam, transmission line or pipeline must buy certificates, separately from and additional to its ordinary mitigation obligations. TWO QUESTIONS FOLLOW: if a listed project is near you, has it acquired certificates, and from whom? And if you hold or manage conserved land, you may be the counterparty rather than only the objector. Covered categories include protection of water resources and biodiversity; transactions are made once only.

trackers.name: CONADERNA's compliance list — a map of who is supposed to enforce it
trackers.desc: A PARLIAMENTARY COMMISSION URGING COMPLIANCE IS EVIDENCE THAT COMPLIANCE HAS BEEN PATCHY — and its address list is a map of who is meant to enforce Ley 3001. The Senate's Comisión Nacional de Defensa de los Recursos Naturales presented a Declaration urging full compliance in high-impact works, directed to MADES, the Ministry of Public Works (MOPC), INFONA, the binational hydroelectric entities Itaipú and Yacyretá, ANDE, the national public procurement directorate (DNCP), the Central Bank, the Banco Nacional de Fomento, private banks, PETROPAR, the Contraloría General, the Supreme Court and the Ministerio Público. Note the procurement authority and the banks are on that list — which means a financing or tender route exists alongside the environmental one. AND THE LAW IS STILL BEING STRENGTHENED: on 30 September 2025 the Cámara de Diputados gave media sanción to a bill making certificate acquisition obligatory for all public institutions and state enterprises for high-impact works, through tender processes. Check its current status — media sanción is one chamber only, not enactment. ALSO RECORDED, AS A PROPOSAL ONLY: a Fondo Ambiental was presented at a workshop run by Proyecto Paraguay Biodiversidad and opened by Itaipú Binacional and the environment minister. This entry does not assert that fund exists — verify before relying on it; the Ley 3001 obligation on Itaipú and Yacyretá is the firmer hook.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Zambia — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: ZambiaLII

trackers.name: CFMG recognition — the Chief can endorse the map, and rights start on filing
trackers.desc: TWO CONSENTS, TWO STAGES — conflating them wastes months. Under the Forests Act 2015 and SI No. 11 of 2018, a community forest management group is a group recognised by a Chief and local authority under section 29; the separate Community Forest Agreement with the Department is what actually secures user rights. WHAT REGULATION 6 REQUIRES: consent of the Chief through endorsement of the application or map signifying consent — note the alternative, the Chief may endorse the map rather than the form — plus a statement of intent in Form I showing a balance between forest protection and management, development, utilisation and forest enterprise development. A pure-protection statement does not match what the form asks; the balance is the requirement. Further information comes on Form II, rejection with reasons on Form III, and regulation 15 provides appeals. THE PROVISION MOST PEOPLE MISS: regulation 9 sets out rights and responsibilities upon submission of an application — rights attach when you file, not when you are approved — and regulation 16 provides assistance with control of restricted activities. A group that has filed is not powerless while it waits.

trackers.name: The Agreement gives exclusive use — unlike Cambodia's CPAs
trackers.desc: WHAT THE COMMUNITY FOREST AGREEMENT ACTUALLY DELIVERS. The Director may transfer authority to control access, use and management of a designated forest area after consulting the Chief and local authority; the group gains the right to issue community permits and collect revenue for products and uses in the management plan; and the area is for the exclusive use of the local community represented by the group. THAT LAST POINT IS THE DIFFERENCE THAT MATTERS — compare Cambodia, where Community Protected Area communities hold management rights but not exclusion rights. Zambia grants exclusive use, which is the difference between managing a forest and being able to keep others out of it. COVERED RIGHTS include medicinal herbs, honey, grass and grazing, produce for community-based industries, eco-tourism and recreation, plantations, and timber or fuel wood; rights may also be assigned. WHERE IT APPLIES: land under customary authority as well as Local and National Forests, plus open areas and Game Management Areas. A PRESUMPTION WORTH QUOTING: major forest produce on State Land and customary areas shall be conserved for the use and benefit of the local community in those areas, subject to stated exceptions. THE SCALE OF THE THREAT: Zambian forests are disappearing at 275,000 hectares per annum.

trackers.name: ZEMA call for comments — the appeal window is reported as ten days, the shortest found anywhere in this region, and the route is disputed
trackers.desc: TEN DAYS. IF THAT IS RIGHT — AND IT IS THE FIGURE IN THE STANDARD REGIONAL REFERENCE — IT IS THE TIGHTEST OBJECTION CLOCK IN AFRICA, AND MOST PEOPLE WILL MISS IT WHILE DECIDING WHO TO WRITE TO. An aggrieved party appeals a decision of the environment agency in writing to the Minister responsible for the environment within ten days of receiving the decision, and the Minister should decide within fourteen days; from there the route runs to the High Court. BUT THE ROUTE ITSELF IS CONTESTED: the assessment regulations still in force date from 1997 and send the appeal straight to the Minister, while the Environmental Management Act of 2011 provides for review and appeal first to the Agency's own Board and only then to the Minister. Revised regulations were prepared and sent for approval years ago and had not been enacted when this was written. The safe course is to lodge in writing within ten days, address it to the Board, copy the Minister, and say in the letter that you are proceeding under both routes — cheaper than being told you used the wrong one after the time has run. WHERE TO WATCH FOR THE TRIGGER: the Agency publishes an EIA call-for-comments section and a downloadable repository of environmental impact statements, so the document you need to object to is usually obtainable without a request; it also offers an SMS subscription for updates, which matters where data is expensive. The Act separately obliges the Agency to maintain a central environmental information system and an environmental information registry open to public viewing. Plot 6975, corner of Church and Suez Roads, Lusaka; +260 211 254023 or 254059; info@zema.org.zm; open 08:00 to 17:00 on weekdays. CAVEATS: the ten-day and fourteen-day figures come from a development-bank regional handbook and an assessment-commission country profile, not from the Agency's own pages, which publish no appeal deadline at all — treat ten days as the working assumption and confirm at the counter. This URL is the call-for-comments section as listed in the Agency's own site navigation; the page verified for this entry was its parent.

trackers.name: Zambia Land Alliance — paralegal officers in district branches across all ten provinces, and they have got grabbed land returned
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a network of Zambian NGOs on land rights that works through a national secretariat in Lusaka and district branches across all ten provinces, plus District Land Alliances that are separate registered organisations in their own right — so the first contact is usually local, not national. WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE IN PRACTICE, from a documented case: a family in Solwezi whose land had been taken by a church was advised by a ZLA paralegal officer to start with the Area Development Committee, given a referral letter, and when the other side refused to attend the convened meeting, advised to bring civil proceedings — which they won, with an order to vacate. That is the whole sequence a household needs and cannot usually find: who to go to first, the letter that makes them act, and when to stop negotiating and sue. It also runs Community Land Advocacy Committees with traditional leaders in districts including Kafue, Mkushi, Serenje and Kalumbila, and uses participatory land use planning to turn communities into land use negotiators before an investor arrives. District alliances in the Copperbelt describe strengthened paralegal networks reaching thousands of people, funded through the Zambian Governance Foundation, OSISA and Global Greengrants. WHO IT SUITS: rural and peri-urban households and communities facing land grabbing, mining displacement or investor allocations on customary land — particularly women, whose land rights are an explicit focus. Plot 126E Kudu Road, Kabulonga, Lusaka. CAVEATS: ZLA is an advocacy network with paralegals, not a law firm — it refers and advises rather than litigating for you; the national website is thin and partly filled with unrelated template text, so the district alliances are the more reliable point of contact; and no intake criteria or fee information was published.

trackers.name: Zambia's district land alliances — customary land holding certificates issued with the chiefs, and the argument about whether they help
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Chipata and Petauke District Land Alliances, Zambian civil society organisations documenting the land rights of households in Eastern Province. Since 2014 the Chipata alliance has partnered with six customary chiefs to run low-cost participatory documentation using mobile mapping, working through the chiefs, their advisors, village headpersons and each household, and building Village Land Committees that carry the process locally. WHY THIS EXISTS AT ALL: Zambia's government recognises customary tenure but has not legislated to secure it — roughly 14.5 million people rely on undocumented customary land while only about 140,000 leasehold titles exist. Households want documentation to prevent arbitrary takings and to secure fair compensation if land is converted by government, headpersons or chiefs. WHAT THE CERTIFICATE IS AND IS NOT, which is the most important paragraph here: it carries a georeferenced map of the holding plus the identity of the right holder, any joint holders, and any “persons of interest” attached to the parcel — and the issuers deliberately never call it a land title. Conditions printed on the certificate, in English and the local language, state that it does not constitute consent to convert customary land to leasehold. That distinction is the protection: conversion to leasehold is how customary land is lost. THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT: researchers studying the Petauke certificates issued from 2010 concluded, from interviews with farmers, chiefs and the alliance, that the certificates reinforced rather than reversed the commodification of land and inequality of access. Communities have also worried that documentation is a precursor to taxation. Weigh that before starting. WHO IT SUITS: households and villages on customary land in Eastern Province wanting their holding mapped and recorded before someone else claims it. CAVEATS: NEITHER ALLIANCE HAS A VERIFIED SITE OF ITS OWN — this entry points at the tenure programme record that documents them; approach through Zambia Land Alliance, whose entry is also in this file and which pilots chief-issued certificates nationally. The work has been donor-funded and pilot-scale, chiefdom boundaries rest on an out-of-date 1958 map, and the certificate's legal weight is untested.

trackers.name: Zambia's mining-pollution coalitions and the foreign-court route — how Chingola and Kabwe residents got past a company that ignored them at home
trackers.desc: WHAT WORKED, AND WHO TO FIND: Zambian mining-affected communities have repeatedly failed to get remedy at home and succeeded by suing the foreign PARENT company in ITS OWN courts. 1,826 residents of Chingola, whose water and farmland were contaminated by run-off from a copper mine from 2004, won the right to bring their case in the United Kingdom against the parent of the mine's operator — and that case produced compensation. Separately, a class action was filed in South Africa on behalf of an estimated 140,000 women and children in Kabwe alleging lead poisoning from a mine within a British group from 1925 to 1974, closed in 1994 and never cleaned up — an estimated 6.4 million tonnes of lead-bearing waste, soil in places above 3,000 mg/kg against a common regulatory limit of 400. THE ORGANISATIONS AROUND IT: a national development organisation trained Shimulala residents in Chingola on their rights and put community activists on local radio; the Alliance for Lead-Free Kabwe coalesces Zambian and international groups pressing for a clean-up plan; the Zambia Environmental Justice Coalition responded to a later acid spill by demanding the government RENEGOTIATE ALL COMPENSATION AGREEMENTS with the full involvement of affected communities; and a “Zambia's Sacrifice Zone” campaign of young activists, journalists and NGOs uses storytelling and radio to carry community voices. After one spill, 47 households threatened suit in the Lusaka High Court unless compensation was paid. ASK EARLY WHO THE PARENT COMPANY IS AND WHERE IT IS INCORPORATED — that answer decides whether a foreign court is open to you. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian communities living with mine pollution, contaminated water or lead waste, and anyone facing a subsidiary of a foreign-listed mining group. CAVEATS: NO SINGLE VERIFIED SITE EXISTS FOR THESE COALITIONS — this entry points at the international documentation record that names them; foreign litigation took Chingola thirteen years, activists report promised compensation unpaid and weak enforcement, and this route needs foreign counsel. For paralegals, Zambia Land Alliance; for EIA comment, the ZEMA entry.

trackers.name: Mize Community Conservancy, Nyawa Chiefdom — 585 km² registered under the Wildlife Act in the name of the community itself
trackers.desc: WHAT TO REGISTER, AND THE PRECEDENT THAT SHOWS IT CAN BE DONE: the Mize Community Conservancy (MiCC) in the Nyawa Chiefdom, Kazungula District, Southern Province — successfully REGISTERED UNDER ZAMBIA'S WILDLIFE ACT, covering 585 km², in a degraded wildlife corridor connecting Kafue National Park to the neighbouring transfrontier protected areas. A community conservancy in this model is a legally recognised, geographically defined area formed by communities that have united to manage and benefit from wildlife and other natural resources — which is the difference between using land at someone's discretion and holding a registered area in your own name. WHAT THE REGISTRATION TOOK, because the sequence is the useful part: a review of 354 legal texts on wildlife and related sectors, published on a public legal hub, established the basis; a customary law analysis was then run across the chiefdom — 57 participants from 20 villages, including senior headmen, women and youth; and ten new community resource board members, three of them women, were elected, with governance strengthened through exchange visits and training. Legal groundwork, then customary mapping, then an elected board — in that order. The chiefdom encompasses a reported 500 villages. Alongside registration, the work covers habitat and game management, human-wildlife conflict, and livelihoods through fish farming, beekeeping and livestock. Sister conservancies exist at Simalaha in Zambia and Mucheni in Zimbabwe under the same regional model, so there are neighbours who have done it. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian chiefdoms and villages that want a registered conservancy rather than an informal arrangement, especially in wildlife corridors under pressure. CAVEATS: THE CONSERVANCY HAS NO SITE OF ITS OWN — this entry points at the programme record documenting the registration, and the work was donor-funded through a time-limited international programme, so ask what survives its end. Registration is under the WILDLIFE Act and confers management rights over wildlife and resources; it is NOT a land title, and Zambia's customary land questions remain — see the district land alliances entry for certificates, and Zambia Land Alliance for paralegals.

trackers.name: Zambia Legal Aid Board — land disputes are the FIRST case type it lists, and applications are processed in 48 hours
trackers.desc: WHERE TO APPLY: the Legal Aid Board of Zambia, a statutory body operating under the Legal Aid Act No. 1 of 2021, which repealed and replaced the 1967 Act and now also provides for the regulation of LAW CLINICS and the registration of practitioners, legal assistants, PARALEGALS and legal aid service providers. WHY IT LEADS THIS ENTRY: the Board's own published list of case types it deals with BEGINS with “land dispute and related issues”, followed by compensation demands, conveyancing, change of ownership, breach of contract, probate, property settlement and drafting assistance. A legal aid body that names land first is unusual, and it means you do not have to argue that your case belongs. WHAT IT COSTS AND HOW LONG IT TAKES: legal aid is provided FREE OF CHARGE, though after a MEANS TEST a modest contribution may be requested case by case; APPLICATIONS ARE PROCESSED WITHIN 48 HOURS, and you are told if more time is needed — up to 30 days. A published turnaround is rare enough in this file to be worth citing back at them if you are left waiting. You may request a particular lawyer, but assignment depends on availability, expertise and caseload. SCALE AND REACH: in one year the Board received 12,071 applications, granting legal aid — assistance or representation — in 6,397 and giving information and advice to the remaining 5,674; it runs six Legal Services Units at Subordinate Court level across three provinces, and supervises ten legal desks in correctional facilities and police stations staffed by paralegals from civil society organisations. In civil cases it may also provide mediation. Alongside it, the National Legal Aid Clinic for Women (NLACW), established 1990 under the Law Association of Zambia, offers representation, mobile legal clinics and community-level paralegal desks; Plot 110a/150 Musonda Ngosa Road, Villa Elizabetha, Lusaka, +260 211 220595. WHO IT SUITS: Zambians with a land dispute, compensation claim or property matter who cannot pay a lawyer; women and children through NLACW. CAVEATS: A STATE BOARD with a means test, a nominal consultation contribution and a criminal-heavy caseload; it will not act against government policy for you. For paralegals in ten provinces, Zambia's ZLA entry; for EIA comment, ZEMA; for the foreign parent-company route, the mining-pollution entry.

trackers.name: ZCCN, Green Living Movement, WECSZ and CBE — a member-governed network that sits on the government's climate technical committee, Copperbelt paralegals and radio, and the group that got 67 companies to commit on the Kafue
trackers.desc: THE NETWORK WITH A SEAT, AND THE ORGANISATIONS WITH PARALEGALS: the ZAMBIA CLIMATE CHANGE NETWORK (ZCCN, zccnzambia.org), A MEMBERSHIP-BASED ORGANISATION EXISTING AS A CIVIL SOCIETY NATIONAL PLATFORM on climate and environmental justice, at Mulungushi International Conference Centre, Annex Building Rooms 18 and 20, Great East Road, LUSAKA. ITS GOVERNANCE AND ITS SEAT ARE BOTH THE POINT: THE GENERAL MEMBERSHIP FORMS THE FOUNDATION OF THE NETWORK — CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS, INDIVIDUALS AND OTHER STAKEHOLDERS — THE BOARD IS ELECTED BY THE MEMBERS, AND AT NATIONAL LEVEL THE NETWORK HAS BEEN IDENTIFIED BY THE GOVERNMENT AS AN IMPORTANT STAKEHOLDER WITHIN THE CORE STRUCTURE OF CLIMATE CHANGE POLICY PROCESSES, SITTING ON THE TECHNICAL COMMITTEE, THE THIRD HIGHEST LEVEL. A member-elected network holding a seat on a government technical committee is a route from a village meeting into national policy — and ZCCN explicitly invites LOCAL COMMUNITY GROUPS and youth leaders to join, not only registered NGOs. Its named thematic areas include LAND USE AND MANAGEMENT. GREEN LIVING MOVEMENT (GLM), A ZAMBIAN NGO FOUNDED IN 2000 by Zambian environmental and social development enthusiasts, works natural resource management through community participation — and, the operative detail, EXTENDS ITS PRESENCE TO MISAKA IN KITWE, FISENGE IN LUANSHYA, CHIEFTAINESS LESA IN MPONGWE AND THE BROADER COPPERBELT PROVINCE THROUGH RADIO PROGRAMMES AND THE PROVISION OF PARALEGAL SERVICES. Paralegal services delivered alongside radio across named chiefdoms is the combination that reaches people who cannot travel to Lusaka. Ask GLM whether your chiefdom is covered — and its guiding motto is that unless you enter the den you cannot get the cubs. THE WILDLIFE AND ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION SOCIETY OF ZAMBIA (WECSZ), ESTABLISHED 1953, a non-profit running COMMUNITY-BASED CONSERVATION INITIATIVES IN IMPORTANT AREAS AND ZAMBIA'S SOLE NATIONWIDE ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION PROGRAMME. Seventy years and the only national education programme means WECSZ has a presence in schools everywhere — the cheapest way to reach a district is often through its teachers. AND THE ONE WITH A DOCUMENTED WIN: CITIZENS FOR A BETTER ENVIRONMENT (CBE), STARTED 1997, at 67 Afcom House, KITWE, with a named founder who is A MINING ENGINEER AND ENVIRONMENTAL AUDITOR who helped write the 1996 Zambian Republican Constitution and sits on several national environmental committees. CBE PROMOTES THE SOCIAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS OF LOCAL COMMUNITIES AFFECTED BY THE MALPRACTICE OF MULTINATIONAL MINING COMPANIES — AND IN 2000, WITH THE ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL OF ZAMBIA, IT SECURED COMMITMENTS BY 67 COMPANIES SURROUNDING THE KAFUE RIVER TO OPERATE ACCORDING TO THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AND POLLUTION CONTROL ACT. Sixty-seven companies signing up to obey the existing law is a settlement a coalition can demand again. And an executive director who is a qualified environmental auditor can read a mine's own monitoring returns — that is rarer and more useful than a campaigner. Its recorded field method is direct: meeting aggrieved farmers whose stream was polluted by a named mine, then inspecting the works done to stop the tailings discharge. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian communities on the Copperbelt, near a mine, or seeking a national platform. CAVEATS: SOME OF THIS RECORD IS HISTORICAL — confirm current activity and contacts. For paralegal officers in district offices, Zambia's Zambia Land Alliance entry; for customary land holders, the district land alliances entry; for the foreign-court route against a parent company, the mining-pollution coalitions entry; for a 585 km2 community conservancy, the Mize entry.

trackers.name: The Zambia Alliance for Agroecology and Biodiversity and its members — Namfumu Conservation Trust, Caritas Zambia and an organic farm that trains converts — plus the documented warning about community resource boards
trackers.desc: THE ALLIANCE A FARMING COMMUNITY CAN JOIN: the ZAMBIA ALLIANCE FOR AGROECOLOGY AND BIODIVERSITY (zambianagroecology.org) PUBLISHES ITS MEMBERSHIP WITH A DESCRIPTION OF EACH ORGANISATION — including NAMFUMU CONSERVATION TRUST, WHICH ENDEAVOURS TO PROMOTE STRONG ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION PARTNERSHIPS TO CONTRIBUTE TO THE MITIGATION OF CLIMATE CHANGE THROUGH HOLISTIC SUSTAINABLE RURAL DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION IN ZAMBIA AND SOUTHERN AFRICA, and which states that it renders its services WITH SKILL, COMPASSION AND RESPECT FOR HUMAN DIGNITY, REGARDLESS OF RACE, CREED OR RELIGIOUS AFFILIATION. A conservation TRUST is a body that can hold assets and outlive its founders — and one that publishes a non-discrimination commitment is one a mixed community can join without a fight about whose it is. CARITAS ZAMBIA, whose agriculture and alternative livelihood programmes focus on CAPACITY BUILDING FOR CROP-DEPENDENT COMMUNITIES IN SMALL LIVESTOCK PRODUCTION, AND ON INITIATIVES TO EMPOWER COMMUNITY MEMBERS TO ENGAGE IN OTHER ECONOMIC ACTIVITIES BESIDES FARMING — including PRODUCTION OF CASH CROPS, TRAINING INITIATIVES FOR FARMERS, AND HARVESTING AND SALE OF FOREST PRODUCTS. Harvesting AND SALE of forest products, run by a church organisation with a national reach, is the income side of keeping a forest standing. If your community holds forest it is being pressed to clear, that is who to ask about the market. AND THE TRAINING DOOR: a named ECOLOGICAL ORGANIC FARM in the alliance PRACTISES MIXED ORGANIC AGRICULTURE AIMED AT MAKING ACCESSIBLE AND AFFORDABLE ORGANIC FOOD, PRODUCES AND SELLS THROUGH VARIOUS OUTLETS, AND OFFERS TRAINING FOR THOSE WANTING TO CONVERT TO ORGANICS OR LEARN HOW TO FARM — with production systems adhering to principles of HEALTH FOR ALL, HARNESSING THE ECOSYSTEM AND FAIRNESS TO EVERYTHING AND EVERYONE. A working farm that both sells and teaches is the practical alternative to offer a household being told the only way to earn more is to clear more. Send someone to the training before you argue the case. THE ALLIANCE'S OWN FRAMING: like many other countries, ZAMBIA HAS NOT BEEN SPARED ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION AND THE EFFECTS OF THE CLIMATE CRISIS, AND ZAMBIAN COMMUNITIES FACE A NUMBER OF ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS. AND THE WARNING THIS FILE OWES ANY COMMUNITY BEING OFFERED A RESOURCE BOARD, FROM A PUBLISHED TWO-COUNTRY STUDY OF COMMUNITIES BESIDE TWO NAMED NATIONAL PARKS: THE SURVEY REVEALED A GENERAL INCONGRUENCE BETWEEN COMMUNITY PERCEPTIONS AND EXPECTATIONS OF THE PURPOSE AND ROLES OF THE COMMUNITY RESOURCE BOARDS AND THOSE OF THE RESPECTIVE WILDLIFE AUTHORITIES — AND AFTER TWO DECADES OF IMPLEMENTATION THERE APPEARS TO BE SIGNIFICANT CONFUSION AMONG COMMUNITIES REGARDING CBNRM THAT SEEMS TO TRANSLATE INTO UNFULFILLED EXPECTATIONS AND FRUSTRATIONS, HIGHLIGHTING INADEQUACIES IN IMPLEMENTATION WITH REGARD TO OUTREACH AND INCLUSION. Twenty years in, communities and wildlife authorities still did not agree on what the resource board was FOR. Before you constitute one, write down what your community expects it to do and what revenue it expects to receive, get the authority to write down the same, and compare the two documents. The incongruence is the documented failure mode — catch it at the start, not at year twenty. A separate study of a named game management area records that CBNRM WAS INSTITUTIONALISED IN THE ZAMBIAN WILDLIFE ACT IN 1998 AND IS PART OF THE CONSERVATION STRATEGY FOR PROTECTED AREAS INCLUDING GAME MANAGEMENT AREAS. It is in the Act. Whatever its record, the legal footing exists — the problem this research names is delivery, not authority. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian farming communities, forest-holding villages, and anyone being offered a community resource board. CAVEATS: THE CBNRM RECORD IS MIXED AND THIS FILE SAYS SO PLAINLY. For a 585 km2 community conservancy registered in a chiefdom, Zambia's Mize entry; for a network with a seat on the government's climate technical committee and Copperbelt paralegals, the ZCCN and Green Living Movement entry; for paralegal officers in district offices, Zambia Land Alliance; for the foreign-court route against a parent company, the mining-pollution coalitions entry.

trackers.name: Kasempa Conservation Foundation's 30 community forest scouts over 160,000 hectares outside Kafue, and Rainforest Trust — a funder that pays for private reserves, community forests and indigenous land titling, with its eligibility rule printed
trackers.desc: THIRTY SCOUTS, AND A FUNDER THAT WILL PAY FOR TITLE — the Zambian example first, because every number is on the record: A STRATEGIC ALLOCATION OF A USD 5 MILLION GLOBAL ENVIRONMENT FACILITY GRANT EMPOWERED LOCAL COMMUNITIES TO TAKE THE LEAD IN CONSERVATION — AND THROUGH THE KASEMPA CONSERVATION FOUNDATION, 30 COMMUNITY FOREST SCOUTS WERE TRAINED AND DEPLOYED, WHO HAVE SUCCESSFULLY CURBED POACHING AND ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES IN NEARLY 160,000 HECTARES OUTSIDE KAFUE NATIONAL PARK — WITH THE RETURN OF ELEPHANTS TO THE AREA AFTER DECADES OF ABSENCE. Three things to take. The vehicle is a community FOUNDATION with a place name on it, not a project office. The scouts are thirty local people on the payroll. And the ground is OUTSIDE the national park — which is where most of the communities in this file actually live. A hundred and sixty thousand hectares of unprotected land held by thirty people from the area is the ratio to quote when somebody says community protection cannot cover a large landscape. And the elephants returning after decades is the outcome a funder will pay for. If your area once had something it no longer has, that absence is the case — name the species and the decade it left. THE APPROACH BEHIND IT, IN THE FUNDER'S OWN WORDS: THE SOLUTION LIES NOT IN PROTECTING NATURE FROM PEOPLE, BUT IN EMPOWERING COMMUNITIES TO BE THE STEWARDS OF THEIR LAND — NOTING THAT INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND LOCAL COMMUNITIES COLLECTIVELY MANAGE AT LEAST A QUARTER OF THE WORLD'S LANDS, OFTEN ACHIEVING GREATER CONSERVATION RESULTS THAN GOVERNMENT-PROTECTED AREAS. Often achieving greater results than government-protected areas, said by a large international conservation organisation. That sentence, from that source, is worth more in a ministry meeting than the same claim from a village — cite who said it. THE FUNDER THAT PAYS FOR LAND AND PUBLISHES ITS CATEGORIES: RAINFOREST TRUST PARTNERS WITH LOCAL CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS TO CREATE NEW PROTECTED AREAS, AND ITS FOUR PROTECTED-AREA TYPES ARE PRINTED — PRIVATE RESERVES, BEING PARCELS OF LAND SECURED FOR CONSERVATION AND MAINTAINED BY ITS PARTNERS IN PERPETUITY; NATIONAL PARKS, RECOGNISED AND PROTECTED BY THE NATIONAL GOVERNMENT WITH SUPPORT FROM ITS PARTNERS; COMMUNITY FORESTS, IN WHICH LOCAL PEOPLE ARE DIRECTLY INVOLVED AS CRITICAL STAKEHOLDERS IN THE MANAGEMENT OF THE PROTECTED LAND AND WORK WITH PARTNERS AND GOVERNMENT TO MAKE LAND-USE DECISIONS; AND INDIGENOUS LAND TITLING, IN WHICH INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES GAIN LEGAL RIGHTS TO THEIR LAND WITH THE HELP OF PARTNERS AND GOVERNMENT. INDIGENOUS LAND TITLING is a funded category. A donor that will pay for a community to obtain legal rights to its own land is the single most on-brief thing in this file, and it is listed as one of four standard project types rather than an exception. If titling is what your community needs, that is the word to use in the application. THE ELIGIBILITY RULE, WHICH IS SHORT: THE APPLICANT ORGANISATION MUST BE AUTHORISED TO WORK WITHIN THE COUNTRY OF THE PROPOSED PROJECT, WITH LEGAL DOCUMENTATION REQUIRED AT A LATER STAGE, AND THE PROPOSED PROJECT MUST BE BASED IN THE SUBTROPICS OR TROPICS. IT ALSO OFFERS RAPID FEASIBILITY AWARDS, WHICH CAN BEGIN SOON AFTER APPROVAL. Two conditions only, and the documentation comes later. That is a low bar compared with most of the funders in this file — and a RAPID FEASIBILITY AWARD is money to find out whether a purchase is possible before you commit to raising the price. Ask for that first. THE SMALLER DOOR, WITH A CEILING: A SMALL GRANTS PROGRAMME RUN BY AN ALBERTINE RIFT CONSERVATION SOCIETY INVITES CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS TO SUBMIT PROJECT PROPOSALS WITH BUDGETS NOT EXCEEDING USD 5,000, UNDER SIX NAMED AREAS — NATURE BASED COMMUNITY ENTERPRISES; ECOSYSTEM SERVICES AND SUSTAINABLE BENEFITS; POLICY ANALYSIS AND ADVOCACY; CLIMATE CHANGE AND COMMUNITY ADAPTATION; NATURAL RESOURCES MANAGEMENT GOVERNANCE; AND BIODIVERSITY THREAT MITIGATION. Five thousand dollars is a size a village committee can absorb and account for, and POLICY ANALYSIS AND ADVOCACY is one of the six eligible areas — which means a grant can pay for the objection itself, not only for planting. Small ceilings usually mean simpler forms; ask for the application pack. AND THE LARGEST COMMUNITY GRANT SOURCE, FOR SCALE: an established small grants programme operating in 129 COUNTRIES HAS SUPPORTED OVER 25,000 COMMUNITY-BASED PROJECTS, with SPECIAL CONSIDERATION FOR INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, WOMEN, YOUTH AND PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES, and has CONCENTRATED ITS EFFORTS ON PROTECTED AREAS AND INDIGENOUS AND COMMUNITY CONSERVED AREAS. Twenty-five thousand community projects funded. Whatever your community is proposing, somebody has been funded to do something like it — ask the national coordinator for examples from your own country before you draft. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian communities outside Kafue, and any African organisation seeking money to buy land, title it, or run a small project. CAVEATS: RAINFOREST TRUST FUNDS PARTNER ORGANISATIONS, so you need a registered local partner; and this file's own record includes a case where conservation land purchase preceded evictions — read the World Land Trust entry's caution alongside this one. For a 585 km2 community conservancy registered in a chiefdom, Zambia's Mize entry; for the agroecology alliance and the honest CBNRM warning, the Zambia Alliance entry; for paralegal officers in district offices, Zambia Land Alliance.

trackers.name: The five funders that put up the first risk capital for community funds, the guarantee facility behind them, the alliance that will NOT fund construction, and the land-sharing arrangement that leaves the owner his value
trackers.desc: LAND SHARING, NOT LAND LOSING — placement note first: THESE ARE INTERNATIONAL FUNDERS, FILED UNDER ZAMBIA BECAUSE IT IS ONE OF THE NINE AFRICAN COUNTRIES WHOSE NATIONAL COMMUNITY FUND THIS MONEY CAPITALISES. THE ARRANGEMENT TO LEARN FIRST: LOW-INCOME COMMUNITIES HAVE NEGOTIATED LAND SHARING OR LAND LEASING ARRANGEMENTS WITH LOCAL AUTHORITIES AND PRIVATE LANDOWNERS, AND THEN ACCESSED LOW-COST HOUSING LOANS AND INFRASTRUCTURE SUBSIDIES TO UPGRADE THEIR NEIGHBOURHOODS — THE AIM BEING TO HELP LANDOWNERS CAPTURE THE COMMERCIAL VALUE OF THEIR LAND WHILE REDUCING POVERTY AND VULNERABILITY. Land sharing means the occupants keep part of the site and the owner develops the rest, so the owner gets his value and nobody is evicted. This file is full of cases framed as all-or-nothing — the community leaves or the project stops. Land sharing is the third answer, and it has been negotiated in practice with both councils and private owners. If you are being told there are only two outcomes, that is the arrangement to put on the table. WHO PUT UP THE FIRST MONEY, NAMED: FIVE ORGANISATIONS — MISEREOR, CORDAID, HOMELESS INTERNATIONAL, SELAVIP AND A RAUSING TRUST — PROVIDED THE INITIAL RISK CAPITAL TO ENABLE FEDERATIONS TO ACCESS LOANS FOR PROJECTS THAT WOULD OTHERWISE NOT HAVE BEEN POSSIBLE. RISK CAPITAL is the specific thing to ask for. Not a project grant — the first money that makes a lender willing to lend, because somebody else is carrying the first loss. A community fund that cannot borrow usually lacks that layer, not the borrowers. Five named organisations have supplied it before. AND THE LIMIT THE SECTOR STATES ABOUT ITSELF, WHICH IS WORTH TRUSTING: NORTHERN NGOs HAVE LIMITS ON THE QUANTUM OF FUNDING THEY CAN PROVIDE AND CANNOT HOPE TO COME NEAR TO PROVIDING THE LEVELS NEEDED TO CATALYSE LARGE SCALE UPGRADING ON A WIDE GEOGRAPHIC BASIS — HENCE THE NEED TO ATTRACT PUBLIC SECTOR AND BI-LATERAL FUNDING, NOT ONLY TO INCREASE THE SIZE OF THE FUNDS BUT ALSO TO ENSURE A WIDER LOCAL ENGAGEMENT WITH THE OBJECTIVES. Foreign charity cannot fund this at scale and says so. The scale money is public and bilateral — which means the ministry and the aid agency in your own country are the target, and the foreign NGO grant is the thing that proves the model works so they will fund it. Plan the sequence in that order. THE GUARANTEE LAYER, WHICH ALMOST NOTHING ELSE IN THIS FILE MENTIONS: A FACILITY INITIATED BY A PRIVATE INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT GROUP — COMPRISING SEVERAL EUROPEAN BILATERAL AID AGENCIES AND A DEVELOPMENT BANK — HAS BEGUN TO OFFER GUARANTEES. A guarantee is not money; it is somebody standing behind your fund so a commercial bank will lend to it. For a community fund that has savings and a track record but no collateral, that is the missing piece — ask your national fund whether it has ever sought one. THE LIMIT THAT SAVES A WASTED APPLICATION: CITIES ALLIANCE PROVIDES TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE GRANTS AND SEEKS TO ENHANCE KNOWLEDGE SHARING AND DONOR CO-ORDINATION — IT DOES NOT DIRECTLY FUND SLUM UPGRADING CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS. Written down plainly, so nobody wastes months applying for building money from a body that funds studies. Ask that question of every funder in this file before you draft: does it pay for construction, or only for advice? THE MODEL THAT LEVERAGES THE STATE: COMMUNITIES TYPICALLY COMBINE THEIR SAVINGS IN CITY DEVELOPMENT FUNDS, WHICH ALLOW THEM TO LEVERAGE PUBLIC FINANCE FROM NATIONAL AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS, OR EVEN FROM INTERNATIONAL DONORS — ALLOWING COMMUNITIES TO TAKE ON MUCH LARGER DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS. A CITY development fund rather than a national one. The city is the level where land is actually allocated, and a fund at that level can match municipal money. If your country's fund is national and remote, a city fund is the intermediate structure to ask for. AND THE TECHNICAL SUPPORT THAT COMES WITH IT: ARCHITECTS AND URBAN PLANNERS WHO HELP THE URBAN POOR TO MAP THEIR LIVING CONDITIONS AND DRAW UP COMPREHENSIVE SITE PLANS FOR UPGRADING OR RELOCATION PROJECTS. A site plan drawn by an architect, held by the community, before the municipality produces its own. Whoever arrives with the plan sets the terms of the discussion — and these networks supply the professionals to draw it. WHO IT SUITS: Zambian and other African community funds seeking risk capital or guarantees, and any settlement being told it must move or stay. CAVEATS: THESE ARE FUNDERS OF FUNDS AND FEDERATIONS, not of individual communities — you reach them through a national affiliate, and one of them explicitly does not pay for building. For capital for national community funds in nine African countries, Zimbabwe's Urban Poor Fund International entry; for the network whose board is majority slum dwellers, South Africa's SDI entry; for the agroecology alliance and the honest CBNRM warning, the Zambia Alliance entry; for paralegal officers in district offices, Zambia Land Alliance.

trackers.name: 176 Zambian community members won the right to a pollution trial — and the mining company appealed to the Supreme Court to avoid it; plus what SALC supplies to local lawyers, in twelve named countries, with its Johannesburg address and phone
trackers.desc: THE COMPANY WENT TO THE SUPREME COURT TO AVOID A TRIAL — and that sentence tells you more about how these cases are fought than any manual: A MINING COMPANY TOOK A ZAMBIAN POLLUTION CASE TO THE SUPREME COURT IN A BID TO AVOID TRIAL, APPEALING A HIGH COURT RULING THAT HAD CLEARED THE WAY FOR 176 COMMUNITY MEMBERS TO HAVE THEIR CASE HEARD — THE HIGH COURT HAVING ALREADY DISMISSED THE COMPANY'S APPLICATION TO THROW THE CASE OUT, WITH A TRIAL DATE SET AND THE MATTER DESCRIBED AS A LANDMARK HUMAN RIGHTS AND ENVIRONMENTAL CASE. Read what the company did, not what it said. It did not argue the pollution did not happen; it argued the case should not be heard at all, twice, up to the highest court in the country. Expect that as the first phase of any serious case: months spent on whether you are allowed to sue before a word about the harm. Budget for it, and treat surviving the strike-out application as a real victory — 176 people did. AND THE NUMBER MATTERS: 176 COMMUNITY MEMBERS, together, in one case. This file records the two-or-more threshold at the development bank and the 165 residents who won at Isiolo. A group of neighbours filing jointly is the standard shape of a winnable environmental case in Africa, not an exceptional one. WHAT THE LITIGATION CENTRE SUPPLIES, AND IT IS TWO THINGS AT ONCE: TECHNICAL AND MONETARY SUPPORT TO LOCAL AND REGIONAL LAWYERS AND ORGANIZATIONS IN LITIGATING HUMAN RIGHTS AND RULE OF LAW CASES; TRAINING IN HUMAN RIGHTS AND RULE OF LAW ISSUES; AND IT FACILITATES NETWORKS OF HUMAN RIGHTS LAWYERS AND ORGANIZATIONS THROUGHOUT SOUTHERN AFRICA. MONETARY as well as technical. Money and expertise to the lawyer already acting for you, rather than a foreign firm taking over the file — which is the arrangement this file keeps recommending. If your advocate says the case is right but the resources are not there, this is a body that supplies both to him. ITS PUBLISHED FOCUS LIST NAMES WHAT YOU NEED: COMMUNITY AND CUSTOMARY LAND RIGHTS; ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE; POLICY ADVOCACY; RIGHT TO INFORMATION; AND, IN ITS OWN PROGRAMME LANGUAGE, SOCIO-ECONOMIC RIGHTS, EXTRACTIVES, LAND RIGHTS, CLIMATE JUSTICE AND BUSINESS AND HUMAN RIGHTS. CUSTOMARY LAND RIGHTS and EXTRACTIVES as named, funded workstreams of a regional litigation centre. Very few organisations in this file list both — and the mine-versus-village case is exactly where the two meet. THE TWELVE COUNTRIES ARE NAMED, SO CHECK WHETHER YOURS IS ONE: ANGOLA, BOTSWANA, THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO, ESWATINI, LESOTHO, MALAWI, MOZAMBIQUE, NAMIBIA, SOUTH AFRICA, TANZANIA, ZAMBIA AND ZIMBABWE — AND IT ALSO SUPPORTS LITIGATION IN SOUTH AFRICAN COURTS THAT ADVANCES HUMAN RIGHTS IN THE WIDER REGION. Cases brought in South African courts on behalf of the region is a separate door. Where a company is headquartered or listed in South Africa and operating in your country, that is where a claim may be able to go — this file records the same logic in the arms-export challenge the centre has filed in a South African high court. WHY IT EXISTS, WHICH TELLS YOU WHAT IT IS FOR: ESTABLISHED IN 2005 BY AN INTERNATIONAL BAR ASSOCIATION AND A SOUTHERN AFRICA OPEN SOCIETY INITIATIVE TO FILL A PERCEIVED GAP IN LITIGATION EXPERTISE IN THE REGION, WITH THE AIM OF INCREASING THE CAPACITY OF LOCAL LAWYERS AND CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS TO USE LITIGATION AND ADVOCACY — AND IT PROVIDES SUPPORT TO COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANIZATIONS BY OFFERING LEGAL ASSISTANCE AND ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY STRENGTHENING. COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANIZATIONS named as recipients of both legal assistance and capacity strengthening. Your association does not have to be a legal body to approach it — and the second half, strengthening the organisation itself, is what stops a case collapsing because the group behind it fell apart. THE PEOPLE GROUPS IT NAMES INCLUDE ACTIVISTS, PEOPLE EXPERIENCING HOMELESSNESS OR LIVING IN INFORMAL SETTLEMENTS, INFORMAL WORKERS, PEOPLE AFFECTED BY DISPLACEMENT, AND INDIGENOUS PEOPLE. AND THE CONTACT IS PUBLISHED IN A DIRECTORY OF PUBLIC INTEREST LEGAL SERVICES ORGANISATIONS: A NAMED JOHANNESBURG STREET ADDRESS IN ROSEBANK, A TELEPHONE NUMBER, AND AN ENQUIRIES EMAIL ADDRESS. That directory itself is worth opening — a searchable list of public interest legal services organisations with addresses and phone numbers is exactly what a community with no lawyer needs, and there is one. WHO IT SUITS: communities in the twelve named countries facing a mine, a pollution claim or a customary land dispute, and their existing lawyers. CAVEATS: IT SUPPORTS LOCAL LAWYERS RATHER THAN ACTING DIRECTLY — and the Zambian case above shows the timescale. For the centre's own stub, Zambia's SALC entry; for the five funders that supply risk capital and the land-sharing arrangement, the risk capital entry; for paralegal officers in district offices, Zambia Land Alliance; for the USD 5M community forest grant and 30 scouts, the Kasempa entry.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Accountability State Authority
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Egypt, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Egypt e-Tenders
trackers.desc: Egypt's government e-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Egypt, and for how much.

trackers.name: CAPMAS
trackers.desc: Egypt's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Egypt.

trackers.name: Court of Cassation (Egypt)
trackers.desc: Egypt's highest ordinary court; publishes many civil and some criminal judgments online. · Find here: information and selected rulings of Egypt's Court of Cassation.

trackers.name: GAFI
trackers.desc: Egypt's General Authority for Investment company registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: African Convention on Nature — check WHICH version binds your state
trackers.desc: THERE ARE TWO AFRICAN CONVENTIONS OF THIS NAME, AND CITING THE WRONG ONE IS THE AVOIDABLE ERROR HERE. The Algiers Convention was signed 15 September 1968, in force 16 June 1969. The revised Maputo Convention was adopted by the Assembly of the Union in Maputo on 11 July 2003 and entered into force 23 July 2016 — thirteen years later. THE OPERATIVE RULE: the 1968 Convention remains in force for those countries that have not ratified the 2003 revisions, so the two coexist and which binds your state depends on its ratification status. Commentary records only about 30 percent of African states had ratified Maputo. This entry does not assert which binds your state — the African Union publishes a Status List alongside the treaty text at au.int. Check it first. WHY THE DELAY IS AN ARGUMENT FOR IT: commentary attributes the thirteen years to the revised text containing strong provisions that could create accountability and also slow down social and economic development — a treaty resisted for creating accountability is one worth invoking where it applies. PROVISIONS TO KNOW: article XXXIX — no reservation may be made to this Convention, so a ratifying state takes all of it; article XL — withdrawal takes effect only one year after written notification; and no instrument of accession to the 1968 Algiers Convention may be deposited any longer, so the older text is closed to new entrants. THE OBJECTIVES ARE BROADER THAN USUAL: conservation, utilisation and development of soil, water, flora and fauna for present and future welfare, from an economic, nutritional, scientific, educational, cultural and aesthetic point of view — so a claim resting on cultural or aesthetic value has a treaty basis. BUT IF THE 1968 TEXT IS WHAT BINDS YOU, EXPECT LITTLE: parties were encouraged to cooperate but were not required to submit regular reports on implementation, and there were no financial mechanisms — no reporting trail, no funding attached. Article XLI also provides for interim secretariat arrangements, so check current institutional capacity. IUCN publishes a commentary on each provision in English and French.

trackers.name: Egyptian Center for Economic and Social Rights — has litigated expropriation for public utility, and keeps legal representatives in more than twenty governorates
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an Egyptian non-governmental legal institution founded in 2009 that works through strategic litigation rather than reporting alone, and whose landmark cases include the expropriation for public utility case and litigation over the privatisation of public property — the two ways land moves out of people's hands in Egypt. It also runs housing and eviction work. WHERE IT CAN REACH YOU: the main office is in downtown Cairo with branches in Alexandria, Daqahliya and Aswan, plus legal representatives in more than twenty governorates — which in a country where nearly every rights organisation is Cairo-only is the difference between a case and a press release. Its published record shows it filing urgent proceedings before the Administrative Court, pressing the government over non-implementation of a court ruling that banned Nile pollution at Aswan, and bringing a suit to protect the Pyramids from vibration and laser damage caused by concerts — evidence it will litigate a site-protection claim, not only a labour or welfare one. WHO IT SUITS: communities and households facing expropriation, eviction, or industrial pollution, and workers' groups. CAVEATS, AND THEY ARE SERIOUS: Egyptian civic space is heavily constrained — ECESR's offices have been raided by police and staff detained, its founder is a prominent opposition lawyer, and association with it carries risk that a community should weigh before approaching. Its site publishes case news rather than an intake procedure, much of the material is Arabic-first, and no fee or eligibility information was found.

trackers.name: EIPR — Cairo rights organisation with a standing right-to-housing file, legal aid and strategic litigation on evictions
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, an independent Cairo organisation established in 2002, working through research, documentation, legal aid, strategic litigation and advocacy on civil liberties, economic and social rights and criminal justice — with a declared focus on the rights closest to a person: body, privacy and house. WHY IT IS FILED HERE: it maintains a standing published Right to Housing file, which is the rare thing a resident can read BEFORE the demolition crew arrives. Its documentation includes the demolition of the homes of almost 1,000 families at Izbat al-Nakhl in February 2014, carried out with riot police, without prior notice or consultation — some residents rehoused, others left homeless — within a period in which more than twenty forced eviction operations were recorded without reparation or fair compensation. THE ARGUMENT TO USE: it grounds housing claims in Article 78 of the Egyptian constitution, and has analysed the state budget to show the government failed to adopt policies supporting the poor's right to adequate housing. It also works the tenancy side, proposing rent subsidy through the state housing and mortgage fund with a legal rent-to-income ratio capped at 20 per cent, and arguing that tenants who paid key money or financed unfinished units and infrastructure themselves have built a long-term usufructuary entitlement distinct from ordinary tenancy — a useful line for anyone whose own money went into the building they are being moved out of. WHO IT SUITS: Egyptian households facing demolition, eviction, resettlement or rent liberalisation, especially in Greater Cairo. CAVEATS: EGYPTIAN CIVIC SPACE IS SEVERELY CONSTRAINED AND EIPR'S OWN SENIOR STAFF HAVE BEEN DETAINED; approach with that in mind. It supports litigation rather than acting as a general legal aid office, and for expropriation cases and its regional branches, Egypt's ECESR entry is the other route.

trackers.name: Egypt's environment and land organisations by name — Habi Center for Environmental Rights, the Land Center for Human Rights, the Housing Rights centre, HMLC with its Aswan office, and HEPCA on the Red Sea
trackers.desc: THE ENVIRONMENT AND LAND ORGANISATIONS BY NAME, because this file has held only Cairo general-rights bodies for Egypt: HABI CENTER FOR ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS; the LAND CENTER FOR HUMAN RIGHTS; the EGYPTIAN CENTER FOR HOUSING RIGHTS; the ASSOCIATION OF LEGAL ASSISTANCE ON HUMAN RIGHTS; and the GENERAL INDEPENDENT FEDERATION OF EGYPTIAN FARMERS. A centre named for environmental rights and another named for land are the two doors an Egyptian facing a project should knock on first — a general rights organisation will refer you to them anyway. AND A FARMERS' FEDERATION IS THE MEMBERSHIP BODY BEHIND A RURAL CLAIM: bring it in before you are alone. THE LAWYERS AND THEIR REACH: the HISHAM MUBARAK LAW CENTER (HMLC), founded 1999 in DOWNTOWN CAIRO WITH A SECOND OFFICE IN ASWAN, works through LITIGATION, CAMPAIGNS AND LEGAL RESEARCH, and its Cairo office PROVIDES SPACE FOR MANY ACTIVIST GROUPS — including this file's ECESR — acting as a HUB AND MEETING SPACE for civil society. An office in Aswan matters more than the Cairo address if your land is in the south: ask HMLC which office covers your governorate, and note that its Cairo premises are where other groups physically meet. ON THE COAST: HEPCA (Hurghada Environmental Protection and Conservation Association, hepca.org), ESTABLISHED 1992 BY DIVE CENTRES in Hurghada and Safaga, a registered ASSOCIATION with OVER 700 EMPLOYEES, working on MARINE AND LAND CONSERVATION in the RED SEA GOVERNORATE. Seven hundred staff makes HEPCA the largest non-state conservation employer recorded for Egypt in this file — and it was founded by an industry whose income depended on the reef, which is the coalition shape worth copying: find the businesses that lose money if the ecosystem dies. THE RISK, STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT IS PART OF USING THESE: many of these organisations — HMLC, EIPR, ECESR and others — have been named among NGOs targeted under a FOREIGN-FUNDING CASE, subjected to inspection and review; military police RAIDED the Cairo offices of HMLC and ECESR in February 2011, arresting 28 researchers, lawyers and journalists including both directors.
