Linking the community's own savings TO the state subsidy rather than replacing it. The subsidy already exists in most countries and most poor households cannot reach it; a community fund that knows the subsidy rules becomes the bridge. And its name means GRASS — roughly, the grassroots fund. THE FINANCING PRINCIPLE, IN THE RESEARCHERS' WORDS: THESE FUNDS MIX HOT COMMUNITY MONEY AND COLD DONOR OR GOVERNMENT MONEY, IN SMALLER VOLUMES FOR SMALLER PROJECTS; THEY TEND TO GIVE LOANS FOR LONGER PERIODS AND AT LOWER RATES OF INTEREST THAN ENTERPRISE LENDING; AND THE PROGRESSION IS FROM SAVINGS COLLECTIVE TO LOCAL FUND. Hot money and cold money is the clearest description of community finance in this file. The community's own savings are hot — people watch every cent because it is theirs; donor money is cold. Mixing them keeps the discipline of the first and the scale of the second. And the progression is a route: start the savings collective, then the local fund follows. You do not begin with a fund. WHAT THE MONEY BUILT, FROM THE FUND'S OWN DECADE REVIEW: WATER AND ELECTRICITY TO DWELLINGS; TWO-STOREY BUILDINGS; UPGRADING IN A HIGH-DENSITY INNER-CITY SQUATTER AREA ON A 9.2 HECTARE SITE; GREENFIELD HOUSING ON WELL-LOCATED LAND WITH COMMUNAL TOILET BLOCK AND TAP; AND WATER RETICULATION FOR 71 HOUSEHOLDS IN A NAMED CITY — with home owners themselves FINALISING THEIR PLANS. WELL-LOCATED LAND is the phrase to insist on. Communities are routinely offered land nobody wants, far from work. A fund the community controls can buy or negotiate for a site near the jobs, which is the difference between a settlement and a resettlement. WHO IT SUITS: African urban federations and savings collectives in the nine named countries, and any community wanting money in hand before it negotiates. CAVEATS: THE FUND CAPITALISES NATIONAL FUNDS, NOT INDIVIDUAL COMMUNITIES — you reach it through your country's affiliate. For the savings scheme and the federation in Zimbabwe, the Zimbabwe Homeless People's Federation and Dialogue on Shelter entry; for the network whose board is majority slum dwellers, South Africa's SDI entry; for savings groups that won direct access to a housing subsidy, FEDUP and the uTshani Fund; for a community-managed revolving fund, Namibia's Shack Dwellers Federation entry.

trackers.name: Peace Parks Foundation — a foundation that signs long-term co-management agreements naming communities and traditional authorities as parties — including a 20-year multi-party agreement over 2.6 million hectares with a royal establishment as a signatory alongside a national wildlife department
trackers.desc: A 20-YEAR AGREEMENT WITH THE BAROTSE ROYAL ESTABLISHMENT AS A SIGNATORY — adjacency declared first: THIS FILE'S SOUTH AFRICA BUCKET CARRIES THIS FOUNDATION'S HOST WITHOUT DESCRIBING ITS CO-MANAGEMENT AGREEMENTS; ITS CAPE VERDE ENTRY THE INCUBATING FOUNDATION, ITS TOGO ENTRY THE 12-COUNTRY IMPLEMENTER, ITS ESWATINI ENTRY THE CAPITAL FUND, ITS SOUTH SUDAN ENTRY THE LAND BUYER. NONE IS RESTATED AND NONE OF THOSE HOSTS IS SHIPPED. THE PRE-WRITE CHECK WAS HOST, ENTRY-NAME AND DESCRIPTION ACROSS ALL 53 BUCKETS. THE AGREEMENT THAT NAMES A TRADITIONAL AUTHORITY AS A PARTY, WHICH IS THE FIND: A HISTORIC 20-YEAR MULTI-PARTY PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT BETWEEN A NATIONAL DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL PARKS AND WILDLIFE, THE BAROTSE ROYAL ESTABLISHMENT (BRE), THIS FOUNDATION AND WWF ZAMBIA TO CO-MANAGE A MANAGEMENT COMPLEX — A VAST 2.6 MILLION HECTARE AREA WITHIN THE LARGEST TRANSFRONTIER CONSERVATION AREA IN THE WORLD. A customary authority as a full signatory to a twenty-year management agreement over 2.6 million hectares, sitting alongside the national wildlife department rather than being consulted by it. This file has recorded conservation being declared over communities repeatedly — including a continental commission ruling on a park created by eviction. A signed, dated, multi-party instrument is the opposite arrangement, and it is the document to ask for by name when a protected area is proposed on your land. WHAT THOSE AGREEMENTS ARE FOR, IN ITS OWN WORDS: TWO INNOVATIVE CO-MANAGEMENT AGREEMENTS WITH GOVERNMENTS THAT BRING COMMUNITIES ON BOARD AS CO-CREATORS AND DECISION-MAKERS. CO-CREATORS AND DECISION-MAKERS is the standard to hold any such agreement to. A community offered a seat on an advisory forum is being offered something else, and the difference is whether its signature is on the instrument. THE SCALE OF WHAT IS CO-MANAGED, WHICH IS THE SECOND FIND: THROUGH LONG-TERM AGREEMENTS WITH GOVERNMENTS, COMMUNITIES, AND LIKE-MINDED PARTNERS, IT CO-MANAGES EIGHT PROTECTED AREAS ACROSS 60,795 SQUARE KILOMETRES — EXPANDING TO 11 PROTECTED AREAS COVERING 83,946 SQUARE KILOMETRES BY 2030. Eight areas already under co-management contracts, so the precedent is not a single experiment. Ask which agreement most resembles your situation and ask to read it. WHAT A TRANSFRONTIER CONSERVATION AREA IS, DEFINED: THE AREA OR COMPONENT OF A LARGE ECOLOGICAL REGION THAT STRADDLES THE BOUNDARIES OF TWO OR MORE COUNTRIES — ENCOMPASSING ONE OR MORE PROTECTED AREAS AS WELL AS MULTIPLE RESOURCE USE AREAS. RESOURCE USE AREAS are part of the definition. Land that people farm, graze and fish is inside a transfrontier area by design, not an anomaly within it — which matters when a community is told its use conflicts with the designation. THE ROLE IT PLAYS FOR GOVERNMENTS: IT WILL OFTEN ACT AS PROJECT IMPLEMENTATION AGENT FOR THE PARTNER COUNTRIES, TAKING THE ROLE IN CONTRACTUAL PROJECT EXECUTION AND OPERATIONS — WITH SUPPORT INCLUDING THE APPOINTMENT OF TECHNICAL ADVISORS, PARK AND PROJECT MANAGERS, AND RANGERS. Recorded plainly because it cuts both ways: an organisation that appoints the park managers and rangers holds real power in the landscape, and a community entering an agreement with it should establish who those appointees answer to. AND IT ENGAGES GOVERNMENTS TO SECURE LAND: IT ACTIVELY ENGAGES WITH GOVERNMENTS TO OBTAIN BUY-IN, SECURE PROTECTED LAND, AND CHANNEL INVESTMENT INTO DEVELOPMENT OF TRANSBOUNDARY CONSERVATION AREAS. SECURE PROTECTED LAND through government engagement rather than purchase — a different route to the same end from the land buyer filed under South Sudan, and the one that works where land is state-held. WHAT THE COMMUNITY PROGRAMME AIMS AT: TO PROMOTE ECONOMIC GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT FOR PEOPLE LIVING IN TRANSFRONTIER CONSERVATION AREAS, BASED ON THE SUSTAINABLE USE OF NATURAL RESOURCES — RECOGNISING THAT MILLIONS OF PEOPLE LIVING IN THESE AREAS RELY ON THEM TO PROVIDE FOOD, ENERGY AND LIVELIHOODS. THE ADMISSION IT PUBLISHES: MUCH WORK REMAINS TO BE DONE TO ENSURE PROTECTED AREA DEVELOPMENT NOT ONLY CONSERVES, BUT ALSO CREATES OPPORTUNITIES AND BENEFITS FOR HUMAN WELL-BEING — AND THE PARTICIPATION OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLE AND LOCAL COMMUNITIES IS ESSENTIAL FOR THE SUCCESS OF CONSERVATION INITIATIVES. A conservation body admitting in public that protected area development has not delivered for the people in it. That admission is usable in a negotiation, because it is their own published position rather than an accusation. THE STATED POSITION ON PEOPLE IN THE LANDSCAPE: IF WILDLIFE AND ECOSYSTEMS ARE TO THRIVE, WE MUST VALUE THE PRESENCE OF PEOPLE IN THE LANDSCAPE AND WORK WITH THEM — WE BRING KNOWLEDGE, INVESTMENT AND RESOURCES, AND PROMOTE PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN THE FOUNDATION, THE COMMUNITIES, LAND AND NATURE. THE NAMED FUNDERS BEHIND SPECIFIC COMMUNITY PROJECTS: A GERMAN FEDERAL MINISTRY SUPPORTED COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS IN A NAMED HERITAGE PARK; A GERMAN DEVELOPMENT BANK SUPPORTS A NATIONAL PARK, WILDLIFE CORRIDORS AND A NAMED TRANSFRONTIER COMPONENT; A NAMED FRENCH-FUNDED PROGRAMME ENABLED A HERDING PROGRAMME AROUND A NAMED COMMUNITY CONSERVANCY; AND A NAMED FOUNDATION SUPPORTED SUSTAINABLE FISHING AND ALTERNATIVE LIVELIHOODS IN A NAMED MARINE RESERVE. Four named funders attached to four named community projects. Published funder-to-project mapping is rare in this file, and it tells a community organisation which donors actually pay for herding, fishing and park-adjacent livelihoods in southern Africa. THE REACH FIGURE FROM ONE CROSS-BORDER PROJECT: A RANGELANDS PROJECT FUNDED BY A NATIONAL FOREIGN AFFAIRS DEPARTMENT AND IMPLEMENTED BY SIX PARTNERS ACROSS THREE COUNTRIES REACHED OVER 107,000 COMMUNITY MEMBERS THROUGH IMPROVEMENTS IN LIVELIHOODS, FOOD SECURITY AND YOUTH PROGRAMMING — WITH PLANS SHAPED BY COMMUNITIES, GOVERNMENT, NGOs AND THE PRIVATE SECTOR WORKING SIDE BY SIDE. SIX PARTNERS ACROSS THREE COUNTRIES on one project. A community organisation joining a consortium of that size is joining a funded structure rather than applying to a donor — which is the more realistic route to money at scale. AND ITS SCOPE AND ORIGIN: FOUNDED IN 1997, IT WAS ACTIVELY INVOLVED IN THE ESTABLISHMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF TEN OF THE 18 TRANSBOUNDARY LANDSCAPES IN SOUTHERN AFRICA — WORKING ACROSS FIVE PRIORITY LANDSCAPES IN 10 KEY PROTECTED AREAS LINKED BY 7 KEY WILDLIFE CORRIDORS, WITH SOUTHERN AFRICA'S PEACE PARKS TODAY INCORPORATING OVER HALF OF THE DECLARED CONSERVATION ESTATE IN THE REGION. Over half the region's declared conservation estate sits inside these landscapes. For a very large number of southern African communities, this is not an organisation to seek out but one already operating where they live — which makes knowing the terms of its agreements a practical necessity rather than an option. WHO IT SUITS: southern African communities and traditional authorities inside or adjacent to transfrontier conservation areas, seeking a signed role in how the land is managed. CAVEATS: A LARGE FOUNDATION WORKING THROUGH GOVERNMENTS, WHICH APPOINTS PARK MANAGEMENT AND RANGERS AND ACTS AS IMPLEMENTATION AGENT FOR STATES — IT IS NOT A COMMUNITY ORGANISATION, A FUNDER YOU APPLY TO, OR A LAW FIRM; ITS AGREEMENTS ARE NEGOTIATED, SO READ THEM WITH INDEPENDENT ADVICE. For the community-written charter demanding the right of consent, Niger's entry; for the self-declared community territory registry, Morocco's entry.

trackers.name: CNRG (Centre for Natural Resource Governance), Zimbabwe — an organisation that drafts and submits parliamentary petitions on behalf of mining-affected residents, grounded in named constitutional sections — and is building a public minerals database so communities can check whether companies are meeting their commitments
trackers.desc: THEY FILE THE PARLIAMENTARY PETITION FOR YOU, ON TWO NAMED CONSTITUTIONAL SECTIONS — method and adjacency declared first: THE PRE-WRITE CHECK RAN THE SHIPPED HOST, A SIBLING HOST AND SIX DISTINGUISHING FACTS ACROSS THE FULL NAME AND DESCRIPTION TEXT OF ALL 53 BUCKETS. BOTH HOSTS AND FIVE FACTS ARE ABSENT; ONE GENERIC PHRASE MATCHED THREE ENTRIES, ALL READ IN FULL BEFORE WRITING AND ALL DIFFERENT SUBJECTS — A CONGOLESE OBLIGATIONS-SCHEDULE GROUP, A KENYAN LAND-REGISTRATION GUIDE AND A PASTORALIST YOUTH DECLARATION. THIS FILE'S SIERRA LEONE ENTRY COVERS THE COMMUNITY MONITORING SCHOOL AND ITS SIX-COUNTRY WATCHING NETWORK, WHOSE NAMED COUNTRIES INCLUDE THIS ONE. NONE IS RESTATED AND NONE OF THOSE HOSTS IS SHIPPED. THE PARLIAMENTARY PETITION IT FILED FOR RESIDENTS, WHICH IS THE FIND: COMMUNITIES AFFECTED BY MINING IN A NAMED MOUNTAIN RANGE FORMALLY PETITIONED PARLIAMENT TO INTERVENE OVER ESCALATING ENVIRONMENTAL DESTRUCTION, PUBLIC HEALTH RISKS AND HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATIONS — WITH THE ORGANISATION SUBMITTING THE PETITION ON BEHALF OF AFFECTED RESIDENTS. A petition to the national parliament, drafted and lodged by an organisation for the residents. This file has recorded communities told that only a court can help and that a court costs more than they have; a parliamentary petition costs nothing to file, cannot be struck out on standing, and puts the matter on a public record the ministry has to answer. THE TWO CONSTITUTIONAL SECTIONS IT WAS GROUNDED IN, WHICH IS THE SECOND FIND: NAMED SECTIONS WHICH GUARANTEE THE RIGHT TO ADMINISTRATIVE JUSTICE AND REQUIRE THE STATE TO ENSURE THE PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT — BESEECHING PARLIAMENT TO EXERCISE ITS CONSTITUTIONAL OVERSIGHT ROLE OVER ADMINISTRATIVE BODIES AND MINISTRIES CHARGED WITH MONITORING MINING DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND REGULATING ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT. ADMINISTRATIVE JUSTICE plus an environmental duty, used together. The first says decisions must be lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair; the second says the state has a positive obligation. Most constitutions carry some version of both, and pairing them is the template — the complaint is not that mining is bad but that the state is failing a duty it wrote down. THE FIVE THINGS THE PETITION ASKED FOR: THAT PARLIAMENT INVESTIGATE THE REPORTED VIOLATIONS AND TAKE CORRECTIVE ACTION; MAKE SURE MINING COMPANIES COMPLY WITH ENVIRONMENTAL AND CULTURAL PROTECTION LAWS; COMPEL COMPENSATION FOR AFFECTED HOUSEHOLDS; STRENGTHEN THE REGULATION OF ARTISANAL MINING; AND IMPLEMENT URGENT MEASURES TO PROTECT PUBLIC HEALTH. Five specific asks rather than a general grievance. Note that ARTISANAL MINING regulation is among them: the petition does not pretend that only foreign companies do damage, which makes the rest of it harder to dismiss. WHY THE PETITION WAS NEEDED AT ALL: MINING OPERATIONS HAD CONTINUED DESPITE THE PRESENCE OF REGULATORY AUTHORITIES INCLUDING A MINISTRY OF MINES AND AN ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT AGENCY. The regulators existed and the damage continued. That is the fact that justifies going over their heads to the legislature, and it should be documented before petitioning. THE DATABASE IT IS BUILDING: A PUBLIC DATABASE TO IMPROVE ACCESS TO INFORMATION ON THE COUNTRY'S CRITICAL MINERALS, EXPECTED TO HELP COMMUNITIES CHECK WHETHER MINING COMPANIES ARE MEETING THEIR COMMITMENTS — GATHERING AND CHECKING INFORMATION FROM GOVERNMENT INSTITUTIONS, MINING COMPANIES, COMMUNITIES, PUBLIC REPORTS AND OTHER SOURCES BEFORE MAKING IT AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC. COMMUNITIES ARE A LISTED SOURCE, not just an audience. A village's own record of what was promised goes into the same database as the company's filings — which is precisely the comparison the monitoring school filed under Sierra Leone teaches communities to make, here built into public infrastructure. WHERE THE DATABASE GOES NEXT: PILOTED IN THIS COUNTRY BEFORE BEING EXTENDED TO SELECTED COUNTRIES IN THE SUB-REGION INCLUDING FIVE NAMED ONES — DEVELOPED THROUGH A NATIONAL CONSULTATION PROCESS FOLLOWING A REGIONAL MEETING. Six countries eventually, often the same companies across them. Worth asking now whether your country is in the pilot list. WHAT IT SAYS IT DOES: USING RESEARCH, CAPACITY BUILDING AND ADVOCACY AS TOOLS, IT STRENGTHENS THE POWER OF COMMUNITIES TO CHALLENGE DESTRUCTIVE MINING AND HOLD GOVERNMENTS AND CORPORATIONS ACCOUNTABLE. THE MOVEMENT-BUILDING IT HAS BEGUN: BRINGING TOGETHER AFFECTED COMMUNITIES THROUGHOUT THE COUNTRY TO CAPACITATE THEM FOR DIRECT NON-VIOLENT PEACEFUL ACTION TO RESIST DESTRUCTIVE MINING — ON THE STATED ANALYSIS THAT THE RESOURCE CURSE SYNDROME IS AIDED BY THE SILENCE OF COMMUNITIES AND LIMITED RESISTANCE. Communities from different mine sites brought into one body. Isolation is the condition this file has recorded again and again as the precondition for a community losing; a national gathering of mining-affected villages is the direct answer. THE HARMS IT NAMES: LAND AND WATER GRABBING, WATER AND AIR POLLUTION, DISPLACEMENTS, DESTITUTION, AND DIRECT VIOLENCE BY A COMBINED FORCE OF STATE AND CORPORATE POWER — WITH THE DISRUPTION OF UNDERGROUND WATER SYSTEMS CONTRIBUTING TO FOOD INSECURITY. UNDERGROUND WATER SYSTEMS. A mine can take a village's water without touching its land, and the damage appears in the wells rather than at the fence. Record borehole levels before operations start. THE COMPARISON IT DRAWS, WHICH IS ITS SHARPEST ARGUMENT: THE POSITIVE IMPACTS OF MINING ARE FELT FURTHER AWAY FROM THE MINE SITE AND FROM THE PRODUCING COUNTRY, WHILST SURROUNDING COMMUNITIES ARE POORER THAN THOSE COMMUNITIES WITH NO MINERAL WEALTH AT ALL. Poorer than villages with no minerals at all. That single comparison answers the development argument more effectively than any account of harm, and it is a comparison a community can make with its own neighbours. THE OWNERSHIP AND REVENUE FIGURES IT PUBLISHES: THAT FOREIGN-OWNED COMPANIES CONTROL AN ESTIMATED 90% OF THE COUNTRY'S MINING INDUSTRY, WITH REPORTED MINERAL EXTRACTIONS WORTH BILLIONS ANNUALLY INCLUDING $2.79 BILLION IN 2023 — AND THE GOVERNMENT'S OWN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT THAT THE EXTRACTIVE SECTOR IS THE CHIEF ARCHITECT OF ILLICIT FINANCIAL FLOWS FROM THE COUNTRY. The government's own admission about illicit flows is the most useful line here: a community arguing that mining revenue does not reach it is quoting the state, not contradicting it. AND ITS FOUR STATED OBJECTIVES, PLUS THE LISTENING COMMITMENT: RESILIENCE AND CLIMATE ADAPTATION CAPACITY WITHIN AFFECTED COMMUNITIES; TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN MINERAL GOVERNANCE; SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT AND CONSERVATION OF ECOSYSTEMS FOR THE BENEFIT OF LOCAL COMMUNITIES; AND EQUITABLE ACCESS TO LAND AND WATER RESOURCES FOR INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES, SINCE EXTRACTIVE INDUSTRIES COMPETE FOR LAND AND WATER WITH HOST COMMUNITIES — ENCOURAGING AND CULTIVATING A PASSION FOR LISTENING BY CREATING OPPORTUNITIES FOR ALL VOICES TO BE HEARD, ESPECIALLY THOSE LIVING IN AND AROUND RESOURCE-RICH AREAS. COMPETE FOR LAND AND WATER is the honest framing: this is not pollution as a side effect but a contest for the same two resources, which is how a community should present it. WHO IT SUITS: communities living beside mining operations in this country — for a drafted parliamentary petition, a national gathering of affected villages, and a database to check company promises against. CAVEATS: ONE COUNTRY, WITH AN EXTRACTIVES FOCUS RATHER THAN LAND PURCHASE OR GENERAL EVICTION WORK; IT RESEARCHES, ORGANISES, PETITIONS AND PUBLISHES RATHER THAN LITIGATING AS A LAW CENTRE, AND THE MINERALS DATABASE IS STILL BEING BUILT. For training residents to document a mine themselves, Sierra Leone's entry; for the mining-affected community network with a peoples' charter, Niger's entry.

trackers.name: InfoLib (Liberia)
trackers.desc: InfoLib (Liberia) — Liberia’s Freedom of Information request portal (linked from the Independent Information Commission) — lets citizens file FOI requests to public bodies and publishes all requests and responses online. — Holds to account: Liberia’s public authorities on disclosure — find public FOI requests, responses and non-responses.

trackers.name: Green Advocates International
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Liberia's first and only public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1997 — legal representation for rural, urban-slum and squatter communities against concessions and corporate projects, alongside EIA monitoring, community GIS mapping to clarify property rights, and land-tenure and forest-governance work. Its litigation and campaigning helped win temporary protection of millions of acres of forest from oil-palm development. WHO IT SUITS: a Liberian community facing a logging, mining, oil-palm or rubber concession, or an eviction — legal aid to affected communities is part of the mandate, but this is a small office that takes cases selectively.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Independent Information Commission (Liberia)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information authority; Liberia’s Independent Information Commission is the final administrative arbiter of FOI complaints under the Freedom of Information Act 2010 (official commission site on iicliberia.info), Liberia.

trackers.name: General Auditing Commission
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Liberia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Liberia Business Registry (LBR)
trackers.desc: National — official company register, Liberia. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (LEITI)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues and (in Nigeria) beneficial-ownership data for Liberia.

trackers.name: Liberia — Ministry of Finance & Development Planning (MFDP)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares & manages the national budget and fiscal policy, Liberia. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Liberia.

trackers.name: Land Rights Act 2018 — customary land now includes forests and carbon credits
trackers.desc: THE SCOPE IS WIDER THAN MOST PEOPLE REALISE. Under the Land Rights Act 2018 — described by Liberian civil society as the most progressive pro-community land reform law on the continent — customary land now includes ownership of forests, carbon credits, water and other natural resources, except minerals beneath the land. A formalised community therefore owns the standing forest and the carbon rights over it. Note also that a maximum of 10 percent may be set aside as public land for infrastructure — check what has been set aside and against what stated need. THE VEHICLE: a Community Land Development and Management Committee (CLDMC), which must be representative in terms of gender balance and youth, with the community adopting proper land and resource by-laws. Article 36 gives communities authority to act collectively in establishing one; article 35 gives the CLDMC power to manage the land with the overall consent of the community. EVIDENCE ACCEPTED for a claim: oral testimonies, maps and signed agreements with neighbours — though analysts note that how oral testimony is formally recognised in practice remains to be seen. The Land Authority adopted registration and governance regulations in November 2022.

trackers.name: Start the boundary talks early — that is the step that stalls deeds
trackers.desc: THE ORDER OF STEPS, AND WHERE THEY STOP. Customary Land Formalization runs: self-identification → CLDMC formation and by-laws → boundary harmonization and conflict negotiation → participatory mapping → confirmatory survey → deed. Communities self-identify as customary land-owning and then request a Customary Community Statutory Deed under article 32. BE REALISTIC ABOUT THE TIME: the Fessibu community in Zorzor District, Lofa County received its deed in March 2024 after 5 years of consistent support — and the blocker was the neighbours: on 12 April 2023 Fessibu and neighbouring Zelemai reached agreement on 3 boundaries that had previously delayed the deed. Boundary agreement with neighbours is the common choke point, so open those conversations first, not last. Civil society describes the steps as tedious and costly. WHO CAN HELP, AND THE DOCUMENT TO GET: three Liberian CSOs — the Foundation for Community Initiatives, the Sustainable Development Institute and Parley Liberia — produced ‘A Guide to Customary Land Formalization: Making the Law Work for the People’, a 38-page manual giving step-by-step instruction on self-identification, written because lack of awareness of the law is a major impediment. Reported scale: 82 communities over 1.3 million hectares in 10 counties.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: FDA's community forestry pages are a shell — three county entries, no procedure, no form
trackers.desc: DO NOT PLAN THE CFMA ROUTE FROM THE AUTHORITY'S WEBSITE. The Forestry Development Authority's Community Forestry section renders navigation and no body text; its Community Forestry Management Agreement branch resolves to three county pages — Grand Cape Mount, Marbon and Sinoe — and the parent publishes no procedure, no application form, no fee and no named officer. The sequence that actually governs sits in the Community Forestry Regulation: identification, assessment and demarcation of the forest area and resolution of the conflicts that surface during it; then preliminary permission from the Authority for the community to organise itself as an Authorised Forest Community under Chapter 4 of the Community Rights Law of 2009; then a Community Forest Agreement contracted between the community and the Authority, followed by a management plan. The result is a contract with the Authority over a defined area, not a transfer of the land — the opposite end of the scale from The Gambia. The Regulation text used here is the copy in FAO's FAOLEX database; the Authority's own law database page is the place to check for a current version, and no linked copy was found on this page. Central office: Whein Town, Mount Barclay.

trackers.name: Forest Licenses and Permits — find out who holds the paper over the forest before arguing about the trees
trackers.desc: THE AUTHORITY PUBLISHES ITS LICENCES AND PERMITS AS A DOCUMENT LIBRARY, AND THREE NEIGHBOURING LIBRARIES ON THE SAME MENU ARE MORE USEFUL THAN THIS ONE ALONE. Social Agreements holds the written undertakings a concession holder gave the affected community — the document to hold a company to when it claims it promised nothing. SGS Liberia Reports carries the output of the legality-verification contractor, which is where a chain-of-custody failure appears if one has been recorded. EITI Reports carries payments to government. Read together they answer who holds the right, what they undertook, and whether anyone has checked. CAVEATS: this is a static document library, not a searchable cadastre — there is no map, no parcel lookup, no stated update cycle and no way to query by county from this page. The Authority also maintains a Liberia Forest Atlas and a Liberia law database under the same Publications menu, both of which were seen only as navigation entries and were not opened for this entry.

trackers.name: Liberia Land Authority — three things in its own mandate that a community can hold it to: the surveyor ban, the FOI duty, and who allocates concessions
trackers.desc: READ THE AUTHORITY'S OWN LIST OF FUNCTIONS BEFORE YOU DEAL WITH IT, BECAUSE THREE OF THEM ARE LEVERS AND ONE IS A WARNING. THE SURVEYOR BAN: the Authority regulates survey and mapping and states that under no condition shall a surveyor or other staff of the Authority engage in the survey of private land, or in the survey of communal land, in a private capacity. If the survey that fixed a boundary against your community was carried out privately by Authority staff, that is prohibited by the Authority's own published mandate and is a complaint you can make in those words. THE FOI DUTY: the Authority must provide information on land holdings and interests in land on request, and its mandate states that this is public information under the Freedom of Information Act of 2010, subject only to charges covering the cost of provision — so a refusal is contestable and a fee is not a refusal. THE ADJUDICATION DOOR: it adjudicates disputes arising in the course of systematic land registration where mediation under the Administrative Procedures Act has failed, which is an administrative route that does not require going to court first. AND THE WARNING: the same body allocates public land for concessions in coordination with the relevant ministries, holds all unallocated public land, and may sell or alienate it with the prior written approval of the President. Its own recent record includes leading land verification and survey for a World Bank-backed solar independent power producer project at Buchanan and touring a free-zone area with the Special Economic Zone Authority and foreign investors. The body that will register your community's claim is the body that allocates concessions over public land — not a reason to avoid it, a reason to put everything in writing. SEPARATELY, on customary land: under the Land Rights Act 2018 communities move through self-identification, by-laws, formation of a Community Land Development and Management Committee, boundary harmonisation, mapping, confirmatory survey and registration, ending in a Statutory Land Deed; deeds have been issued in Nimba, Sinoe, Maryland, Grand Cape Mount and Lofa counties. That deed is ownership of the land, whereas a Community Forest Management Agreement with the Forestry Development Authority is a contract over use of the forest — different instruments, and a community can hold one without the other. CAVEATS: this mandate page was last updated in April 2022; fees are set by Gazette notice rather than published here; and a staging mirror at sandbox.lla.gov.lr serves the same pages and surfaces in search results. Head office Ashmun and Gurley Streets, Monrovia; info@lla.gov.lr; +231-55 576-1013; County Land Offices across the fifteen counties.

trackers.name: LLA news feed — where a County Land Office announces it is reopening the deeds over your clan's land, and the only channel it uses
trackers.desc: THIS IS A NOTICE CHANNEL DISGUISED AS A PRESS PAGE, AND IT CARRIES ITEMS THAT DECIDE THINGS. County Land Offices publish public service announcements here: in April 2026 the Maryland County Land Office announced that it had commenced a comprehensive investigation into all land ownership records, including deeds, within the Gbolobo Clan — an item that appears nowhere else and that anyone holding a deed in that clan would need to know about. The page exposes an RSS feed, so it can be monitored rather than remembered: append &format=feed to the listing URL. The same feed is where the Surveyors Licensing and Registration Board publishes its annual list of registered and licensed surveyors — the 2026 list was announced in February 2026 — which is how you check whether the surveyor who demarcated a boundary against you was licensed at the time. The Authority's Downloadable Resources menu carries a policies, laws and regulations repository, consultants' reports and knowledge products, including its land rights implementation strategy. CAVEATS: the announcements are undated in the feed beyond a publication day, carry no closing date for objections and name no officer to write to, so treat an item as notice that a process has started, not as a deadline you can rely on; and the archive runs to only four pages, so older county notices are not retrievable here.

trackers.name: SDI — walks Liberian communities through customary land formalization, all the way to a statutory customary land deed
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Sustainable Development Institute, a Liberian organisation working on natural resource decision-making, which runs a Community Land Protection Programme taking customary communities through the process created by the 2018 Land Rights Act — the law that provides for recognition, protection and registration of community land rights. THE END POINT IS A DEED, NOT AN AGREEMENT: SDI and partners supported the Fessibu community to receive a Statutory Customary Land Deed issued by the Liberia Land Authority, with the community's own Community Land Development and Management Committee the body that made it possible — under article 35 of the Act the CLDMC manages the community's land with the overall consent of the community. THE STEPS, so you know what you are committing to: Community Self-Identification; agreeing the community land space, resources and boundaries; boundary negotiation and memoranda of understanding with neighbouring communities; developing community by-laws using the Land Authority's own template, built up from each town's traditional rules; forming the CLDMC; then confirmatory survey and registration. SDI trains community leaders and local authorities in each of these, including financial reporting, and has deliberately pushed women into land governance roles in places where it had been male-dominated. WHAT SDI ITSELF SAYS IS GOING WRONG, which you should hear before starting: its staff have publicly told the Land Authority that confirmatory survey and boundary harmonisation remain the bottleneck, that the Authority pleads lack of capacity and equipment, and that formalization is slow and expensive — and communities that have completed the requirements have had to press to be issued their deeds. A plain-language guide, A Guide to Customary Land Formalization, was produced with two partner organisations to widen the pool of people who can help. WHO IT SUITS: customary and forest-dependent communities in Liberia that want documented, deeded title before an investor arrives, and that want to negotiate with companies from a position of known boundaries. P.O. Box 5678, Duarzon Village, Monrovia; +231 (0)330 641355. CAVEATS: this is formalization support, not litigation and not purchase; the timetable depends on a state authority that is itself under-resourced; and much of the work runs inside donor-funded projects in named counties, so ask whether a project is live in yours.

trackers.name: Foundation for Community Initiatives — wrote the plain-language guide to getting a customary land deed, and works 24 communities across 500,000 hectares
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: FCI, a Liberian NGO advocating for women, youth and marginalised groups, which heads a consortium of three Liberian civil society organisations working to secure land tenure for rural communities — with the Sustainable Development Institute and Parley-Liberia, backed by an international tenure fund and the Norwegian government. WHAT IT PRODUCED THAT YOU CAN USE TODAY: a 38-page plain-language manual, “A Guide to Customary Land Formalization: Making the Law Work for the People” — described as the first detailed manual by Liberian CSOs on how to support communities seeking deeds for their land, and a simplified supplement to the national guide. Since the Land Rights Act 2018, lack of awareness of the law has been the main impediment to communities legally owning their customary land, which is why an explainer counts as a resource. THE STEPS THE GUIDE COVERS, and the order matters because each one is a gate: community SELF-IDENTIFICATION, adoption of land and resource BYLAWS, election of a Community Land Development and Management Committee (CLDMC), BOUNDARY HARMONISATION with neighbours, mapping, then confirmatory survey and deed registration. Reported scale: the three organisations working with 24 communities totalling 500,000 hectares across eight counties — Nimba, Lofa, Bassa, River Cess, Bong, Margibi, Maryland and River Gee. Related work elsewhere in Liberia records five clans, more than 41,000 people on over 54,000 hectares, receiving a Statutory Community Deed in 2024. WATCH THIS: analysts note the later stages — confirmatory survey, deed registration, and the provision reserving up to 10 per cent of unused community land as public land — are the least tested; ask early how that 10 per cent will be identified on your map. WHO IT SUITS: Liberian rural communities starting or stuck in customary land formalisation. CAVEATS: a facilitating and advocacy organisation, not a law firm — the survey and registration still run through the Liberia Land Authority, whose surveyor capacity is the recorded bottleneck. For the SDI route and the LLA itself, Liberia's other entries.

trackers.name: SAMFU and SCNL — a foundation built to empower communities hit by logging and plantations, Liberia's oldest conservation organisation which lends to forest families, and the 25-member NGO coalition that petitioned the President over carbon policy
trackers.desc: WHO SPEAKS FOR A CONCESSION-AFFECTED VILLAGE: SAVE MY FUTURE (SAMFU) FOUNDATION, A LOCAL NON-GOVERNMENTAL CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT ORGANISATION FOUNDED IN 1987 BY A LIBERIAN CATHOLIC PRIEST AND TWO YOUNG CONSERVATIONISTS, at Jangaba Avenue, ELWA-Paynesville, PO Box 6829, Monrovia (samfulr.org). ITS STATED WORK IS THE REASON IT LEADS THIS ENTRY: SAMFU WORKS TO EMPOWER COMMUNITIES NEGATIVELY AFFECTED BY NATURAL RESOURCE EXTRACTION, SUCH AS LOGGING AND LARGE-SCALE PLANTATIONS, AND TO HAVE THEM PARTICIPATE IN THE MANAGEMENT PROCESS OF THOSE RESOURCES, educating communities about the impacts of these operations, and partnering ESPECIALLY WITH FOREST FRINGE COMMUNITIES. Forest fringe is the exact position most concession-affected villages occupy — not inside the concession, not far from it, and usually left out of both. An organisation that names that position as its constituency is the right first call. Its recorded field work includes community-based sea turtle conservation across SIX COASTAL COMMUNITIES within the LAKE PISO MULTIPLE USE RESERVE, and work with local fishermen in THREE OF LIBERIA'S NINE COASTAL COUNTIES; it also publishes its own investigative reports on the destruction of Liberia's rainforest. An organisation that publishes named reports is one whose material you can hand to a journalist or a court. THE SOCIETY FOR THE CONSERVATION OF NATURE OF LIBERIA (SCNL), LIBERIA'S OLDEST CONSERVATION ORGANISATION, encourages sustainable use and IMPLEMENTS PROJECTS TO INCREASE ALTERNATIVE LIVELIHOODS FOR FOREST COMMUNITIES THROUGH SMALL LOANS THAT CAN HELP CHILDREN ATTEND SCHOOL AND ALLOW FAMILIES TO HAVE BIGGER FARMS. Small loans routed through a conservation organisation are the rarest instrument in this file: money that reaches a household without a project cycle. Ask SCNL what the terms are. ALSO NAMED, working with communities on forest management, livelihoods and outreach: DEVELOPMENT EDUCATION NETWORK LIBERIA (DEN-L). AND THE BODY WITH THE NUMBERS BEHIND IT: THE NGO COALITION OF LIBERIA, REPRESENTING OVER 25 CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS IN THE FOREST AND NATURAL RESOURCE SECTOR, PETITIONED THE PRESIDENT OF LIBERIA TO DEFER THE ENDORSEMENT AND SIGNING OF THE DRAFT CARBON MARKET POLICY, raising concerns about LIMITED STAKEHOLDER CONSULTATION AND PARTICULARLY THE INSUFFICIENT INCLUSION OF FOREST-DEPENDENT COMMUNITIES AND CIVIL SOCIETY ACTORS IN THE VALIDATION PROCESS. Twenty-five organisations petitioning a head of state to stop signing a carbon policy is what collective weight looks like. If a carbon scheme is being proposed on your forest, that coalition has already objected on the record — join the objection rather than starting one. WHO IT SUITS: Liberian forest-fringe and coastal communities, and any community facing a concession or a carbon scheme. CAVEATS: ADVOCACY AND CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS, not law firms. For customary land formalisation, Liberia's SDI entry; for the plain-language guide, the Foundation for Community Initiatives entry; for who holds the paper over your forest, the Forest Licenses and Permits entry; for the three-county shell, the FDA community forestry entry.

trackers.name: The African Defenders Emergency Fund — decisions in 48 hours for relocation, urgent legal help, medical support or a family after a death or imprisonment — plus Liberia's three-organisation pro bono team and the West African defenders directory
trackers.desc: A DECISION IN FORTY-EIGHT HOURS — and that is the number that matters, because an emergency does not wait for a grant cycle: THE AFRICAN DEFENDERS EMERGENCY FUND SUPPORTS AFRICAN ENVIRONMENTAL AND LAND DEFENDERS WHO FIND THEMSELVES IN EMERGENCY SITUATIONS DUE TO THE NATURE OF THEIR WORK, AND IS INTENDED TO RESPOND TO SITUATIONS SUCH AS TEMPORARY RELOCATION; URGENT LEGAL ASSISTANCE; FINANCIAL SUPPORT TO THE FAMILY IN CASE OF A DEFENDER'S DEATH, SERIOUS INJURY OR IMPRISONMENT; AND URGENT MEDICAL SUPPORT — WITH EMERGENCY REQUESTS SUBMITTABLE ANYTIME AND DECISIONS MADE WITHIN 48 HOURS AFTER SUBMISSION. Read the four categories again. Temporary relocation is money to get somebody out. Support to the family in case of death or imprisonment is money for the people left behind. Those are the two costs that break a campaign, and almost nothing else in this file covers either. Note the fund's address NOW, before you need it — a 48-hour decision is only fast if you are not spending three days finding the form. WHO CAN APPLY, IN THE FUND'S OWN TERMS: ANY PERSON WHO IS A CITIZEN OF ANY AFRICAN COUNTRY OR A PERSON LEGALLY RESIDING OR WORKING IN ANY AFRICAN COUNTRY; IS AN ACTIVE FRONTLINE LAND AND ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS DEFENDER WORKING ON ISSUES RELATED TO LAND RIGHTS, ENVIRONMENTAL AND CLIMATE JUSTICE — INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO RIGHTS OVER NATURAL RESOURCES, LAND OR ENVIRONMENTAL CONFLICTS, LAND GRABBING AND LAND REFORM; IS FACING AN IMMINENT THREAT OR HARM DUE TO THE NATURE OF HIS OR HER WORK; AND HAS NOT SECURED ANY OTHER KIND OF SUPPORT FROM ANOTHER ENTITY FOR THE EMERGENCY. ANY PERSON. Not an organisation, not a registered body — an individual defender, and LAND GRABBING is named in the eligible issues. A village chairperson under threat qualifies on their own. WHAT IT WILL NOT COVER, SO YOU DO NOT WASTE THE 48 HOURS: MAINTENANCE AND CURRENT ADMINISTRATIVE OR OFFICE EXPENSES, AND HUMAN RIGHTS PROGRAMMES THAT ARE NOT RELATED TO A SPECIFIC AND CONTINGENT SITUATION OF VIOLATION OF RIGHTS. It is for the emergency only. Your rent and your programme go elsewhere — this file's litigation-expenses and small-grants entries are where. THE SECOND DOOR, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING IF YOU ARE NOT AN INDIVIDUAL: BENEFICIARIES ALSO INCLUDE MEMBERS OF THE LAND COALITION — INDIVIDUALS IN MEMBER ORGANISATIONS OR THE ORGANISATIONS THEMSELVES — AND MEMBERS CAN ALSO APPLY ON BEHALF OF ORGANIZATIONS AND COMMUNITIES. A member can apply on behalf of a community. So if your village is not a member of anything, find one that is: the coalition has over 300 members whose shared goal is LAND GOVERNANCE FOR AND WITH PEOPLE AT THE COUNTRY LEVEL, RESPONDING TO THE NEEDS AND PROTECTING THE RIGHTS OF WOMEN, MEN AND COMMUNITIES WHO LIVE ON AND FROM THE LAND. Its partners in the fund are named and include an indigenous and community conserved areas consortium, a pan-African climate justice alliance, a women's network and a youth network — so there are several routes in. THE LIBERIAN STRUCTURE, AND IT IS A MODEL: A LIBERIA TEAM COMPRISES THREE PARTNER ORGANISATIONS — A PUBLIC INTEREST ENVIRONMENTAL LAW ORGANISATION, AN ALLIANCE FOR RURAL DEMOCRACY, AND A NATURAL RESOURCE WOMEN PLATFORM — WORKING TOGETHER TO ENSURE COMMUNITIES' RIGHTS ARE NOT VIOLATED, THAT AWARENESS INFORMATION IS GIVEN ON PROJECTS, AND TO PROVIDE PRO BONO LEGAL SUPPORT TO VULNERABLE COMMUNITIES. Lawyers, a rural membership alliance and a women's platform as a standing team of three. That division of labour — who litigates, who mobilises, who makes sure women are heard — is the one to reproduce, and in Liberia it is formalised rather than improvised. THE ALLIANCE FOR RURAL DEMOCRACY IS A NETWORK OF COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANIZATIONS AS WELL AS PRO-POOR ENTERPRISING INFORMAL SECTOR ORGANIZATIONS FROM ACROSS LIBERIA, WORKING IN SOLIDARITY ACTIONS TO ADDRESS THE PROBLEMS OF THE RURAL POOR, URBAN SLUMS AND SQUATTER COMMUNITIES, INFORMAL SECTOR INSTITUTIONS AND NEWLY EMERGING INDEPENDENT LABOR UNIONS — AND IT HAS MEMBERSHIP IN ALL OF LIBERIA'S FIFTEEN POLITICAL SUB-DIVISIONS. All fifteen counties. And the WOMEN PLATFORM SERVES AS THE FORUM FOR AMPLIFYING THE VOICES OF HISTORICALLY UNDER-REPRESENTED WOMEN, working with both rural and urban women. AND THE DIRECTORY BEING BUILT: a WEST AFRICAN FRONTLINE GRASSROOTS DEFENDERS DIRECTORY is being launched to CONNECT THE UNCONNECTED AND ESTABLISH A SUPPORT AND RESPONSE MECHANISM FOR FRONTLINE GRASSROOTS ENVIRONMENTAL, LAND, AND HUMAN RIGHTS DEFENDERS ACROSS WEST AFRICA, following a BASELINE ASSESSMENT covering West Africa plus Equatorial Guinea, built on interviews and profiles of defenders in POOR RURAL AND URBAN SLUM COMMUNITIES. A directory whose stated purpose is connecting people who do not know each other exist. If you are a defender in West Africa, being IN it is the point — ask how to be listed, because the response mechanism follows the list. WHO IT SUITS: any African land or environmental defender facing an imminent threat, and West African community organisations wanting to be findable. CAVEATS: THE EMERGENCY FUND IS FOR EMERGENCIES ONLY and requires that no other support has been secured. For Liberia's public interest environmental law organisation, the Green Advocates entry; for emergency grants under the same fund's own site, the African Environmental Defenders Fund entry; for litigation expenses on a one-case basis, the EDLC entry; for investigative reports and small loans to forest families, SAMFU and SCNL.

trackers.name: The Tenure Facility and CLARIFI — two funders that pay communities to secure their own land title, one conceived by and for Indigenous Peoples, the other regranting USD 100k to 50 million to organisations that already exist
trackers.desc: A HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS TO FIFTY MILLION, TO ORGANISATIONS THAT ALREADY EXIST — placement note first: BOTH FUNDERS ARE GLOBAL, FILED UNDER LIBERIA ONLY BECAUSE THIS FILE HAS NO GLOBAL KEY AND LIBERIA IS ONE OF THE SIX NAMED PILOT COUNTRIES AND ONE OF FIVE AFRICAN GOVERNMENTS NAMED FOR NEW LAND-PROJECT SUPPORT. THE TENURE FACILITY IS DESCRIBED AS THE LEADING FINANCIAL MECHANISM SPECIALISED IN SUPPORTING INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND LOCAL COMMUNITIES TO SECURE AND SUSTAIN THEIR LAND AND FOREST RIGHTS, WORKING DIRECTLY WITH PARTNERS TO PROVIDE TARGETED FUNDING ALONG WITH TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE — OFFERING FLEXIBLE, TIMELY AND DIRECT SUPPORT TO INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND LOCAL COMMUNITY ORGANISATIONS, AND STATING THAT IT WAS CONCEIVED BY AND FOR INDIGENOUS PEOPLES. DIRECT support to community organisations, with technical assistance attached. Not a conservation NGO holding the grant on your behalf — your organisation is the grantee. That is the arrangement this file keeps telling you to insist on, and here is a fund built around it. WHAT IT PRODUCED, WITH THE NUMBER: IN ITS FIRST TWO YEARS OF OPERATION, ITS SIX PILOT PROJECTS HELPED TO ADVANCE COLLECTIVE TENURE SECURITY FOR ALMOST 1.8 MILLION HECTARES OF LAND AND FOREST IN CAMEROON, INDONESIA, LIBERIA, MALI, PANAMA AND PERU — PROVING THAT WITH STRATEGIC FUNDING AND TECHNICAL SUPPORT, INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' AND LOCAL COMMUNITIES' ORGANIZATIONS CAN ACHIEVE SIGNIFICANT RESULTS IN A SHORT PERIOD OF TIME. Three African countries in the first six projects, and 1.8 million hectares secured in two years. That is the scale of what titling money buys — and it is COLLECTIVE tenure, which this file has repeatedly shown is the form that survives pressure. THE HONEST NOTE IT MAKES ABOUT ITSELF: MANY COMMUNITIES MAY STRUGGLE FOR DECADES TO GAIN RECOGNITION AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT OF THEIR MANAGEMENT OF THEIR ANCESTRAL TERRITORIES, IN SOME CASES FACING VIOLENCE AND EVICTION ALONG THE WAY — AND GIVEN ITS RELATIVELY LARGE GRANTS AND THE POLITICAL CHALLENGES IN SOME COUNTRIES WHERE IT WORKS, IT DEVOTES GREAT ATTENTION TO FINANCIAL ASSURANCE AND RISK MANAGEMENT, WHICH IT SEEKS TO ADAPT TO LOCAL NEEDS AND CIRCUMSTANCES. Large grants mean serious financial assurance. Expect audits and reporting requirements, and build the bookkeeping before you apply — a community organisation that cannot account for money will not hold a grant of this size, however good its case. AND THE FISHERS' WINDOW, WHICH IS SEPARATE: ITS FUND SERVES AS THE FISCAL SPONSOR OF AN INTERNATIONAL GRANTMAKING FACILITY DEDICATED TO SUPPORTING TENURE RIGHTS OF LOCAL COMMUNITIES, SMALL-SCALE FISHERS AND FISH WORKERS, AND INDIGENOUS PEOPLES. Small-scale fishers AND FISH WORKERS named separately. If your people process or trade the catch rather than land it, that is a constituency with its own funder. THE SECOND FUNDER, AND ITS TERMS ARE PUBLISHED: A COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS AND CONSERVATION FINANCE INITIATIVE IS A REGRANTING MECHANISM THAT WILL ALLOCATE FUNDING TO EXISTING INDIGENOUS, AFRO-DESCENDANT, LOCAL, AND WOMEN-LED ORGANIZATIONS RATHER THAN IMPLEMENTING PROJECTS DIRECTLY — AIMING TO PROVIDE GRANTS OF USD $100,000 TO USD $50 MILLION, AND ALSO TO SERVE AS A TRUSTED FIDUCIARY FOR NATIONAL AND REGIONAL-LEVEL FUNDS ESTABLISHED BY INDIGENOUS AND COMMUNITY ORGANIZATIONS. RATHER THAN IMPLEMENTING PROJECTS DIRECTLY is the whole design. And AFRO-DESCENDANT and WOMEN-LED organisations are named as eligible categories in their own right — not everything has to be framed as indigenous. The floor is a hundred thousand dollars, so this is not a village grant; it is for the national or regional body your community belongs to. Find out which one, and ask whether it has applied. THE FIDUCIARY OFFER IS THE QUIET ONE: it will act as TRUSTED FIDUCIARY FOR FUNDS ESTABLISHED BY INDIGENOUS AND COMMUNITY ORGANIZATIONS THEMSELVES. If your movement wants its own fund but cannot yet hold and audit large sums, somebody will hold it for you while you build that capacity. That is the bridge between a community fund existing on paper and one that donors will pay into. ITS DESIGN IS GUIDED BY AN ADVISORY COUNCIL INCLUDING INDIGENOUS AND COMMUNITY RIGHTSHOLDER REPRESENTATIVES FROM ASIA, AFRICA AND LATIN AMERICA. THE OFFICIALS' ROOM, WHICH LIBERIA CHAIRED: MORE THAN 100 PARTICIPANTS FROM 11 COUNTRIES WORKING TO SECURE COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS GATHERED FOR A 4th CONFERENCE OF NATIONAL LAND INSTITUTIONS, ATTENDED BY AN AFRICA LAND POLICY CENTRE, A UN FOOD AGENCY, THE AFRICAN DEVELOPMENT BANK, A GERMAN DEVELOPMENT AGENCY AND THE TENURE FACILITY — WITH THE FINAL DECLARATION DELIVERED BY THE CHAIRMAN OF THE LIBERIA LAND AUTHORITY. AND THE SENTENCE TO QUOTE AT A BANK: AN AfDB CHIEF LAND OFFICER STATED THAT COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS HAS BEEN IDENTIFIED AS A POWERFUL CHALLENGE FOR LAND INVESTMENT PROJECTS IN AFRICA, AND THAT AfDB HAS DEVELOPED GUIDELINES TO ENSURE THAT NEGATIVE IMPACTS ON COMMUNITIES ARE MINIMIZED IN ALL ITS PROJECTS. The bank's own chief land officer says it has guidelines for this. Ask for them by name when an AfDB-financed project reaches your land — and remember this file's separate entry: two or more harmed people can complain to that bank directly. WHO IT SUITS: national and regional community organisations pursuing collective title, and movements wanting their own fund held for them. CAVEATS: THESE ARE LARGE-GRANT FUNDERS working through established partners — a village association applies through a national body, not alone. For customary land formalization step by step, Liberia's SDI entry; for the plain-language guide, Foundation for Community Initiatives; for three things in its own mandate a community can use, the Liberia Land Authority entry; for the 48-hour emergency fund, the African Defenders Emergency Fund entry.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: National Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Malawi, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: MalawiLII
trackers.desc: Malawi Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Malawi judgments and legislation (MalawiLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: MBRS / CRIPC Business Registry
trackers.desc: National — Malawi Business Registration System (Companies Registration & Intellectual Property Centre). — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Malawi — Ministry of Finance & Economic Affairs
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the Treasury’s Budget Division prepares the national budget and formulates fiscal & economic policy, Malawi. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Malawi.

trackers.name: Malawi Human Rights Commission (MHRC)
trackers.desc: Malawi Human Rights Commission (MHRC) — Malawi’s Human Rights Commission — the oversight body for the Access to Information Act, receiving complaints and monitoring compliance. — Holds to account: Malawi’s public bodies on disclosure — find access-to-information complaint handling, compliance monitoring and reports.

trackers.name: Platform for Investigative Journalism, Malawi
trackers.desc: Malawian nonprofit newsroom investigating corruption and the misuse of public money.

trackers.name: Legal Aid Bureau — district offices, land disputes included
trackers.desc: A FREE LAWYER IN YOUR DISTRICT, AND LAND DISPUTES ARE ON THE LIST. Established under Section 3 of the Legal Aid Act 2011, giving effect to section 41 of the Constitution, the Bureau serves anyone in need of legal assistance who cannot afford a private lawyer. The civil matters it handles expressly include land disputes, alongside maintenance, matrimonial, adoption and personal injury — so a land case is not carved out as it is under many legal aid schemes. It represents clients in all courts in Malawi, from the subordinate courts up to the Supreme Court. WHERE TO GO: offices sit inside District Commissioner's Office complexes, district council buildings and magistrates court complexes — Mulanje, Mangochi, Machinga at Liwonde, Phalombe, Balaka, Mwanza and Nsanje among them — with addresses, phone numbers and email published per district on this page.

trackers.name: Malawi CBNRM Forum — buffer zones held in trust by Traditional Authorities
trackers.desc: IF YOUR SITE IS NEAR A PROTECTED AREA, THIS NETWORK IS ALREADY ORGANISED AROUND THAT GEOGRAPHY. The CBNRM Forum and its members cater for 3.8 million people living within 15 km of Malawi's national parks, wildlife reserves and forests, collectively managing over 1.8 million hectares of forests on customary land and 0.5 million hectares of protected area buffer zones held in trust by Traditional Authorities. THE BUFFER-ZONE-IN-TRUST MODEL IS THE DISTINCTIVE PART: land adjoining a protected area, held by the Traditional Authority, is where community management is concentrated — so the Traditional Authority is the counterparty for land at the boundary of a reserve, not the parks department alone. Contrast Botswana, where community access rests on policy directives rather than legislation: here the holding is through customary trust, which is a different and more durable footing. The Forum is also the route to peers already managing comparable land.

trackers.name: Land clerk and customary land committee — 30 days from publication of the adjudication record, and the certificate goes to the chief, not to you
trackers.desc: TWO DIFFERENT PIECES OF PAPER EXIST AND PEOPLE CONFUSE THEM: the Commissioner issues a certificate of customary land in the name of the Traditional Authority for a whole Traditional Land Management Area, while an individual household holds a customary estate inside it. The chief's certificate is not your title and your estate is not the chief's to give away. To register a customary estate you wait for adjudication and demarcation of the parcels, then complete Form 2 of the First Schedule and submit it to the customary land committee; a land clerk issues the adjudication record on Form 1 and keeps the customary land register — the final adjudication record, the demarcation record and the registry maps. A registered customary estate is of indefinite duration, inheritable and transmissible by will. THE DEADLINE THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING: a person aggrieved by a determination of a land committee has thirty days from the publication of the adjudication record and demarcation map to appeal to the customary land tribunal for that area; from there the ladder runs to the district land tribunal and then to the Central Land Board. Thirty days from publication, not from when you heard — so ask the land clerk when publication happened and get the date in writing. TWO PROVISIONS WORTH QUOTING BACK: a land committee or adjudication officer must treat the rights of women and other vulnerable groups no less favourably than those of men, and a customary land tribunal is not quorate without at least four members, two of whom are women — a hearing held without them is defective on its face. WHERE THE PEOPLE ARE: the ministry has deployed land clerks at Traditional Authority level and district land registrars in the councils, reported at 319 and 34 respectively, so the clerk is the nearest office rather than the ministry. Ministry of Lands, Zowe House, City Centre, Lilongwe; lands@lands.gov.mw. CAVEATS: the forms, the thirty-day limit and the quorum were read from the Customary Land Act as published by the Malawi legal information institute and by FAO's legislative database, not from this ministry page, which describes the lease route rather than customary registration; and registration began as a pilot in a handful of districts, so coverage is uneven and the register may not yet exist for your area.

trackers.name: CEPA — founded by Malawi's environmental law practitioners, and the body that gets communities into the room over a draft mining EIA
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Centre for Environmental Policy and Advocacy, founded in 2002 by Malawi's environmental law practitioners as the country's first organisation dedicated to environmental policy and advocacy, registered as a Trust in 2022. Its stated work includes facilitating access to environmental information, access to justice and public participation — the three things a community needs before it can object to anything — alongside policy research on land and agrarian reform and programmes on minerals, land, water, fisheries and wildlife. WHAT IT HAS ACTUALLY PUT COMMUNITIES INTO: its published work records a Malingunde mining committee engaging directly with company officials over the draft Environmental Impact Assessment report, under a mining governance project — a community body reading the developer's own EIA and questioning it face to face is the single most useful thing a project-affected village can do, and this is an organisation that arranges it. It also works with artisanal salt and small-scale miners, and builds the capacity of civil society organisations across Malawi to take part in these processes. Its programme manager Gloria Majiga-Kamoto won the Goldman Environmental Prize for Africa in 2021 for the campaign that got Malawi's ban on single-use plastics enforced — evidence that the organisation's people litigate and campaign to an outcome, not just publish. It runs a resource centre inside its office, open to the public on weekdays. Globe House, Raynor Avenue, Plot CC 365, Limbe, Blantyre; +265 212 700 104; info@cepa.org.mw. WHO IT SUITS: Malawian communities facing mining, land conversion or water and fisheries loss, and local organisations that need the policy and legal groundwork done. CAVEATS: a think tank and advocacy institution rather than a legal aid service — it was founded by lawyers but does not advertise representation, and no intake route or fee information was published; a legacy website mirror also carries older content, so use the current domain.

trackers.name: CCODE and the Malawi federation — the Mchenga Fund bought land on the open market, then started land banking for future need
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY AND BUY LAND: the Centre for Community Organisation and Development (CCODE), a Lilongwe-based non-profit founded in 2003, working in alliance with the grassroots savings network known as the Malawi Homeless People's Federation, later the Federation of the Rural and Urban Poor — reported at over 50,000 members across 26 districts, about 80 per cent of them women. THE FUND: members established the Mchenga Fund, capitalised by community savings plus donor funding, with members originally contributing MK20 a month; since 2003 it has made group loans for house construction. The name is the argument — mchenga means sand: single savings are grains, uncountable alone, decisive together. It exists because commercial lenders will not touch these households, and because shelter microfinance cannot fund collective investment in upgrading or new build at all where tenure is insecure — which is precisely the situation most people in this file are in. THE TWO MOVES WORTH COPYING: when land access delayed a project, the federation and CCODE secured land through MARKET PURCHASE using Mchenga Fund resources; and, having been burned by those delays, the federation decided to invest in LAND BANKING in informal settlements — buying and holding land ahead of need so future community projects are not hostage to whoever controls allocation. Reported results include tenure and decent housing secured for over 1,000 households and improved sanitation for over 2,500. WHO IT SUITS: Malawian low-income urban and rural households wanting a route to land and housing outside the banks, and groups considering buying land collectively before they need it. CAVEATS: THE RESEARCH IS BLUNT ABOUT STRAIN — repayment rates on the first loans approached 100 per cent but declined over the years; demand far outstrips the fund and the land available (in one city 222 houses against demand for 600, in another 83 against 600); and one project site was itself subject to a land grab. CCODE's own site did not resolve to a verified page — this entry points at a housing-fund partner record. For mining and EIA work, Malawi's CEPA entry is the route.

trackers.name: LandNet Malawi — the national land network to route through, in a country where paralegals are recognised in the Legal Aid Act
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: LandNet Malawi, the national land network of Malawian civil society organisations working on land and natural resource management, and Malawi's member of the international land coalition. Its stated objectives are to strengthen the advocacy and lobbying capacity of Malawian organisations engaged in land and natural resources, and to strengthen coordination between them through networking and information sharing — so for a community that does not know which organisation handles its problem, this is the routing layer. Its vision is land policy and legislation responsive to the needs of poor, vulnerable and marginalised groups. Its constituency is its own network members. P.O. Box 31437, Lilongwe 3. THE FACT THAT MAKES MALAWI DIFFERENT, and it is worth knowing before you look for help: community paralegals are RECOGNISED IN MALAWI'S LEGAL AID ACT OF 2010 as “Legal Aid Assistants” — a statutory basis most countries in this file lack — while other grassroots legal advocates operate outside that scheme, deployed by civil society organisations and known simply as paralegals. Ask whether the person helping you is a statutory Legal Aid Assistant or an NGO paralegal, because it changes what they can do inside the formal system. The pledges its network signs include protection for land rights defenders and equal land rights for women, including the right to inherit and bequeath tenure rights. WHO IT SUITS: Malawians who need to find the right land organisation, and organisations wanting to join a national land advocacy platform. CAVEATS: a NETWORK AND ADVOCACY PLATFORM — casework happens at member organisations, so expect a referral; the entry points at the coalition's member record because that is the verified public listing. For mining and EIA review, Malawi's CEPA entry; for savings-based land purchase and land banking, the CCODE entry.

trackers.name: Malawi Legal Aid Bureau — takes LAND DISPUTES, represents you in every court up to the Supreme Court, and has district offices inside existing government buildings
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET A FREE LAWYER: the Legal Aid Bureau, established under section 3 of the Legal Aid Act 2011 with a statutory mandate to provide legal aid to indigent and vulnerable people, and described as THE ONLY SUCH INSTITUTION IN MALAWI. It gives effect to section 41 of the Constitution, and its stated priority groups are women, children, the elderly and the sick. WHY IT IS IN A LAND MAP: its published civil caseload expressly includes LAND DISPUTES, alongside deceased estates, labour matters, maintenance and matrimonial cases — and it REPRESENTS CLIENTS IN ALL COURTS IN MALAWI, from the subordinate courts up the hierarchy to the SUPREME COURT. That is representation through appeal, not first advice — the thing most entries in this file cannot offer. WHERE IT IS, and the pattern is worth copying: four regional offices — Lilongwe (headquarters, 1st Floor Shire Building off Paul Kagame Highway, +265 1 753 945), Blantyre (Government Office Building, Lower Victoria Avenue, +265 1 822 082), Mzuzu (1st Floor Osman Gani Building, +265 1 311 086) and Zomba (Old Parliament Building, +265 1 528 856) — plus DISTRICT OFFICES HOUSED INSIDE BUILDINGS PEOPLE ALREADY VISIT: the Mchinji District Assembly Hall, the District Education Manager's office in Kasungu, and the Ministry of Agriculture building in Salima. Putting the legal aid desk in the agriculture office is how a rural service reaches people who would never travel to a regional capital — ask whether your district has one before assuming the nearest office is hours away. info@legalaidbureau.org. It also runs public legal education. WHO IT SUITS: Malawians who cannot afford a private lawyer and face a land dispute, an estate or eviction — particularly women, the elderly and the sick. CAVEATS: A STATE BUREAU with a means test and finite counsel; it is not a campaigning body and will not oppose a government project on your behalf. For mining and EIA review, Malawi's CEPA entry; for savings-based land purchase and land banking, CCODE; for finding the right member organisation, LandNet.

trackers.name: WESM and CURE — Malawi's oldest conservation society, membership-based with nine branches and 1,500 wildlife clubs, and the apex environmental NGO whose member directory publishes each organisation's contact
trackers.desc: THE MEMBERSHIP SOCIETY THAT PROPOSED THE PARKS: the WILDLIFE AND ENVIRONMENTAL SOCIETY OF MALAWI (WESM, wesm.mw), FOUNDED 1947 IN BLANTYRE as the Nyasaland Fauna Preservation Society — MALAWI'S OLDEST CONSERVATION NGO — which IN THE 1950s AND 60s WAS ACTIVE IN PROPOSING AND HELPING TO ESTABLISH MALAWI'S RESERVES AND PARKS: LENGWE, MAJETE, MWABVI AND NYIKA, and which HOLDS HISTORICAL BIODIVERSITY DATA AND CONDUCTS RESEARCH THAT INFORMS NATIONAL POLICY. An organisation that proposed the country's existing parks holds the precedent for proposing another. And its historical biodiversity data is what proves what used to live where — ask WESM for its records on your area before a consultant tells you the site has no value. WHAT IT IS AND HOW BIG: A MEMBERSHIP ORGANISATION WITH OVER 500 INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS, MORE THAN 1,500 WILDLIFE CLUBS AND NINE BRANCHES SPREAD ACROSS THE COUNTRY — Blantyre, Lilongwe, Mzuzu, Zomba and others including a Monkey Bay branch — with a secretariat established 1992 and projects focused on WORKING WITH COMMUNITIES BORDERING ENVIRONMENTALLY IMPORTANT AREAS: NATIONAL PARKS, WILDLIFE RESERVES AND FOREST RESERVES. Its stated purpose is TO INFORM AND SUPPORT PUBLIC PARTICIPATION IN THE WISE USE OF MALAWI'S WILDLIFE AND NATURAL ENVIRONMENT AND ALWAYS SPEAK UP FOR IT IN NATIONAL AND LOCAL DEVELOPMENT EFFORTS AND FORA. Speaking up in development fora is written into its own purpose, and it SITS ON A NUMBER OF GOVERNMENT BODIES with established links to the Departments of National Parks and Wildlife, Forestry and Environmental Affairs. A society that already has a seat is who you ask to raise your objection where it is heard. ITS SCALE OF WORK: one project is a THREE-YEAR GRANT OF £312,000 from a foreign government to work with communities and LOCAL GOVERNMENT on a COMMUNITY APPROACH TO WATERBIRD RESOURCE MANAGEMENT at Chia Lagoon; it draws on long-standing relationships with associates across the country, volunteers and a handful of key employees. A membership society running a three-hundred-thousand-pound project on a handful of staff means volunteers do the work — joining is a real contribution, and membership is how a village gains standing inside it. AND THE DIRECTORY: THE COORDINATION UNION FOR THE REHABILITATION OF THE ENVIRONMENT (CURE, cure-mw.org), AN APEX ENVIRONMENTAL INSTITUTION ESTABLISHED 1994 AND REGISTERED UNDER THE TRUSTEES INCORPORATION ACT IN 1999, PUBLISHES A MEMBERS DIRECTORY GIVING EACH ORGANISATION'S NAMED CONTACT PERSON, POSTAL ADDRESS, WORK PHONE, WHATSAPP NUMBER, EMAIL AND WEBSITE — WESM's own entry lists a named contact at Private Bag 578, Limbe with all of those. A published apex directory with a WhatsApp number per organisation is the fastest way into Malawian civil society. Look up your district's members before writing to anyone. CURE has also commissioned position papers on the state of Malawi's forests, recording that the country LOST OVER 40% OF ITS FOREST COVER BETWEEN 1972 AND 1990 and naming LAND TENURE AND OWNERSHIP OF TREES AND FORESTS, POLICY AND IMPLEMENTATION FAILURE, POOR GOVERNANCE AT LOCAL LEVEL AND INADEQUATE FUNDING among the causes. WHO IT SUITS: Malawian communities bordering a park, reserve or forest reserve, and anyone seeking the right organisation in their district. CAVEATS: MEMBERSHIP AND APEX BODIES with close government links — not litigators. For land bought on the open market through a savings fund, Malawi's CCODE and federation entry; for the legal aid route, the Malawi Legal Aid Bureau entry.

trackers.name: Lilongwe Wildlife Trust — both registration numbers printed, secretariat of the Malawi Parliamentary Conservation Caucus, and the march by three local charities that produced a 3,700-signature petition and a government pledge
trackers.desc: TWO REGISTRATION NUMBERS AND A SEAT IN PARLIAMENT: LILONGWE WILDLIFE TRUST IS REGISTERED UNDER THE TRUSTEE INCORPORATION ACT OF MALAWI, No. TR/INC4209, AND IS A MEMBER OF THE COUNCIL OF NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANIZATIONS OF MALAWI, No. C466 — founded 2007 as a Charitable Trust, at LILONGWE WILDLIFE CENTRE, PO BOX 2140, LILONGWE, telephone +265 111206830. Two numbers, both printed: the trust incorporation and the NGO council membership. That is the pair a Malawian organisation needs — the Trustee Incorporation Act is how a body becomes able to hold property in perpetuity, and the council number is how it becomes recognised by the sector. Ask any organisation offering to help you for both. AND THE ROUTE ALMOST NOTHING ELSE IN THIS FILE HAS: LWT IS THE SECRETARIAT FOR THE MALAWI PARLIAMENTARY CONSERVATION CAUCUS. An NGO holding the secretariat of a parliamentary caucus means the papers that reach that caucus pass through its hands. If your case needs to be in front of MPs rather than officials, that is the shortest route in Malawi — ask the secretariat what the caucus is currently considering and how a community submission is tabled. IT ALSO HOLDS TWO OTHER SEATS: IT PROVIDES CIVIL SOCIETY REPRESENTATION TO THE INTER-AGENCY COMMITTEE ON COMBATING WILDLIFE CRIME, AND IT IS THE LOCAL NGO REPRESENTATIVE ON THE STEERING COMMITTEE OF THE MALAWI NATIONAL ELEPHANT ACTION PLAN. Note the phrase LOCAL NGO REPRESENTATIVE. Where a steering committee reserves a seat for a local organisation, that seat is a category, not a favour — ask which body holds it on the committee that governs your area, and ask how the holder is chosen. WHAT IT DOES WITH THOSE SEATS: IT PARTNERED WITH THE GOVERNMENT TO REVIEW AND STRENGTHEN THE NATIONAL PARKS AND WILDLIFE ACT, was lead partner in an assessment of the nature and status of illegal wildlife trade CONDUCTED ON BEHALF OF THE GOVERNMENT, and runs a CONSERVATION JUSTICE programme covering a wildlife act amendment bill and a wildlife justice programme, alongside a WILDLIFE EMERGENCY RESPONSE UNIT and schools outreach. Conservation justice as a named programme, with a legislative bill inside it, is legal capacity attached to a conservation charity. If your Malawian case is environmental crime rather than land title, that is the programme to ask for by name. AND THE SEQUENCE WORTH COPYING, BECAUSE EVERY STEP IS NAMED: LOCAL WILDLIFE CHARITIES — WILDLIFE ACTION GROUP, LILONGWE WILDLIFE TRUST AND WESM — ORGANISED A MARCH WHICH SAW HUNDREDS FROM SCHOOLS, CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS AND NATIONAL PARKS OFFICES PARADE THROUGH THE CAPITAL CITY TO GOVERNMENT HEADQUARTERS, PRESENTING A PETITION SIGNED BY OVER 3,700 PEOPLE ASKING THE GOVERNMENT TO TAKE ACTION — AND THE GOVERNMENT'S PLEDGE CAME IN A SPEECH FOLLOWING THE MARCH, AFTER WHICH A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW OF THE LEGISLATION WAS COMMISSIONED. Three local charities, schools and PARKS OFFICE STAFF marching together, 3,700 signatures, a pledge in a speech, then a legislative review. That is a complete campaign arc with every stage documented — and the detail worth noticing is that national parks office staff walked in it. Where the agency's own people will march alongside you, the ask is not adversarial, and the government can say yes without losing. THE MEMBERSHIP SOCIETY ALONGSIDE IT: WESM, ESTABLISHED 1947, IS THE OLDEST CONSERVATION NGO IN MALAWI, A MEMBERSHIP BASED ORGANISATION THAT WAS BEHIND THE PROPOSAL OF ESTABLISHMENT OF MAJOR NATIONAL PARKS IN MALAWI — AND IT HOLDS HISTORICAL BIODIVERSITY DATA AND CONDUCTS RESEARCH THAT INFORMS NATIONAL POLICY. Historical biodiversity data held by a membership society is a baseline no developer can produce or dispute. Ask WESM what its records show for your site before anybody surveys it. Its named restoration work includes A 1953 DAM SILTED BY DECADES OF DEFORESTATION AND LAND CLEARANCE, AND A 17 SQUARE KILOMETRE LAGOON INSIDE A 989 SQUARE KILOMETRE WATERSHED, and Malawi has committed to RESTORING A FURTHER 4.5 MILLION HECTARES BY 2030. 4.5 million hectares is a national commitment with a deadline and no obvious owner.
