THIS FILE'S SOMALIA ENTRY NAMES A COASTAL LINKS ORGANISATION IN A LIST OF EIGHT MOVEMENTS WITHOUT DESCRIBING IT OR SHIPPING THIS HOST; ITS NIGER AND RWANDA ENTRIES USE THE RIGHT-TO-SAY-NO PHRASE IN OTHER ENTRIES; ITS MALI ENTRY THE FISHERS' CO-OPERATIVE LITIGATION. NONE IS RESTATED AND NONE OF THOSE HOSTS IS SHIPPED. THE COURT CASE AND WHAT IT FORCED, WHICH IS THE FIND: IN 2004 LEGAL ACTION WAS LAUNCHED AGAINST THE MINISTER CONCERNED, CITING CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS TO FOOD SECURITY, CULTURE, AND THE RIGHT TO OCCUPATIONS AND LIVELIHOODS — AND IN 2007 THE MINISTER SIGNED AN OUT OF COURT AGREEMENT THAT OBLIGED THE GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP A NEW FISHERIES POLICY ACCOMMODATING THE SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC RIGHTS OF 30,000 SMALL-SCALE FISHER PEOPLE. Not damages for one community — a national policy, written because a fishers' organisation sued. Three years from filing to settlement, and the remedy was legislative. That is the largest ratio of effort to outcome recorded in this file, and the grounds are worth copying: FOOD SECURITY, CULTURE, AND OCCUPATION, rather than property. A community with no title has all three. THE STRUCTURE OF THE ORGANISATION THEY BUILT, WHICH IS THE SECOND FIND: ESTABLISHED IN 2003, WITH OVER 2,000 MEMBERS ACROSS 89 COASTAL TOWNS IN FOUR PROVINCES IN ONE ACCOUNT AND 4,000 IN ANOTHER — WITH PROVINCIAL, REGIONAL, SUB-REGIONAL AND BRANCH STRUCTURES; EACH BRANCH HAS A COMMITTEE WITH ELECTED OFFICIALS WHO REPRESENT THEM ON THE REGIONAL COMMITTEE, AND A REGION ELECTS A REGIONAL SECRETARY AND CHAIRPERSON. Four tiers, every one elected from below. That is the constitutional shape to copy for any scattered set of villages: the branch elects its committee, the branch committee sits regionally, the region elects its own officers. Nobody is appointed downward, which is what this file records going wrong when a national body speaks for communities it did not consult. THE APPEAL COURT RULING BEHIND IT: A 2018 SUPREME COURT OF APPEAL RULING RECOGNISED THE RIGHTS OF SMALL-SCALE FISHERS TO CONTINUE CUSTOMARY FISHING PRACTICES. Customary practice recognised by an appellate court — the same argument this file's Guinea-Bissau entry records being made about customary land, won here on water. THE TRIBUNAL AND WHAT IT WAS FOR: A FISHER PEOPLE TRIBUNAL HELD OVER THREE DAYS IN A NAMED CHURCH, THE COUNTRY'S FIRST PEOPLE'S TRIBUNAL FOCUSED ON FISHING COMMUNITIES — ATTEMPTING TO DOCUMENT AND EXPOSE OCEAN GRABBING AND THE VIOLATIONS OF FISHING COMMUNITIES' RIGHTS, AND TO CHECK IF THEIR RIGHTS ARE BEING MET; A JURY VERDICT WAS LAUNCHED PUBLICLY AFTERWARDS. A people's tribunal with a jury and a published verdict, held in a church hall over three days. It has no legal force, and that is the point: where the state will not hold a hearing, the community holds its own, on the record, with testimony that can then be used elsewhere. Cheap, and entirely within a coalition's own control. WHAT THE CAMPAIGNING ACTUALLY CONSISTED OF: STREET CAMPAIGNS, MEDIA COVERAGE, DIPLOMATIC MEETINGS WITH LOCAL AND NATIONAL GOVERNMENT, AND THE COURT CASE — WHICH LED TO ONE OF THEIR MOST SIGNIFICANT VICTORIES. Four instruments used together. The litigation is listed last and did not stand alone. THE THREATS THE MEMBERSHIP ORGANISATION NAMES: THE PRIVATISATION OF COASTAL LAND THAT LIMITS ACCESS TO THE SEA; ASSERTING COMMUNAL AND CUSTOMARY RIGHTS; RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF TRADITIONAL FISHING PRACTICES; GENDER EQUITY AND THE ROLE OF WOMEN AND YOUTH; PARTICIPATION IN CO-MANAGEMENT; STRENGTHENING LOCAL BRANCHES AND DISSEMINATING THE POLICY AT BRANCH LEVEL; AND AN IMPROVED EXEMPTION ALLOCATION UNTIL THE POLICY IS IMPLEMENTED. PRIVATISATION OF COASTAL LAND THAT LIMITS ACCESS TO THE SEA is the fishing equivalent of enclosure: the water is still public, but the road to it is not. Worth naming early wherever a coastal development is proposed. WHAT MAKES FISHING UNVIABLE, IN ITS OWN LIST: CORPORATE MONOPOLIES, OVERFISHING, POLLUTION OF THE OCEANS AND GOVERNMENT ACTION — WITH MANY POOR COMMUNITIES DENIED ACCESS BY ELITE GROUPS WHO PLACE NARROW COMMERCIAL INTERESTS ABOVE THE RIGHT OF FISHERS TO EARN A LIVING. THE INLAND EXTENSION, WHICH IS RARELY COVERED: IN 2017 IT TURNED ITS ATTENTION TO ASSISTING INLAND FISHING COMMUNITIES, WITH CURRENT LEGISLATION NOT RECOGNISING SMALL-SCALE FISHING FOR LIVELIHOODS IN RIVERS AND DAMS — WORKING ON A DAM FISHERY PROJECT, HELPING COMMUNITIES SET UP COMMITTEES IN NAMED TOWNS AND ENGAGING GOVERNMENT, RECREATIONAL FISHERS AND A UNIVERSITY. River and dam fishers are invisible in law almost everywhere, and this file has recorded dam projects displacing them with no category to claim under. An organisation that has taken that on, and works with the recreational fishers rather than against them, is a rare model. WHAT IT DOES BEYOND CAMPAIGNS: IT FACILITATES THE FORMATION AND GROWTH OF MASS BASED COMMUNITY ORGANISATIONS IN POOR COASTAL AREAS, AND DEVELOPS DISCUSSION PAPERS THAT SPEAK IN THE VOICE OF TRADITIONAL SMALL-SCALE FISHERS AND CRITICALLY ANALYSE CONCEPTS AND DEFINITIONS RELATED TO FISHERY POLICY. DEFINITIONS is where these fights are won or lost: who counts as a small-scale fisher decides who gets a permit, and the definition is written in policy documents most communities never read. THE PROGRAMME'S FOUR OBJECTIVES: EMPOWERMENT FOR SOCIAL ACTIVISM ESPECIALLY YOUTH; DEMONSTRATING FOOD SOVEREIGNTY THROUGH PROVINCIAL AND MICRO-PROJECTS; SYSTEMIC CHANGE THROUGH ACCOUNTABLE LEGAL AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORKS COMMITTED TO PARTICIPATORY GOVERNANCE; AND GLOBAL SOLIDARITY AMONGST SMALL-SCALE FOOD PRODUCERS. THE CONSERVATION ARGUMENT IT MAKES: SMALL-SCALE FISHERS ARE THE CUSTODIANS OF NATURAL RESOURCES BECAUSE THEY DEPEND ON THESE RESOURCES IN ORDER TO SURVIVE — WITH A STAFF MEMBER TRAVELLING COMMUNITY TO COMMUNITY, REACHING THREE OF THE FOUR COASTAL PROVINCES AT LEAST TWICE IN A SINGLE YEAR. The counter-argument to conservation-by-exclusion, made by the people excluded. And the travel figure is the honest cost of holding a coastal membership together. AND THE ALLIANCES ON RECORD: MEMBERS HAVE PARTICIPATED IN INTERNATIONAL FORUMS INCLUDING A UNITED NATIONS FOOD AND AGRICULTURE BODY; THE ORIGINAL LITIGATION WAS RUN WITH A HUMAN RIGHTS LITIGATION ORGANISATION; THE TRUST CO-FOUNDED A NATIONAL RURAL EDUCATION COLLECTIVE IN 1980; AND IT ISSUES JOINT PRESS RELEASES WITH A CAMPAIGN ASSERTING COMMUNITIES' RIGHT TO REFUSE OIL AND GAS DEVELOPMENT ON A NAMED STRETCH OF COAST. The fishers did not litigate alone: a public-interest law organisation ran the case with them. That pairing — a membership organisation plus a litigation partner — is the combination behind most of the wins recorded in this file. WHO IT SUITS: coastal and inland fishing communities losing access to water or shore, and any scattered membership wanting a four-tier elected structure or a people's tribunal model. CAVEATS: ONE COUNTRY, WITH A FISHERIES AND FOOD-SOVEREIGNTY FRAME RATHER THAN LAND PURCHASE; IT ORGANISES, RESEARCHES AND CAMPAIGNS AND LITIGATES THROUGH LEGAL PARTNERS RATHER THAN AS A LAW CENTRE. For the organisation that builds rural bodies before the land claim, Somalia's entry; for the co-operative named as co-applicant in offshore litigation, Mali's entry.

trackers.name: Natural Justice: Lawyers for Communities and the Environment
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an African public-interest law organisation — lawyers and paralegals working with communities facing mining, oil and gas, logging and large infrastructure, combining legal empowerment, community protocols, policy work and litigation. Hubs in Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, staff in Madagascar, Botswana and Guinea, and country programmes in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal and South Africa. It also runs the Environmental Lawyers Collective for Africa and an EIA Process Tracker. WHO IT SUITS: an Indigenous or rural community whose land, water or customary rights are threatened by an extractive or infrastructure project. It takes selected cases and works project-to-project outside its programme countries, so expect an approach-and-assess conversation rather than open intake. IS THERE AN OFFICE NEAR YOU? NO — this is project-to-project country. Natural Justice's 3 hubs are Cape Town, Nairobi and Dakar, with additional staff in Antananarivo, Botswana and Guinea; elsewhere it works across African countries on a project-to-project basis. So you are asking them to take on a project, not walking into an office — approach with a defined case and expect that answer to depend on their current programme. Its team page does list staff and fellows beyond the hub countries. WHAT IT DOES: founded 2007 in Cape Town, it supports communities to know the law, use the law and shape the law — access to land and governance of natural resources, the struggle against harmful extractive and infrastructure developments, traditional knowledge and benefit sharing, community rights within conservation, and climate action. ITS SIGNATURE TOOL IS THE COMMUNITY PROTOCOL — a documented instrument letting a community set out its biological, cultural and spiritual resources, norms and values, and assert existing rights under customary, domestic and international law, aimed squarely at laws and projects developed by government and industry without consultation. Ask for it by name. Contact: 63 Hout Street, Cape Town 8001; +27 21 426 1633; info@naturaljustice.org.

trackers.name: African Environmental Defenders Fund (emergency grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the African Environmental Defenders Fund — an emergency grant fund run by Natural Justice with the International Land Coalition Africa, ICCA Consortium, PACJA, Oxfam Novib, FEMNET and others, giving up to US$5,000 to land and environmental defenders anywhere in Africa who are under threat because of their activism. It can cover the cost of legal representation where a defender is arrested, summoned or prosecuted, plus relocation and other short-term transitional costs. WHO IT SUITS: an individual frontline defender who is a citizen or legal resident of an African country, facing an imminent threat, and not already supported by another body — it is not project or core funding, and routine office and administrative costs are excluded. HOW IT DIFFERS: applications are rolling, by email or helpline, not to a grant round. Natural Justice's own site names Burkina Faso, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa and Botswana as its country programmes, which is where this entry is placed; the fund's stated eligibility is any African country, so apply from elsewhere on the continent too.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional litigation centre supporting and co-counselling cases across Angola, Botswana, DR Congo, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its socio-economic rights work challenges large-scale agricultural and extractive land use that dispossesses customary landholders without adequate consent, consultation or compensation, and covers mining, pollution and climate justice — live matters include a Zambian community's pollution claim against copper processors and San and Bayei claims to ancestral land in Botswana. WHO IT SUITS: in-country lawyers and community organisations who need a partner with regional capacity and resources; SALC generally works through local counsel and partners rather than taking clients directly. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Namibia e-Procurement
trackers.desc: Namibia's government e-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Namibia, and for how much.

trackers.name: NamibLII
trackers.desc: Namibia Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Namibian judgments and legislation (NamibLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor-General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Namibia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Business and Intellectual Property Authority (BIPA)
trackers.desc: Namibia’s official registry of businesses and intellectual property — company incorporation and registration numbers.

trackers.name: BIPA Beneficial Ownership Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Namibia
trackers.desc: Supreme Court of Namibia — supreme court in Namibia (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: High Court of Namibia
trackers.desc: High Court of Namibia — supreme court in Namibia (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Communal conservancies — the community defines the area
trackers.desc: THE STRONGEST COMMUNITY LAND MODEL IN THIS MAP, AND THE REASONS ARE STRUCTURAL. A communal conservancy holds conditional rights to use the wildlife within a self-defined area, with fixed boundaries agreed with adjacent conservancies, communities or landowners — negotiated laterally with neighbours, not drawn by a ministry and handed down. It is a self-governing, democratic entity run by members through an elected committee, and it is recognised by the ministry but not governed by it: MEFT facilitates registration and monitors compliance, and may de-register a non-complying conservancy, but does not run it. AND IT REVERSED A CRIMINAL STATUS: before independence, residents on communal land who hunted game were treated as poachers; as legal entities with wildlife utilisation plans, conservancies were allowed to hunt under quotas based on annual game counts carried out by the ministry and the conservancies together. TO ESTABLISH ONE: an elected committee meets the requirements set under the 1996 amendment of the 1975 Nature Conservation Ordinance, then the Minister declares it in the Government Gazette. Obligations: wildlife management plans, annual general meetings and financial reports. SCALE: from 4 gazetted in 1998 to 86 conservancies and 43 community forests over 180,083 km² — community conservation areas now cover 20 percent of Namibia.

trackers.name: CCFN — a conservation fund that pays your legal costs
trackers.desc: THE WINDOW ALMOST NOTHING ELSE IN THIS MAP OFFERS. Alongside Minimum Support Packages and Payments for Ecosystem Services, CCFN provides financial aid to communities to meet their legal costs in pursuing their contract liberties and realising their benefits from contracts relating to their rights over their natural resources — expressly for conservancies that have been disadvantaged and/or shortchanged in contractual or other legally recognised arrangements. A conservation fund paying a community's legal fees to enforce a bad joint-venture contract is rare anywhere. Separate application forms exist for Conservancy Grants and JV Grants; check the Project Guidelines under Resources. There is also a human-wildlife conflict window — Germany through KfW announced a N$72.5 million HWC grant for communal conservancies, with the 43 worst-affected registered conservancies qualifying plus the Kyaramacan Association in Bwabwata National Park. LONG-TERM: ‘Namibia for Life’ secured N$1 billion in long-term financing with CCFN, NACSO, WWF and Enduring Earth. BUT KNOW THE TRANSITION: the movement is described as moving from a largely donor-funded development phase to a longer-term maintenance phase, with conservancy numbers expected to plateau around 90–100 — so new registrations are nearing a ceiling and the money is shifting toward sustaining what exists.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Environmental Clearance Certificate portal — an appeal costs N$1,000, more than three applications, and only registered parties may comment
trackers.desc: TWO NUMBERS DECIDE WHETHER ORDINARY PEOPLE USE THIS SYSTEM. AN APPLICATION FOR A CLEARANCE CERTIFICATE COSTS N$300; AN APPEAL COSTS N$1,000. Objecting is priced higher than applying, and the same N$1,000 applies to a transfer of certificate. Fees are not payable online: they must be paid by affixing a revenue stamp or a revenue franking impression to the document, so budget the trip as well as the money. THE SECOND GATE IS REGISTRATION, AND IT CLOSES QUIETLY: under the assessment regulations only a registered interested and affected party is entitled to comment in writing on submissions made to the Environmental Commissioner. Registering on a project's register is not a formality you do when you have something to say — it is the thing that gives you standing to say it, and it has to be done while the consultation is open. WHAT THE PORTAL ACTUALLY OFFERS, WHICH IS MORE THAN MOST IN THE REGION: online registration and application with status tracking against your email address; a Report Environmental Noncompliance form that lets you attach a photograph and lets you withhold your own details unless you want to be contacted; a screening questionnaire that tells you whether a project needs an assessment at all; a list of activities that may not be undertaken without a certificate; and a plain-language guide to the environment Act that carries section numbers so you can find the provision itself. There is also a Public Comments on new Projects list with a validity date against each project — that list rendered empty when this entry was written, so check it in a browser rather than assuming nothing is open. CAVEATS: the Commissioner is required to acknowledge an application within three days and to notify a decision within seven days of finalising review, and an appeal lies to the Minister — those timings and the registration rule were read from the assessment regulations and from a legal-alliance summary of them, not from this portal, which publishes fees and FAQs rather than deadlines. Note also that whether a public hearing happens at all is discretionary.

trackers.name: NACSO — how a Namibian community becomes a registered conservancy or community forest, which is the strongest community land right in this region
trackers.desc: WHERE THE RIGHT COMES FROM: Namibia wrote environmental protection into its constitution after independence and then, by legislation in the mid-1990s, established the right of people on communal land to organise themselves as conservancies and benefit directly from managing the natural resources there. The first conservancies were registered in 1998 and the first community forests in 2006. This is devolution to the community itself — not, as in Zimbabwe, to the district council — and it is why Namibia is usually described as Africa's leading case of devolved rights and responsibilities. WHAT EXISTS NOW: by the end of 2017 there were 83 registered communal conservancies and 32 registered community forests, plus one community association inside a national park, covering 166,267 km²; the count has since grown to around 87 conservancies with more communities electing to self-organise. Over seven million hectares of communal land are managed as conservancies. WHO TO ENLIST AND WHAT TO ASK: the environment ministry facilitates registration and monitors compliance; NACSO is the umbrella of the support organisations that help communities through it — technical assistance, governance support, the annual game counts, monitoring, and policy advocacy. Ask them what your area would have to do to register, because a registered conservancy is a legally recognised entity with rights to manage the resources in its defined jurisdiction, which is a far better position from which to refuse a project than being residents with no standing. Income comes from tourism, conservation hunting, meat and crafts, and a national fund has been established to move conservancies off donor dependence. In October 2024 a National Communal Conservancies and Community Forest Alliance was launched as the umbrella body representing conservancies and community forests at national policy level. WHO IT SUITS: communal-area communities in Namibia that want legal standing over their land and resources before a project arrives. CAVEATS: registration is a process with the ministry, not a purchase, and it takes time and organisation; conservancy income depends on tourism and hunting markets; and NACSO is a support and coordination association, not a legal service — for an objection to a specific project, Namibia's environmental clearance portal entry is the route.

trackers.name: Shack Dwellers Federation of Namibia and NHAG — a community-managed revolving fund that lends to its own savings groups, and has secured land for thousands of families
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY AND BUY LAND: the Shack Dwellers Federation of Namibia (SDFN), founded in October 1998 by around 30 grassroots housing groups active since the late eighties, a national network of housing savings schemes open to people who are unemployed or earn less than about N$5,000 a month; and the Namibia Housing Action Group (NHAG) Trust, established 1992 as its support organisation. THE INSTRUMENT: in 1996 communities established the Twahangana Fund, a COMMUNITY-MANAGED REVOLVING development fund that lends to the savings groups themselves — members' savings combined with government and international contributions. Each saving group manages its own savings and holds its own bank account. Community savings have been used to secure land and to leverage additional government contributions. WHY IT EXISTS IN THOSE TERMS: the federation's own account is that 89 per cent of Namibians do not qualify for conventional home loans and cannot access commercial housing — so the savings group is not a supplement to the mortgage market, it is the replacement for it. REPORTED SCALE, AND THE FIGURES VARY BY SOURCE AND DATE: from 605 schemes with 20,400 members, land secured for roughly 6,230 families and 3,488 houses built, up to over 1,000 saving groups, 30,000–33,000 members, savings above N$34 million, and 7,000–7,700 brick houses, each with its own toilet and water connection. About two-thirds of members are women, and the negotiation with authorities has been driven mainly by women. A member's account of the route is exact: save small amounts regularly, then buy a plot, then build. Town councils have partnered with NHAG to open land for low-income buyers. WHO IT SUITS: Namibians in shacks, rented rooms or without accommodation who cannot borrow commercially, and groups wanting to buy land collectively rather than individually. CAVEATS: this is slow and incremental — members describe consolidation of the erven delaying construction for years — and Namibia's housing backlog is reported above 300,000 against this output. It secures and develops land for members; it is not a defence against a project, and for communal conservancy registration Namibia's NACSO entry is the route.

trackers.name: Legal Assistance Centre, Windhoek — a land and environment law project with a paralegal phone line and published walk-in hours
trackers.desc: WHO TO INSTRUCT: the Legal Assistance Centre (LAC), Namibia's public interest law organisation, whose Land, Environment and Development (LEAD) project covers inheritance, conservancies, ILLEGAL FENCING, environmental issues and issues affecting especially disadvantaged groups including the Himba and the San. HOW TO REACH IT, WHICH IT PUBLISHES PLAINLY: phone a paralegal on +264-61-22-3356, or come to the office at 4 Marien Ngouabi Street, Windhoek — open for basic advice Monday to Friday, 08h00–11h30 and 14h00–16h00, closing 15h00 on Fridays. THE FIGHT IT IS BUILT FOR, and the numbers explain why: about 39 per cent of Namibia's land area is communal, with the 2013/2014 agricultural census recording 169,984 agricultural households — 907,715 people — holding tenure rights in communal areas; and LAC's own analysis identifies ELITE LAND GRABBING in communal areas and ILLEGAL PRIVATE ENCLOSURES that reduce communal grazing and worsen overgrazing, at a time when traditional authorities' ability to enforce customary tenure has weakened. Illegal fencing is the quiet way communal land is taken — no permit, no notice, just posts — and this is the organisation that has litigated and published on it. It also trains Communal Land Boards in environmentally sound decision-making and conflict management, runs workshops for communities and for traditional leaders, police and officials on the Communal Land Reform Act and conservancy legislation, and comments publicly on live disputes including a mining conflict framed as a test of constitutional environmental rights. THE REGIONAL DOOR IT OPENS: LAC belongs to the Southern African Legal Assistance Network (SALAN), a network of legal aid and legal assistance NGOs spanning South Africa, Lesotho, Botswana, Mozambique, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe and Tanzania — so a community in any of those countries can ask LAC who its national equivalent is. WHO IT SUITS: Namibians facing illegal fencing, communal land allocation disputes, inheritance problems or environmental harm — and southern African communities looking for the nearest legal aid organisation. CAVEATS: a public interest law organisation with finite capacity, and it notes shrinking resources for civil society; the walk-in service is basic advice, not automatic representation. For conservancy registration, Namibia's NACSO entry; for savings-based land purchase, the Shack Dwellers Federation.

trackers.name: Namibian Chamber of Environment and the Namibia Nature Foundation — 63 member NGOs whose council is the members themselves, grants with no overhead deduction, and a foundation that will hold and administer funds for a community
trackers.desc: THE CHAMBER, THE ZERO-OVERHEAD GRANTS AND THE TRUST: the NAMIBIAN CHAMBER OF ENVIRONMENT (NCE, n-c-e.org), A MEMBERSHIP-BASED AND MEMBER-DRIVEN UMBRELLA ORGANISATION ESTABLISHED AS A VOLUNTARY ASSOCIATION UNDER NAMIBIAN COMMON LAW, currently holds 63 FULL MEMBERS — NAMIBIAN REGISTERED NGOs whose main business is environmental matters in Namibia — AND 13 ASSOCIATE MEMBERS. ITS GOVERNANCE IS THE POINT: THE MEMBERS CONSTITUTE THE COUNCIL, WHICH IS THE HIGHEST DECISION-MAKING ORGAN, AND THE COUNCIL ELECTS THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE AT AN AGM. An umbrella where the members ARE the governing body cannot be steered over their heads. If your organisation joins, you get a vote in the chamber, not just a newsletter. AND THE MONEY ARRANGEMENT IS UNUSUAL ENOUGH TO COPY: CORE FUNDING FOR THE NCE IS PROVIDED BY A SINGLE CORPORATE DONOR, WHICH MEANS ALL ADDITIONAL FUNDING RECEIVED IS INVESTED DIRECTLY INTO ENVIRONMENTAL PROJECTS AND PROGRAMMES — THERE ARE NO OVERHEAD COSTS — AND THE NCE DELIBERATELY FOCUSES ON CORPORATE SUPPORT AND AVOIDS TARGETING FUNDING SOURCES THAT MAY COMPETE WITH ITS MEMBERS. A grant-maker whose overheads are already paid passes on every kwacha it raises, and one that refuses to chase its own members' donors is not a rival. Ask what it funds: emphasis is placed on LEGACY INITIATIVES WITH TANGIBLE OUTCOMES. Its secretariat is two people, only one full-time — so approach with a specific, finished proposal. ITS MEMBERS, published with descriptions, include a nature trust established to manage and conserve the land hosting a named lodge, a conservancy association whose stated purpose is TO REPRESENT AS MANY PROPERLY ESTABLISHED CONSERVANCIES AS POSSIBLE AND ACT AS THEIR COORDINATING BODY, a desert lion research project, DEVELOPMENT WORKSHOP NAMIBIA on informal settlements and disadvantaged communities, and the NAMIBIAN ENVIRONMENT AND WILDLIFE SOCIETY, an NCE founding member whose potential partners are ALL ORGANISATIONS IN NAMIBIA with conservation, environmental research or environmental education as their main aim. A nature trust formed to hold the land under a lodge is a template: a private landholding placed inside a non-profit that exists to conserve it. THE FOUNDATION THAT WILL HOLD YOUR MONEY: THE NAMIBIA NATURE FOUNDATION (NNF, nnf.org.na), 76-78 Frans Indongo Street, WINDHOEK, FOUNDED 1987 AND REGISTERED UNDER A DEED OF TRUST WITH THE MASTER OF THE NAMIBIAN HIGH COURT, one of Namibia's oldest and largest homegrown environmental organisations and an IUCN member since 1991, whose stated objects include RAISING FUNDS FOR CONSERVATION AND ENVIRONMENTAL INITIATIVES AND ADMINISTERING AND MANAGING FUNDS FOR PARTNERS, DONORS, PRIVATE SECTOR, GOVERNMENT, COMMUNITIES AND PROJECT IMPLEMENTERS. A registered trust that will administer funds on a community's behalf solves the problem that stops most village groups being funded at all — no bank account, no audit history. And one partner records that through NNF's technical support their team MANAGED TO ESTABLISH A FULLY REGISTERED NGO. Ask NNF for that support before asking anyone for money. WHO IT SUITS: Namibian community groups needing registration, a fiscal host, a grant or an umbrella. CAVEATS: SMALL SECRETARIATS; NCE core funding comes from a mining company — know that before you approach. For how a community becomes a registered conservancy, Namibia's NACSO entry; for land bought through community savings, the Shack Dwellers Federation and NHAG entry; for the land and environment lawyers, the Legal Assistance Centre entry; for the appeal against a clearance certificate, the ECC portal entry.

trackers.name: IRDNC — forty years of Namibian community conservation that trains and employs villagers as rangers — and the four-country KAZA consortium roster with a law centre inside it
trackers.desc: RANGERS HIRED FROM THE VILLAGE, AND A LAW CENTRE IN THE CONSORTIUM: INTEGRATED RURAL DEVELOPMENT AND NATURE CONSERVATION (IRDNC, irdnc.org.na) IS A NAMIBIAN NGO WITH MORE THAN 40 YEARS OF EXPERIENCE IN SUSTAINABLE NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND COMMUNITY-DRIVEN CONSERVATION, based at WINDHOEK WEST, WINDHOEK. ITS METHOD IS THE POINT: BY TRAINING AND EMPLOYING LOCAL COMMUNITY MEMBERS AS RANGERS, IT PROTECTS DESERT-ADAPTED ELEPHANTS, LIONS AND BLACK RHINOS WHILE SAFEGUARDING LIVELIHOODS AND STRENGTHENING LONG-TERM COEXISTENCE BETWEEN PEOPLE AND WILDLIFE, working to reduce human-wildlife conflict in the north-west. Forty years, and the ranger is a person from the village on a wage. That is the difference between a conservation project and a local institution: the salary stays in the community and the knowledge does not leave when the funder does. If an organisation proposes protection on your land, ask how many of the posts will be filled locally and at what pay — IRDNC is the Namibian precedent for the answer being all of them. THE ROSTER THAT MATTERS MOST, BECAUSE IT NAMES WHO TO APPROACH IN FOUR COUNTRIES FOR ONE LANDSCAPE: the consortium partners for a sustainable wildlife management programme in the KAVANGO-ZAMBEZI TRANSFRONTIER CONSERVATION AREA — THE WORLD'S LARGEST — ARE THE ASSOCIATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION AND INTEGRATED RURAL DEVELOPMENT (ACADIR) IN ANGOLA; ECOEXIST IN BOTSWANA; IRDNC; THE KAZA SECRETARIAT; THE LEGAL ASSISTANCE CENTRE; THE NACSO NATURAL RESOURCE WORKING GROUP; THE NAMIBIA NATURE FOUNDATION; THE NAMIBIA DEVELOPMENT TRUST; SAVE THE RHINO TRUST; TRAFFIC; AND WWF ZAMBIA AND WWF ZIMBABWE. A LEGAL ASSISTANCE CENTRE sitting inside a wildlife consortium is the detail to take away. It means the legal capacity is already at the table with the conservation bodies, so a community inside KAZA does not have to find a lawyer separately — ask the consortium which partner handles the land and rights questions, and note that the answer is a named public interest law firm. And a transfrontier consortium means an Angolan, Botswanan, Namibian, Zambian or Zimbabwean community facing the same landscape has counterparts named in the same document. ACADIR in Angola is a body this file's Angolan record does not otherwise hold — an association combining environmental conservation AND integrated rural development is exactly the pairing a southern Angolan village needs. THE PROGRAMME'S OWN OBJECT IS WORTH QUOTING BACK: TO RECONCILE THE CHALLENGES OF WILDLIFE CONSERVATION WITH THOSE OF FOOD SECURITY, PROMOTING SUSTAINABLE AND LEGAL USE OF RESILIENT ANIMAL POPULATIONS BY INDIGENOUS RURAL POPULATIONS, WHILE INCREASING AND DIVERSIFYING THE PROTEIN SUPPLY. Food security and protein supply written into a conservation programme's object is the counter to the argument that protection means going hungry. Cite it. THE SCALE AND WHERE THE MONEY GOES, ON THE RECORD: a global environment facility grant of USD 7.1 MILLION FORMED PART OF A TOTAL OF USD 32.43 MILLION for scaling up community-based ecosystem management, covering a conservancy network then numbering 29 REGISTERED CONSERVANCIES WITH 150,000 RESIDENTS ACROSS 75,000 SQUARE KILOMETRES — and an earlier USD 26.5 MILLION in donor support went to the same programme, under which LOCAL COMMUNITIES WERE GRANTED RIGHTS TO MANAGE THE LAND AND REAP THE BENEFITS FROM TOURISM, WITH ANY INCOME GENERATED PAID OUT DIRECTLY TO INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS OF CONSERVANCIES OR POOLED TO PAY FOR NECESSITIES LIKE WATER TANKS, WIND PUMPS AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF LOCAL INFRASTRUCTURE. Paid out directly to individual members, OR pooled for water tanks and wind pumps — and the conservancy chooses which. That is the clause to write into your own constitution before the first revenue arrives, because the argument about how income is split is the one that breaks community bodies. Decide it while there is still nothing to divide. The programme's activities are also named: COMMUNITY-BASED TOURISM FACILITIES INCLUDING JOINT VENTURES WITH THE PRIVATE SECTOR, TROPHY HUNTING, GAME MEAT PRODUCTION, THE COMMERCIALISATION OF INDIGENOUS PLANTS AND CRAFT PRODUCTION. Commercialisation of indigenous plants is the quiet earner on that list, and the one least likely to divide a community. WHO IT SUITS: Namibian communal communities, anyone inside the KAZA landscape in five countries, and conservancies deciding how to split income. CAVEATS: TROPHY HUNTING IS PART OF THIS MODEL and communities differ sharply on it — decide before you join a programme built around it. For how a community becomes a registered conservancy or community forest, Namibia's NACSO entry; for 63 member NGOs governing the council themselves with no overhead on grants, the Namibian Chamber of Environment and NNF entry; for a land and environment law project, the Legal Assistance Centre entry; for a community-managed revolving fund, the Shack Dwellers Federation entry.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund (CBF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional environmental endowment established in 2012, managing an endowment plus a sinking fund for Ecosystem-based Adaptation, which it disburses mainly through partner National Conservation Trust Funds rather than directly — it helped establish several of them, including the Dominica, Grenada, Jamaica, St Kitts & Nevis, St Lucia and St Vincent funds. Its EbA window runs open calls for proposals. WHO IT SUITS: organisations doing on-the-ground ecosystem work that reduces climate vulnerability. Check whether your country has a national trust fund first — that is usually the door, and the CBF itself is the wholesaler behind it. HOW IT DIFFERS: endowment income committed for the long term, so it funds sustained protected-area management rather than a campaign. APPLY TO YOUR NATIONAL FUND, NOT TO CBF — for most of the money. CBF is a regional umbrella: at national level the partner National Conservation Trust Funds (NCTFs) lead the grantmaking process, with endowment proceeds held in country-based subaccounts and channelled through them. So for the Conservation Finance stream, the regional body is the wrong door — find your NCTF. THE EXCEPTION IS THE EbA FACILITY, which awards through competitive calls for proposals and is a direct route. THE NUMBERS: EbA medium grants USD 250,000–1 million, large grants up to USD 2 million — large by the standards of most funds here, and not aimed at a small unincorporated group acting alone. Eligible recipients expressly include NCTFs, NGOs, community-based organisations, government agencies, universities and the private sector. SCOPE CHECK: the EbA Facility covers the marine and coastal zone of the insular Caribbean, so an inland project must show its connection to marine and coastal ecosystems. IF YOU ARE TOO SMALL FOR EbA: CBF partners with GEF SGP across 12 shared countries — that is the sibling route for community-scale grants, and it is recorded separately in this map. Endowment disbursements go to NCTFs that have signed agreements with CBF, the first in 2016 with Fondo MARENA in the Dominican Republic.

trackers.name: Cour supérieure des comptes et du contentieux administratif (Haïti)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Haiti — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Haiti — Ministère du Commerce et de l’Industrie (Guichet MCI)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the Ministry of Commerce & Industry registers businesses — via the online Guichet MCI platform (launched 2024) issuing a secure certificate, with company-name antecedent search & application tracking, Haiti. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Haiti — Ministère de l’Économie et des Finances (MEF)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; coordinates preparation & execution of the general State budget and manages the treasury, Haiti. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Haiti.

trackers.name: Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF)
trackers.desc: A FUND WHOSE SMALL-GRANT APPLICATION IS A SINGLE LETTER. CEPF (founded 2000; a joint initiative of the French Development Agency, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, the Government of Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank) has funded more than 2,500 grantees. FOR SMALL GRANTS THE LETTER OF INQUIRY IS THE ENTIRE APPLICATION — no longer project proposal is required — reviewed by the hotspot's Regional Implementation Team, with an offline template provided in the call's languages. Large grants go through the ConservationGrants portal and only then invite a full proposal. Reported averages: small grants around US$15,000, large around US$150,000; the small/large threshold varies by call (US$20,000 and US$50,000 both recorded), so read it. TIMING: calls run 6–8 weeks and notification comes several months after closing — but CEPF stops accepting letters once the designated funds are committed, so an open call can close early. WHO IS DISQUALIFIED: individuals cannot apply — you need a legally registered organisation with its own bank account — and government cannot apply. Community groups, farmers' cooperatives, Indigenous Peoples' organisations and women's groups all can, and CEPF welcomes first-time applicants. TWO RULES THAT SINK GOOD APPLICATIONS: your letter must aim at one single strategic direction; and site-based directions are geographically bound — community management work must be in a listed priority KBA, corridor work in a named corridor, while civil-society strengthening can be anywhere in the hotspot. THE STEP MOST PEOPLE SKIP: CEPF encourages you to contact RIT staff to discuss the idea before submitting — free, and the cheapest way to learn whether it fits.

trackers.name: ANAP — it approves plans AND must follow their implementation
trackers.desc: A THREE-PART DUTY WORTH SEPARATING OUT. The Agence Nationale des Aires Protégées was created by the décret-cadre published in Le Moniteur, 26 January 2006, its mission drawn from article 54: protect biodiversity and manage the Système National des Aires Protégées. The decree requires it to elaborate and approve the plans d'aménagement for protected areas in its jurisdiction and follow their implementation — so a plan that exists but is not being followed engages the same body that approved it. Other statutory functions: coordinating preparation and implementation of the national protected areas management plan, and protecting biodiversity in situ and ex situ. THE ENFORCEMENT ARM: the Brigade de Sécurité des Aires Protégées (BSAP) is an operational direction of ANAP for environmental surveillance of protected area units and ecological sites, and also provides support to control bodies — the named body if your issue is unlawful activity inside a protected area. THE DEFINITION IS BROAD: a protected area is any zone delimited, regulated OR managed for conservation of biodiversity and associated natural and cultural resources — regulation alone can suffice. FOR A SMALL SITE, CATEGORY III (monument ou élément naturel) covers a topographic feature, a mountain, an underwater cavern, a grotte, or even a living element such as an ancient wooded islet, and these are generally quite small areas. ANAP became a Direction Générale by presidential arrêté of 10 May 2017.

trackers.name: The capacity gap is documented — and so is the shared-responsibility principle
trackers.desc: PLAN FOR THE MINISTRY NOT ACTING UNAIDED. A USAID-commissioned Biodiversity and Tropical Forest Assessment records that responsibilities at the heart of the MDE's mandate as set forth in the decree are generally not addressed by the MDE due to a lack of resources — with delineation of national parks among the functions listed. A statutory duty undischarged for want of resources is still a statutory duty, and that assessment is a citable source for the gap — but a campaign depending on unaided ministry action is likely to stall. Note too that before 2012 ANAP was a technical direction barely operational. THE OPENING FOR PARTICIPATION IS IN THE SYSTEM'S OWN FOUNDING PRINCIPLE: the National Environmental Management System proceeds from collective responsibility, to be shared between sectoral ministries and between the Government and citizens. WHERE A DEVELOPMENT CROSSES SECTORS: the Comité Interministériel d'Aménagement du Territoire (CIAT), led by an Executive Secretariat and composed of the Ministries of Planning, Agriculture, Environment, Public Works and Interior, is where those ministries sit together. CONTEXT: protection efforts date from 1926; the SNAP and ANAP were created in 2006; post-earthquake the PSDH treats biodiversity as a pillar through the Programme pour la Protection de l'Environnement and the Programme de Gestion des Bassins Versants. Parc national La Visite covers 30 km².

trackers.name: Freedom of Information Unit (Office of the Prime Minister)
trackers.desc: National right-to-information portal; Trinidad & Tobago’s FOI Unit administers the Freedom of Information Act 1999, with refusals reviewable by the Office of the Ombudsman, Trinidad & Tobago.

trackers.name: Fishermen and Friends of the Sea (FFOS)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a non-profit formed by fishers and citizens in 1996 and incorporated in 2000, with the strongest public-interest litigation record in the country — three separate appeals to the Privy Council, over a Certificate of Environmental Clearance for a highway beside the Aripo Savannas, over water pollution fees and the polluter-pays principle, and over judicial review time limits. It also runs a public route to report an environmental emergency. WHO IT SUITS: fishing communities and coastal residents facing oil spills, seismic survey, port or highway projects. Structurally it matters because section 5(6) of the Judicial Review Act lets a bona fide third party bring judicial review for people who cannot file themselves because of poverty or disadvantage. Courts have been strict on the duty to act promptly, so make contact early.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund (CBF)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional environmental endowment established in 2012 which disburses mainly through partner National Conservation Trust Funds and runs open calls under its Ecosystem-based Adaptation window. WHO IT SUITS — READ THIS FIRST: this country is NOT a core eligible country for the EbA facility. CBF's own trustee report lists it among territories that can benefit ONLY where they are included in a regional project in which eligible countries form a three-quarters majority. So the realistic route is joining a regional consortium led from an eligible country, not applying alone. HOW IT DIFFERS: long-horizon endowment money for sustained ecosystem management, not campaign funding. APPLY TO YOUR NATIONAL FUND, NOT TO CBF — for most of the money. CBF is a regional umbrella: at national level the partner National Conservation Trust Funds (NCTFs) lead the grantmaking process, with endowment proceeds held in country-based subaccounts and channelled through them. So for the Conservation Finance stream, the regional body is the wrong door — find your NCTF. THE EXCEPTION IS THE EbA FACILITY, which awards through competitive calls for proposals and is a direct route. THE NUMBERS: EbA medium grants USD 250,000–1 million, large grants up to USD 2 million — large by the standards of most funds here, and not aimed at a small unincorporated group acting alone. Eligible recipients expressly include NCTFs, NGOs, community-based organisations, government agencies, universities and the private sector. SCOPE CHECK: the EbA Facility covers the marine and coastal zone of the insular Caribbean, so an inland project must show its connection to marine and coastal ecosystems. IF YOU ARE TOO SMALL FOR EbA: CBF partners with GEF SGP across 12 shared countries — that is the sibling route for community-scale grants, and it is recorded separately in this map. Endowment disbursements go to NCTFs that have signed agreements with CBF, the first in 2016 with Fondo MARENA in the Dominican Republic.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional technical non-profit founded in 1989, headquartered in Trinidad and legally registered as a non-profit in this country, working with grassroots and community-based organisations directly involved in natural resource management. What it actually supplies is capacity rather than representation: coaching, mentoring and training of trainers, facilitated multi-stakeholder dialogues for planning and policymaking, participatory research, and unusual practical tools — participatory GIS mapping, three-dimensional modelling, participatory video and photojournaling — for communities that need to evidence their own case. It also channels funding and technical support to civil society organisations. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations and CSOs that need to be equipped to hold their ground in a planning or policy process. It is not a litigator, and its re-granting runs through time-limited donor projects rather than a standing open call — ask what is currently running. IS YOUR SITE A KBA? CHECK BEFORE YOU WRITE ANYTHING. CANARI publishes the CEPF Caribbean Islands Biodiversity Hotspot Ecosystem Profile, which identifies 45 Key Biodiversity Areas and 6 conservation corridors covering 28 KBAs as priorities for funding support, with maps — formulated through a process engaging over 200 stakeholders from more than 160 organisations. A campaign whose site is a KBA, or sits in one of the six corridors, has a materially stronger funding case and should say so explicitly. CORRECTED — AND THIS STREAM IS CLOSING. CEPF returned for a Phase II running August 2021 to July 2027, and CANARI is once again the Regional Implementation Team, managing US$11.8 million. THE ELEVENTH AND FINAL SMALL-GRANT CALL offers USD 5,000–50,000 for projects of up to 12 months between April 2026 and March 2027, and the tenth call was the final open call for large grants in the region — so treat the current call as the last scheduled opportunity, not one of many, though targeted solicitations may still fill portfolio gaps. ELIGIBILITY NARROWED IN PHASE II: the Phase I list of 11 countries no longer applies; Phase II calls name Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines, with CEPF stating 7 countries initially eligible. BUT THE SITE TEST CAN OUTRANK THE COUNTRY TEST: applicants based outside the eligible countries may submit provided activities focus on a conservation need within a priority corridor or site. THREE RULES: applicants must not be a government agency (government-owned bodies qualify only with independent legal personality and authority to receive private funds); joint projects are eligible with one lead organisation; and NGOs, community groups, universities and private enterprises may all apply. ASK BEFORE YOU DRAFT: RIT Manager Nicole Brown, caribbeanrit@canari.org — applicants uncertain about eligibility are expressly encouraged to make contact first. A Grievance Redress Mechanism exists for concerns about a funded project. WHAT CANARI ITSELF IS: a non-profit technical institute of thirty years' standing that acts as a conduit, channelling funding, information and technical support to CSOs — not a standing grant fund. Its project pattern is small grants plus technical coaching for partner CSOs to run participatory community vulnerability assessments and then design a project from the results.

trackers.name: Registrar General – Companies Registry
trackers.desc: National — Companies Registry, Registrar General’s Department, Trinidad & Tobago. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Central Statistical Office
trackers.desc: Trinidad and Tobago's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Trinidad & Tobago.

trackers.name: Companies Registry (Trinidad & Tobago)
trackers.desc: Official company and business register of Trinidad and Tobago — incorporation records.

trackers.name: Trinidad & Tobago — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares & administers the national budget and publishes the annual budget statement & estimates, Trinidad and Tobago. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Trinidad & Tobago.

trackers.name: TTEITI Disclosure
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Judiciary of Trinidad and Tobago
trackers.desc: Official judiciary portal publishing Supreme Court of Judicature judgments. · Find here: judgments and information of the Judiciary of Trinidad and Tobago.

trackers.name: Direct private party action — anyone with a general interest has standing
trackers.desc: THE WIDEST STANDING PROVISION IN THIS MAP. Section 69 of the Environmental Management Act, Ch. 35:05, creates a direct private party action: a private party may bring proceedings before the Environmental Commission against any person violating environmental requirements — including failure to obtain a Certificate of Environmental Clearance, or failure to comply with the terms and conditions in one. The test, in s.69(2): any individual or group expressing a general interest in the environment, or a specific concern about the claimed violation, is deemed to have standing. No registration, no membership floor, no charter wording — against Finland's rules-defined area of operation, Italy's ministerial list and Korea's denial of NGO standing for the environment itself. The Attorney General may intervene as of right. THE FORUM is a special environmental court with the powers of a superior court of record, hearing appeals from EMA decisions, enforcement applications, compensation assessments and private party complaints; decisions are final on fact, with appeal to the Court of Appeal on any question of law. AND THE HONEST PART: practitioners record that the Commission has not produced a wealth of jurisprudence, attributed to violators settling with the Authority through the consent agreement mechanism and to limited public awareness that a private party can initiate proceedings at all.

trackers.name: The CEC system — 44 designated activities, and a 3-year expiry
trackers.desc: WHAT A PRIVATE PARTY ACTION WOULD BE ENFORCING. Under s.35(2) no person may proceed with an activity the Minister has designated as requiring a Certificate without first obtaining one, and the Designated Activities Order 2001 as amended defines 44 activities requiring a CEC. YOUR PUBLIC COMMENT CAN BECOME ENFORCEABLE: the Authority may issue a Certificate subject to such terms and conditions as it thinks fit, including required mitigation measures, after considering the comments or representations made during the public comment period (s.36(1)) — and breach of those conditions is itself a ground for a private party action. A representation that becomes a condition is one you can later enforce in court. CHECK THE EXPIRY: if the activity has not commenced within 3 years, the Certificate ceases to have validity, force or effect — an old CEC on a dormant project may already be dead. DESIGNATION ROUTES for a place or a species: the Environmentally Sensitive Areas Rules 2001 and Environmentally Sensitive Species Rules 2001. INFORMATION: the Authority may release compiled environmental information on written request and payment of the prescribed fee. RULE-MAKING: draft Rules go out for public comment, with a public hearing if there is sufficient public interest.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Association of Indigenous Village Leaders in Suriname (VIDS)
trackers.desc: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname — founded in 1992 and representing the traditional leaders of all 51 Indigenous villages in Suriname (Kaliña, Lokono, Trio, Wayana and others). It promotes and defends Indigenous peoples’ rights nationally and internationally, campaigns for the legal recognition of collective land and territorial rights and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC), and presses Suriname to honour its obligations under the binding rulings of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights; it was awarded the inaugural EU Human Rights Award for the region. WHEN THE STATE DID NOT ACT ON THE INTER-AMERICAN COURT JUDGMENT, IT DID NOT LOBBY — it submitted its own initiatiefwet (private member's bill) on collective rights of Indigenous and tribal peoples to Parliament, including recognition of the right to traditional living areas. An organisation that drafts and tables legislation is a legal actor, not only a monitor. ASK FOR THE FPIC PROTOCOL: VIDS holds a national FPIC protocol dated November 2024, announced for formal handover to government — a community-authored national protocol is a document to point a developer and a ministry at. On 3 September 2025 it adopted resolutions demanding legal recognition of collective rights, an immediate halt to land allocation in Indigenous and tribal areas, rejection of the ‘5-kilometre law’ and compliance with the Kaliña and Lokono judgment. The eight villages of Beneden-Marowijne are organised as KLIM and work with VIDS; the chairman is recorded as Theo Jubitana, and it runs the campaign ‘Met elkaar in Suriname’. THE BILL YOU WILL MEET: a proposed Wet Bescherming Woon- en Leefgebieden would create a protection zone of 5 kilometres around villages — objected to on the ground that it is no real solution to the land-rights question and leaves large parts of traditional territory exposed to logging, mining and oil exploration.

trackers.name: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund — regional conservation finance
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a regional umbrella environmental fund providing continuous finance for conservation, through an Endowment Fund and a Climate Change Program whose Ecosystem-based Adaptation Facility runs competitive calls for proposals — around 100 projects funded. WHO IT SUITS: Caribbean community and conservation groups. HOW IT DIFFERS: mostly you do NOT apply to CBF directly — partner National Conservation Trust Funds lead the grantmaking in each country, so find your national trust fund first. CBF states it works across 14 Caribbean countries; check its 'Where We Work' map for yours. APPLY TO YOUR NATIONAL FUND, NOT TO CBF — for most of the money. CBF is a regional umbrella: at national level the partner National Conservation Trust Funds (NCTFs) lead the grantmaking process, with endowment proceeds held in country-based subaccounts and channelled through them. So for the Conservation Finance stream, the regional body is the wrong door — find your NCTF. THE EXCEPTION IS THE EbA FACILITY, which awards through competitive calls for proposals and is a direct route. THE NUMBERS: EbA medium grants USD 250,000–1 million, large grants up to USD 2 million — large by the standards of most funds here, and not aimed at a small unincorporated group acting alone. Eligible recipients expressly include NCTFs, NGOs, community-based organisations, government agencies, universities and the private sector. The CORE project targets climate resilience of vulnerable groups in 8 beneficiary countries — Belize, Dominica, Grenada, Guyana, Jamaica, St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, and Suriname — with beneficiaries expressly including women's rights organisations, environmental organisations and youth organisations as well as NCTFs. trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the basin-wide confederation of Amazonian Indigenous organisations, founded to act for 511 Indigenous peoples across the nine Amazon countries, around 66 of them in voluntary isolation or initial contact. It works through one national member organisation per country — in this country that is OIS, Organizaciones Indígenas de Surinam — and its governing Council brings those presidents together. Its standing work areas are territorial rights and natural resources, human and sociocultural rights, and international law, and it has issued a formal declaration on the defence of Amazonian Indigenous defenders. USE IT: go to OIS first — COICA is the regional weight behind a national organisation, not a direct service. It is the route to carry a territorial case or a threat against leaders from your community into regional and international forums.

trackers.name: ACT Suriname — Amazon Conservation Team Suriname
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a Surinamese foundation established under Surinamese law in September 2002, working in partnership with Indigenous and Maroon communities of the southern interior. Its flagship is the Amazon Conservation Rangers programme, launched in Suriname in 2007: community-appointed rangers, 42 currently active, trained and equipped to monitor their own territory — reviewing satellite imagery for deforestation, testing water quality, and detecting illegal intruders such as loggers and gold miners. It also facilitates Community Life Plans, territorial management documents a village can put in front of a government agency or a company. USE IT: in a country that still has no legal recognition of Indigenous land rights, this is the practical substitute — evidence and governance documents a community controls itself.

trackers.name: Suriname — Ministerie van Financiën en Planning
trackers.desc: National budget authority; monitors State revenues & expenditures and prepares the State budget (Staatsbegroting), Suriname. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Suriname.

trackers.name: Suriname — Kamer van Koophandel en Fabrieken (KKF)
trackers.desc: National company registry; Suriname’s official business registry maintaining the mandatory public Handelsregister with online registration, name reservation & digital extracts, Suriname. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Kaliña and Lokono — six orders, all deadlines passed, nothing done
trackers.desc: THE ORDERS ARE BROAD AND ONE IS ABOUT COURT ACCESS ITSELF. The Inter-American Court gave judgment on 25 November 2015, in force 28 January 2016, ordering Suriname to: legally recognise the collective legal personality of ALL Indigenous and Tribal (Maroon) peoples, not only the applicants; recognise their land rights and grant collective title; establish an effective mechanism for delimiting, demarcating and titling territories; create or adapt domestic remedies to guarantee effective collective access to the courts; create a community development fund; and run permanent programmes on Indigenous human rights. THAT FOURTH ORDER IS THE ONE FOR THIS LENS: where a Surinamese court turns away a collective claim for want of a domestic mechanism, that refusal is itself the subject of an outstanding international obligation. THE COMPLIANCE POSITION, PLAINLY: the judgment's deadlines have all passed without the measures being carried out; at nearly 11 years, IKSur records territories still not fully recognised, delimited or demarcated while concessions for logging, gold mining and oil exploration continue to be granted. IKSur's framing is worth borrowing: protection without formal recognition is not a land right. BACKDROP: the Constitution does not explicitly recognise Indigenous and tribal peoples and there is no statutory regime for collective land rights; Suriname was also condemned in Saramaka (2007). CITE ALONGSIDE: UNDRIP arts. 19 and 32 on FPIC — authoritative though not a treaty — and ILO Convention 169, which Suriname has NOT ratified but whose standards are widely applied regionally as a minimum. State that ratification position honestly when citing it.

trackers.name: Access to Information Unit (Office of the Prime Minister)
trackers.desc: Jamaica's Access to Information Unit, which administers the ATI Act 2002 and is secretariat to the Access to Information Appeal Tribunal. You CAN get: any official document held by a public authority — correspondence, budgets, maps, photographs, computerised records — with acknowledgement within 7 working days and a decision within 30 days, extendable once by a further 30. If refused or ignored you have an internal review within 60 days, then an appeal to the Tribunal within 60 days of the decision or of the date the answer was due. The Tribunal can inspect the document itself and overrule the authority, and critically THE BURDEN IS ON THE PUBLIC AUTHORITY to prove its refusal was justified, not on you to prove it was wrong. You may appear yourself; a lawyer is optional. You CAN'T get: free copies — reproduction is charged, though viewing and inspecting are free — or documents an authority never created, since it need not make a record to answer you. For activists: this is how the Jamaica Environment Trust prised environmental records out of agencies that had withheld them at a permit-holder's request. It is also an offence to destroy or conceal a record to prevent disclosure. WHEN NOT TO USE IT: if the body is private, it falls outside the Act.

trackers.name: Jamaica Environment Trust (JET)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Jamaica's principal environmental watchdog, litigating in the public interest — it brought the Cockpit Country constitutional case decided in January 2023 — and campaigning against bauxite leases granted up to the edge of the Cockpit Country Protected Area, which still has no protection under Jamaican law. WHO IT SUITS: communities facing mining, coastal hotel development or industrial pollution. Its sharpest routine tool is the Access to Information Act: JET has appealed refusals to the Access to Information Appeal Tribunal and won, prising out records agencies withheld at a permit-holder's request, and it publishes the resulting cases and monitoring reports on its own site for reuse.

trackers.name: CANARI — Caribbean Natural Resources Institute
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a regional technical non-profit founded in 1989, headquartered in Trinidad and legally registered as a non-profit in this country, working with grassroots and community-based organisations directly involved in natural resource management. What it actually supplies is capacity rather than representation: coaching, mentoring and training of trainers, facilitated multi-stakeholder dialogues for planning and policymaking, participatory research, and unusual practical tools — participatory GIS mapping, three-dimensional modelling, participatory video and photojournaling — for communities that need to evidence their own case. It also channels funding and technical support to civil society organisations. WHO IT SUITS: community organisations and CSOs that need to be equipped to hold their ground in a planning or policy process. It is not a litigator, and its re-granting runs through time-limited donor projects rather than a standing open call — ask what is currently running. IS YOUR SITE A KBA? CHECK BEFORE YOU WRITE ANYTHING. CANARI publishes the CEPF Caribbean Islands Biodiversity Hotspot Ecosystem Profile, which identifies 45 Key Biodiversity Areas and 6 conservation corridors covering 28 KBAs as priorities for funding support, with maps — formulated through a process engaging over 200 stakeholders from more than 160 organisations. A campaign whose site is a KBA, or sits in one of the six corridors, has a materially stronger funding case and should say so explicitly. CORRECTED — AND THIS STREAM IS CLOSING. CEPF returned for a Phase II running August 2021 to July 2027, and CANARI is once again the Regional Implementation Team, managing US$11.8 million. THE ELEVENTH AND FINAL SMALL-GRANT CALL offers USD 5,000–50,000 for projects of up to 12 months between April 2026 and March 2027, and the tenth call was the final open call for large grants in the region — so treat the current call as the last scheduled opportunity, not one of many, though targeted solicitations may still fill portfolio gaps. ELIGIBILITY NARROWED IN PHASE II: the Phase I list of 11 countries no longer applies; Phase II calls name Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Saint Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines, with CEPF stating 7 countries initially eligible. BUT THE SITE TEST CAN OUTRANK THE COUNTRY TEST: applicants based outside the eligible countries may submit provided activities focus on a conservation need within a priority corridor or site. THREE RULES: applicants must not be a government agency (government-owned bodies qualify only with independent legal personality and authority to receive private funds); joint projects are eligible with one lead organisation; and NGOs, community groups, universities and private enterprises may all apply. ASK BEFORE YOU DRAFT: RIT Manager Nicole Brown, caribbeanrit@canari.org — applicants uncertain about eligibility are expressly encouraged to make contact first. A Grievance Redress Mechanism exists for concerns about a funded project. WHAT CANARI ITSELF IS: a non-profit technical institute of thirty years' standing that acts as a conduit, channelling funding, information and technical support to CSOs — not a standing grant fund. Its project pattern is small grants plus technical coaching for partner CSOs to run participatory community vulnerability assessments and then design a project from the results.

trackers.name: Forest Act declaration — name your share and your term
trackers.desc: A PRIVATE OWNER CAN APPLY TO HAVE THEIR OWN LAND DECLARED, and the procedure is short. Under the Forest Act 1996, write to the CEO and Conservator of Forests stating your interest, giving the exact location (parish, district, volume and folio number of the title), the size proposed and what percentage of the property that represents, and the time period over which declaration would apply. SO A PARTIAL, TIME-LIMITED DECLARATION IS BUILT IN — as with Costa Rica's servidumbre, you are not committing the whole property forever; you name the share and the term. At least 90 days notice applies, and declaration is by Gazette or newspaper. THE INCENTIVE: the Act provides property tax remission for private landowners with land in protected areas, forest management areas or forest reserves, once they comply with directions under the Act. AND A POWER THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS: the Minister may declare any land not in a forest reserve to be a forest management area, including private land, if satisfied its use should be controlled for the protection of the national interest. Jamaica has over 150 gazetted forest reserves.

trackers.name: Local Forest Management Committees — a letter starts the process
trackers.desc: THE LOWEST BARRIER TO CO-MANAGEMENT RECORDED IN THIS MAP. A Local Forest Management Committee is the body created in watershed management units to enable community participation in co-management of forested areas managed by the Forestry Department — and in the Department's own words, any community interested in forming one needs only to write to the CEO and Conservator of Forests indicating its interest, after which the agency makes contact and begins the process. 18 LFMCs exist across the island. A letter, not an application pack. AND FOR LARGER AMBITION, MANAGEMENT IS DELEGATED TO NGOs BY INSTRUMENT: the Jamaica Conservation and Development Trust manages the Blue and John Crow Mountains National Park, the Negril Coral Reef Preservation Society the Negril Marine Park, and the Caribbean Coastal Area Foundation another area. FUNDING: the Jamaica Protected Areas Trust (2004) administers the Forest Conservation Fund, capitalised through debt-for-nature swaps. ESTABLISH WHICH STATUTE GOVERNS YOUR SITE FIRST: NEPA works under the Natural Resources Conservation Authority Act, the Wild Life Protection Act and the Beach Control Act — each using different terminology — alongside the Forest Act, Fishing Industry Act and JNHT Act.

trackers.name: Amerindian Peoples Association (APA)
trackers.desc: Indigenous-led human-rights organization founded in 1991 that represents the Amerindian (Indigenous) peoples of Guyana — formed to confront human-rights abuses against Indigenous communities, including police brutality and the impacts of mining and logging on their lands, it provides legal empowerment and access-to-justice support, pursues land- and territorial-rights claims through participatory mapping and the courts (and international bodies such as the Inter-American Commission and UN forums), documents violations, and campaigns to bring Guyana’s Amerindian Act into line with international Indigenous-rights standards; it works through some 40+ community units across the interior regions.

trackers.desc: National — Deeds & Commercial Registries Authority company register, Guyana. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.
