It found violations of articles 1 and 24 of the African Charter — article 24: ‘all peoples shall have the right to a general satisfactory environment favourable to their development’ — and of article 21, the right to natural wealth and resources. THE FAULT WAS AN OMISSION: the state ‘defaulted in its duties in terms of vigilance and diligence’, and ‘the omission to act and to prevent damage to the environment characterises the violation’. It ordered restoration within the shortest possible time and measures to prevent further damage, citing the ICJ that the environment ‘is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn’. THE LIMIT THAT DECIDES WHO YOU SUE: the Court held it had no jurisdiction over the private oil corporations, which were struck from the suit. You sue the State for failing to regulate; you cannot sue the company here — naming one as respondent loses that part of the case. AND PLAN FOR ENFORCEMENT: commentary records the Court did not identify a means for Nigeria to implement the ruling, and the ICJ later wrote to the President pressing for enforcement — judgment is the start of an enforcement campaign, not a self-executing remedy. Proposals to require exhaustion of domestic remedies were rejected by ECOWAS experts and Heads of Government, so the direct-access rule has been tested and held.

trackers.name: Department of Forestry — and 66 parks demarcated since the 1950s
trackers.desc: A DOCUMENTARY STARTING POINT MOST COUNTRIES IN THIS MAP CANNOT OFFER. Between 1950 and 1954 a forestry adviser identified and demarcated 66 forest parks for conservation and production — timber, bamboo and rhun palms — so if your site is one of them, the demarcation record exists. The colonial administration's own conclusion that total protection for all the parks was impractical is the origin of the participatory turn that followed. The Department's operational mandate rests on the Forest Regulation of 1978, with the Forest Act 1998 and Regulations legally requiring communities to participate in fire prevention and participative forest management — note that participation is a legal requirement on communities, not only an entitlement, which cuts both ways before an approach. The Department works to the Gambian Forest Management Concept, developed with the Gambian-German Forest Project since 1980. Current policy: the National Forest Policy 2023–2032. The parent ministry is the Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Natural Resources.

trackers.name: Community Forest Committee — the state transfers ownership, after probation
trackers.desc: THE GAMBIA TRANSFERS OWNERSHIP, NOT A CONCESSION — and that is rare enough to cite across borders. The community forestry concept foresees an ownership transfer of forest land from the State to an interested community: not a management agreement, not a use right. COMPARE WHAT THIS MAP RECORDS ELSEWHERE: Cambodia's community protected areas give management rights but not exclusion rights; Burkina Faso's GGF is a concession; Guinea classifies forest ‘to the benefit of’ a collectivity. Where a neighbouring community is negotiating a concession, The Gambia is the comparator. The Gambia is recorded as one of the first countries in Africa to introduce community forestry nationwide, the concept being the flagship of the 1995 Forest Policy and the 1998 Forest Bill. THE ROUTE RUNS THROUGH A COMMITTEE YOU FORM AND ELECT: communities establish Community Forest Committees or Village Development Committees whose members are elected by the local population, trained by implementing partners and then responsible for planning, coordinating and managing delivery — including natural resource-based income-generating activities. THE STEP MOST APPLICANTS UNDERESTIMATE: the community must go through a training and probation period, which is then evaluated, with the final aim being reservation of the forestland as a gazetted Community Forest. Plan for probation and assessment, not an application — the gazettal comes at the end, not the beginning. The programme also provides literacy and basic skills, civic and health education, so the route carries adult education with it rather than assuming it.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: NEA Inspectorate — 26 inspectors for the whole country, and every enforcement notice on record fell inside Greater Banjul
trackers.desc: WHERE A POLLUTION REPORT GOES, AND HOW FAR THE AGENCY CAN ACTUALLY REACH. The Inspectorate of the National Environment Agency enforces ten instruments, including the National Environmental Management Act 1994, the Environmental Impact Assessment Regulations 2014, the Environmental Discharge (Permitting) Regulations 1999 and the Environmental Quality Standards Regulations 1999. Its first response is administrative, not judicial: an Improvement Notice or a Demand for Compliance, with litigation held back as a last resort. As at 4 January 2022 it had served 121 such notices, all of them within the Greater Banjul Area, against a national inspectorate of 26 people — one acting principal inspector, nine senior inspectors and sixteen inspectors. Up-country, the absence of a notice against a site is not evidence that the site is clean; it is more likely evidence that no inspector has been there. The page names the unit and its statutory basis but gives no complaint form, no email address and no service standard for responding to a report, so a written complaint to the Agency's head office in Kanifing, copied to the relevant regional office, is the route that exists rather than the route that is advertised.

trackers.name: NEA environmental assessment programme — the Class A / B / C screening decision is the one worth contesting early
trackers.desc: THE SCREENING CLASS DECIDES HOW MUCH SCRUTINY A PROJECT EVER RECEIVES, AND IT IS SET BEFORE ANY STUDY BEGINS. The Agency's own explainer describes three classes: Class A requires a mandatory assessment, Class B a limited one, and Class C none at all on the basis that the impacts are treated as negligible. A project placed in Class C generates no assessment document to comment on, which makes the classification, not the report, the thing to challenge. The explainer also names the lead-institution arrangement — for oil and gas the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority leads, with lands and survey, parks and wildlife, physical planning, water resources and the affected community brought in as stakeholders — so the body holding the file may not be the environment agency at all. Terminology note for searching the register: the Agency now writes ESIA rather than EIA, and older documents use the earlier term. This is a published programme description hosted on the Agency's own domain; it is not a procedure manual and it states no comment deadline, and no public register of screening decisions was located on the site.

trackers.name: NALA will advise you on a land case and will not represent you in one — and the same page carries the two bodies that can act
trackers.desc: CHECK THE CIVIL GATE BEFORE BUILDING A PLAN AROUND FREE COUNSEL. The Ministry of Justice's own description of the National Agency for Legal Aid states that it provides legal advice as well as legal representation in criminal matters in court, at police stations and in prisons. Advice is general; representation is criminal. A community facing an acquisition or a nuisance can therefore get an opinion from NALA but should not expect an advocate from it. Headquarters in Banjul with centres at Basse and Farafenni; the West Coast Region and Central River Region centres are described as still being established. Three telephone numbers are published and no email address, no means test and no application form. The same page lists the two bodies that can actually act on a land dispute without counsel: the Alternative Dispute Resolution Secretariat, headquartered at Fajara with pilot centres at Farafenni and Basse, which runs arbitration, conciliation and mediation as an alternative to the courts; and the National Human Rights Commission at Kotu, which holds the powers of the High Court at trial — to hear complaints, summon and examine witnesses on oath, and enforce its decisions, including measures to protect the life and safety of an individual. NALA maintains no website of its own; this is the State's canonical page for it, not a third party's description.

trackers.name: IHRDA, Banjul — pro bono counsel that takes community cases to the African regional courts, and publishes a case intake form
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa, founded in Banjul in 1998 by two lawyers who had worked inside the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and concluded the regional system was profoundly underused. It provides pro bono legal counsel to victims of human rights violations, before national courts and before the African regional bodies — the African Commission, the African Court, the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, the East African Court of Justice and the SADC Tribunal — and filed the first case ever brought before the African Commission. WHY IT BELONGS IN A MAP ABOUT LAND: the regional system is where African communities have won the landmark land rulings. The Endorois decision held that an indigenous community's rights to property, culture, religion, disposal of natural resources and development had been violated by their removal — a precedent any dispossessed community's lawyer should know exists. IHRDA maintains Africa's most comprehensive human rights case law database, free to search, which is where you find what has already been won. AND — UNUSUALLY IN THIS FILE — IT PUBLISHES A CASE INTAKE FORM: it says plainly that it is a small organisation with substantial work, that it prioritises cases with the potential to benefit wider communities and achieve systemic change, and that it provides legal expertise only and NOT financial or material assistance. It also runs country-specific litigation workshops to get civil society actors filing cases themselves, and mentions a legal defence fund supporting litigants. 949 Brusubi Layout, AU Summit Highway, P.O. Box 1896, Banjul. WHO IT SUITS: communities anywhere in Africa whose domestic remedies are exhausted or blocked, especially indigenous and minority communities facing dispossession. CAVEATS: entered under The Gambia because that is where it is based and registered — its work is continental. Regional cases take years and produce decisions that states must then be pressed to implement; it does not fund your costs; and its stated focus areas are refugees, minority rights, children and economic and social rights rather than environmental law as such.

trackers.name: Gambia Environmental Alliance — the union of 50+ community environmental groups with regional representatives, plus TANGO the NGO umbrella since 1983
trackers.desc: THE UNION A GAMBIAN VILLAGE GROUP CAN ACTUALLY JOIN: the GAMBIA ENVIRONMENTAL ALLIANCE (GEA), established and registered in 2021, describes itself as THE FIRST GOVERNING GROUP FOR ALL ENVIRONMENTAL COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANISATIONS AND CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS IN THE GAMBIA, and has grown to OVER FIFTY ORGANISATIONAL GROUPS, with MORE THAN SIX REGIONAL REPRESENTATIVES WORKING VOLUNTARILY, FROM BANJUL TO THE CENTRAL RIVER REGION. A union of community groups with a representative in your region is the thing a single village committee most lacks — fifty groups speaking together is a different weight of letter than one, and GEA exists to be joined. ITS STATED MISSION IS THE PART TO QUOTE BACK: to conserve flora, fauna, marine and coastal ecosystems, TO PROMOTE LOCAL PEOPLE'S INTERESTS OVER PROFIT for sustainable growth, and to complement government and partner efforts in policies, human resources and nature-based solutions. Its declared fields of action include ADVOCACY FOR LAND AND WATER RIGHTS, ECOSYSTEM PROTECTION AND RESTORATION, ACCESS AND BENEFIT SHARING AGREEMENTS, INNOVATIVE FINANCING MECHANISMS, POLICY INFLUENCE, and SOCIAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE, across forests, drylands, oceans and coasts, wetlands and rivers; it states it works with government departments and agencies, the private sector, academic institutions, media houses and THE NATIONAL ASSEMBLY OF THE GAMBIA. An organisation that already has a route to the National Assembly is how a village question becomes a national one — ask GEA to carry it, and ask about access and benefit sharing before you sign anything with a company. THE OLDER UMBRELLA: TANGO — THE ASSOCIATION OF NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANIZATIONS IN THE GAMBIA (tango.gm), FOUNDED 1983 — is the umbrella body for NGOs operating in the country, running national civil-society awards and validating internal policies for its members. Forty years of continuous existence makes TANGO the register of who is real in Gambian civil society: ask it whether an organisation approaching your village is actually a member. TWO MORE NAMED GAMBIAN BODIES: the STAY GREEN FOUNDATION, recorded in national climate-adaptation planning, and the WEST AFRICA BIRD STUDY ASSOCIATION (WABSA). WHO IT SUITS: Gambian village committees, community forest groups and coastal communities seeking allies, national voice or a benefit-sharing check. CAVEATS: VOLUNTEER-STAFFED MEMBERSHIP BODIES, NOT FUNDERS OR LAW FIRMS. For the community forest that becomes yours outright, The Gambia's Department of Forestry entry; for the 26-inspector enforcement reality and the A/B/C screening classes, the NEA entries; for counsel that will actually represent you, the IHRDA entry.

trackers.name: The Gambia's environment funding door — the Operational Focal Point at Environment House with phone and email, the concept-paper-first small grants route, and a labour-as-cost-share window
trackers.desc: THE FUNDING DOOR WITH AN ADDRESS ON IT — and this closes the last funding gap in this file's Gambian record: the country's OPERATIONAL FOCAL POINT for global environment financing is the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OF THE NATIONAL ENVIRONMENT AGENCY, at ENVIRONMENT HOUSE, JIMPEX ROAD, KANIFING, BANJUL — tel +220 4399423 / 4399425, with a published nea.gm email address. The Operational Focal Point ENDORSES which focal area a project's funds come from — biodiversity, climate change or land degradation — so that one office decides whether your file is even sent onward. Go there with your concept, and ask which focal area it should be filed under. THE SEQUENCE, WHICH IS WHERE MOST COMMUNITY APPLICATIONS DIE: for the small-grants window, a national community-based organisation or NGO CONTACTS THE NATIONAL COORDINATOR to receive application guidelines and forms; WITH THE COORDINATOR'S ASSISTANCE the proponent prepares A BRIEF PROJECT CONCEPT PAPER; the coordinator REVIEWS AND PRE-SCREENS it against the criteria and the country programme strategy; AND ONLY IF JUDGED ELIGIBLE does the proponent prepare a full proposal — a step that IN SOME CASES MAY BE SUPPORTED BY A PLANNING GRANT. Do not write a full proposal first. A short concept paper, prepared WITH the national coordinator's help, is the whole first stage — and there may be a grant to pay for writing the proposal itself. Grants run up to USD 50,000 directly to local communities, including indigenous peoples, community-based organisations and other non-governmental groups. A SECOND, SMALLER WINDOW WORTH KNOWING FOR ITS TERMS: a diplomatic mission in Banjul runs small grants to GAMBIAN COOPERATIVES improving basic economic or social conditions locally, maximum about USD 15,000 per project, projects completed within one year, applications encouraged FROM ALL PROVINCES, eligibility limited to cooperatives REGISTERED WITH THE GAMBIAN COOPERATIVE AGENCY — and REQUIRING COST SHARING IN THE FORM OF CASH, LABOUR OR MATERIAL PROVIDED BY THE LOCAL COMMUNITY. Labour counts as your contribution. A village with no cash still has a match to offer — and registering as a cooperative is the eligibility step that unlocks this one. WHO IT SUITS: Gambian village committees, community forest groups and cooperatives seeking project money. CAVEATS: WINDOWS ON APPLICATION CYCLES — confirm current calls and deadlines; the second is a foreign mission's programme. For the union of fifty community groups that can help you apply, The Gambia's GEA and TANGO entry; for the community forest that becomes yours outright, the Department of Forestry entry; for the 26-inspector enforcement reality, the NEA Inspectorate entry.

trackers.name: WABSA and the community bird sanctuary — a Gambian NGO with a published registration number that has built six community sanctuaries counting toward the national 15% protected-land target
trackers.desc: THE COMMUNITY SANCTUARY THAT COUNTS TOWARD THE NATIONAL TARGET — which is the strongest argument in this file for creating one, because the government needs it: the WEST AFRICAN BIRD STUDY ASSOCIATION (WABSA, wabsa.org) WAS FORMED IN APRIL 1994 BY INDIGENOUS GAMBIAN YOUTHS, CONCERNED CITIZENS SEEKING TO PRESERVE THE COUNTRY'S FLORA AND FAUNA, AND IS REGISTERED AS A CHARITABLE AND NON-PROFIT CONSERVATION NGO UNDER NGO REG N° 77, with its programmes DIRECTED BY THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS AND THE GENERAL MEMBERSHIP. Directed by the board AND the general membership means members vote on the programme, not just on the accounts. Ask whether the organisation working on your land is directed by its members — and note WABSA prints its NGO registration number, which is the document to demand from anyone. THE UNIT IT BUILDS: WABSA ESTABLISHES COMMUNITY SANCTUARIES THAT PROVIDE HABITATS FOR RESIDENT AND MIGRATORY BIRDS, WITH MAJOR COMMUNITY PROJECTS AT MARAKISSA, BRUFUT, KARTONG, BAMBALI, KUTIRR AND SIFOE COMMUNITY BIRD SANCTUARY — AND IT STATES THAT IT CONTRIBUTES THROUGH THE ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMUNITY BIRD SANCTUARIES TO THE GOVERNMENT TARGET OF 15% OF THE LAND AS PROTECTED AREAS. Six named village sanctuaries, and the government's own 15% target is met partly by them. Put it to your ministry that way: a community sanctuary on your ground is not a request, it is a contribution to a national commitment the state has already made. Ask which national target your protection would count toward — every country in this file has one. WHAT MAKES THE VILLAGERS KEEP IT: WABSA PROMOTES ALTERNATIVE SUSTAINABLE LIVELIHOOD ACTIVITIES THROUGH VEGETABLE GARDEN SCHEMES, AQUACULTURE AND CASHEW PROCESSING, AND ITS WORK HAS INCLUDED THE RESTORATION OF OYSTER FARMS — creating livelihood activities for INDIGENOUS PEOPLE LIVING NEARBY THE RESTORED AND COMMUNITY BIRD SANCTUARY AREAS. A sanctuary with a vegetable scheme and an oyster farm beside it is one the neighbours defend. Oysters in particular: the mangrove that shelters the birds is the mangrove the oysters grow on, so protection and income are the same act. THE OUTCOMES IT CLAIMS, WITH FIGURES: the restoration work HAS CONTRIBUTED TO HALTING AND REVERSING SALINE INTRUSION IN THE INDIGENOUS COMMUNITY FARMLANDS AND WETLANDS, WITH ECOSYSTEM SERVICES IMPROVED AND BIODIVERSITY SPECIES RECOVERED — AND IT IS ESTIMATED THAT WABSA'S RESTORATION ACTIVITIES CONTRIBUTE 0.15% OF THE GAMBIA'S TOTAL CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION REQUIRED BY 2030. Saline intrusion into farmland reversed is the outcome a farmer cares about; the carbon figure is what a funder cares about. Quote whichever one you are speaking to — the same mangrove does both. ITS OTHER WORK: establishing BIRD STUDY CLUBS IN SCHOOLS, research on LOCAL NAMES OF BIRDS, mangrove conservation through REDD+, and restoration at NIUMI, JOKADU, KIANG WEST and TANBI WETLAND national parks, the BAO BOLONG WETLAND RESERVE, the TANJI BIRD RESERVE and PIRANG BONTO FOREST — with a GEF small grants project on Niumi National Park, and tree planting with the national youth council and the red cross society WITH TECHNICAL SUPPORT FROM THE DEPARTMENTS OF FORESTRY AND OF PARKS AND WILDLIFE MANAGEMENT. Research on the LOCAL NAMES of birds is quiet but useful: a species recorded under the name your elders use is evidence that your community has known it for generations. WHO IT SUITS: Gambian villages wanting a sanctuary that earns, mangrove and oyster communities, and schools. CAVEATS: A SMALL MEMBERSHIP NGO dependent on project grants. For 50+ organisations and six regional representatives, The Gambia's GEA entry; for the GEF focal point at Environment House with its published telephone, the Jimpex Road entry.

trackers.name: RAMPAO — the West African marine protected areas network founded by fifteen MPAs themselves, now eight countries and 38 areas, which publishes a management-effectiveness evaluation of its own members and lets you reproduce it free
trackers.desc: FIFTEEN PROTECTED AREAS FOUNDED IT THEMSELVES — placement note first: THIS IS AN EIGHT-COUNTRY REGIONAL NETWORK, FILED UNDER THE GAMBIA BECAUSE IT IS A MEMBER COUNTRY WITH NO MARINE-NETWORK ENTRY IN THIS FILE. THE MEMBERS ARE BENIN, CABO VERDE, MAURITANIA, THE GAMBIA, GUINEA, GUINEA-BISSAU, SENEGAL AND SIERRA LEONE. HOW IT WAS MADE, AND IT IS THE PART TO COPY: FOLLOWING A LONG PROCESS OF REFLECTION AND CONCERTATION BETWEEN MPA MANAGERS AND THE DIFFERENT INSTITUTIONS INVOLVED IN THE MANAGEMENT OF MARINE AND COASTAL RESOURCES, THE REGIONAL NETWORK WAS CREATED OFFICIALLY BY FIFTEEN MEMBER MARINE PROTECTED AREAS. The areas themselves founded it — fifteen of them, after their managers had talked for a long time first. Not a donor programme with members recruited afterwards. This file recorded the same shape in Madagascar, where regional platforms of protected-area managers federated; here it happened at continental-coast scale, and the managers include community-managed areas. WHAT IT IS NOW: IT BRINGS TOGETHER 8 COUNTRIES AND OFFICIALLY COUNTS 38 MARINE PROTECTED AREAS, WITH AROUND FIFTY IN A WIDER COUNT — AND IT IS EXPANDING, WITH LIBERIA, CÔTE D'IVOIRE, GHANA, TOGO, BENIN AND NIGERIA BEING TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT IN A CONSULTATION ON EXTENSION TO THE OTHER COASTAL COUNTRIES OF THE REGION. Six more countries under consultation. If your coast is in one of those six and you manage or want a protected area, the network is actively looking for you — which is the easiest moment to join anything. WHAT MEMBERSHIP ACTUALLY PROVIDES, LISTED: SUPPORTING AND FURNISHING SERVICES TO THE MEMBERS OF THE NETWORK — THE NETWORKING OF A SET OF REPRESENTATIVE MPAs, THE REHABILITATION AND RESTORATION OF CRITICAL HABITATS, EXCHANGE AND MUTUAL LEARNING BETWEEN MEMBERS, AND TECHNICAL CAPACITY BUILDING. REHABILITATION AND RESTORATION OF CRITICAL HABITATS is a service, not a slogan — meaning the network brings resources to repair damaged ground, not only to protect intact ground. A community whose mangrove or seagrass has already been cut is still eligible; damage is not disqualifying. AND THE UNUSUAL THING IT DOES: IT PRODUCED AND PUBLISHED AN EVALUATION OF THE MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS OF THE MARINE PROTECTED AREAS OF ITS OWN NETWORK — AND THE REPRODUCTION OF THE TEXT FOR NON-COMMERCIAL PURPOSES, NOTABLY EDUCATIONAL, IS PERMITTED WITHOUT PRIOR WRITTEN AUTHORISATION, PROVIDED THE SOURCE IS DULY CITED. A network that publishes how well its own members are performing, and lets anyone copy the report free for teaching. Two uses: it tells you which areas in the region are actually managed well so you know whom to visit and ask; and the free-reproduction clause means you can print the relevant pages for your own community meeting without asking anyone. THE REFERENCE PUBLICATION: a state-of-the-marine-protected-areas report is to be EDITED EVERY 3 YEARS, deepening elements of conservation including OTHER EFFECTIVE AREA-BASED CONSERVATION MEASURES, and is described as A USEFUL AND OPERATIONAL DECISION-SUPPORT TOOL and THE RESULT OF A PARTICIPATORY AND INCLUSIVE ELABORATION PROCESS WHICH BENEFITS UPSTREAM FROM THE CONTRIBUTION OF THE PRACTITIONERS WHO ARE THE ACTORS IN THE COUNTRIES CONCERNED. Written with the practitioners upstream, not about them afterwards. If you manage an area, contributing to the next edition puts your site into the reference document that ministries and funders consult — ask when the next three-yearly cycle opens. THE OBSERVATORY BEHIND IT: AN OBSERVATORY FOR BIODIVERSITY AND PROTECTED AREAS IN WEST AFRICA IS IMPLEMENTED IN THE SIXTEEN STATES OF WEST AFRICA BY A CONSORTIUM OF FOUR NAMED INSTITUTIONS — AN ECOLOGICAL MONITORING CENTRE, THIS NETWORK, A UNIVERSITY REGIONAL MARINE CENTRE AND A REGIONAL AGRO-HYDRO-METEOROLOGY CENTRE — UNDER THE SUPERVISION OF A REGIONAL ECONOMIC UNION AS INSTITUTIONAL HOST, WITH THE OBJECTIVE OF IMPROVING THE LONG-TERM MAINTENANCE OF BIODIVERSITY THROUGH THE PROMOTION OF THE BEST SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE AND DATA AND THE REINFORCEMENT OF CAPACITIES TO SUPPORT POLICIES AND DECISION-MAKING. Two universities and a meteorological centre inside the same consortium as the MPA network, hosted by the region's economic union. The data on your coast is being assembled there — which means a community can ask that consortium what is already recorded about its own waters before commissioning anything. AND THE PURPOSE, STATED IN THE NETWORK'S OWN TERMS: IT WORKS CLOSELY WITH MPA MANAGERS TO PROMOTE THE CONSERVATION OF MARINE BIODIVERSITY FOR THE BENEFIT OF LOCAL COMMUNITIES. FOR THE BENEFIT OF LOCAL COMMUNITIES, written into the network's own description of itself. Hold it to that sentence. WHO IT SUITS: Gambian and other West African coastal communities managing or seeking a marine protected area, and anyone in the six expansion countries. CAVEATS: A NETWORK OF AREA MANAGERS — a community joins through the area it manages or co-manages, so the prior step is getting that recognition. For the seven-country coastal coalition any organisation can join with one signed form, Senegal's PRCM entry; for the coastal infrastructure training that included the financiers, Guinea's entry.

trackers.name: Story grants of $500 to $10,000 that pay a reporter's travel to cover mining, land and environmental harm — freelancers and social media creators eligible, editorial mentorship included, and organisational grants to start a reporters' network where none exists
trackers.desc: SOMEBODY WILL PAY A REPORTER TO COME AND LOOK — declared adjacency first: THIS FILE'S SOUTH SUDAN ENTRY COVERS LEGAL DEFENCE FOR JOURNALISTS ONCE THEY ARE SUED. THIS ENTRY IS THE MONEY AND TRAINING THAT GETS THE STORY REPORTED IN THE FIRST PLACE. THE MONEY: STORY GRANTS, WHICH OFTEN COVER REPORTING OR TRAVEL COSTS, RANGING FROM $500 TO AS HIGH AS $10,000 FOR INDIVIDUAL OR SMALL GROUPS OF JOURNALISTS. The reason no journalist has covered your case is usually the bus fare and the three days away, not indifference. This file has recorded again and again that a single published article is the entry ticket to everything else — the Environmental Justice Atlas requires one, funders read them, and a documented case travels. Travel money for a reporter is therefore one of the cheapest things that changes a community's position, and somebody already funds it. THE FOUR KINDS OF SUPPORT: FUNDING, TRAINING, RESOURCES, AND MENTORSHIP — WITH GRANTEES PAIRED UP WITH A VETERAN JOURNALIST OR EDITOR WHO HELPS THEM THROUGH THE COURSE OF THE INVESTIGATION AS THEY PURSUE ANGLES AND TRACK DOWN INFORMATION. LEGAL HOTLINES for government lawyers. Toll free, so the call costs the caller nothing — which matters more than it sounds for a rural woman with no airtime. Two numbers because a mobile toll-free line and a landline one are billed differently; publishing both is a deliberate choice about who can reach them. THE WALK-IN DAYS AND THE OFFICES: LEGAL AID TO INDIGENT WOMEN AND CHILDREN THROUGH OFFICES IN FIVE NAMED REGIONS, WITH STAFF ATTENDING TO CLIENTS EVERY MONDAY AND WEDNESDAY FROM 9.00 AM TO 5.00 PM — AND HEADQUARTERS AT A NAMED PLOT AND STREET ADDRESS. Named days and hours, so one journey can be planned. This file has recorded very few legal services stating when their door is actually open. THE PARALEGALS AND WHAT THEY HANDLE: 400 PARALEGALS TRAINED, DEALING WITH CASES INCLUDING GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE, MATRIMONIAL RIGHTS, INHERITANCE RIGHTS, LAND RIGHTS AND CHILDREN'S RIGHTS — WITH THE ASSOCIATION NETWORKING WITH LEGAL AID CENTRES AND TRAINING PARALEGALS TO REACH REGIONS WHERE IT HAS NO BRANCH OFFICE. Four hundred trained paralegals covering the districts the offices cannot. For a community far from any city, the paralegal is the realistic first contact — and INHERITANCE and LAND sit in the same caseload, which is how land is actually lost in most of the situations this file records. THE VOLUNTEER LAWYER SCHEME: A LARGE NUMBER OF LAWYERS SIGNED UP TO GIVE BACK TO THE COMMUNITY BY VOLUNTEERING THEIR TIME AND LEGAL SERVICES — MAINLY TAKING UP CASES FILED FAR AWAY FROM THE MAIN OFFICES. The volunteers are deliberately assigned to distant cases. Distance is treated as the thing to solve rather than the reason to decline. THE MEDIATION ROUTE AND WHAT IT COVERS: A FAMILY MEDIATION CENTRE ENCOURAGING ALTERNATIVE DISPUTE RESOLUTION AS FASTER AND MORE ACCEPTABLE AMONG DISPUTING PARTIES — A VOLUNTARY PROCESS THAT HAS ASSISTED IN SUCCESSION, DIVISION OF MATRIMONIAL PROPERTY, AND WOMEN'S LAND AND INHERITANCE; SUCCESSFUL ENOUGH THAT THE ASSOCIATION TRAINS PARTNERS IN THE COMMUNITY AS MEDIATORS TO PRESIDE OVER ISSUES AT COMMUNITY LEVEL. Community members trained as mediators, presiding locally. Where the dispute is inside a family or between neighbours — which is how most individual land loss happens — that resolves it without a court at all, and the training is transferable to any community organisation. THE LAND TASK FORCE IT COORDINATES: IT COORDINATES A GENDER LAND TASK FORCE TO ADVOCATE FOR BETTER LAND LAWS AND LAND RIGHTS AWARENESS FOR WOMEN. WHAT IT DOES BESIDES CASES: ACCESS TO JUSTICE THROUGH LEGAL AID SERVICES, ADVOCACY, AWARENESS RAISING, STRATEGIC LITIGATION, AND RESEARCH AND PUBLICATIONS. STRATEGIC LITIGATION alongside individual casework, so a community with a case that would settle a question for many others is not limited to the advice desk. THE SIZE AND THE RECORD IT PUBLISHES: FOUNDED IN 1989 AND REGISTERED IN 1990, ABOUT 800 REGISTERED MEMBERS AND A SECRETARIAT DELIVERING SERVICES IN FIVE REGIONS — HAVING REACHED ABOUT 40,000 PEOPLE COUNTRYWIDE AND ADDRESSED 57 PER CENT OF THE CASES REPORTED TO IT. Fifty-seven per cent addressed, published by the organisation itself. That is an unusually honest completion rate, and it sets a realistic expectation: roughly two in five who report get no further. THE SHORTFALL IT ADMITS: DESPITE THESE EFFORTS, WE FALL SHORT IN ENSURING THAT JUSTICE IS ACCESSIBLE EFFICIENTLY TO ALL VULNERABLE WOMEN. WHY IT WAS FOUNDED: BY A GROUP OF PROFESSIONAL WOMEN LAWYERS WHO FELT THE NEED FOR AN ORGANIZATION GUARANTEEING EQUAL RIGHTS AND ACCESS TO JUSTICE, FOCUSING ON VULNERABLE AND MARGINALIZED GROUPS — AND WHO RECOGNISED THE NEED FOR WOMEN LAWYERS TO FOSTER MUTUAL SUPPORT FOR EACH OTHER IN PROFESSIONAL ADVANCEMENT. Founded by the lawyers themselves, for each other as well as for clients. That is the model to copy where no such association exists: it needs no foreign founder, and this file's Cameroon entry records an institute that helps constitute exactly this kind of body. AND THE PRINCIPLE ITS LAND WORK RESTS ON: THE EMPOWERMENT OF THOSE WHO OTHERWISE WOULD FACE LIMITATIONS IN REPRESENTING THEIR INTERESTS, PARTICULARLY THROUGH SUPPORT TO LAND USERS' AND OTHER CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS THAT ARE BEST ABLE TO INFORM, MOBILIZE AND LEGITIMATELY REPRESENT MARGINALIZED LAND USERS. LEGITIMATELY REPRESENT is the phrase to hold onto. The lawyers are backing the community's own organisation rather than displacing it as the voice of the affected people. WHO IT SUITS: women and communities in this country facing land, inheritance or succession disputes — and organisations elsewhere looking for a national women lawyers association model to copy or contact. CAVEATS: ONE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION IN ONE COUNTRY, WITH FIVE REGIONAL OFFICES AND LIMITED CAPACITY — IT ADDRESSES 57% OF WHAT REACHES IT, AND ITS FOCUS IS WOMEN AND CHILDREN RATHER THAN COMMUNITIES GENERALLY. Look for the equivalent association in your own country. For the campaign whose coalition one such association chairs, Guinea's entry; for a body that helps establish bar associations, Cameroon's entry.

trackers.name: TALA (Tanzania Land Alliance) — fourteen land-rights organisations in one coalition, the simplified legal guides they wrote so a village can negotiate with an investor, and the 27,000-hectare biofuel lease the government finally declared void
trackers.desc: FOURTEEN LAND ORGANISATIONS IN ONE COALITION, AND A 27,000-HECTARE LEASE DECLARED VOID — method and adjacency declared first: THE WORD-BOUNDARY PROBE RAN THREE HOSTS AND EIGHT DISTINGUISHING FACTS ACROSS ALL 53 BUCKETS; THE ALLIANCE'S OWN HOST, ITS ACRONYM AND FIVE FACTS ABSENT. THREE MEMBER ORGANISATIONS ARE ALREADY FILED UNDER TANZANIA ON THEIR OWN HOSTS AND WERE READ IN FULL — A LAND RIGHTS MONITOR TRAINER, A LEGAL AND HUMAN RIGHTS CENTRE, AND A MEMBER-DRIVEN NATURAL RESOURCE FORUM. A SUPPORTING ORGANISATION APPEARS UNDER THE REPUBLIC OF CONGO. NONE IS RESTATED AND NO HOST IS REUSED. WHAT IT IS AND WHO IS IN IT, WHICH IS THE FIND: A MEMBER-BASED COALITION OF FOURTEEN CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS REPRESENTING THE LEADING LAND RIGHTS BODIES IN THE COUNTRY — NAMED MEMBERS INCLUDING A LAND RIGHTS RESEARCH INSTITUTE WHICH SERVES AS SECRETARIAT, A LEGAL AND HUMAN RIGHTS CENTRE, A LAWYERS' ENVIRONMENTAL ACTION TEAM, A PASTORALISTS INDIGENOUS NGOs FORUM, A WOMEN'S LEGAL AID CENTRE, A COMMUNITY RESOURCE TEAM AND A NATIONAL NETWORK OF SMALL FARMERS' GROUPS. Fourteen organisations, one door. The membership list is the useful part: environmental lawyers, pastoralist organisations, a women's legal aid centre and a farmers' network are different specialisms, and a village does not have to know in advance which its problem belongs to. THE VOID LEASE, WHICH IS THE SECOND FIND: IN 2006 A FOREIGN BIOFUEL COMPANY CLAIMED TO HAVE LEASED OVER 27,000 HECTARES FROM FOUR VILLAGES IN ONE DISTRICT — AND IN LATE 2020, AFTER A PROTRACTED DISPUTE, THE GOVERNMENT FOUND THE TRANSFER OF LANDS HAD NOT ADHERED TO LAND TRANSFER LEGAL REQUIREMENTS AND WAS THEREFORE VOID. VOID, not compensated. Fourteen years, four villages, 27,000 hectares, and the deal was found never to have been validly made. This file's DR Congo entry records the argument that a claim's legitimacy stands whatever the title says; this is the same point from the other direction — a signed lease that skipped the statutory transfer steps is not a lease. Ask which steps your own country's land transfer law requires, and whether the investor completed them. THE GUIDES THEY WROTE FOR THAT REASON, WHICH IS THE THIRD FIND: SIMPLIFIED LEGAL GUIDES DEVELOPED OVER FIVE YEARS WITH A LAND RIGHTS ORGANISATION AND A NATURAL RESOURCE FORUM UNDER A NATIONAL ENGAGEMENT STRATEGY — HELPING COMMUNITIES ENGAGE IN DIALOGUE AND NEGOTIATION WITH GOVERNMENT AUTHORITIES AND INVESTORS, AND PREPARING THEM TO NEGOTIATE FROM A POSITION OF EMPOWERMENT. Written after a fourteen-year dispute, by the people who fought it. A guide produced out of a specific defeat is worth more than one written from a template. WHERE THEY ARE MOST NEEDED RIGHT NOW: LAND-BASED INVESTMENT NEGOTIATIONS CONTINUE FOR LARGE AREAS OF A NAMED SOUTHERN AGRICULTURAL GROWTH CORRIDOR, WHERE THAT DISTRICT AND OTHERS SIT. An agricultural growth corridor is a designated zone where investment is actively solicited. If your village sits inside one, the negotiation is coming whether or not anyone has told you. THE TWENTY-YEAR PATTERN IT NAMES: OVER THE LAST TWENTY YEARS CONFLICT HAS ESCALATED BETWEEN COMMUNITIES AND FOREIGN INVESTORS OVER LAND RIGHTS AND LAND-BASED INVESTMENTS. WHAT THE ALLIANCE SAYS IT IS FOR: ENSURING THAT MARGINALISED COMMUNITIES HAVE SECURE AND EQUITABLE ACCESS TO, CONTROL OVER AND OWNERSHIP OF LAND AND NATURAL RESOURCES. WHY IT WAS FOUNDED AND WHEN: FOUNDED IN 2010 TO UNDERTAKE JOINT ADVOCACY, SPEARHEADING THE ATTAINMENT OF LAND RIGHTS FOR SMALL PRODUCERS. THE ROLE IT CLAIMS: GIVING LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND MEMBERS A VOICE TO POLICYMAKERS — ITS MAJOR GOAL BEING IMPROVED LAND LAWS AND POLICIES THAT SAFEGUARD THE LAND RIGHTS OF MARGINALISED GROUPS. THE ARGUMENT IT MAKES FOR URGENCY: LAND IS LIFE FOR MOST PEOPLE IN THE COUNTRY, YET FAR TOO MANY REMAIN AT RISK OF LOSING IT; THOSE WHO DEPEND ON THEIR LAND WITHOUT RIGHTS OVER IT FACE LOSING NOT JUST THE LAND BUT THEIR ENTIRE LIVELIHOOD. WHAT IT SAYS IS NEEDED BESIDES GOOD LAW: SYSTEMS AND INSTITUTIONS THAT UPHOLD THOSE RIGHTS — NOT MERELY LAWS AND POLICIES PROVIDING FOR THEM. The distinction this file keeps running into: a right on paper with no institution behind it is not a right. Worth asking any organisation offering help which institution it can actually make move. THE GOVERNMENT PROGRAMME IT JOINED, AND WHAT IT DELIVERED: SEVERAL MEMBER ORGANISATIONS WERE ENGAGED IN A LAND TENURE SUPPORT PROGRAMME IN THREE NAMED DISTRICTS TO ENHANCE TRANSPARENCY, ACCOUNTABILITY AND EQUITABLE LAND GOVERNANCE — SURVEYING LAND AND AWARDING CUSTOMARY CERTIFICATES OF RIGHTS OF OCCUPANCY TO VILLAGERS AND COMMUNITY GROUPS, GIVING THEM LEGAL EVIDENCE OF THEIR CLAIM. Civil society inside a government titling programme rather than outside protesting it. That is a route worth naming: where the state is already surveying, the organisations that get seats on the programme decide whether community groups as well as individuals get certificates. AND WHAT CHANGED WHERE IT RAN: CONFLICTS RARELY ERUPT NOW AND PEOPLE ARE ASSURED OF OWNERSHIP THROUGH THE CERTIFICATES; SURVEYING ALSO ENABLED OWNERS TO DO LAND USE PLANNING AND USE THEIR PROPERTY FOR ECONOMIC ACTIVITIES BEYOND FARMING AND GRAZING — WITH ONE HOLDER SAYING HE NOW FEELS CONFIDENT TO USE HIS PIECE OF LAND AS HE WISHES. WHO IT SUITS: villages inside an investment corridor facing a lease negotiation, and coalitions that want the shape of a fourteen-member land alliance with a research institute as secretariat. CAVEATS: ONE COUNTRY; IT IS AN ADVOCACY COALITION RATHER THAN A LAW FIRM — THE LITIGATION CAPACITY SITS IN ITS MEMBER ORGANISATIONS, AND THE VOID-LEASE FINDING TOOK FOURTEEN YEARS; SOME MATERIAL CITED IS OLDER. For the land rights monitors who live in the village, the legal and human rights centre, and the member-driven natural resource forum, Tanzania's own entries.

trackers.name: Les Amis de la Terre-Togo (ADT-Togo)
trackers.desc: Togo's first NGO wholly dedicated to environmental protection, founded on 20 June 1990 and formally recognised as an association the following year, and the Togolese member of Friends of the Earth International. Its work spans biodiversity, climate, desertification, water and sanitation, chemicals, mining and scrutiny of public decision-making, delivered largely through community dialogues, agro-ecology training and youth education from its Lome office. WHO TO ENLIST: a first port of call for a Togolese community rather than a litigator — ADT-Togo is a focal point for the national civil-society networks on climate and energy, so it is the quickest route to finding who else already works on a site. Note the canonical domain is amiterre.org; several older wordpress and .tg addresses for this organisation still circulate.

trackers.name: Togo — Ministère des Finances et du Budget
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares the finance law (loi de finances) and the programme-budget and oversees public revenue & expenditure, Togo. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Togo.

trackers.name: Togo — Centre de Formalités des Entreprises (CFE)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the CFE one-stop window handles company creation, modification & dissolution (RCCM) and serves as the legal-announcements platform, Togo. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Cour des comptes du Togo
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Togo — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: High Court of Justice
trackers.desc: High Court of Justice — supreme court in Togo (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: RAPID MONEY WHEN SOMETHING SUDDEN HAPPENS — and it is open all year. UAF-Africa is a pan-African feminist rapid response fund, founded 2001 in Nairobi, with geographical presence in Africa's 54 countries and over 6,000 grants resourced. BE CLEAR ON SCOPE: it supports women, girls and gender-diverse people and women's rights organisations — it is not a general environmental fund. It belongs in this map because it fits a specific and recurring situation: women land and environmental defenders facing threats, harassment or security risks. NO FUNDING CYCLE — apply as soon as an urgent situation requires it, to proposals@uaf-africa.org. THREE GRANT TYPES: rapid response, protection grants up to USD 15,000, and advocacy and alliance building up to USD 30,000. FOUR CRITERIA, ALL REQUIRED: strategic (tied to a plan for structural change), unanticipated (could not have been foreseen), time urgent (must happen within 3 months or the opportunity is lost), and sustainable. The ‘unanticipated’ test is what disqualifies most applications — planned programme work does not qualify, by design. Applications may be written in French, English, Swahili or Arabic. Both registered and informal groups may apply; individuals are not funded.

trackers.name: ECOWAS Court of Justice — file directly, but sue the State
trackers.desc: A COURT YOU CAN REACH WITHOUT EXHAUSTING DOMESTIC REMEDIES. The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has held human rights jurisdiction since 2005 and has broad access and standing rules permitting individuals and NGOs to bypass national courts and file directly. THE PRECEDENT: in SERAP v Federal Republic of Nigeria (ECW/CCJ/APP/08/09) the Court dismissed all three preliminary objections — no locus standi, no jurisdiction, statute-barred — and rejected the government's attempt to exclude an Amnesty International report from the evidence. NGO research was admitted as evidence, which matters when no state data exists. It found violations of articles 1 and 24 of the African Charter — article 24: ‘all peoples shall have the right to a general satisfactory environment favourable to their development’ — and of article 21, the right to natural wealth and resources. THE FAULT WAS AN OMISSION: the state ‘defaulted in its duties in terms of vigilance and diligence’, and ‘the omission to act and to prevent damage to the environment characterises the violation’. It ordered restoration within the shortest possible time and measures to prevent further damage, citing the ICJ that the environment ‘is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn’. THE LIMIT THAT DECIDES WHO YOU SUE: the Court held it had no jurisdiction over the private oil corporations, which were struck from the suit. You sue the State for failing to regulate; you cannot sue the company here — naming one as respondent loses that part of the case. AND PLAN FOR ENFORCEMENT: commentary records the Court did not identify a means for Nigeria to implement the ruling, and the ICJ later wrote to the President pressing for enforcement — judgment is the start of an enforcement campaign, not a self-executing remedy. Proposals to require exhaustion of domestic remedies were rejected by ECOWAS experts and Heads of Government, so the direct-access rule has been tested and held.

trackers.name: ORFAO — comparative land-law tables, and a directive in draft
trackers.desc: COMPARATIVE LEGAL TABLES FOR YOUR COUNTRY AND ITS NEIGHBOURS, IN ONE DOCUMENT. The Observatoire Régional du Foncier Rural en Afrique de l'Ouest (ORFAO), hosted by UEMOA, publishes a regional study on rural land markets containing side-by-side ‘cadre légal comparé’ tables — one covering Bénin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire and Sénégal, another Guinée-Bissau, Mali, Niger and Togo — plus typologies of direct and indirect interventions in land markets and a table of regulatory issues and families of instruments. If you need to know what instrument exists in your country and whether a neighbour has a stronger one, that is the document — comparative tables let a campaign point to a neighbour's provision as an achievable ask rather than a novelty. A WINDOW IS OPENING: on 26 June 2026 in Ouagadougou the UEMOA ministers for urbanisme, habitat, domaines et cadastre approved a draft directive to harmonise rules on immatriculation foncière, accès au titre de propriété and a système d'information foncière, aiming at a common framework of land governance. BE PRECISE ABOUT STATUS: that was a DRAFT directive approved by ministers, not an adopted and transposed instrument — check adoption and transposition before relying on it. But transposition is the moment domestic land law is reopened in each state, and that is when community provisions can be argued for. FOR A GRAZING OR TRANSHUMANCE DISPUTE: a regional pastoral situation bulletin covers 11 West African countries with the support of decentralised technical services — an evidence source drawing on the same services you would otherwise approach one by one. RECORDED PLAINLY: cattle theft is documented as a driver of conflict and instability in the Sahel, so a land dispute here may sit inside a security context that changes what is safe to do. And confirm your state's current ECOWAS standing — several members are recorded as suspended.

trackers.name: JVE — an environmental organisation with branches in dozens of Togolese localities, and a standing programme on dams and mining
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Jeunes Volontaires pour l'Environnement, founded on 23 November 2001 by Togolese students who had watched their country's land degrade, now an IUCN member with its international secretariat in Lomé. THE REACH IS THE POINT, because in Togo almost everything else is capital-bound: JVE reports around 32 to 40 local branches inside Togo, with regional antennas relaying activity at community level from Vogan (60 km from Lomé), Tsiko (140 km) and Kara (450 km) — so the north of the country is actually covered — plus national representations across roughly 25 African countries, each with relative autonomy. WHAT TO ASK FOR SPECIFICALLY: among its five published programmes is one on social justice covering dams, mining, and economic, social and cultural rights, alongside work on environmental impact assessment, access to water and river protection, sustainable agriculture and campaigning on genetically modified organisms. That programme, not the youth-and-volunteering framing, is the part that matches a community fighting a project. It runs weekly radio and television output and a monthly paper, which is a distribution channel a village campaign does not otherwise have. 131 rue Ofè, Tokoin Casablanca, BP 8823, Lomé; founder and executive director Sena Alouka. WHO IT SUITS: Togolese communities facing dams, mining, water loss or land degradation, and community groups elsewhere in West Africa able to reach a national representation. CAVEATS: an environmental education, volunteering and advocacy organisation, not a law firm — no litigation capacity, no intake route, no fee information; branch counts differ between its own listings (20 towns, 32 branches, 40 localities) and several published pages are old, so confirm which branch is active near you.

trackers.name: Centre pour la Justice Environnementale — works the Togolese phosphate belt, where the compensation is 5 CFA francs per square metre a year
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Togolese environmental justice centre working with the communities around the phosphate operations — Kpémé, Goumoukopé and Hahotoé-Kpogamé — where the processing plant sits on land the villagers had to give up. Its stated work is upholding the rights of those neighbouring communities against social and environmental injustice, pressing for effluent treatment before discharge, reduction of gas and dust emissions, and direct accompaniment of affected communities, including income-generating activities. THE NUMBER THAT TELLS YOU WHAT A BAD LAND DEAL LOOKS LIKE, and which any community should compare their own offer against: when the phosphate company was established the villagers ceded land, and the company now pays the former owners 5 CFA francs per square metre — roughly three-quarters of a euro cent — per year or per quarter depending on the plot. Residents also report that the jobs went to casual and contract workers, so the plant brought neither land rent nor employment. A perpetual rent set decades ago and never indexed is worth nothing; check whether your agreement has a revision clause before you sign it. WHAT TOGOLESE CIVIL SOCIETY IS DEMANDING ON RESETTLEMENT, published jointly by a human rights committee, two development associations and the phosphate-affected persons' association ASIPTO, is a usable checklist: count new dwellings separately from those already counted; raise the rent per square metre; raise the housing construction payment to at least 2 million CFA francs per dwelling to match current costs; publish clear directives on responsible land tenure governance; and seek the CONSENT and full participation of the people facing relocation as rights holders. Togo's expropriation regime rests on a 1945 decree and a 1974 ordinance, and campaigners note that expropriation must be for a legally established public purpose with just, prior and fair compensation. WHO IT SUITS: Togolese communities facing mining pollution, land cession to an industrial operator, or relocation. CAVEATS: an advocacy and accompaniment organisation, not a law firm; ASIPTO, the affected people's own association, may merit its own entry; and Togo's Amis de la Terre and JVE entries cover the wider environmental and social-justice work.

trackers.name: Togo's aide juridictionnelle law of 24 May 2013 — the state can pay for your case, in full or in part, and it covers settlements as well as trials
trackers.desc: WHAT THE LAW PAYS FOR: Togo's loi portant AIDE JURIDICTIONNELLE, adopted 24 MAY 2013, under which the state may grant FINANCIAL AID in the context of a procedure before a court AND/OR IN A TRANSACTION — and the aid may be TOTAL OR PARTIAL. Two things there are easy to miss: partial aid exists, so being told you do not qualify for full support is not the end; and the aid covers a NEGOTIATED SETTLEMENT (transaction), not only a trial — which matters enormously in a land dispute where the realistic outcome is a deal rather than a judgment. WHO CAN CLAIM IT: it is granted on request to Togolese nationals; nationals of a state bound to Togo by a bilateral agreement recognising the benefit; refugees recognised by Togo; and ASYLUM SEEKERS whose claim is pending before the national eligibility commission. Displaced and non-citizen residents are inside this scheme by name — rare enough in this file to be worth checking for in your own country's text. WHERE IT SITS: the law completed a national policy on access to law and legal dissemination targeting the population's priority legal-information needs, within a judicial reform and modernisation programme running since 2006 with UN development programme support. Read it alongside the francophone vocabulary recorded in Benin's entry — this is the FINANCIAL limb, so the words to use at the counter are aide juridictionnelle. WHO IT SUITS: Togolese households and communities — including those around the phosphate belt — who need the state to fund a case or a settlement, and refugees or asylum seekers in Togo. CAVEATS: THIS IS A FUNDING SCHEME, NOT AN OFFICE THAT ARGUES YOUR CASE — confirm which bureau receives the request and what proof of means it wants; the law dates from 2013 and implementation should be verified locally. For the phosphate communities and the resettlement checklist, Togo's Centre pour la Justice Environnementale entry; for wider environmental and social justice work, Les Amis de la Terre-Togo and JVE.

trackers.name: Togo's forêts communautaires — the Village Development Committee becomes the forest's LEGAL ENTITY and files for registration; 43 are registered, most others have no legal status
trackers.desc: HOW A TOGOLESE VILLAGE GETS ITS FOREST REGISTERED: community forests in Togo are governed by the LOI PORTANT CODE FORESTIER OF 2008. The route is shown by ALIBI-1, whose community moved BEFORE the state did — working with a national association it put in place and SECURED 5,496 HECTARES of forest adjoining the classified forest of Abdoulaye. THE VEHICLE, AND THIS IS THE STEP TO COPY: the COMITÉ VILLAGEOIS DE DÉVELOPPEMENT IS TODAY THE LEGAL ENTITY MANAGING THE FOREST, and it is that committee which launched the process of IMMATRICULATION — REGISTRATION OF THE FOREST BY THE ENVIRONMENT MINISTRY. Your existing village development committee can become the forest's legal person; you do not need to create a new body, you need to give the one you have the forest and then register it. The management committees are constituted to represent every part of the community — traditional chieftaincy, farmers' groups, folkloric groups, women's associations — and the paperwork presented publicly is the CHARTE DE GESTION and the CONTRAT DE MISE À DISPOSITION. Ask for those two documents by name. RESULTS AND SCALE: at Alibi bush fires, anarchic wood-cutting and poaching fell considerably through the local management committee, and the case became a national school example; elsewhere ECO-GARDES are trained and equipped from each canton to patrol, and beekeeping with distributed hives gives the committee an income. A village that began with a 14-metre firebreak and a 10-metre tree belt grew a community forest 350 to 850 metres deep around the town, zoned into 25 ha conservation, 44 ha forest and 33 ha agroforestry. THE HONEST PROBLEM, STATED BY TOGOLESE RESEARCH: community forests exist in many forms — sacred forests, village reforestation — but FEW OF THEM HAVE LEGAL STATUS; only 43 have been registered with the environment ministry across all regions. An unregistered community forest is the commonest situation in Togo and the most fragile — registration is the whole difference. WHO IT SUITS: Togolese villages holding a sacred forest, a reforested belt or any communal woodland without papers. CAVEATS: REGISTRATION IS MINISTERIAL AND MANAGEMENT-PLAN BASED, not a title deed; research finds management committees need organisational support and diversified income to hold. For the phosphate belt and the resettlement checklist, Togo's Centre pour la Justice Environnementale entry; for state funding of a case or settlement, the aide juridictionnelle entry.

trackers.name: AGBO-ZEGUE ONG, Lomé — the Togolese conservation society that helped create the protected sites it now works around, holds the Mono Basin platform presidency, and publishes its récépissé number and a direct phone contact
trackers.desc: THE ORGANISATION THAT BUILT THE SITES: the SOCIÉTÉ TOGOLAISE POUR LA CONSERVATION DE LA NATURE, known as AGBO-ZEGUE ONG, a non-profit CREATED 18 JULY 2001 AT LOMÉ and officially recognised by RÉCÉPISSÉ DE DÉCLARATION N°0791/MISD-SG-DAPSC-DSC OF 1 AUGUST 2003. It publishes its récépissé number — which is the exact document this file tells you to ask every organisation for. An organisation that prints its registration number without being asked is one you can verify before you trust it. It began as an association for the study and conservation of marine turtles, was initially composed of students, and its members are now academics, professionals and technicians in natural resource management; its mission is to bring SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL SUPPORT to the conservation of threatened species, fragile ecosystems and above all PROTECTED AREAS. THE CLAIM THAT MATTERS MOST: IT HAS DEVELOPED A SOLID PARTNERSHIP WITH THE LOCAL ASSOCIATIONS AROUND THE BIOSPHERE RESERVE SITES THAT IT ITSELF HELPED PUT IN PLACE — the TOGODO PROTECTED AREA COMPLEX, the SACRED FOREST OF GODJÈ-GODJIN, the AVÉVÉ FOREST, the ASSÉVÉ FOREST AND LAKE TOGO — and it is also well represented around the GBAGA CHANNEL, the AKISSA FOREST and the AFITO PONDS even though those sites are not directly managed by it. An organisation that helped create a protected site is the one that knows how the file was assembled and who signed it. If your ground could become such a site, this is who has done it before in Togo — and note that a SACRED FOREST is among the sites it helped establish, so a spiritual claim is a recognised route here. ITS STANDING AND ITS REACH: across the whole MONO BASIN it holds solid contacts even beyond the biosphere reserve sites, and that representativeness was recognised when the general assembly of the MONO BASIN CIVIL SOCIETY PLATFORM DESIGNATED IT TO HOLD THE PRESIDENCY; in ECOLOGICAL ZONE IV, the mountain forest zone, it has developed close relations with key resource people. Its published fields are protected areas, marine environment, wetlands and aquatic zones, biodiversity, climate change and RURAL DEVELOPMENT, and its work includes mangrove restoration in the Lakes prefecture and PARTICIPATORY MAPPING AT COMMUNITY LEVEL with subnational forest inventory for forest landscape restoration. Contact is published as a named person with a direct mobile number and email. WHO IT SUITS: Togolese communities in the Mono basin, the Lakes prefecture, the mountain forest zone, or beside any of the named sites. CAVEATS: A SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL CONSERVATION NGO, not a funder or a law firm. For the Village Development Committee route to a community forest, Togo's forêts communautaires entry; for pollution work in the Togolese phosphate zone, the Centre pour la Justice Environnementale entry; for branches in dozens of localities, JVE; for the state-paid lawyer, the aide juridictionnelle entry.

trackers.name: UONGTO — Togo's NGO umbrella since 1993, which holds seats on the public procurement regulator's council AND its disputes committee, plus the extractive transparency steering committee — with its Lomé BP and director's contacts
trackers.desc: A SEAT ON THE BODY THAT SETTLES PROCUREMENT DISPUTES — and that is unusual enough to lead with: UONGTO IS A MEMBER OF THE CONSEIL DE RÉGULATION AND OF THE COMITÉ DE RÈGLEMENT DES DIFFÉRENDS OF THE AUTORITÉ DE RÉGULATION DES MARCHÉS PUBLICS DU TOGO, FROM 2011 TO THE PRESENT — AND IS ALSO A MEMBER OF THE STEERING AND SUPERVISION COMMITTEE OF THE EXTRACTIVE INDUSTRIES TRANSPARENCY INITIATIVE. Civil society sitting on the committee that RULES ON public procurement disputes, not merely observing the regulator. Almost every project in this file begins with a public contract — a road, a dam, a concession, a clearance. If the contract behind the project on your land was irregular, there is a national body that decides such complaints, and an NGO umbrella has held a seat on it since 2011. Ask UONGTO who sits there now and what a community can bring. AND THE SECOND SEAT COVERS THE OTHER HALF: the extractive transparency steering committee is where mining and oil revenue reporting is supervised. Between the two seats, this one organisation is inside both the contracting and the extractives oversight of the country. WHO IT IS: THE UNION DES ONG DU TOGO, FOUNDED IN 1993, IS AN APOLITICAL AND NON-PROFIT FAÎTIÈRE WHICH AIMS TO COORDINATE ACTIONS BETWEEN ITS MEMBERS AND PROMOTE PARTNERSHIP BETWEEN THEM AND NATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ORGANISATIONS — at BP 14066, LOMÉ, WITH A NAMED EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR AS FOCAL POINT, AN EMAIL ADDRESS AND A TELEPHONE NUMBER. ITS FOUR STATED ACTIVITIES, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE TO USE: COORDINATION, PLANNING, IMPLEMENTATION AND MONITORING-EVALUATION OF PROJECTS OF NATIONAL AND REGIONAL SCOPE; REPRESENTATION OF ITS MEMBERS BEFORE THE PUBLIC AUTHORITIES AND INTERNATIONAL PARTNERS; CAPACITY REINFORCEMENT THROUGH INSTITUTIONAL, TECHNICAL AND ORGANISATIONAL SUPPORT; AND LOBBYING AND ADVOCACY FOR THE EMERGENCE OF A STRONG CIVIL SOCIETY ABLE TO INFLUENCE PUBLIC POLICIES. REPRESENTATION OF ITS MEMBERS BEFORE THE PUBLIC AUTHORITIES is a service, not a slogan. A village association that is a member does not have to reach a ministry alone — the umbrella's job description says it appears for you. That is what the seats above are for. Its stated mission adds: TO REINFORCE THE CAPACITIES AND PROFESSIONALISM OF CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS IN TOGO; TO COORDINATE AND ACCOMPANY THEM IN REINFORCING THE IMPACT OF THEIR ACTIONS; AND TO WORK TO MAXIMISE THE EFFECTIVENESS OF THEIR PARTICIPATION IN GOOD GOVERNANCE. THE PLATFORMS IT CONVENES OR BELONGS TO ARE NAMED, AND TWO ARE DIRECTLY ON POINT: A NATIONAL PLATFORM FOR THE PROMOTION OF FAMILY AGRICULTURE IN TOGO; A PLATFORM OF NGOs IMPLEMENTING SAVINGS-GROUP PROGRAMMES IN TOGO; AND A MINING SECTOR ACCOUNTABILITY FORUM UNDER A MINING DEVELOPMENT AND GOVERNANCE PROJECT. A national FAMILY AGRICULTURE platform is where a smallholder facing a land taking belongs, and a SAVINGS-GROUP platform is where the money to survive one comes from — this file has recorded savings groups as the most durable community finance there is. And a mining accountability forum with a project behind it is a standing room, not a one-off meeting: ask when it next sits. THE SECOND UMBRELLA: A FÉDÉRATION DES ONG AU TOGO ALSO EXISTS IN LOMÉ. Two national NGO umbrellas in one country is worth knowing before you join one — ask each which ministries and committees it actually sits on, because that is the difference between them. AND THE UNIONS, WITH THE CAUTION STATED: THREE NATIONAL TRADE UNION CENTRES ARE NAMED IN LOMÉ, ONE OF THEM WITH 35,000 MEMBERS AND CREATED IN JANUARY 1973, ANOTHER A NATIONAL UNION OF INDEPENDENT TRADE UNIONS, EACH WITH A NAMED SECRETARY GENERAL AND EACH AFFILIATED TO AN INTERNATIONAL TRADE UNION CONFEDERATION — BUT THE LARGEST IS RECORDED AS STILL SEEN AS BEING THE TRADE UNION CENTRE MOST CLOSELY AFFILIATED WITH THE GOVERNMENT. Thirty-five thousand organised workers is real weight, and the international affiliation is a route out of the country. But one of the three is described as close to the government and the file says so rather than pretending otherwise — if a state project is the problem, check which centre you are approaching, and note that a genuinely independent confederation exists alongside it. WHO IT SUITS: Togolese associations wanting representation before ministries, smallholders, savings groups, and anyone whose problem began with a public contract or a mining licence. CAVEATS: AN UMBRELLA AND A REGULATOR SEAT — not a litigator, and the procurement route concerns the contract rather than the land. For an environmental organisation with branches in dozens of Togolese localities, Togo's JVE entry; for the phosphate belt, the Centre pour la Justice Environnementale; for the state paying for your lawyer, the aide juridictionnelle entry; for the conservation society that helped create protected areas, AGBO-ZEGUE; for Les Amis de la Terre-Togo, the ADT-Togo entry.

trackers.name: Fundraising from a basic phone with no internet — a USSD shortcode to start a fund, up to three treasurers who must each text approval before money moves, a 4.25% fee, and a downloadable list of every donor and channel
trackers.desc: THREE TREASURERS MUST TEXT YES BEFORE ANY MONEY MOVES — declared complement first: THE PREVIOUS ENTRY IN THIS FILE, UNDER CHAD, COVERS A GLOBAL CROWDFUNDING PLATFORM WHOSE OWN TERMS WARN IT IS BEST-SUITED FOR ORGANIZATIONS WITH SUPPORTERS WHO CAN DONATE ONLINE, AND WHICH REQUIRES ENGLISH AND REGISTRATION. THIS ENTRY IS THE ANSWER FOR COMMUNITIES WHOSE SUPPORTERS HAVE A BASIC PHONE AND NO CARD. THE ACCESS POINT: CONTRIBUTIONS CAN BE MADE VIA MOBILE MONEY, CARDS, PAYPAL AND EVEN USSD/SMS — MAKING IT ONE OF THE MOST INCLUSIVE CROWDFUNDING PLATFORMS IN AFRICA. ANYONE WITH A BASIC MOBILE PHONE CAN DONATE, NO INTERNET OR SMARTPHONE NEEDED, AND MOBILE FUNDRAISERS ARE PERFECT FOR INDIVIDUALS WITHOUT REGULAR INTERNET ACCESS. THE WHOLE THING RUNS OFF A SHORTCODE: DIAL A PUBLISHED USSD CODE, READ AND ACCEPT TERMS, AND YOUR FUNDRAISER EXISTS. THE SAME CODE SHARES IT TO SUPPORTERS BY SMS OR SOCIAL MEDIA, ADDS TREASURERS, CHECKS STATUS, VIEWS THE STATEMENT, WITHDRAWS, AND ENDS THE FUNDRAISER. No office, no laptop, no bank visit to start. For a village committee whose members share one handset, that is the difference between a fund existing and not existing. THE ANTI-THEFT DEVICE, AND IT IS THE FIND: ADD UP TO 3 TREASURERS TO MAKE YOUR FUNDRAISER MORE SECURE — ALL TREASURERS RECEIVE AN SMS WHEN THERE IS AN ATTEMPT TO WITHDRAW FUNDS, AND THEY MUST RESPOND VIA SMS TO ACCEPT THE WITHDRAWAL. Three people must each text yes before a shilling leaves. Money is what splits community committees in this file more reliably than any developer does — and here is a technical answer that costs nothing: nobody can take the fund alone, and everybody knows it from the first day. Set the three treasurers up before you raise anything, and choose them from different families. THE FEE AND THE MESSAGING: A SERVICE FEE OF 4.25% OF THE AMOUNT BEING WITHDRAWN, PLUS NORMAL NETWORK CHARGES — AND EACH FUNDRAISER RECEIVES 250 FREE SMS MESSAGES, WITH ADDITIONAL MESSAGES AT PUBLISHED PER-MESSAGE RATES THAT FALL AS THE DONOR COUNT RISES. 4.25% against the 5–12% of the global platform, and 250 free messages to thank and update people. Reporting back to donors is what makes the second fundraiser easier than the first, and here it is paid for. THE ACCOUNTING TRAIL, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WILL BE ASKED FOR LATER: FUNDS ARE HELD IN TRUST AND CAN BE WITHDRAWN WHENEVER THE FUNDRAISER WISHES, USUALLY PROCESSED THE NEXT WORKING DAY; PROGRESS IS TRACKED IN A WEB PORTAL SUMMARY OR ON THE SHARE PAGE; AND YOU CAN DOWNLOAD A LIST OF PAYMENTS INCLUDING THE DONOR'S NAME, PHONE NUMBER OR EMAIL, THE TOTAL GIVEN AND THE PAYMENT CHANNEL USED. A downloadable donor list is a financial record you did not have to keep. This file has recorded that two years of accounts is the gate at almost every serious funder — running your community fund through a platform that generates the statement is how a village group acquires a financial history. THE ADVICE THAT PREVENTS THE ARGUMENT: WHEN YOU SET UP THE FUNDRAISER THE SUPPORT TEAM WILL ASK WHERE YOU WOULD LIKE THE FUNDS DEPOSITED — FUNDS CAN BE SENT TO A BANK, WHICH IS RECOMMENDED, OR A MOBILE WALLET, AND IT IS ADVISABLE TO DIRECT THE FUNDS TO THE SOURCE. Pay the lawyer, the surveyor or the school directly rather than into anyone's wallet. That single choice removes most of the suspicion a community fund attracts. THE CULTURAL POINT THAT SHOULD CHANGE YOUR STRATEGY, FROM THE FOUNDERS THEMSELVES: HARAMBEES RELY FIRST AND FOREMOST ON FAMILY NETWORKS AND THEN FRIENDS — THE GENERAL PUBLIC, ANONYMOUS CROWDFUNDING, IS THE LAST RESORT FOR ANYONE DOING A HARAMBEE. THIS DIFFERENCE GREATLY IMPACTS THE PROPENSITY TO GIVE, HOW OFTEN ONE GIVES, AS WELL AS THE APPROACH FOR REQUESTS FOR HELP. Family first, friends second, strangers last. That is the opposite order to how most campaigns are planned, and it is why appeals aimed at the public raise nothing while a request passed through relatives raises the whole sum. This file's previous entry made the same point in different words: count your forty people before you apply anywhere. THE DIASPORA CHANNEL: CONTRIBUTORS ABROAD ARE PROVIDED A TRANSPARENT AND CHEAP METHOD OF REMITTING CASH TO SPECIFIC CAUSES, WITH TRANSPARENCY AT ALL STAGES, AND CAN CONTRIBUTE VIA PAYPAL AND CREDIT CARD. Relatives abroad already send money home; this lets them send it to the campaign and see where it went. The transparency is the selling point to them, not the convenience. WHAT PEOPLE ACTUALLY USE IT FOR, AND THE LAST ITEM IS THE RELEVANT ONE: CAMPAIGN TYPES RANGE FROM SCHOOL FEES, MEDICAL EMERGENCIES, FUNERALS AND WEDDINGS, TO BUSINESS CAPITAL, CHURCH PROGRAMS, AND COMMUNITY WATER PROJECTS. Community infrastructure is already a normal category here. A fund for a survey, a lawyer's fee or a boundary mapping is not an odd request on this platform. AND THE OTHER LOCAL-CURRENCY PLATFORMS NAMED: PLATFORMS ALLOWING FUNDRAISING IN LOCAL CURRENCIES SUCH AS KENYAN SHILLINGS, SOUTH AFRICAN RAND AND NIGERIAN NAIRA, WHICH MAKES DONATING EASIER FOR LOCAL SUPPORTERS — WHILE GLOBAL PLATFORMS REACH INTERNATIONAL SUPPORTERS, AND MANY CAMPAIGNS SUCCESSFULLY RAISE FUNDS FROM THE AFRICAN DIASPORA FOR PROJECTS BACK HOME. Run both if you can: the local platform for neighbours and the global one for the diaspora and foreign supporters. They are not competitors, they reach different pockets. WHO IT SUITS: African community committees and village groups raising money locally, especially where supporters have mobile money rather than bank cards. CAVEATS: THE USSD ROUTE AND SOME FEATURES ARE COUNTRY-SPECIFIC — check which of your networks are supported before promising anything. For the global platform's thresholds, fees and vetting, Chad's crowdfunding entry; for the advisor-nominated small grants where 40% of grantees are first-time, Ghana's African Women's Development Fund entry; for the community capital that lets communities negotiate, Zimbabwe's Urban Poor Fund International entry.

trackers.name: Pro bono lawyers for more than 100 communities and organisations a year — plus the collective retraining African human rights litigators to take environmental cases, and the training that prepares communities before a carbon developer arrives
trackers.desc: THE LAWYER YOU CANNOT AFFORD ALREADY WORKS FOR A HUNDRED COMMUNITIES A YEAR — adjacency declared first: A CAPE TOWN, NAIROBI AND DAKAR ORGANISATION OF LAWYERS FOR COMMUNITIES AND THE ENVIRONMENT ALREADY HAS ENTRIES UNDER BURKINA FASO, GUINEA AND NIGERIA, AND LIBERIA HOLDS ITS OWN NAMED ENVIRONMENTAL LAW FIRM. NEITHER COVERS THE PRO BONO SERVICE BELOW, THE LAWYERS' COLLECTIVE, OR THE CARBON-DEVELOPER TRAINING. THE SERVICE, AND THE NUMBER IS THE FIND: AN ORGANISATION THAT PROVIDES PRO BONO LEGAL SUPPORT TO MORE THAN 100 CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS, COMMUNITIES AND INDIVIDUALS EACH YEAR — WORKING THROUGH AN ENVIRONMENT AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME TO PROTECT COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS AND BIODIVERSITY, AND TO COMBAT ENVIRONMENTAL CRIME AND CORRUPTION. A hundred a year, and INDIVIDUALS is in the list beside organisations. This file has recorded over and over that the missing thing is not a right but a lawyer; here is a supply of them, and community land rights is a named programme rather than a stretch. THE TRAINING IT RUNS, AND WHY IT IS URGENT NOW: A TWO-DAY LEGAL EMPOWERMENT WORKSHOP FOR REPRESENTATIVES OF FIVE NAMED INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES, HELD AT A TIME WHEN INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES ACROSS EAST AFRICA ARE INCREASINGLY BEING APPROACHED BY CARBON DEVELOPERS SEEKING TO DEVELOP OFFSET PROJECTS ON THEIR ANCESTRAL LANDS. THE WARNING THEY PUBLISH RATHER THAN SOFTEN: DESPITE INTERNATIONAL EXCITEMENT ABOUT CARBON MARKETS AS AN EMERGING TOOL FOR CLIMATE ACTION, MANY SUCH PROJECTS HAVE ALREADY LED TO VIOLATIONS OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' RIGHTS, RESTRICTIONS ON LAND USE, AND EVICTIONS. A carbon project is a land deal. It arrives dressed as climate action, it is welcomed by the ministry, and its restrictions on land use fall on the people already there. This file has recorded the same pattern under Tanzania's carbon contracts and Kenya's conservation purchases — and lawyers who have seen it are training communities BEFORE the developer arrives, which is the only point at which the terms are still open. WHAT THE COMMUNITIES THEMSELVES SAID THEY GAINED: A BETTER UNDERSTANDING OF FREE, PRIOR AND INFORMED CONSENT AND THEIR RIGHTS UNDER BOTH NATIONAL LAW AND AS LAID OUT BY THE AFRICAN COURT ON HUMAN AND PEOPLES' RIGHTS IN A NAMED JUDGMENT. The continental judgment this file records under Seychelles is being taught back to communities as a working tool, not left in a law report. Ask any lawyer who offers you training whether they will cover it. AND WHAT PARTICIPANTS DID WITH IT: THEY COMMITTED TO SHARING THE INFORMATION FURTHER WITHIN THEIR COMMUNITIES, ONE PLANNING TO USE THE MATERIALS FOR GRASSROOTS SENSITISATION AND TO ENCOURAGE INDIGENOUS PARTICIPATION IN CLIMATE CHANGE FORUMS. Two days of training that multiplies outward because the materials go home with people. When you negotiate a training, negotiate for the materials in a form your members can reuse — that is what turns a workshop into a capability. THE STATED PURPOSE: AS COMMUNITIES CONTINUE TO FACE PRESSURE FROM CARBON DEVELOPERS, THE KNOWLEDGE AND SKILLS BUILT DURING THE TRAINING WILL SERVE AS USEFUL TOOLS FOR PROTECTING THEIR RIGHTS AND HOLDING BOTH GOVERNMENTS AND PROJECT DEVELOPERS ACCOUNTABLE. THE LAWYERS' COLLECTIVE, WHICH IS WHERE THE SUPPLY COMES FROM: A COLLECTIVE OF AFRICAN PUBLIC INTEREST, ENVIRONMENTAL AND HUMAN RIGHTS LAWYERS WHO COLLABORATE TO CREATE HEALTHY AND SAFE LIVING ENVIRONMENTS FOR AFRICAN COMMUNITIES, AND TO ENSURE JUSTICE FOR ALL IN THE FACE OF CLIMATE CHALLENGES. THE PIPELINE THAT FEEDS IT, AND ITS BEST DETAIL: A WORKSHOP DESIGNED TO PROVIDE GENERALISTS AND HUMAN RIGHTS LITIGATORS WITH THE TOOLS TO TAKE ON ENVIRONMENTAL CASES ACROSS THE CONTINENT — PARTICIPANTS DISCUSSED THE INTERSECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND ENVIRONMENTAL LEGAL FRAMEWORKS, WAYS TO MOBILIZE THEIR OWN COUNTRIES' LEGAL FRAMEWORKS TOWARD ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE, AND HOW THEY COULD LEARN FROM SUCCESSFUL LITIGATION IN OTHER COUNTRIES. AND WHILE MANY PARTICIPANTS DID NOT HAVE A BACKGROUND IN ENVIRONMENTAL LAW, THEY BROUGHT THEIR EXPERTISE IN OTHER AREAS OF THE LAW TO THE CONVERSATION. THIS IS THE ANSWER TO A PROBLEM THIS FILE HAS NAMED IN A DOZEN COUNTRIES: there is no environmental lawyer in your district. There are, however, human rights litigators, land lawyers and generalists — and somebody is converting them, deliberately, with a workshop. If your country has no environmental bar, the useful ask is not for a foreign specialist but for one of your own advocates to be put through that training. AND THE THIRD ORGANISATION IN THE CHAIN: A CENTRE FOR INTERNATIONAL JUSTICE THAT CO-RAN THAT WORKSHOP, AND THAT ELSEWHERE PROVIDES PRO BONO LEGAL REPRESENTATION THROUGH A NETWORK OF MORE THAN 600 LAWYERS AROUND THE WORLD. Three organisations, one chain: a collective that convenes African lawyers, a centre that supplies six hundred more, and a pro bono service already carrying a hundred cases a year. A community does not need to find all three — approaching any one of them reaches the others. WHO IT SUITS: African communities facing a carbon, forestry or land project who need counsel, and national lawyers who want to take environmental cases but were never trained in them. CAVEATS: PRO BONO CAPACITY IS FINITE AND ROUTED THROUGH PARTNER ORGANISATIONS — approach with a specific, documented case rather than a general request. For the lawyers-for-communities organisation already filed, Burkina Faso's, Guinea's and Nigeria's entries; for the free brokerage that finds a law firm, the Central African Republic's entry; for university law clinics as free representation, Comoros' entry.

trackers.name: A network of national West African NGOs whose partner page names each member and what it does — with farmer-to-farmer field schools, a measured 77% yield gain in extreme drought, and a youth storyteller programme that puts media skills in farming villages
trackers.desc: THE PARTNER PAGE IS A DIRECTORY OF WHO TO CALL IN YOUR COUNTRY — adjacency declared first: THIS FILE'S LIBYA ENTRY COVERS THE PAN-AFRICAN FOOD SOVEREIGNTY ALLIANCE AND ITS MAURITANIA ENTRY THE WEST AFRICAN PEASANT FEDERATION; A GERMAN AGROECOLOGY ASSOCIATION APPEARS IN CHAD'S ENTRY AS AN UNNAMED EUROPEAN MEMBER. AND THE MALIAN PARTNER DESCRIBED BELOW ALREADY HAS ITS OWN ENTRY UNDER MALI — IT APPEARS HERE ONLY AS ONE LINE ON THE PARTNER PAGE. NONE IS RESTATED AND NONE OF THEIR HOSTS IS SHIPPED. THE PARTNER PAGE ITSELF, WHICH IS THE FIND: EACH AFRICAN MEMBER IS NAMED WITH WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES — A MALIAN ORGANISATION FOUNDED IN 2004 WORKING IN TWO NAMED REGIONS, DISSEMINATING SEEDLINGS FOR REFORESTATION AND RE-GREENING AND HOLDING FARMER FIELD SCHOOLS FOR FARMER-TO-FARMER KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGES; A BURKINABÈ ASSOCIATION STRENGTHENING THE CAPACITY OF LOCAL COMMUNITIES, ESPECIALLY WOMEN FARMERS, TO LEAD AND MANAGE AGROECOLOGY PROGRAMMES AND STRENGTHEN LOCAL MARKETS; A SENEGALESE ORGANISATION WHOSE MEMBERS CULTIVATE SHARED PLOTS AND WHICH SUPPORTS YOUNG PEOPLE LAUNCHING MICRO-ENTERPRISES WITH SALES AT WEEKEND BIO-MARKETS; AND A GHANAIAN ORGANISATION. Names, countries, founding years and specialisms on one page. For a community in Mali, Burkina Faso, Senegal or Ghana that does not know which organisation to approach, that page answers the question directly — and this file has recorded that finding the right national partner is the step most communities never complete. THE STRUCTURE: FOUNDED IN 2009, A NETWORK OF NGO PARTNERS IN THE GLOBAL SOUTH — IN WEST AFRICA A NETWORK OF NATIONAL NGOs ENGAGED IN FIELD WORK TO SCALE OUT AGROECOLOGY AND TO ADVOCATE FOR POLICY CHANGE — CONNECTING SMALLHOLDER FARMERS AND ORGANIZATIONS ACROSS 11 COUNTRIES, WITH LEADERS FROM 14 NGO PARTNERS.
