This file's Benin entry records the published boundary where a paralegal must hand a land title dispute to an advocate; a clinic like this is what exists on the near side of that line, and for most people it is the only thing that exists at all. THE MOBILE CLINICS AND WHAT THEY ARE FOR, WHICH IS THE SECOND FIND: THE SECOND ORGANISATION RUNS AN INITIATIVE FOCUSED ON ENHANCING ACCESS TO JUSTICE AND BRIDGING THE GAP BETWEEN INFORMAL AND FORMAL JUSTICE SYSTEMS IN RURAL AREAS, THROUGH THE TRAINING OF COMMUNITY PARALEGALS AND MOBILE LEGAL CLINICS. BRIDGING INFORMAL AND FORMAL JUSTICE is the precise problem for a rural community: the chief's forum will hear you tomorrow and cannot bind a company, the magistrate can bind it and sits three hours away. An organisation that works both sides is worth more than one fluent in only the second. WHERE THE FIRST ONE CAN BE WALKED INTO: A PUBLISHED STREET, AREA AND PLOT NUMBER IN THE CAPITAL, WITH A PUBLISHED POSTAL BOX AND EMAIL. WHAT ITS REGISTRATION LETS IT DO: FOUNDED IN FEBRUARY 1995 AS A NON-PROFIT, APOLITICAL, VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATION REGISTERED UNDER MALAWI'S TRUSTEES INCORPORATION ACT OF 1962 — AUTHORIZED TO PROVIDE ITS SERVICES ANYWHERE IN THE COUNTRY, ITS REGISTRATION PROVIDING THE BASIS THAT DEFINES ITS MANDATE AND SCOPE OF WORK, WITH PROGRAMMES IN ALL THREE REGIONS. AUTHORIZED ANYWHERE IN THE COUNTRY, by the terms of its registration. That is a thing to check about any organisation offering help: some registrations are district-limited, and a body that cannot lawfully operate where you are cannot act for you. WHO FOUNDED IT: FORMER STUDENT EXILES WHO RETURNED HOME TO THE PROMISES OF A NEW DEMOCRACY IN 1994. ITS STANDING AT THE CONTINENTAL BODY: IT IS LISTED AMONG THE NGOs OF THE AFRICAN COMMISSION ON HUMAN AND PEOPLES' RIGHTS, WHOSE SECRETARIAT SITS IN BANJUL, THE GAMBIA. A paralegal clinic that is also accredited at the continental commission. That combination is rare and it is the useful one: the same organisation that takes a walk-in complaint can carry it upward if the domestic route fails. WHAT KINDS OF CASE THE CLINIC ACTUALLY HANDLES: CASES RANGING FROM GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE AND LABOUR TO IMMIGRATION ISSUES AND POLICE MATTERS. Land is not on that published list. Recorded plainly so nobody arrives expecting it — but LABOUR and POLICE are, which covers the farm worker dismissed with his housing and the person arrested at a protest. WHAT THE FIRST ORGANISATION SAYS ITS MISSION IS: TO CONTRIBUTE TOWARDS THE PROTECTION, PROMOTION AND CONSOLIDATION OF GOOD GOVERNANCE BY EMPOWERING RURAL AND URBAN COMMUNITIES TO INCREASE AWARENESS OF AND EXERCISE THEIR RIGHTS THROUGH RESEARCH, EDUCATION, ADVOCACY AND NETWORKING — THROUGH TWO CORE PROGRAMMES, COMMUNITY MOBILIZATION AND EMPOWERMENT, AND HUMAN RIGHTS MONITORING AND TRAINING. THE NETWORK IT SITS INSIDE: THE HUMAN RIGHTS CONSULTATIVE COMMITTEE (HRCC) DESCRIBED AS A NETWORK OF CHURCH INSTITUTIONS, HUMAN RIGHTS NGOs AND THE COUNTRY'S LAW SOCIETY, WHICH WORKS TOGETHER ON HUMAN RIGHTS, ADVOCACY AND INFORMATION SHARING — ITS FORMER DIRECTOR HAVING CHAIRED THAT COMMITTEE AND BEEN ONE OF THE PRIMARY ORGANIZERS OF THE 20 JULY 2011 MALAWIAN PROTESTS. THE LAW SOCIETY sitting in the same network as the churches and the NGOs. That is the door to the private bar: a community that reaches the consultative committee is one step from the professional body that can find it an advocate. WHAT THE SECOND ORGANISATION IS AND WHERE: A NON-PROFIT IN BLANTYRE, ASSISTING MARGINALIZED PEOPLE WITH HUMAN RIGHTS ISSUES AND LEGAL ADVICE AND FACILITATES ACCESS TO JUSTICE FOR THE POOR — PART OF ITS ADVOCACY BEING REFORM OF THE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM, PARTICULARLY IN PRISONS. Two organisations in two different cities, which matters in a long country where a single capital office reaches nobody in the south. ITS BAIL PROGRAMME, WHICH IS THE THIRD FIND: A PIONEERING INITIATIVE EMPOWERING ECONOMICALLY DISADVANTAGED INDIVIDUALS WITH ESSENTIAL LEGAL KNOWLEDGE TO NAVIGATE THE BAIL APPLICATION PROCESS EFFECTIVELY, THROUGH DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATION AND TARGETED TRAINING, AIMING TO INCREASE THE APPROVAL RATE — ALONGSIDE A PROJECT TO ERADICATE TORTURE AND ILL-TREATMENT IN DETENTION THROUGH VICTIM SUPPORT, ENHANCED REPORTING AND ACCOUNTABILITY WITHIN LAW ENFORCEMENT. Teaching people to make their own bail application, rather than only representing them. A detained land defender whose community can be taught the bail process does not have to wait for a lawyer to become available — and this file has recorded that the wait is where the harm happens. AND THE JOINT ACTION ON RECORD: IN JULY 2024 THE SECOND ORGANISATION WAS ONE OF MANY THAT SIGNED AN OPEN PROTEST LETTER TO THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE. It signs collective letters, which tells you it will lend its name to a coalition rather than only acting alone. WHO IT SUITS: people in this country needing free first-line legal advice, rural communities who need the clinic to come to them, and anyone detained who needs the bail process explained. CAVEATS: ONE COUNTRY, AND BOTH ARE PARALEGAL AND ADVICE BODIES RATHER THAN LAW FIRMS — THE PUBLISHED CASE LIST DOES NOT INCLUDE LAND, AND A TITLE DISPUTE WILL NEED AN ADVOCATE; SOME MATERIAL CITED IS OLDER, SO CHECK CURRENT CLINIC LOCATIONS AND HOURS. For the published rule on when a paralegal must escalate a land case, Benin's entry; for the commission's own complaint procedure, Eritrea's entry.

trackers.name: Ålands Natur & Miljö
trackers.desc: Åland's independent environmental folkrörelse, with around a thousand members in a population of just over thirty thousand — proportionally one of the deepest memberships of any body in this file, which is why it is taken seriously in a small polity. WHO TO ENLIST when a wind farm, a plan or a permit lands on the islands. You CAN: use it as a formal consultee — it gives utlåtanden in impact-assessment procedures, including on whether Finland should take part in the transboundary assessment of an offshore wind expansion. It also sits on the monitoring committee for Åland's structural fund programme and its CAP interventions, so it has a seat where the money is allocated, not only where the permit is decided. For activists: it owns its own forest in the archipelago at Nötö and had it professionally surveyed as untouched natural forest, so it holds land as well as opinions. Expect campaigning, consultation responses and evidence rather than litigation.

trackers.name: Åland — Government of Åland, Budget (Finansavdelningen)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the autonomous Government of Åland (Finance Department) prepares the annual budget submitted to the Lagting, and publishes budget proposals, supplementary budgets & fiscal data, Åland. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Åland.

trackers.name: Åland — Landskapsrevisionen (Audit Authority)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution; Landskapsrevisionen is the independent audit authority under the Åland Parliament (Lagting), established by landskapslag 2013:25, performing annual financial audit, performance audit & audit of EU structural-fund support, Åland.

trackers.name: Nordic Council of Ministers — Åland counts toward the three
trackers.desc: YOU COUNT AS A FULL ENTITY, NOT A JUNIOR PARTNER — that is the whole point of this entry. The Nordic Council of Ministers requires that at least three of the following must be involved: Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, Finland, the Faroe Islands, Greenland, or Åland. The Faroe Islands, Greenland and Åland count toward the three alongside the five states, so a project involving only those three autonomous territories satisfies the requirement without any larger country. The central criterion is that projects provide added value to the Nordic countries, the Faroe Islands, Greenland, and Åland — the three are named again in the added-value test, so the benefit need not accrue to the states. ASK WHICH ROUTE APPLIES BEFORE PREPARING ANYTHING: the Council issues direct calls on particular topics from time to time, but the majority of projects are run by an ‘administrative body’, usually a national agency in the Nordic Region, commissioned by the Council — so most of the money is not distributed by the Council itself. The environment and climate working groups fund Nordic projects as a second layer within the same structure. ÅLAND HAS WON AT THIS LEVEL TWICE: the Agenda 21 office, Åland Natur & Miljö took the Nordic Council Environment Prize in 1999, and the City of Mariehamn won it in 2022 for management of wetlands — usable as precedent that Ålandic environmental work is recognised at Nordic level.

trackers.name: ÅMHM — anyone may comment in the 21 days; only a party may appeal
trackers.desc: COMMENT FIRST, WHILE ANYONE MAY. Ålands miljö- och hälsoskyddsmyndighet is the permitting authority, with its electronic noticeboard at amhm.ax and decisions also available in the reception at Norragatan 17, Mariehamn during the stated period. Under Landskapslag (2008:124) om miljöskydd, notice of an application must be published on that noticeboard for at least 21 days before the authority decides, stating the nature of the matter and where the application and all documents added during preparation are available — so ask for the full file, not the application alone. AND THE COMMENT RIGHT IS OPEN: ‘var och en har rätt att ... skriftligen yttra sig över ansökan’ — everyone may submit written views during publication. No standing test applies at the comment stage, which is materially different from the appeal stage, where the appellant must be a sakägare. The 21-day window is the moment the file is open and anyone can be heard — use it. HONEST CONTEXT FROM THE LAGTING'S OWN MATERIAL: handling times have been criticised, decisions often did not gain legal force, and the body was problematised by high staff turnover. The procedure has been publicly argued to be too complicated and costly with long review processes; the recorded counter-argument is that effective environmental protection requires proper prior examination. Expect a slow process, contested from both directions.

trackers.name: Ålands förvaltningsdomstol — ask expressly for the works to be stopped
trackers.desc: AN APPEAL THAT DOES NOT STOP THE WORKS MAY BE DECIDED AFTER THE SITE IS GONE. Appeals against the permitting authority's decisions go to Ålands förvaltningsdomstol, and the law provides that ‘besvärsmyndigheten kan förbjuda verkställighet’ — the appeal authority may prohibit execution of the decision, for both inspection decisions and permit decisions. Ask for the prohibition expressly when you file. THE DEADLINE, AND HOW TO COUNT IT: a published ÅMHM notice records 30 days from the day the decision was delivered (delgavs), with delivery deemed to occur a set number of days after publication — calculate from the deemed delivery date, not the publication date. The ground is lagligheten av beslutet, the lawfulness of the decision, and the original decision or a copy must be attached to the appeal document. A PROTECTION BUILT INTO THE LAW: execution may not be granted for a permit under chapter 3 of the Water Act concerning permission to dispose of another's property — so where a permit would let an operator use land or water belonging to someone else, immediate execution is unavailable as a matter of law. CHECK THE STAGE BEFORE: rättelseyrkande (request for rectification) is part of the administrative procedure preceding the appeal proper — establish whether one is required first. Åland's competence here flows from the självstyrelselag.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Eurosite / ELCN — who already holds land near you, and the easement route
trackers.desc: A DIRECTORY OF THE PEOPLE WHO ALREADY HOLD AND MANAGE LAND IN YOUR COUNTRY — which is who you need when the answer to a development is getting the land into protective hands. Eurosite, established 1989, is one of the largest pan-European organisations bringing together NGOs, governmental organisations and private bodies, with members from the Atlantic islands to the Black Sea and from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. ITS ELCN STRAND IS ABOUT PRIVATE LAND SPECIFICALLY: the European Land Conservation Network was built to support private landowners — non-public bodies or individuals — willing to engage in conservation ON AT LEAST PART OF THEIR LAND. That last phrase is the opening: a landowner who will not sell may still protect a portion, and there is a European network built to make that happen. The three tools it promotes are conservation easements, privately protected areas, and land stewardship agreements. AND A FUNDING ROUTE IS ATTACHED: ELCN and the ILCN have run sessions on using EU LIFE funding for private land conservation, aimed at landowners and conservationists preparing a LIFE project proposal; in November 2025 Eurosite-ELCN launched a working group on nature finance and land stewardship focused on finance mechanisms that mobilise private investment, co-chaired by the former head of the EU LIFE Programme. IF YOUR FIGHT IS A QUARRY, ASK FOR THIS BY NAME: Eurosite and partners published work on project selection criteria for conservation easements to protect nature in European quarries — a published European method for putting an easement over one. The network also co-hosts meetings of the Commission's Expert Group on the Nature Directives (NADEG) on tools and incentives for private land conservation — the most important working-level platform between the Commission, member states and interest groups. IF EUROSITE DOES NOT REACH YOUR COUNTRY, the International Land Conservation Network (founded 2014, the first global network of private land conservation practitioners) is the wider net, active from Canada to Australia to Latin America. BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT THESE ARE: networks of practitioners — they connect you to the organisation that can act; they do not buy land themselves. Ask the network who operates in your country; membership is not asserted here.

trackers.name: Government of Bermuda
trackers.desc: Bermuda government portal, including budget statements and public-finance information. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Bermuda.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Bermuda
trackers.desc: Supreme Court of Bermuda — supreme court (Bermuda).

trackers.name: Bermuda National Parks Act s.6 — private land can join by agreement
trackers.desc: A VOLUNTARY ROUTE INTO THE STATUTORY PARK SYSTEM, WITHOUT SALE OR EXPROPRIATION. The Bermuda National Parks Act 1986 establishes a National Parks System under section 3, comprising land and water specified in the First or Second Schedule — and section 6 provides that private land may become part of the system by agreement between the Minister and the owner. For a private owner who wants durable protection without giving up the land, that is the provision. Section 5 sets the objectives a protected area shall have; a National Parks Commission exists under section 9 with functions at section 10; administration is entrusted to the Director of the Department of Parks (functions at section 8); and an area management plan shall be prepared by the Director for each protected area under sections 11 to 14. THE SCHEDULES ARE POPULATED BY NOTICE, SO CHECK THE CURRENT ONE: the National Parks Protected Areas Notice 1991 filled the First Schedule and a further Notice followed in 2004 (BR 25/2004). NOTE THE SPLIT ADMINISTRATION: nature reserves are managed separately — the Department of Environment and Natural Resources' Terrestrial Conservation team manages over 300 acres of government-owned nature reserves, described as critical habitat for the island's most threatened species. Establish whether your site is a national park or a nature reserve, because different departments hold them. FUNDING: this territory is eligible for Darwin Plus, the Overseas Territories Environment and Climate Fund — around £3 million annually, with a small-scale Darwin Plus Local window alongside the Main Rounds. Applications go to an external administrator, BCF-Darwin@niras.com, not to Defra directly.

trackers.name: Department of Planning — object by email, and subscribe to be told when
trackers.desc: ONE OF THE SIMPLEST OBJECTION ROUTES IN THIS MAP, AND YOU CAN BE TOLD WHEN TO USE IT. Letters of objection and/or representation should be emailed to planningfrontdesk@gov.bm, referencing the PLAN or SUB number in the subject line — the reference format matters, because an objection without it may not be matched to the application. And you can subscribe to the Department's mailing list to receive an email notification whenever new planning applications are advertised in the Official Gazette — which removes the commonest failure recorded across this map: finding out too late. READ THE PUBLISHED RECORDS BEFORE DRAFTING: the Department publishes Development Applications Board agendas and minutes, a list of all delegated and appeal decisions, and Tribunal Reports containing the results of deliberations between the Objections Tribunal Board, technical officers and objectors — the closest thing available to a guide on which arguments have actually succeeded. Also published: zoning maps under the Bermuda Plan, the Listed Building Register, and listed building consultation records including the assessment of any requests to ‘delist’ structures — which is where an attempt to remove protection first appears. A WARNING FROM THE OMBUDSMAN: if you are a neighbour asked to sign Letters of Consent, make sure the developer gives you a copy of the plan that will be submitted to the Board, to ensure the plan shown to you is not different from the one submitted. Keep your copy. The Department publishes its capacity as 33 full-time positions with 9 vacancies.

trackers.name: Ombudsman, Supreme Court, Court of Appeal — one is free, one needs no lawyer
trackers.desc: THREE FORUMS ABOVE THE DEPARTMENT, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. THE OMBUDSMAN investigates complaints about the administrative actions of public authorities, including departments, boards and bodies established or funded by the Legislature — an independent, non-government office offering dispute resolution less formal, more flexible and more accessible than the courts, and services are free and available to everyone. It has done this work: a published investigation concerned Marine and Ports' failure to implement a planning decision. BUT EXHAUST THE DEPARTMENT FIRST — the Office may refer you back where you have not raised the issue with the correct authority or not yet exhausted that authority's own complaint procedure (s.9(1)(b), Ombudsman Act 2004), and some matters are exempt under the Schedule (employment, court proceedings, criminal investigation). THE SUPREME COURT judicially reviews public decision makers, on a jurisdiction substantially similar to England and Wales; leave must be sought ex parte, and applications must be ‘prompt’ and in any event filed no later than 6 months after the decision — six months is the outer limit, not the target; ‘prompt’ is the actual test. THE COURT OF APPEAL: you do not need a lawyer to file an appeal and may file in person, though guidance is encouraged for drafting — notice of appeal within 6 weeks of a final decision with a $200 revenue stamp; a non-final decision needs permission. Onward appeal lies to the Privy Council under the Appeals Act 1911 — so the Eco-Sud standing reasoning recorded here for Mauritius is persuasive authority in Bermuda.

trackers.name: Darwin Plus — an individual can lead and take £20,000
trackers.desc: ONE PERSON CAN BE THE LEAD APPLICANT AND DRAW DOWN £20,000 — which is the fact most local groups miss. Darwin Plus states that the Lead Partner can be an organisation OR an individual who agrees to manage the grant, its finances, reporting and governance, and who must be based in one of the Overseas Territories. So a community group that has not incorporated is not shut out — one resident can lead. Eligible applicants include environmental NGOs, community groups, research institutions, government bodies and individuals. THE FOUR SCHEMES: Local — up to £50,000 for organisations, £20,000 for individuals, projects up to 12 months; Main — £50,000 to £1 million over up to 3 years; People & Skills — up to £100,000 for training and capacity building; Strategic — £1 million to £3 million. A Fellowships Fund supports nationals of the Territories. THE AWARD RATE IS THE ARGUMENT FOR APPLYING: since January 2024 alone, Darwin Plus has supported nearly 130 projects worth over £20 million across fourteen small territories — this is not a lottery-odds fund. THE MOST TRANSFERABLE PRECEDENT: Bermuda's Microforest Restoration Initiative received £50,000 — the full Local ceiling — a small-scale habitat restoration project on a small island, funded to the cap. Deep-sea research at the Bermuda Institute of Ocean Sciences received £316,829. HOW TO FRAME IT: the fund delivers the UK Overseas Territories Biodiversity Strategy, which emphasises protecting globally significant and unique species, ecosystem resilience, invasive non-native species and building local capacity, and says it aligns investment with locally identified priorities — so write the application as a locally identified priority and as habitat or species protection, in the strategy's own words. The territories hold over 90% of the UK's globally unique species. Where a territory has no permanent population, an applicant must demonstrate a long-term meaningful connection to it.

trackers.name: Buy Back Bermuda — a standing campaign whose purpose is buying land off developers
trackers.desc: THE MOST LITERAL ANSWER IN THIS FILE TO ‘WHO WILL BUY THE LAND’. Buy Back Bermuda is a joint initiative of the Bermuda National Trust and the Bermuda Audubon Society ‘to purchase and safeguard precious open space to protect it from development’. Since 2004 it has raised funds for and acquired three properties, restored as nature reserves open to the public — and further acquisitions are planned. A community with a threatened site does not have to argue the principle: the vehicle exists and is looking. Worked example: Somerset Long Bay East, open free from dawn to dusk, with interpretive trail and bird hide. THE PARENT BODY IS THE ISLAND'S LARGEST LANDOWNER: the Bermuda National Trust was created by a public Act of Parliament in 1969, modelled on the National Trust for England and Wales, and holds more than 82 properties including open space and farmland. YOUR MEMBERSHIP VOTE CARRIES WEIGHT: since 2021, ten directors are elected by the membership against three government appointees. AND THE ROUTE MOST OWNERS DO NOT KNOW: many people have entrusted their open space by GIFT OR BEQUEST so that it will be preserved in perpetuity — gifted reserves include Devonshire Marsh, Scaur Lodge, Gladys Morrell and the islands of Morgan's, Palm, Saltus and Rogue.

trackers.name: Government of Niue
trackers.desc: Government portal for Niue, a self-governing state in free association with New Zealand and using the New Zealand dollar. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Niue.

trackers.name: SPREP — three conventions, and 26 members is not 12 parties
trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. SPREP is an independent intergovernmental organisation, autonomous since the Agreement Establishing SPREP was signed at Apia on 16 June 1993, with the Article 2 purpose of providing assistance to protect and improve the environment and ensure sustainable development for present and future generations. It has 26 members — 14 Pacific island countries, 7 territories and 5 metropolitan states — and is headquartered in Apia, Samoa. ESTABLISH WHICH CONVENTION FITS YOUR ISSUE: the Noumea Convention (1986, in force 1990), described by UNEP as the only comprehensive multilateral umbrella agreement for protection of natural resources and environment in the region; the Waigani Convention on hazardous and radioactive waste imports; and the Apia Convention on nature conservation. THE NOUMEA CONVENTION IS UNDER ACTIVE REVIEW — WHICH IS AN OPENING: a 2021 Review produced recommendations now being implemented through a Noumea Workplan and Budget whose stated aim is to elevate the work of the Convention and enhance awareness and implementation, with a Communications Plan and a Finance Strategy named as critical. BUT CHECK WHETHER YOUR STATE IS A PARTY: SPREP has 26 members while the Noumea Convention has only 12 contracting parties — membership and party status are different things, and this entry does not assert the latter. GOVERNANCE POINT WORTH KNOWING: the SPREP Meeting is the plenary decision-making body; the Executive Board (established 2015) is subordinate to it and has no power to make decisions requiring input of all Members — so a decision affecting all members must go to the Meeting. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so no incorporated body is required, which removes the commonest barrier recorded across this map. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest; only successful applicants are invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted — wasted work, and expensive wasted work where drafting means travelling. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. READ THE PUBLISHED GRANT RECORD BEFORE DRAFTING: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25 — showing what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries. That is better evidence of what will succeed than any guidance note. CHECK BEFORE EXPECTING A UNDP OFFICE: UNDP's Pacific Office provides only regional support to this state — not country-level — so do not assume an in-country presence when planning a second funding route.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN NIUE: the sources reviewed record no RTI law and do not list Niue either way — this is a gap in the evidence, not a finding that no right exists. Check locally, and rely on the Boe commitment above.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — individuals can apply
trackers.desc: INDIVIDUALS CAN APPLY, NOT JUST ORGANISATIONS — the third fund in this file with that feature, and consistently the thing local groups do not realise. New Zealand's Pacific Development and Conservation Trust distributes up to $250,000 a year in grants to groups and individuals for conservation, cultural heritage, development and goodwill, prioritising community projects including those involving representative, endangered, threatened or unique habitats and species. Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu and Samoa are all expressly on its eligible list, alongside every other Pacific state and territory. TWO OF ITS FUNDING CRITERIA ARE UNUSUALLY USEFUL: it funds projects that ‘improve legal access to facilities or resources necessary for social, cultural and economic sufficiency’ — broad enough to cover securing a community's access to land and water, which is not how most conservation funds are written — and projects that develop local capacities, particularly for indigenous ecological knowledge development. So documenting customary knowledge of a threatened site is itself a fundable project, and that documentation is often exactly the evidence an objection needs. The Trust is committed to communities working in partnership with iwi, hapū, aiga and local indigenous people — a proposal led by a customary group is what it is looking for, not an exception it tolerates. Apply via New Zealand's communitymatters service. THE OTHER REGIONAL FUNDER, WITH ITS LIMITS STATED: the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund invested in the Polynesia-Micronesia hotspot — backed by AFD, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank, run through CI's team in Apia with SPREP support — funding over 90 projects in 13 countries, including 58 community-based projects. That five-year programme ran 2008–2013 and this entry does NOT assert an open window — check CEPF directly. A RESULT WORTH CITING: in Fiji the National Trust of Fiji, Pacific Invasives Initiative, BirdLife and the local community eradicated goats and rats on Monuriki, creating a haven for the Critically Endangered Fiji crested iguana. AND A FIGURE THAT STRENGTHENS ANY APPLICATION FROM HERE: only 21 percent of the region's original vegetation remains pristine, across a hotspot of 4,500 islands whose total land area is about the size of Switzerland.

trackers.name: Centro de Periodismo Investigativo
trackers.desc: Puerto Rico's investigative-journalism center exposing corruption and the mishandling of public funds.

trackers.name: Fideicomiso de Conservación — it buys land AND constitutes easements
trackers.desc: A BODY THAT DOES BOTH HALVES OF THE ACQUISITION LENS. The Conservation Trust of Puerto Rico is a private non-profit whose stated method is acquiring natural areas to be protected and constituting conservation easements, alongside habitat and species restoration — purchasing outright and holding easements over land it does not own. Few entries in this map name an organisation doing both. ITS RECORD IS NOT THEORETICAL: it purchased the Inés María Mendoza Nature Reserve in 1975 and the Northern Zone Aquifers in 1977 — an aquifer bought as a conservation holding, which is the instructive case: where groundwater is the value at risk, the recharge zone itself can be the thing purchased. It is accredited by the Land Trust Accreditation Commission — the same standard used by US land trusts, which matters when assessing whether a counterparty can hold land durably — and is an IUCN member. ITS TARGET IS PUBLISHED AND QUOTABLE: through Para la Naturaleza, launched June 2013, the goal is to raise protected land from 8 percent to 33 percent by 2033. A dated numerical target is something a campaign can hold it to — and something a landowner can offer to help meet. Para la Naturaleza also runs volunteer and citizen science events and manages the Trust's visitor centres, including Hacienda Buena Vista (Ponce) and Hacienda La Esperanza (Manatí) — citizen science run by the land-holding body is a route to evidence for a site without commissioning survey work.

trackers.name: DRNA — its organic law points at section 19 of Article VI
trackers.desc: A DEPARTMENT WHOSE FAILURES CAN BE FRAMED CONSTITUTIONALLY. The Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales was created by Ley Núm. 23 of 20 June 1972, and is responsible for implementing the public policy contained in section 19 of Article VI of the Constitution. Cite Ley 23 and section 19 together — the organic law points directly at the constitutional provision. ASK WHICH OF THREE STATUTES APPLIES before writing, because they are separate instruments with separate designations: Ley 416-2014, the Ley sobre Política Pública Ambiental; Ley 182-2014, the Ley del Bosque Modelo de Puerto Rico — a landscape-scale model forest instrument that is easy to overlook, worth checking if your site falls in its footprint; and Ley Núm. 133 of 1 July 1975, the Ley de Bosques. ESTABLISH WHO MANAGES YOUR SITE BEFORE ADDRESSING ANYONE: protected natural areas here are managed by Puerto Rico government agencies, US federal agencies, and non-governmental organisations, with marine reserves managed by or jointly with DRNA. The federal layer is a real and separate route that does not exist in most jurisdictions in this map. The US Forest Service publishes a compiled geospatial map of protected areas by administration — that is the tool for working out who holds what — and notes that designation is a dynamic process resulting from the constant evolution of values in different sectors of society.

trackers.name: Te Ipukarea Society (TIS)
trackers.desc: The Cook Islands' first environmental NGO, registered as an incorporated society in 1996, membership-based, working across biodiversity, climate, eco-sustainable development and waste, and a member of IUCN and BirdLife International. WHO TO ENLIST: TIS when a development is being framed as opportunity — its record is campaigning to protect Suwarrow, opposing destructive fishing practices, and challenging deep seabed mining, including calling for a pause while independent baseline research is done. You CAN draw on an unusual piece of standing: TIS was the first national NGO in the Pacific accepted as an observer at the International Seabed Authority, which lets it make statements in ISA Assembly and Council meetings on behalf of a Cook Islands view. For activists: it acts alongside Kōrero O Te ‘Ōrau and Ocean Ancestors, so an approach to one tends to reach the others. KNOW THEIR FUNDING POSITION BEFORE YOU APPROACH: in their own words, ‘we have no core funding, and rely on projects and membership fees for all income’ — so expect to bring or find the project money rather than receive it, and joining as a member is itself materially useful because fees are part of how they survive. What they bring instead of money is ‘well respected scientists and active campaigners’ among staff and membership — expertise and standing, which is what a technical objection needs.

trackers.name: Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Cook Islands, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: SPREP — three conventions, and 26 members is not 12 parties
trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. SPREP is an independent intergovernmental organisation, autonomous since the Agreement Establishing SPREP was signed at Apia on 16 June 1993, with the Article 2 purpose of providing assistance to protect and improve the environment and ensure sustainable development for present and future generations. It has 26 members — 14 Pacific island countries, 7 territories and 5 metropolitan states — and is headquartered in Apia, Samoa. ESTABLISH WHICH CONVENTION FITS YOUR ISSUE: the Noumea Convention (1986, in force 1990), described by UNEP as the only comprehensive multilateral umbrella agreement for protection of natural resources and environment in the region; the Waigani Convention on hazardous and radioactive waste imports; and the Apia Convention on nature conservation. THE NOUMEA CONVENTION IS UNDER ACTIVE REVIEW — WHICH IS AN OPENING: a 2021 Review produced recommendations now being implemented through a Noumea Workplan and Budget whose stated aim is to elevate the work of the Convention and enhance awareness and implementation, with a Communications Plan and a Finance Strategy named as critical. BUT CHECK WHETHER YOUR STATE IS A PARTY: SPREP has 26 members while the Noumea Convention has only 12 contracting parties — membership and party status are different things, and this entry does not assert the latter. GOVERNANCE POINT WORTH KNOWING: the SPREP Meeting is the plenary decision-making body; the Executive Board (established 2015) is subordinate to it and has no power to make decisions requiring input of all Members — so a decision affecting all members must go to the Meeting. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers. YOUR STATE IS RECORDED AS A NOUMEA CONVENTION PARTY: it was among those represented at the 18th Conference of the Parties, Apia, 5 September 2025 — so the Convention's obligations and its Workplan apply here.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so no incorporated body is required, which removes the commonest barrier recorded across this map. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest; only successful applicants are invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted — wasted work, and expensive wasted work where drafting means travelling. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. READ THE PUBLISHED GRANT RECORD BEFORE DRAFTING: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25 — showing what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries. That is better evidence of what will succeed than any guidance note. CHECK BEFORE EXPECTING A UNDP OFFICE: UNDP's Pacific Office provides only regional support to this state — not country-level — so do not assume an in-country presence when planning a second funding route.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN THE COOK ISLANDS: the Official Information Act 2008 — the first RTI law adopted by any Pacific island country.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Te Ipukarea Society — they have already beaten a proposal here
trackers.desc: A LOCAL NGO WITH A DOCUMENTED WIN AGAINST A NAMED PROPOSAL IS THE MOST USEFUL KIND OF ALLY — they have done it before in your jurisdiction. Te Ipukarea Society ran the successful ‘Save Our Suwarrow’ campaign, which opposed a proposal, and a recovery programme for the Rarotonga monarch, down to about 38 individuals in 1987. Set up in 1996 after a restructure of the government Environmental Service, both as an environmental watchdog and to promote harmony between Cook Islanders and their environment through awareness, projects, and liaison with government and other NGOs. The name means approximately ‘looking after our heritage’. It is the BirdLife International partner for the Cook Islands and a member of IUCN — international backing behind a local objection. IF YOU NEED A DIFFERENT ORGANISATION, TWO DIRECTORIES WILL FIND YOU ONE: PIANGO publishes a member directory of national umbrella NGOs across 25 Pacific countries, with named contacts and addresses — an umbrella body is the fastest route to the right local organisation when you do not know who to call. PICAN lists members including the Anglican Church of Melanesia (nine dioceses across Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia) — a community-level network with reach no NGO in the region matches — and Vanuatu's Campaign for Justice, whose stated mission is to actively confront and expose those who obstruct natural justice with impunity. Live & Learn runs Climate Resilient Islands with rural communities in Fiji, Tonga, Vanuatu, Tuvalu, Solomon Islands, PNG and Samoa, with outcome areas including nature-based land management, and publishes filterable case studies and fact sheets. AND A FUNDING MODEL PACIFIC NGOs HAVE STUDIED: at Mida Creek in Kenya, 22 organisations share resources and finances around one protected area, funding guided eco-tours and alternative livelihoods such as beekeeping to relieve harvesting pressure — pooling finances around a single site is a funding model, not just a partnership.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — individuals can apply
trackers.desc: INDIVIDUALS CAN APPLY, NOT JUST ORGANISATIONS — the third fund in this file with that feature, and consistently the thing local groups do not realise. New Zealand's Pacific Development and Conservation Trust distributes up to $250,000 a year in grants to groups and individuals for conservation, cultural heritage, development and goodwill, prioritising community projects including those involving representative, endangered, threatened or unique habitats and species. Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu and Samoa are all expressly on its eligible list, alongside every other Pacific state and territory. TWO OF ITS FUNDING CRITERIA ARE UNUSUALLY USEFUL: it funds projects that ‘improve legal access to facilities or resources necessary for social, cultural and economic sufficiency’ — broad enough to cover securing a community's access to land and water, which is not how most conservation funds are written — and projects that develop local capacities, particularly for indigenous ecological knowledge development. So documenting customary knowledge of a threatened site is itself a fundable project, and that documentation is often exactly the evidence an objection needs. The Trust is committed to communities working in partnership with iwi, hapū, aiga and local indigenous people — a proposal led by a customary group is what it is looking for, not an exception it tolerates. Apply via New Zealand's communitymatters service. THE OTHER REGIONAL FUNDER, WITH ITS LIMITS STATED: the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund invested in the Polynesia-Micronesia hotspot — backed by AFD, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank, run through CI's team in Apia with SPREP support — funding over 90 projects in 13 countries, including 58 community-based projects. That five-year programme ran 2008–2013 and this entry does NOT assert an open window — check CEPF directly. A RESULT WORTH CITING: in Fiji the National Trust of Fiji, Pacific Invasives Initiative, BirdLife and the local community eradicated goats and rats on Monuriki, creating a haven for the Critically Endangered Fiji crested iguana. AND A FIGURE THAT STRENGTHENS ANY APPLICATION FROM HERE: only 21 percent of the region's original vegetation remains pristine, across a hotspot of 4,500 islands whose total land area is about the size of Switzerland.

trackers.name: Office of the Auditor General
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Vatican City, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Pareri tecnici precede a works authorisation — and check the law's version
trackers.desc: EVEN HERE, AN ENVIRONMENTAL TECHNICAL OPINION PRECEDES A WORKS AUTHORISATION. Under the Legge sul Governo dello Stato della Città del Vaticano (25 November 2018), the Direzione's functions include la tutela dell'ambiente e dell'ecologia nello Stato, la manutenzione dei giardini, delle strade e delle fontane — and it formula pareri tecnici per il rilascio delle necessarie autorizzazioni relative alla progettazione ed esecuzione di lavori, giving technical opinions for the authorisations required to design and execute works, and may supervise the works. Separate competences are reserved to the Direzione dei Musei e Beni Culturali and to the Commissione permanente per la tutela dei monumenti storici ed artistici della Santa Sede — a standing commission holds monument protection. For verifying places and installations the Direzione may call on the Corpo dei Vigili del Fuoco and the Direzione di Sanità e Igiene. THE CONSTITUTIONAL FOOTING: the Legge Fondamentale lists among the Governorate's competences la tutela della salute, della sanità, dell'igiene pubblica, dell'ambiente e dell'ecologia. WATCH THE VERSION BEFORE CITING AN ARTICLE: the Fundamental Law dates from 1929, was replaced by the text promulgated 26 November 2000 (in force 22 February 2001), then by one of 13 May 2023, with a further text dated 31 July 2026 on vatican.va. State agricultural activity is carried out exclusively through the Direzione delle Ville Pontificie.

trackers.name: A document addressed to dioceses and parishes — usable far from Rome
trackers.desc: THIS ENTRY IS FOR USE ELSEWHERE, NOT IN VATICAN CITY. Where a parish, diocese or Catholic institution is a landowner, a neighbour or a potential ally in a land dispute — as this map records for El Salvador's mining ban and for Lebanon — the relevant text is the 226-page inter-office document ‘In cammino per la cura della casa comune’, released in 2020, which restates Laudato si' and proposes general actions that local dioceses and parishes can take to protect the environment. It is the centre telling dioceses what is expected of them — though it was released only in Italian, which is a real barrier and is stated here rather than glossed. THE STATE'S OWN COMMITMENTS, useful as precedent rather than exhortation: an ‘Ecological Conversion 2030’ programme applying Laudato si' and Laudate Deum; a commitment to climate neutrality; and ratification of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. Recorded measures include reusing the water in the State's fountains, switching to more ecological fertilisers in its gardens, and changing the lighting of the Sistine Chapel. THE COMMITMENT WITH THE WIDEST REACH: a memorandum of understanding of 10 June between the Governorate, APSA — the Holy See's patrimony administration — the Fondazione Fratello Sole and ACEA, applying sustainability criteria across the entire life cycle of infrastructure, including minimisation of emissions, efficient use of water and energy, and protection of soil and ecosystems. A patrimony administration committing to soil and ecosystem protection has reach well beyond the city walls.

trackers.name: JFSC Registry
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.name: SSIs — nine qualifying interests, and four fifths of habitat unprotected
trackers.desc: THE QUALIFYING LIST IS MUCH WIDER THAN ECOLOGY. Under the Planning and Building (Jersey) Law 2002 the environment department must keep a list of places or buildings of special zoological, botanical, ecological, geological, archaeological, architectural, artistic, historical, scientific or traditional interest. ‘Traditional’ and ‘artistic’ interest are grounds for listing in their own right — so a site that fails on biodiversity may still qualify on another limb. SSIs can be in public OR private ownership, so private land is not excluded. The first ecological SSIs were designated in 1996; there are now 28 Sites of Special Ecological Interest and 22 Sites of Special Geological Interest covering 548 hectares, about 5 percent of the island — and three new ecological SSIs covering 17 ha were added at St Ouen's Bay in 2020, so the list still grows. THE OFFICIAL GAP STATEMENT IS YOUR ARGUMENT: the States' own indicator records that only about 20 percent of Jersey's key semi-natural habitats are protected by SSI designation, so a large area of critical natural habitat remains unprotected. THE PLANNING HOOK: the Island Plan requires planning applications that might affect important or protected biodiversity sites to be supported by an appropriate level of ecological information — an application lacking it is incomplete on the Plan's own terms.

trackers.name: Countryside Enhancement Scheme — it funds delivery of treaty commitments
trackers.desc: A GRANT SCHEME THAT EXPRESSLY FUNDS DISCHARGING TREATY OBLIGATIONS. The Government of Jersey's Countryside Enhancement Scheme has options to assist applicants delivering environmental projects that: maintain and improve the Island's internationally significant rural character, landscape, habitats, flora and fauna; enhance, conserve and protect Jersey's natural environment on a local scale; implement Island-wide strategic environmental projects that enhance biodiversity; and assist with the delivery of the Island's commitments to International Multilateral Environmental Agreements and local environmental objectives. THAT LAST LIMB IS THE ONE TO USE: a project framed as discharging an MEA obligation — Ramsar, CBD, Bern, Bonn — is on eligible ground by the scheme's own terms rather than by inference. Identify which convention your site or species engages and say so. AND NOTE THE SCHEME FUNDS TWO SCALES SEPARATELY: local-scale work and island-wide strategic projects are distinct stated purposes, so a modest local proposal is not competing against island-wide programmes. This pairs with the SSI route recorded separately here: the States' own indicator records that only about 20 percent of key semi-natural habitats are protected by SSI designation — a documented gap that CES-funded work on unprotected habitat can address. SEARCHING FOR THIS IS HARDER THAN IT SHOULD BE: ‘Jersey environmental grants’ returns overwhelmingly New Jersey, USA — Sustainable Jersey, the NJ Highlands Coalition, NJ DEP. Search ‘gov.je’ directly.

trackers.name: National Trust for Jersey — it bought three more sites on £500
trackers.desc: THE MOST ENCOURAGING SENTENCE IN THIS FILE FOR ANYONE WHO THINKS THEY CANNOT AFFORD TO ACT: ‘having now acquired its first site and a cash balance of just under £500, the Trust confidently acquired three further sites’ — Le Rât, Le Grand Côtil de la Cote Pallot and Le Saut Geffroi. Eighty years on it manages over 170 sites and about 2% of Jersey's land. Established 1936 as an independent, self-funding charity, its aim is protection ‘via acquiring and conserving land, buildings and artefacts’. DO NOT BE PUT OFF BY THE HERITAGE REPUTATION: in its own words, ‘whilst the Trust's historic building work is well known, the majority of Trust sites are parcels of land managed for wildlife’. PROOF THAT ACQUISITION CHANGES OUTCOMES: on one site acquired in 1975, wild orchids rose from about 8,500 in 2000 to over 60,000 today. IT IS ALSO A PARTNER FOR RAISING THE MONEY, NOT ONLY FOR HOLDING THE LAND: it employs a Fundraising Officer and actively seeks further sources of income through sponsorship or grant schemes. AND IT HAS AN ANSWER TO ‘PROTECTION TAKES LAND OUT OF PRODUCTION’: through Birds on the Edge, with the States of Jersey Department of Environment and Durrell, it achieved the reintroduction of the chough, a conservation grazing flock, and annual winter conservation bird crops on agricultural land — farming continued. Also worth knowing locally: the Association of Jersey Charities.

trackers.name: Cayman Islands General Registry
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.name: National Conservation Act s.41 — the only means of equal consideration
trackers.desc: THE DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENT HAS SAID WHICH PROVISION MATTERS, IN TERMS: ‘the legal requirement for consultation with the NCC enshrined in section 41 of the NCA is also the only legislative means currently available in Cayman to ensure that environmental concerns are given the same level of consideration as economic, human and social issues when national decisions are being made.’ If a decision was taken without National Conservation Council consultation, section 41 is the point of attack. HOW DESIGNATION WORKS: Cabinet may, after consultation with the Council, designate any area of Crown Land or Cayman waters as protected — and the Council, not Cabinet, determines whether a nominated area serves a purpose or objective of the Act, so there is a nomination step. NOTE THE LIMIT: that power reaches Crown Land or Cayman waters — private land is not covered. Each protected area gets a management plan, which may prohibit or regulate activities within it. The Council has 13 voting members, 8 appointed by Cabinet, of whom 4 must have scientific or technical qualifications — a required scientific minority worth knowing when contesting a decision. The Act also continues the Environmental Protection Fund. WATCH THE ORDERS, NOT JUST THE ACT: areas are designated by National Conservation (Protected Areas) Orders, and a 2026 Order repealed the 2023 Order — the schedule is replaced wholesale, not amended, so check the current one. AND ASK ABOUT EXEMPTIONS: the Council may grant a permit exempting an applicant from any of the provisions of this Law. It appears as both ‘Law’ and ‘Act’ 2013 — same instrument. FUNDING: this territory is eligible for Darwin Plus, the Overseas Territories Environment and Climate Fund — around £3 million annually, with a small-scale Darwin Plus Local window alongside the Main Rounds. Applications go to an external administrator, BCF-Darwin@niras.com, not to Defra directly.

trackers.name: National Trust for the Cayman Islands - Land Reserve Fund (buys threatened parcels outright)
trackers.desc: THE ONLY BODY IN CAYMAN THAT BUYS PRIVATE LAND TO STOP IT BEING BUILT ON - AND THERE IS NO FORM, NO NOMINATION PROCESS AND NO DEADLINE. YOU EMAIL THE DIRECTOR. The Land Reserve Fund launched in 2010 to acquire high-priority environmental land; once acquired it is held under the National Trust for the Cayman Islands Law (1987) and protected in perpetuity. The Trust states it currently safeguards 3,623 acres, 6% of the islands' terrestrial land, across Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman - the Mastic Reserve and Salina Reserve were largely assembled this way, and the Brac Parrot Reserve is 282 contiguous acres. Land can be donated as well as bought. THE TIMING TRAP: the Fund buys from willing sellers using money raised for that specific parcel, so the clock is a fundraising clock, not a planning-objection clock. A single 2024 fundraising dinner raised US$250,000 and the Trust described that as more than half of what was needed for one primary-forest parcel - which tells you the order of magnitude and how long assembling it takes. Approach them the moment a parcel looks vulnerable, not when the application is advertised. The whole public-facing page is written as a donation appeal; the only named route in is director@nationaltrust.org.ky (general office info@nationaltrust.org.ky, +1 345 749-1121). Note also that the Trust buys land - it does not fight your permit for you.

trackers.name: Ultimate Beneficiary Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Nature Protection Act 1991 — 31 percent protected, and orders are current
trackers.desc: A DEDICATED CONSERVATION STATUTE WITH UNUSUALLY HIGH COVERAGE. The Nature Protection Act 1991 protects species of plants and animals including threatened ones, and contains provisions to protect habitats such as the Upper Rock Nature Reserve and Windmill Hill Flats. Up to 31 percent of Gibraltar's land area is protected at EU and local level — high by any comparison in this map — with the Government's stated intention being to ensure those sites are adequately managed, which is the commitment to hold it to. MARINE PROTECTION IS DUAL-DESIGNATED: the Southern Waters of Gibraltar were approved as a Site of Community Importance in July 2006 (Commission Decision 2006/613/EC) and then declared a dual Special Area of Conservation and Special Protection Area, with a protection regime running since 1991. DESIGNATION IS BY ORDER, AND ORDERS ARE CURRENT — see the Nature Conservation (Designation of Gibraltar Nature Reserve and Upper Rock Nature Reserve) Order 2023; the Act and its subsidiary orders are published on gibraltarlaws.gov.gi, and a Gibraltar Nature Reserve Management Plan is published by the government. ONE DATA TRAP: JNCC maintains datasets for UK SACs but expressly excludes Gibraltar's two SACs from UK totals, directing users to the Protected Areas in Gibraltar page instead — do not expect Gibraltar sites to appear in UK-wide datasets.

trackers.name: Darwin Plus — ask for ‘Darwin Plus Local’ if you are community-scale
trackers.desc: THE MAIN ROUND IS NOT THE ONLY DOOR. Darwin Plus — the Overseas Territories Environment and Climate Fund, one of Defra's Biodiversity Challenge Funds — funds environmental projects in UK Overseas Territories and fellowships for UKOT nationals, at around £3 million annually. Alongside the Main Rounds runs Darwin Plus Local, a small-scale window — ask for it by name if your project is community-scale. SCALE OF AWARDS: in one recorded round the Falkland Islands secured 3 projects totalling nearly £900,000 over 3 years, so awards can be substantial and multi-year. ELIGIBLE TERRITORIES: Anguilla, Bermuda, British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Cyprus (Sovereign Base Areas), Falklands, Gibraltar, Montserrat, Pitcairn, St Helena and Turks and Caicos — five of which appear in this map, so this is one scheme covering several of them. Part of Darwin Plus is ODA-funded for Montserrat, St Helena, Tristan da Cunha and Pitcairn, giving those four an additional stream. RECORDED PRIORITIES: increasing the area, effectiveness and condition of protected areas, and conservation and restoration of coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests. CONTACTS: policy to darwin.initiative@defra.gov.uk; applications to BCF-Darwin@niras.com — note applications are handled by an external administrator, not Defra directly. Scheme site: darwinplus.org.uk.

trackers.name: Darwin Plus — an individual can lead and take £20,000
trackers.desc: ONE PERSON CAN BE THE LEAD APPLICANT AND DRAW DOWN £20,000 — which is the fact most local groups miss. Darwin Plus states that the Lead Partner can be an organisation OR an individual who agrees to manage the grant, its finances, reporting and governance, and who must be based in one of the Overseas Territories. So a community group that has not incorporated is not shut out — one resident can lead. Eligible applicants include environmental NGOs, community groups, research institutions, government bodies and individuals. THE FOUR SCHEMES: Local — up to £50,000 for organisations, £20,000 for individuals, projects up to 12 months; Main — £50,000 to £1 million over up to 3 years; People & Skills — up to £100,000 for training and capacity building; Strategic — £1 million to £3 million. A Fellowships Fund supports nationals of the Territories. THE AWARD RATE IS THE ARGUMENT FOR APPLYING: since January 2024 alone, Darwin Plus has supported nearly 130 projects worth over £20 million across fourteen small territories — this is not a lottery-odds fund. THE MOST TRANSFERABLE PRECEDENT: Bermuda's Microforest Restoration Initiative received £50,000 — the full Local ceiling — a small-scale habitat restoration project on a small island, funded to the cap. Deep-sea research at the Bermuda Institute of Ocean Sciences received £316,829. HOW TO FRAME IT: the fund delivers the UK Overseas Territories Biodiversity Strategy, which emphasises protecting globally significant and unique species, ecosystem resilience, invasive non-native species and building local capacity, and says it aligns investment with locally identified priorities — so write the application as a locally identified priority and as habitat or species protection, in the strategy's own words. The territories hold over 90% of the UK's globally unique species. Where a territory has no permanent population, an applicant must demonstrate a long-term meaningful connection to it.

trackers.name: GONHS — they advise developers too, and they publish the baseline data
trackers.desc: THEY WORK WITH DEVELOPERS, NOT ONLY AGAINST THEM — and that shapes how you approach them. In their own words: ‘we share our wealth of experience with planners and developers to help them care for the valuable land in their trust’. It cuts both ways: they may already be advising on the scheme you are objecting to — ask — and an approach framed as improving a project may get further than one framed as stopping it. AND THEY HOLD SEATS YOU CANNOT: ‘via our representation in other bodies we can press authorities for improvements in protecting the environment’ — ask which bodies, and whether your issue can be raised there.
